subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is an honour for me this morning to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36 on behalf of a number of residents of Kamloops, British Columbia.
The petitioners point out their ongoing concern with the government's intention to impose the goods and services tax on the people of Canada, and are calling upon the Liberals in the Senate, not only to plan to vote against it but, if necessary, to filibuster this legislation to ensure that this horrid tax never becomes a reality in Canada.

subsubtopic: BILL C-21
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise in accordance with Standing Order 36 to present a petition on behalf of 65 of my constituents in the riding of Port de Grave, Harbour Grace, and Trinity-Bay de Verde.
These people are terribly concerned about Bill C-21. They are concerned that the unemployment insurance program which the government plans to get out of when this particular bill is passed will hurt them because of the high rate of unemployment and the scarcity of jobs. They humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject these cuts in the unemployment insurance system and to come up with a more meaningful program.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36 I rise today with petitions from members of my constituency of Mission- Coquitlam, as well as from people in Langley and the lower mainland who oppose the goods and services tax that this government is planning, or has introduced and passed and is planning to impose on Canadians. The government is planning to impose it on Canadians and they are opposing it on the basis that it is an unfair form of taxation because of its lack of regard for a taxpayer's ability to pay.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise today to present a couple of petitions. The first is a petition from a number of residents of my riding of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre who are opposed to the GST. They call on this government to reform the taxation system so that there is an effective minimum tax on wealthy individuals and corporations and to ensure that if and when there is a broad public consensus on sales tax measures to replace the manufacturers' sales tax. The petitioners say this is not an opportunity for the government to impose a massive tax through the GST.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I also have a petition presented by a number of farmers from the province of Saskatchewan. It calls upon this government to amend immediately the Canadian Wheat Board Act to place oats under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. This would give oats and barley the same protection that wheat presently enjoys under the that act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
That this House commends the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian Forces at Oka and Chateauguay;
That, in the opinion of this House, the laws of Canada must apply on all Canadian territory, including Kahnawake, and that all persons currently at the Kanesatake Treatment Centre should lay down their arms and submit to the processes of Canada's judicial system, thereby encouraging the creation of a constructive climate for discussions between governments and the Mohawk people on land claims and other issues; and
That upon adoption of this motion, the said motion shall be deemed referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General.
He said: Madam Speaker, I rise to debate this motion regarding a most serious matter of particular concern to Canada's native people, but indeed to all Canadians, a motion dealing with an issue which strikes at the roots of what we believe we are as a country. It is a belief in justice and in an earnest endeavour to seek and find an honourable resolution of longstanding native grievances.
It is a belief shared by Indian leaders across Canada. For example, Phil Fontaine, leader of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs said on August 26 of this year: "To improve our lives, the lives of our people, we, in turn, improve this country."
On September 13, one of the chiefs of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations with whom we have
Government Orders
worked so closely on treaty issues in Saskatchewan said: "If ever there was a light at the end of the tunnel where we all have a keen desire for wanting to succeed, the time is now."
These statements come from Indian leaders with whom I have met on many occasions over the past several months. They wish, as do I and the government, to make that light brighter so that under their guidance we can begin in a substantive and committed way to make necessary changes in policy and process and long overdue improvements and resolution of native issues.
We must all be more sensitive and more conversant with the perspective of aboriginal leaders who want actions so that their children and successive generations can live in dignity, with honour and respect. That is what we wish for all Canadians. I sincerely believe that I can play a constructive role in the process to bring this about. The time to begin is indeed now.
We are all aware of the good that can come from working co-operatively through consensus in a spirit of openness and honesty. We are all aware that this project of historic significance has been made increasingly difficult by the events of the last several weeks but also has now made these matters a major imperative for Canada.
The events at Kanesatake and Kahnawake pose a threat to achieving our reasonable goals and objectives. This debate is not about the existence of legitimate longstanding aspirations of native people in this country. This debate is not about the vast majority of native people who are law abiding in pursuing their aspirations in a peaceful way. What this debate is about is the fundamental respect which all Canadians must hold for the rule of law, the threat posed to society by those who reject it, and the efforts of those that seek to uphold it.
The motion states:
That this House commends the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian forces at Oka and Chateauguay; and
That, in the opinion of this House, the laws of Canada must apply on all Canadian territory, including Kahnawake, and that all persons currently at the Kanesatake Treatment Centre should lay down their arms and submit to the processes of Canada's judicial system, thereby encouraging the creation of a constructive climate for discussions between governments and the Mohawk people on land claims and other issues; and

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
That upon adoption of this motion, the said motion shall be deemed
referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor
General.
There are several issues relating to this motion that I want to present and review in the House today.
I want to begin with the role and conduct of the Canadian forces, a role which is now coming to an end. I want also to review the land issue at Oka and our efforts to resolve it. I wish to discuss the rule of law and its fair application throughout Canada. There can be no sovereign enclaves within Canada where the laws of Canada do not apply. I want to discuss the laying down of arms by the warriors as the only means to resolve this situation at Oka peacefully and honourably. This will enable our system of justice, the fairest in the world, to take its course and to ensure that the innocent are not in any way penalized and those guilty of crimes meet the proper remedies under the law.
I want to state that once this occurs, we will immediately begin full discussion on the land issues and aspirations of the Mohawk people at Kanesatake.
In concluding my remarks, I will touch on the broader issues facing Canada's native people and the government's commitment to working towards a solution of their grievances. There will be much fuller debates on these downstream questions in the days and months ahead.
Returning to the motion for today, given the situation at Oka and Chateauguay and the level of tension that has existed over many weeks, the first clause of this motion intends to recognize and commend the exemplary actions of the Canadian forces since they were requisitioned by the Government of Quebec. The nature of this requisition has to be well understood by all Canadians.
The Chief of Defence Staff responded to a requisition from the Attorney General of Quebec on August 8. As required by the assistance to civil authorities provision under Part XI of that National Defence Act, General John de Chastelain implemented a plan which sought to remove the barricades and resolve a continuing disturbance peacefully. That was the undertaking of General John de Chastelain on August 8, and he has led that action without bloodshed.
The forces personnel assigned the responsibility of following the order have carried out that order in a planned, logical, and prudent manner. Throughout their mission, they have attempted to bring about a peaceful resolution to this situation.
In the case of Chateauguay, or Kahnawake as it is known to the Mohawk people, the removal of the blockades leading to the Mercier Bridge had to be an immediate priority. The tension in the community on both sides arising from the blockage of a main commuter artery into the city of Montreal required the Armed Forces to undertake a peacefully negotiated joint removal of the barricades. I think all Canadians were proud on that day to see the soldiers assisted by unmasked Mohawk people taking down those barricades.
All the Canadians saw the skill of military officers in achieving the important first step in restoring the rule of law to Chateauguay. This includes supporting the Surete du Quebec in the investigation into the possession of illegal weapons and their which has been graphically demonstrated and counted by all Canadians by way of television.
At Oka, we witnessed the implementation of a detailed military plan which secured, over one weekend, the peaceful dismantling of the barricades blocking several roadways in the Oka vicinity. If it were not for the intransigence of a small group who have thus far refused to accept the rule of law, the mission of the Canadian forces would have been completed several weeks ago.
As the lines between the two groups narrowed, we saw soldiers come face to face with masked, heavily armed warriors. On behalf of all members and all Canadians, I want to commend in this House those brave young people of the Canadian forces who stood firm and resolute, at the risk of death, and in the face of verbal abuse and violent threats.

Their courage, dedication, and commitment to act with minimum force to fulfil their mission was an example of the effectiveness of their training and the quality of their commanding officers.
As the motion states "This House commends the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian Forces at Oka and Chateauguay" in these trying circumstances.
September 25, 1990

Madam Speaker, all members should commend these men and women who have acted with honour and distinction throughout this tense standoff.

The removal of barricades is not sufficient. What is needed now is a return to normalcy and peace and to a process for the resolution of differences around a table of goodwill and understanding. A table where these matters can be negotiated.
However, the role of the Canadian forces is coming to an end. More and more the situation remaining at the treatment centre will become a provincial policing operation. Support will still be provided as investigations are undertaken and until normalcy is restored to the community of Oka, so that the residents-the children who must return to school, the neighbours, native and nonnative alike-who must live together and the wounds that must be healed may be done so with the security of knowing that there no longer is a militant group of armed warriors in their community. The role, therefore, of the Canadian forces has been to restore the rule of law.
The situation at Oka started out as a dispute over land owned by the municipality and claimed by the Mohawks at Kanesatake. Suddenly, however, it became a dispute over sovereignty, self-government and immunity from the laws by which all Canadians must live together. The vehicle to address these issues is earnest and reasoned dialogue and not military assault weapons and masked warriors.
The rule in law must be applied equally and fairly to all Canadians and all people within the borders of Canada who may choose to visit here. This is the oath I swore when I took my place in the House-to uphold the rule of law. This is the obligation of all of us in the Chamber today share-to uphold the laws of Canada.
The issues of land and self-government have been and will continue to be examined and addressed carefully by the government in the fora appropriate for such matters. I firmly and strongly believe that no one in the country, except a peace officer, should take up a gun or threaten violence in order to get their way. In fact, no one should take up a gun or threaten violence to get their way. I know all Canadians believe this and I assume all hon.
Government Orders
members also agree that an exchange of words is infinitely preferred to an exchange of bullets.
We have witnessed many tragedies this summer, not the least of which was the tragic death of Corporal Marcel Lemay. I know all members of the House will join me in expressing our sorrow and heartfelt sympathies to his widow and family.
We must also feel great sympathy for all people, Mohawk and non-Mohawk people, alike who will bear the wounds and ultimately the scars of these tragic events.
We have seen incidents of racism and intolerance which in this country, my country, our country, are deplorable and unacceptable. We have seen the stoning of men and women; people being pushed and shoved by those who cannot control their hatred-hatred driven by an element in their community hiding behind masks and armed with illegal weapons, hatred that none of us can be proud of. All of us should be ashamed of the conduct of natives and non-natives alike who may have engaged in these acts of hostility toward one another. It has saddened me greatly, Madam Speaker, as it saddens all Canadians.
Throughout the summer Canadians have wondered just how did a tragic circumstance come to be. I want to point out that the Government of Canada through my department had been working diligently on the land question at Oka for some time. Despite court rulings and decisions of previous governments and a decision of confirmation again in 1987 that a specific claim by the Mohawk people at Oka could not be received for negotiation, our government attempted to help the people at Kanesatake to achieve a land base and develop a recognized community.
It was the present Minister of National Defence who initiated a process which led to negotiations and it was the present Solicitor General who appointed a mediator in August 1989 in an attempt to resolve and rectify the land dispute between the municipality of Oka and the Mohawks of Kanesatake. That process commenced over a year ago and the parties endorsed a framework agreement in September 1989 which would have ensured that the land would be preserved for the use and benefit of the Mohawk people at Kanesatake.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
This agreement was to have been ratified by the community by March 1990, but the community was not asked or allowed to vote on the agreement. Instead, the Mohawks chose a new chief who declared an indefinite suspension of negotiations in early March of this year.
The municipality then decided to push plans ahead for developing a golf course expansion on land which they owned by way of an option. This caused the Mohawk people and warriors in particular to put up a barricade on Route 344 around March 12 of this year. The municipality therefore,sought an injunction from the Quebec Superior Court to have the barricades removed.
During May and June I met separately with Minister John Ciaccia of Quebec and representatives of the municipality of Oka, the parish of Oka, the Band Council of Kanesatake and the Longhouse Group in an attempt to bring the parties back to the table. In May I undertook to pursue the negotiation and purchase of the lands which were the subject of the disagreement. At my meeting with leaders of the Mohawk and surrounding villages and communities in late June, I asked that the Mohawk people put their concerns and propose solutions in writing for an improvement in the process, a letter which I never received.
On June 28 I wrote to Chief George Martin, the Grand Chief of the Mohawk community at Kanesatake, and to Mayor Jean Ouellet, asking them to put their differences aside to reduce the tensions between their communities and, whatever the outcome of the injunction request, to return to the table with our federal negotiator and work toward finding a peaceful solution.
That was two weeks before the tragic morning of July 11. On that morning, acting under a court injunction granted by the courts in Quebec, the Surete du Quebec moved in to remove the barricades. Gunfire ensued, resulting in the most tragic death of Corporal Lemay. From that moment on, the issue was no longer one of land. It became one of security and policing which is clearly the jurisdiction of the province, in this case Quebec, as stipulated by the Constitution of Canada, which we all respect and uphold in this House.
Nevertheless, I worked diligently throughout this dispute, having instant contact that very day with the Quebec minister, John Ciaccia, numerous meetings and telephone conversations virtually daily with Minister Ciaccia, Sam Elkas, the minister responsible for public security, and through discussions directly with the premier's office in Quebec. This constant contact included undertakings with respect to the federal willingness to continue the process of resolving the land issue and clear commitments to acquire and purchase the lands in question at Oka in order that we might all find a way to resolve this issue peacefully. Throughout this situation, the federal government has been reasonable, prudent and extremely vigilant to ensure that the interests of the Mohawk people at the community of Kanesatake and at Kahnawake, where a sympathy blockade had been erected on the Mercier Bridge, were fully taken into consideration by the federal government.
On July 27, I announced that my department had taken steps to acquire some 30 acres of the land at Oka and had entered into discussion with the town of Oka for the purchase of additional lands. This was consistent with what we had been trying to accomplish for several years and we had received the willing co-operation of the village of Oka in negotiating an agreement for the purchase of that land.
On August 8, the municipality accepted an agreement by which the ownership of 67 acres of land was transferred to the federal government, within 10 days after the removal of barricades and a return to normalcy. Prior to that, we also secured and purchased the lands owned by a M. Rousseau and his family, which are adjacent to the park held under option by the village of Oka. The transaction with the village of Oka was concluded and finalized on September 14 and we do indeed hold full title to those lands and they will be an important element of the solution to the land issue at Oka, once the weapons are laid down. I point this out because it demonstrates the steps that the federal government has taken, not only since July 11 but for several months and years, to ensure that the threat of adverse land development in the vicinity of the Mohawk community at Kanesatake be removed. Therefore, the resolution of the immediate land issue at Oka is a fulfilment of our offers and intentions stated well before July 11 and had been confirmed, in writing, on a number of occasions since July 11.
September 25, 1990

Government Orders
It is now time for the warriors to put down their arms. Throughout the process I maintained that the Government of Canada was committed to a very important principle. That principle is simply this, that we will not, and no Government of Canada ever will contemplate, I am sure, negotiating sensitive land issues where many people's interests are involved at the point of a gun. To do so would be to yield our constitutional responsibilities to the forces of tyranny. What remains at Oka, at Kahnawake, and in Akwesasne, are situations where groups of heavily armed men from various parts of Canada and the United States are undertaking activities which no law-abiding Canadian can tolerate, smuggling of illegal contraband, illegal gambling and possession of illegal weapons. When the laws of Canada are broken, then those responsible, whether native or non-native must be brought to justice and that is the fundamental principle that we are debating here today. The rule of law is based on a set of commonly agreed upon moral precepts, some of which are ancient and others which are more modem. If we do not uphold the fundamental principles of the rule of law, we endanger the rights of every Canadian and we threaten the very order and security which we seek to maintain on behalf of all Canadians, our children, native and non-native alike, in a democratic society. Without fundamental respect for the rale of law, there can be no justice for anyone in this country.
The efforts of this government at all times have been to ensure that safety and security is restored at Kanesa-take and Kahnawake. It is not possible, legally or constitutionally, to exempt or exclude any community from this rule. To do so would be to encourage the creation of warrior enclaves where illegitimate and illegal businesses could be conducted. As we have seen at Akwesasne, that is something no one, particularly members of this House, should encourage because of the tragedy and virtual civil war which broke out in Akwesasne at the hands of the same warrior element I might add, only a short while ago during the month of May. To bend to warrior demands on their negotiation proposals in this area is unacceptable. Armed violence such as what we have seen recently cannot be condoned. We must all seek to have normalcy established and the rule of law respected.
I have met a number of times during the eight or nine months of my ministry with native leadership from across Canada, but particularly with the legitimate Mohawk leadership of Kanesatake. In fact, I have been visited by community leaders from Kanesatake, Kahnawake and Akwesasne who have all decried the lack of democracy in their communities, the taking over, the taking hostage of their communities by this warrior element and who have expressed their wish for a resolution of the land issue and the continuation of co-operation and respect between their communities and the surrounding non-native communities.
The ongoing holdout of the warriors at the treatment centre and the events prior to it have undermined that mutual respect between native and non-native people in the vicinity of Oka and Kahnawake and we must all work very hard in the months ahead to rebuild that trust and mutual confidence.
The message for the warriors is you're hurting your own people. They want justice. They want safety and security. They want democracy where they can have a say in the land and future needs of their communities after the weapons are laid down.
So respect between native and non-native Canadians has been seriously undermined these past several weeks by a contingent of armed people who have their own base interests at heart, I believe, and who have sought and continue to seek the imposition of their armed will on other members of their own society and all Canadians. In doing so, they have resorted to acts which no law-abiding Canadian can condone.
This motion, therefore, links the resolution of the situation at the Oka Treatment Centre to important discussions between governments and Mohawk people on land claims and other issues. We cannot move on to that important discussion of these broader issues until the guns are laid down and peace and normalcy is returned to those communities.
As I have stated previously, and state once more for emphasis, the warriors have to accept the rule of law and we will deal honourably, fairly and generously with the needs of the Mohawk people and all other aboriginal

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
people, but not through a process of confrontation and the threat of military style activity to achieve these ends.
That is the position of the Government of Canada and it should be the position of all members of this House. That is why this motion deserves the respect and support of all hon. members. The question we must all ask ourselves is: Can we allow any group in Canadian society to take up arms and to proclaim sovereign enclaves where they would be immune from the laws of Canada which apply to us all? Our answer and the answer of all Canadians, certainly those I have heard from this past many weeks, is a strong and forceful no.
The government recognizes the concerns of the Mohawk people at Kanesatake. They have had, until the illegal actions of the warriors, good relations with the rest of the community despite many long, outstanding concerns about land. This issue will now enable us, with the laying down of arms, to settle those issues about land. The government's commitment is to begin this full discussion immediately and the judicial processes, at the same time, must apply to the warriors who are presently still remaining within the treatment centre.
A federal negotiator was appointed in the month of August to conduct the negotiations. He stands ready to start those discussions, immediately the guns are laid down, but the ongoing standoff is preventing that work from commencing. Discussions cannot take place as long as armed warriors seek to dictate their will by the use of force or threat of violence.
Clearly the ends, no matter how honourable, do not justify the means being used. Armed threats will not and will never be condoned as long as this government holds office.
In this stand we are not alone, as the following statements by aboriginal leaders in recent weeks would attest. Recently Elijah Harper was quoted in The Toronto Star as saying: "Everybody supports non-violence, and there has been public support for that. It is essential that the Canadian people support non-violence".
Manitoba's Chief Phil Fontaine of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs said on August 26: "We don't condone violence of any sort, by any group. Our preferred option, our preferred approach is to negotiate and that is in
keeping with our traditions and the teachings of our
elders".
Notably, after a full week of discussions in camera with Canada's national aboriginal chiefs, the head of the Assembly of First Nations emerged and stated on September 15: "Anyone who picks up a gun in this country and is involved in a political cause, is threatening his cause".
Tom Porter, Chief of the Mohawk Nation Council at Akwesasne, which has seen such tragedy in recent months, said on August 20: "I don't condone carrying a gun at any time. We follow the ancient principles of honesty, truth and kindness because that is the real Indian way".
Negotiation, not violence nor the threat of violence, is the way to resolve problems. The Government of Canada believes, as do these native leaders and many others with whom I have spoken, that problems must be settled peacefully and democratically.
One prominent aboriginal leader said to me last week in the north of Canada: "Anyone who takes up an arm against a government of Canada is taking up arms against all the people of Canada".
There are the broader matters of native land claims, specific claims, treaty rights, and the essential economic and social progress which we all want to assist native communities in achieving. The resolution of these issues will take time. They have, however, taken too much time already, and the system of 120 years' duration, at least since Confederation, has not worked for Canada's aboriginal peoples. A system of dependency, supported by government members opposite for decades through this century has been changed in significant ways and must undergo even more major changes in the years ahead, because this government cares and wants to work with and to assist aboriginal people, but only in accordance with their wishes and in accordance with their guidance and advice on the achievement of their just aspirations within Canada.
The government has an agenda which has been in preparation for several months now. It has involved native leaders and will continue to involve native leaders as proposals are transformed into policies. Their perspectives, ideas and wisdom is a necessary and welcome input.

*

September 25, 1990

Over the past eight months as minister I have tried to meet as often as possible with native leaders across Canada, whether in small groups or in large summits. I have heard the voices of discontent and mistrust, as have many members. I have sensed the frustration and the anger. I have heard the earnest and sincere call from chiefs, councillors, and elders for changes in the policies and actions of government in the way we deal with claims, in the way we failed to live up to treaty obligations, and in the way we deal with the social and community needs of our aboriginal people.
I recognize, as I stated to the Assembly of First Nations two weeks ago, that a lot of native Canadians do not trust ministers. They offered the observation that I was not the first minister they had distrusted. In fact it was sort of the common way of dealing with ministers of Indian affairs. I think it is important that that trust be established. I think it is important that all native people trust this Parliament, trust in the laws and Constitution of Canada, and respect the way in which we ensure that those laws are applied fairly to their advantage, to their benefit and to ensuring the peace and security that they and we all seek in our communities.
The tragic situation at Oka will not dissuade me from my objective of earning that trust and confidence of native leaders. I am sensitive to the gulf that exists between native people and ministers. I am cognizant of the need to build a mutual respect and to establish a mutual confidence, confidence to listen and comprehend the extent and nature of the problems we all share.
I have been assigned a difficult and challenging task, one that seeks to implement with native input and endorsement, a set of initiatives which I hope will build in a substantial way upon a more trusting, generous and honourable relationship between government and native people. To do that, I will need and certainly will appreciate the support of all members in this House.
I have in meetings with leaders of first nations broadened my understanding of the honour and pride of Canada's native people. I have respect for the peaceful way in which native people have approached many of the problems in their communities.
Government Orders
The government can, will and must continue to build in this direction, to build on the progress we have already made, and yet to meet a much greater challenge that remains. We will not penalize the vast majority of peace loving native people by delaying progress on these issues because a small group of extremists are breaking the law to achieve their ends.
We have extremists throughout society and extremism which threatens the order and security of society must be dealt with, but at the same time we have much larger obligations. The people at the treatment centre must realize that their actions are helping to delay the settlement of this issue and they hurt the cause of other native people across Canada.
I encourage all members of this House to stand and vote together to encourage the warriors to lay down their arms and accept the army's offer of custody and the honourable application of our system of justice, which is known around the world for being the most fair and honourable system of justice available to mankind. In doing so they will have acted honourably and accepted that the rule of law applies to all people in Canada.
I hope all members of the House will support this motion because I think it in itself represents the key to breaking the impasse with the remaining few warriors confined to the treatment centre at Oka.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to start my speech by quoting the words of a great liberal, a great Democrat, John F. Kennedy: "Those who make peaceful resolutions impossible make violent resolution inevitable." That in no way refers to my condoning violence, absolutely not.
I would like to say that I have listened very carefully to the words of the minister. He has inflamed my sense of humanity, my good sense of reason, and has compelled me to be a bit angry because I feel that there have been reasonable suggestions made over the period of the summer, the last of which was last Thursday when there was a proposal put forward which was ignored and which was not negotiated.
I think another proposal was one that I sent forward to the Prime Minister, to the minister himself, and to the premier of Quebec to have an all-party group go into

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
Kanesatake to speak with the people about a peaceful and an honourable disengagement.
I received a letter from the minister in response to my letter. Just allow me to quote from it. I indicated that the native members of Parliament and senators would be going there to assist in the peaceful disengagement and to encourage that that would occur. The minister responded to me:
I have to say that I am not persuaded that such action would contribute positively towards the conclusion I presume we all seek- that is, a peaceful disengagement which respects the rule of Canadian law.
It goes on to say:
The bottom line for the Warriors appears to be an absolute unwillingness to submit to Canadian law and a parallel insistence on the recognition of a Mohawk state. As these demands are unacceptable to Canada a mass visit by Parliamentarians, however well-intended, may only encourage the Warriors to prolong their intransigent disregard for that Constitution you and I are sworn to uphold.
Let me say that I have a legal opinion which says that under the Constitution the minister has a fiduciary obligation to those people and it is as follows:
1)	aboriginal and treaty rights will survive within the constitutional law no matter how much they have been regulated in the past
2)	aboriginal and treaty rights can no longer be extinguished by federal or provincial legislation
3)	the only possible ways now to extinguish aboriginal and treaty rights would be by constitutional amendment and, perhaps, by aboriginal consent
4)	the federal government is the fiduciary for all aboriginal peoples-
As that I think he should have accepted my invitation. I think that we could have appealed in a humane sort of way to this group of individuals who are also human beings. It continues:
5)	as fiduciary, the federal government must consult with the aboriginal peoples before regulating their rights in any way and can only regulate those rights in a manner that places aboriginal interests first above the interests of any other sector of Canada (but can place conservation of mother earth even higher as this benefits aboriginal people)
6)	violation of the fiduciary obligation will be controlled by the courts through damage awards and declaring laws inapplicable to aboriginal people
7)	the federal government must change its ways of developing policies and laws so that aboriginal people are involved and consent to these new policies or laws.
The conclusion of a legal advisor by the name Brad Morse who is professor of law at the University of Ottawa and legal advisor to the Native Council of Canada and other aboriginal first nations reads:
I would conclude from this that the federal government's demand
for extinguishment of aboriginal and treaty rights is a violation of this
fiduciary obligation itself and must be stopped.
What has happened is that the minister has indicated to us this morning that when a group is armed he will not negotiate with them. I am telling you, Madam Speaker, that my people, the Dene-Metis, are not armed. These people are not armed and they want to negotiate in good faith a comprehensive land claims that will not force them to extinguish their rights, but this government will not allow that. It will not renew an outdated claims policy. This is divisive. This is the way in which this government is dividing the aboriginal community. It is totally unacceptable.
I would like to go from here to dealing with the fiduciary. The government's responsibility is to bring the aboriginal communities together and inspire confidence, not to drive them apart by using one aboriginal person against the other. I told this House yesterday that aboriginal peoples cannot afford to choose between one another, there are not that many of us. We are a community who has to believe in an old-fashioned ideology, that there is strength in unity. This is what Canada should be about. But that is not what is happening.
This countiy has been driven apart by a government that is bankrupt in policy, in ideology and in vision. We are constitutionally belly-up. It is not just an aboriginal problem, it is an anglophone-francophone, it is an eastern-western, it is an aboriginal-non-aboriginal, it is the rich and the poor. I do not think that is a partisan issue, I think it is a human rights issue.
The people of Canada want to belong to one country. They want to work together, to be one people, proud of the countiy they come from but that is not what is happening. This countiy is constitutionally belly-up and we are heading into a recession.
Why would we entertain such an inane motion to commend the exemplary conduct of the men and women in the Armed Forces? These people are pawns being used by the government to circumvent the democratic
September 25, 1990

process. The wrong process has been engaged in and this is not right. What should have happened?
I have a copy of a speech delivered by the Prime Minister on August 18, I believe, wherein he called this an armed insurrection. If it is an armed insurrection, what the government should have invoked was the Emergency Measures Act, which would have had the House reconvene after seven days. Why would this government, in all good sense, want the sole responsibility for this mess? Why could it have not shared it with the other parties? It is ridiculous, it borders on the sublime.
On September 20 I wrote to the Prime Minister to demand that there be an inquiry. In response the government has given this ridiculous motion. There is no way that I am going to publicly chastise or criticize people that are being used. The National Defence Act is used as a shield to circumvent the parliamentary process. I am not going to be that ridiculous and neither are the other members of this Parliament, Madam Speaker.
Why has the government missed a golden opportunity to address the real issues? Why does it continue to put forward these ridiculous motions which, again, circumvents an opportunity to deal with some of the real issues that need to be dealt with, like the government's fiduciary responsibility. This responsibility should be one of advocacy, not one of adversary. The government should be working for these people, Madam Speaker, in an advocacy manner, not in an adversarial manner. It should be promoting brotherhood, not division.
I must say that the response that I have received on the motion that has been put forward by the government is that it totally avoids the basic issues with which we should be dealing. There are certain moral and legal obligations that should be addressed. I am going to attempt to address some of those, as I have with the fiduciary responsibility of the government as set out in the Constitution.
The government during the Meech Lake debate was very much aligning itself with a larger body of legal opinion on what is right for Canada constitutionally. There are bodies of legal opinion that say, and I have a note here called "The News from Queens." "Queen's
Government Orders
legal scholars announce proposal to end Kanesatake stand-off".
Madam Speaker, these 20 lawyers from the Queen's Faculty of Law may not be experts, but they have bothered to come forward with a proposal. I will leave it here so that the minister may have a look at it.
They bring certain matters into question, and I will quote John White, the Dean of Law.
"Canada and the Mohawks are looking for a process which can lead to the laying down of arms and a withdrawal of the military. This inquiry represents a responsible way to avoid further loss of life.
According to the 22 legal academics who signed the letter, the usual criminal process may not suffice in this context. The laws we apply must recognize international law, treaty law and the law of aboriginal rights as well as the ordinary law of criminal procedure."
There have been many concerns about the ensuing investigation that will take place in Kanesatake. Who will be overseeing it? Will it be the Surete du Quebec? I asked the Solicitor General that question yesterday. In a latter I wrote to him I asked if it was possible to have tlie RCMP undertake the ensuing investigation. I referred to the fiduciary responsibility of the government. The minister said: "If Quebec so wills and if Quebec agrees, it can be negotiated". But legal advice this morning tells me that the Solicitor General can, in fact, override that because of the federal government's responsibility for aboriginal people under the Constitution. In fact, it can make provisions, make accommodations and can negotiate. At the very least it should negotiate to show that there is an element of co-operation and to build the trust the minister has spoken about.
In my letter of September 20 to the Prime Minister, I indicated that it is critical that there be a parliamentary investigation into the entire situation at Oka and the subsequent events at Kahnawake and Kanesatake. The Canadian public is entitled to know why Parliament was not recalled to deal with what has become a national issue. They want to know why the federal government chose to neglect its responsibilities to those aboriginal people. This is a very fundamental question.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
Why will the government not negotiate? Why was the army directed to use 3,000 troops to deal with a dispute over land? Why has the army used force and tear gas on women and children who were not armed? Why has communication been cut off between the aboriginal people under siege at Kanesatake and the Canadian public at large? Why has freedom of press has been denied? Why has a native civil servant been fired from the federal government? How can the government justify the continuous use of intrusion and violence against a group of Canadians who are not being protected equally as other citizens? These questions are endless and the implications of not acquiring the answers through a parliamentary investigation are too monumental if the government is serious about dealing with the problems confronting aboriginal people across the country. Madam Speaker, the questions and the concerns are endless.
On August 11, the Liberal MP for Kenora-Rainy River wrote to the Speaker asking for an emergency debate on the situation pursuant to Standing Order 52(1). It is crucial that a full enquiry be called in order to establish the facts surrounding this national crisis.
I will review the incident that brought this situation to a crisis. Let us look at the cumulative of the decisions in Calder-Gerin-Sioui. Sparrow establishes that the Supreme Court of Canada is willing to be flexible in order to allow the proof of aboriginal claims. It is also willing to interpret those sections of the Constitution dealing with aboriginal peoples in a way which gives meaning to the concept of aboriginal rights. The latter three cases have been affected by Section 35 of the Constitution Act of 1982.
Madam Speaker, clearly the Constitution Act of 1982, Section 35, is worth the paper it is written on, especially in relation to the evolution of the rights of aboriginal people. Section 35 was included in the Constitution during the tenure of Justice Minister Jean Chretien. Had the Conservative government adjusted its policies and programs to fit these Supreme Court decisions, then the crisis at Oka might have been averted.
Throughout the summer, calls for the Minister of Indian Affairs to become involved in this dispute were
met with silence in an attempt to pass off responsibility to the Government of Quebec. This whole procedure of a termination policy and sloughing off the responsibility to another jurisdiction and making aboriginal issues and the fiduciary responsibility for aboriginal peoples a political football simply is not going to work any more.
What we need in this country is fundamental change. We need changes. Any government that is in power is going to need fundamental change. You are going to have to look at the profile of the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs for instance. Why is it that when a Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs is appointed, it is considered a demotion? It is considered punishment for not having done a good job elsewhere. Why is that? That is ridiculous. That is the perception and if that is the case then it is up to the government to get the message out that this is a high profile position, a position that has inner cabinet support on aboriginal issues, a position that is sensitive to the needs of aboriginal people that is consultative and not confrontational. This is not a ministry that plays a power game, this is one that plays the game of co-operation with the people that it is supposed to serve.
Prior to the army moving to Oka, there were violations of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Electricity and telephones were cut off, repair crews were denied entry and the actions of the Quebec police were directed towards the cutting off of food and medicine to the Indian people. Media access was also cut off.
The motion put forward by the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs is an attempt to mask his incompetence with the competence of the army. That is what it is-avoiding and not dealing with the issues head on. The army has shown restraint and discipline. We recognize that. Why should we talk about it? But the federal government has pushed many aboriginal peoples to the end of their tether, let me tell you. This issue should have been resolved long ago.
I had warned the minister of the burgeoning crisis at Oka and to my knowledge, nothing was done. When human rights abuses took place he did nothing but to condemn various components and factions, not dealing with the issue head on. This is not how you govern. You deal with the issues that are put to you in a crisis yet you do not avoid them.
September 25, 1990

The army was requested by the Government of Quebec. It was not dispatched by the federal government. This government, this minister and this Prime Minister have sat idly acting as lackeys in refusing to take leadership roles in resolving this crisis. In my mind they have abandoned their constitutional responsibilities. The big question across Canada is, why? People have asked ridiculous questions such as this. Are the aboriginal people being punished for killing Meech Lake? That is a question that is being asked. This is not my question, this is a question that is being asked because there is no trust, no faith and no confidence in this government.
The Liberal Party called for the resumption of Parliament at the outset of this crisis, yet the Prime Minister refused to reconvene Parliament. The Prime Minister speaks glowingly in terms laden with blarney about democratic processes, yet he refused to keep Parliament informed about what was going on. Ironically, he reconvened Parliament when a band of poor, destitute refugees landed on the shores of Canada and he called it a national emergency. He used Parliament to foster racism in Canada. That is how I feel about it.
Now I want to go to the whole issue of human rights. I have an article that was sent to me by Lawanahara, Ross Maracle, a clergyman from the Tyendinaga Reserve in Desoronto. He states:
However, here "at home", the Canadian Native is an endangered species living in increasingly endangered spaces. On September 20th the news media reported that the Prime Minister warned that "violence gets you nothing except heartache, sadness and loss'.
So, what's new? We have always lived with heartache and sadness. You saw on TV, Desmond Thtu stand in a northern Native village whose shacks were devoid of electricity and running water. Yes, we have always lived on the edge of epidemics, our babies have the highest rate of infant mortality and our children are plagued with diseases caused by open trench sewers. Our life expectancy is much beneath that of other Canadians. We know what death is all about. Our babies die of gastro-enteritis, our children expire inhaling gas fumes, our youth increasingly are taking their lives. So, what's new? WE DON'T NEED TEAR GAS TO WEEP!
You will never gauge the depth of my emotions, when I, as a Mohawk clergyman and Reverend Greg Shisheesh, a Cree, attempted to deliver food to Kanesatake that was purchased with money that came from Elijah Harper's Reserve of Red Sucker Lake, Manitoba.
Government Orders
How can I express my feelings! Seeing the razor wire! The searchlights! The helicopters! Thnks! Machine-guns with bayonets! And now dogs and the towers! In Canada! May this not be the resurrection of the ghosts of Dachau and Auschwitz rising out of an abyss of racial intolerance.
This is what he likens it to. He continues:
Give us native Martin Luther King's and Desmond TUtu's, who are not afraid to identify with despised people. Who will, as the Good Samaritan, bind up the emotional and spiritual wounds of our people. Where are those that represent the Jesus Christ who would pour in oil and bind up wounds without checking the colour of his skin or asking him his beliefs?
Well, I can say that we, as Canadians, have to remember that there are two races of people only, men and women, and the rest is just colour.
Our attempt has to be to live in peace and harmony, not to divide, not to create policies that divide people. That is totally unacceptable. I can tell you as an aboriginal person and a Canadian parliamentarian, it is my goal to be fair. It is my goal to be more than partisan. It is my goal to be human and to share that humanity with my fellow parliamentarians and Canadians who put me here to represent them.
My goal is to show you when you look at my people and you look into the eyes of my people, you will see something good, something kind, something tolerant, and that you will not see criminals. You will not see the intolerance that has been spoken about, the violence. Because there is goodness there and it is a goodness that is to be shared. We are a people, as one of my elders said, "a people who have no principle and have no belief and no vision, have no future. They are a people doomed for failure". Well, I see the aboriginal people and the people of Canada as more than that.
There have been other concerns. A member of the Canadian Bar Association, Mr. Sam Stevens, wrote an article in a paper called The National. The Canadian Bar Association membership has 35,000 members. There is a large legal body of opinion. In his comments he said:
The new Native Law Section of the Canadian Bar met with the Minister of Indian Affairs in August 1988 to discuss its proposals and urged him to act quickly. The minister did not adopt any of the recommendations. In the midst of the Oka conflict, CBA again forwarded a copy of its report to the Minister.
We, as Canadians, now face circumstances that no longer allow us to ignore or delay the resolution of these many issues, but it has taken an

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
armed confrontation to force us to begin to deal with the original citizens of this country in a fair and equitable manner.
The Canadian Bar Association in its special report entitled: "Aboriginal Rights in Canada: An Agenda for Action (1989)" made this the central focus of how to resolve aboriginal issues but it also realized there had to be a number of other mechanisms to resolve the hundreds of outstanding claims. Their recommendations are as such: the resumption of the constitutional process; a royal commission to examine, study, and report on treaty issues; a parliamentary inquiry to examine and make recommendations on the plight of the Inuit, Metis, and non-status Indians; and the establishment of a specific claims tribunal and aboriginal rights commission to inquire into aboriginal rights, issues and claims and then to publish reports recommending solutions.
These recommendations are not made by people who scribble out messages on napkins. These are groups of professionals who sit down together, think out, and through consensus come up with an agenda, trying to assist government in taking the right approach.
Mr. Stevens states:
In the end that it will take a very long time before the bitterness at Oka and across the country subsides and aboriginal First Nations, governments and average Canadians can begin to feel good about each other.
What a heavy price to pay for something that could have been completely avoided. The solutions were there, but the commitment to do something about these problems was not there.
Sam Stevens is the Administrator of the Justice of the Peace Program for the Territorial Court in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories.
I will conclude with these comments. This country and this government will go nowhere if there is not fundamental change. We need to endorse a program, an aboriginal agenda, that does a number of things and that gives aboriginal issues within government the highest profile and the role of the minister. We need to look at what happens to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. To empower people, one accelerates devolution and makes sure that those resources and moneys that are intended for aboriginal peoples do reach the people that they are intended for.
We also must look at taking the right procedures now with this one crisis-this is one crisis, there are many that could occur-and that a parliamentary investigation or inquiry does take place. We must, in fact, entertain the recommendations about a royal commission of inquiry but the government should not use it as a blanket not to take action on current issues.
In dealing with land claims the policies, please, I appeal to the government that it should not be divisive. It is are dividing our people. We need to have our people work together. I represent 15,000 aboriginal people. I cannot have those people divided because of policies that divide them, separate them, and force them to choose between one another.
We also need to look at a legislative commission to deal with land claims and we have to deal with issues of sovereignty. We have to deal with issues of self-determination or self-government and we also specifically have to address the whole issue of the outdated claims policy.
From the day that I was elected, I have pushed successive ministers in committee on this issue of selfgovernment and on the extinguishment clause because I could see that we were heading into trouble with the comprehensive claims. There were the former ministers, Mr. McKnight and Pierre Cadieux, and now we have the current minister.
It has been my goal ultimately to have the claims settled but in doing that there are major considerations for my people. What do they want to lose? What will the exchange be? These are the questions that are determined by the policies that government puts forward.
I say once again to Canada: "You have to realize that the aboriginal people are not the enemy." The aboriginal people are the inhabitants of this land, who have been here for thousands of years and who have carried on tradition.
Winandaga, a great peacemaker who was a Huron by birth and a Mohawk by adoption, said: "Our strength shall be in unity. Our way shall be the way of reason, righteousness and peace." What do you think the white forefathers saw when they came upon a group of people that had government based on peace, that had a group of people who were civilized enough to govern themselves? It must have been a pleasant surprise to extract principles of democracy from them for their own constitution.
September 25, 1990

It must have been a great treat to have been able to do that.
The aboriginal people have many considerations: constitutional, political, social, educational, and economic-marginalized on most fronts. But this is a problem that is not going to go away. This is a problem that the government is going to have to grasp and say, "We have the political will to make change," or it is not going to change. It is quite obvious that it is not changing.
I say that we are willing to work things out. We want to work together, but we cannot do it ourselves. I am here as a fellow parliamentarian and I am willing to work with the government on this issue.

That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the
word "Chateauguay" and replacing them with the following:

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I would like to offer my congratulations to the member for Western Arctic who made a very impassioned and a very strong speech as an aboriginal member of this House of Commons. I look forward to the other speeches by aboriginal members because I feel that these are the people who can speak, as the member for the Western Arctic has done, from the heart and identify for us the issues.
Having said that, I would like to enter this debate on motion No. 17 which we are debating today, presented by the Minister of Indian Affairs. I would have to say at the outset how utterly disappointing this motion is. It totally fails to deal with the national and international ramifications of the situation that occurred this summer and still occurs at Kanesatake and Kahnawake. It fails to deal with the root of any of the problems that have led to that situation and it is, in my view, simply a cynical attempt, once again, for the government to refuse to accept its responsibility for the actions that were taken.
If the government had accepted its responsibility, it would have called Parliament back, but it failed in accepting that responsibility. The Government of Canada had an obligation, in a situation as serious as this, to call back Parliament and to hear the solutions, the ideas and the debate of all of the members and parties of this House. This government has not only failed on this issue and failed the aboriginal people, it has failed the people of Canada. What we have seen by successive federal governments has led to what I have seen increasingly over the years become, on the part of aboriginal people,

Government Orders
a rebellion of despair because there is nowhere else to turn. I want to say today in speaking to this motion that it is up to us as politicians to turn that rebellion of despair into a revolution of hope. That is our responsibility. That is the responsibility we want to see.
From the beginning of the situation at Kahnawake and Kanesatake it has been characterized by a wish more to save face on the part of the government than to save lives. That should always be the first consideration of any government. This has been much more than a summer of discontent. It has been a summer of anger and contempt. The images that we have seen this summer must surely be branded on the soul of every Canadian and of every Canadian child who watched what their country was becoming. We have seen the images of Canadians fighting other Canadians on Canadian streets. We have seen Canadians stoning other Canadians as they drive by seniors and children. We have seen masked citizens facing off against helmeted and shielded soldiers and police. I suppose the image that struck me the most is something I read the other day by a reporter who was behind the barricades. He said that he was in the treatment centre and a seven-year old child came in. That seven-year old wanted a piece of candy or something and he said to him to go away and he would talk to him later. He described how the seven-year old turned around with a look of tremendous hate in his eyes for this white reporter. It told a thousand tales. Is that the future we will see as a result of this summer? I sincerely hope not.
As politicians, we have a responsibility not just for the events of today but for what is going to happen tomorrow and as we move on into the decade and the year 2000. The minister spoke often in his comments about the rule of law.
We had a situation where the Canadian Armed Forces acted under the Defence Act and came into the situation at Kahnawake and Kanesatake. I ask the government: Let's talk about the rule of law. Why was the Emergencies Act not enforced?
I would suggest to you, Madam Speaker, that the reason that legislation was not used is that this minister,
this government and this Prime Minister would have had to stand before this House and explain their actions, because under that law they would be forced to do so.
I quote from the preamble of the act: "In order to ensure safety and security during such an emergency, the Governor in Council should be authorized, subject to the supervision of Parliament, to take temporary measures that may not be appropriate in normal times."
By not utilizing this act, are the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Prime Minister saying to us that these are normal times, that what we saw this summer were normal times? I hope not, and I assure you that I and my party will continue to work very hard to ensure that this is not seen as normal times.
Clearly, these were extraordinary times and required the measures that were provided for in this act.
I underline the term in this act that says: "subject to the supervision of Parliament". The language is perfectly clear.
Instead, the Government of Canada, the Government of Quebec and the Liberal premier of Quebec chose to use Section 281 of the Defence Act.
Finally, we have an opportunity now to debate this issue. This motion certainly does not begin to deal with the issue in any substantial way.

And now we are finally here, and if there is anything that illustrates the failure of this government's policies or its lack of policies, it is the fact that the crisis still continues, months after it started. I don't think anyone in this House will disagree with me if I say that this summer was one of the saddest Canada has known. It was a summer of hostility, violence and confrontation, and I believe it has completely changed our concept of Canada.
I was talking recently to a friend who went to Europe this summer. He told me it was the first time in his life that he did not have a feeling of national pride upon returning to his country. For the first time, he wondered whether this country was really more humane, was really a better place to live and bring up children.
September 25, 1990



Today, Canadians are questioning the very character of our nation, and they are finding some of those answers very disquieting.
The crisis at Kanesatake and Kahnawake has deep roots of injustice which have been buried and therefore are easy for many of us to ignore.
The crisis at Kanesatake and Kahnawake is about justice, as the Minister of Indian Affairs says. It is about fair treatment for aboriginal people. It is about hope and dignity, and it is about fundamental human rights.
The experience of Canada's first nations is the experience of a denial of constitutional recognition and the refusal of governments to live up to past agreements.
I remind the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that agreements are the rule of law as well. With that agreement, we have a responsibility to our people.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
But agreements have been broken. Promises have been broken. How could we have expected aboriginal people to have faith in the political system when during the Meech Lake debate, the Prime Minister of Canada promised aboriginal people that he would have a package for them that would address their issues. Once the Meech Lake Accord was defeated, no more was said about that package.
If the injustices remained, then, if a package was necessary to address them and two weeks later it was not there, how could people have faith in the political system?

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Aboriginal people for centuries have had the experience of seeing their resources taken away, their land, water and air polluted without their involvement in any of that and their health and livelihood threatened.
The 1763 Royal Proclamation talked about treaties that endured so long as the sun rises and the river flows. Well, Madam Speaker, I remind the Minister of Indian
Government Orders
Affairs that treaties are law and those are laws that should be respected.
About 120 years after the Royal Proclamation, Chief Piapot, of the Cree described the situation as follows, and I quote: "In order to become the sole masters of our land they relegated us to small reservations as big as my hand and made us long promises, as long as my arm. But next year the promises were shorter and got shorter every year until they are the length of my finger".
That is the history of Canadian respect for the law. [Translation]
Listening to the government's eloquent speeches, we must not forget this is the same government that cut back financing for native newspapers by 100 per cent. This government has stifled the voice of our native people..
That same government also cut financing for native broadcasting services. It has undermined the media that help native people preserve their language and culture. That same government also made substantial cuts in funding for organizations that represent native people and it capped funding for native postsecondary education. It is a decision that is hard to understand if we consider the importance of education for the individual, the community and society as a whole.

Finally, Madam Speaker, it is this government along with successive Conservative and Liberal governments and provincial governments that excluded Canada's First Nations from participation in the constitutional reform process. They were shut out just as the territories of the Yukon and Northwest Territories were shut out. Those are areas where indigenous Canadians make up a sizeable percentage of the population.
Consequently, aboriginal concerns and rights were often ignored or put off to some future date.
Elijah Harper and the First Nations movement in Canada said that would not do. Empty promises were not enough. Real commitments were required and that real and immediate action on aboriginal issues had to take place.
I would say that Mr. Harper has also said that aboriginal peoples speak loudest when they speak with the voice of peace and the voice of peace with justice.

September 25, 1990

I would say that there are probably very few of us in this Chamber, if any, who condone the use of violence. But I also believe that if the rights of Canadian aboriginal people continue to be ignored, our collective rights as a nation will be diminished and our country cannot be whole. It is time to recognize that the future of Canada cannot be separated from the future of Canada's first peoples.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the crisis this summer, to which this motion refers, stems from the frustration of Canada's first peoples who have had their political and constitutional objectives and efforts ignored or obstructed and who have tried to negotiate with governments that are unwilling to negotiate. The role of the Surete du Quebec and the role of the province of Quebec has only added to the problem. That is very sad because it seems to me that the people of the province of Quebec who themselves have been victims of oppression concerning language in their history and of exploitation very often by people from another culture, should be the first people to understand the aspirations of aboriginal people who simply have the same aspirations to some autonomy over their own affairs, to the right to their language and their culture. I think that is a very sad statement for all Canadians.
There are many events that occurred this summer, too many to go into, but I think that too will be one of the scars on the soul of our nation. I have often said that there are three areas that distinguish in many ways Canada from other countries: our vast north land, our territories and northern parts of our provinces; the history of Canada's first people, the aboriginal people; and the fact that we have within Canada, Quebec, with a rich culture, a rich language, and a rich history from which all of us benefit. If we look at our history and indeed if we look at constitutional development, it is exactly in those three areas where we continually fail. We have a chance not to fail.
Today we are discussing a motion, a superficial motion, which does not deal with the roots of one of those three major characteristics of Canada by which we define ourselves as Canadians. Let's not lose that chance. Let's take that chance and say now we are going to do something, we are going to do something noble, we are
going to do something just, and we are going to do it now.
There were many events this summer and this fall. [Translation]
There have been a number of events since then, which I will not describe in detail.
However, we saw provincial police withhold food, water and medical supplies from the Mohawks of Kahne-satake.
There were a number of horrifying incidents involving people from Chateauguay and Mohawks at the Mercier Bridge. The Canadian Forces were brought in. We saw a number of tense face-offs between the military and the Mohawk warriors. There were weapons on both sides. Negotiations were broken off. Three thousand soldiers moved forward and dismantled the barricades. There were a number of violent confrontations between the army and the Mohawks last week in Kahnawake, during which tear gas was used.

We still see food supplies withheld from Mohawk men, women, and children who are behind the barricades. It seems to me that by supplying people with the basic necessities of life we are not necessarily saying that we condone the use of arms. Where is the humanity in this? Surely in Canada we can have negotiations. We do not have to accept the actions of the use of arms and of the use of violence, but at the same time governments have to set an example that we are above that, that we do not deprive people of food, and that we will continue to negotiate.
The fundamental question in all of this in every Canadian's mind is: Who is in control and where has the federal government been? Sadly the answer seems to be that no one is in control.
The Prime Minister, instead of taking a leadership role in trying to find a solution, instead of acknowledging federal constitutional responsibility for aboriginal affairs and for the Armed Forces, has done nothing. I think it has come as a great surprise to Canadians to learn that under the National Defence Act a premier can call in the Armed Forces against Canadian citizens without the involvement of Parliament, without the involvement seemingly of the Prime Minister, and that after that both the Prime Minister and the Liberal premier of Quebec
September 25, 1990

can wash their hands of the situation and say that all of the decisions are now in the hands of the army. We elect politicians; we do not elect the army.
The minister spoke today as well about negotiations. There are many proposals on the table for negotiation, proposals which do not circumvent the Canadian law, and the minister is well aware of this. Minister Ciaccia from Quebec has worked, and I would say has worked nobly, in trying to reach an agreement. Sometimes it seems he has worked, because his feels so fundamentally about the issue, not necessarily under the direction of the premier of that province. Here is a man who obviously wants to find a solution, who wants to find a negotiation, who has put forth a proposal, and this government refuses to listen and says no.
People who are watching this debate have to understand that this proposal does not say and does not in any way intimate that the people involved in the treatment centre, those people who have illegal arms, would be outside Canadian law. The proposal does not say that at all, yet this government says that we will not negotiate.
Having gone to Oka on several occasions myself, having met with Indian chiefs across Canada, I have tried as well to make a number of concrete proposals, as have many, many other people: constitutional experts, legal experts. We have had Bishop Thtu here. Jesse Jackson was here yesterday. Of course as a journalist his freedom of the press was cut off and he was not able to do his job, as Canadians journalists cannot do either. I would say that there are people who have put forward in good faith, not in a partisan way, proposals to end this situation.
I have made a number of those concrete proposals this summer to get negotiations going again, to establish a relationship between first nations and our commitments based on dignity and respect, not based on the desire for humiliation of people who feel that they as Canada's first nations are defending their land. I proposed among other things an aboriginal land claims commission, which clearly in the long term must be considered, a land claims commission that takes it out of the bureaucracy of the Department of Indian Affairs, a commission subject to federal statute and accountable to Parliament. If we
Government Orders
have seen anything this summer, we have learned that we must have Parliament involved in all of these issues and not simply within one ministry.
We must find a solution to the land claims issue. I would add that land claims, as they have done in other agreements, include issues of self-government. We must find a mechanism for co-operation and consultation instead of conflict and violence. We can do this.
I have had a number of other recommendations which I will mention very briefly. First, I have asked the Prime Minister to order the army immediately to restore food and basic necessities to the people in the treatment centre, to restore communications to the journalists on site, and to continue negotiations.
Second, I have also asked that an all-party committee be dispatched to Kanesatake and Kahnawake to investigate the situation and also for politicians to show that we are interested. I am sure the people of Canada must be wondering: Are politicians even interested? For our leaders to come out and say it is all in the hands of the army must be very curious to Canadian citizens. We have to take that responsibility.
Third, I have asked for a public inquiry, not a judicial inquiry, that should be struck immediately to investigate how this crisis has been created and how it has been handled.
Finally, I believe that the government could indeed demonstrate some good faith by restoring funding to the aboriginal programs, funding that was cut in the last budget. It is probably very ironic to those organizations that we have spent ten times the amount of money on the army, on the police, than would have been needed simply to restore the funding to those programs.
The political process must be responsive to the needs and the aspirations of Canada's aboriginal people or it will be rejected by them. We must create real hope for peaceful change. We must have real change for peace and hope.
Today I want to close by reminding the House that the year 1992 marks the 500th anniversary of contact between Europeans and the first peoples of North America. It also marks the 125th anniversary of Confederation. I believe we should look at the year 1992 as a target date

Government Orders
for resolution of conflicts between first nations and peoples who have settled there.
The motion put forward by the government is cynical. It does not deal with the root of the problem. As you know, Madam Speaker, I am only allowed to amend the amendment put forward by the Liberals, but I would have to say that if I had the opportunity I would have wanted to change the first part of the motion as well.
The Liberal Party has accepted to commend the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian forces at Oka and Chateauguay. I am not against the Armed Forces at Oka and Chateauguay, but the forces work under the direction of the politicians. Once again this clause which the Liberal Party has accepted and I cannot amend takes away the responsibility of the government.
I would say that it is not a question in my mind of the conduct of anyone in this situation, except the conduct of the federal government and the Government of Quebec. However, given those limitations, I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting the words "this House
condemns the complete failure of the government" and replacing
them with:
"this House condemns the complete failure of the current and past governments".

Mr. Speaker, the World Summit for Children Week in Winnipeg started yesterday and ends this weekend when the actual summit begins in New York. The week-long observance aims to focus the attention of Canadians to the plight of all children, to guarantee their basic rights to food, shelter, good health and education, and to secure their active role in society.
The Winnipeg Free Press recently headlined the lamentable story that slightly over half a million Canadian children turn to food banks every year; that "in Winnipeg the number of hungry who are turning to food banks to feed themselves and their families has swelled by 30 per cent in the last year."
We cannot long afford to fail them. We cannot long endure their continued loss to hunger, illness, ignorance and abuse.
The country will pay the price if we in Parliament who can act fail to act now.
I therefore urge Parliament and this government to give top priority to development of strategies that would eliminate or significantly minimize poverty within this decade.
A war on poverty on behalf of the children of Canada and of the world is a war worth our effort.
