Mr. Speaker, the World Summit for Children scheduled to be held in New York this weekend has been hailed by this government as a vehicle to advance the causes of children everywhere in the world. The summit will be chaired by our very own Prime Minister and is to bring to the forefront of world leaders' minds the plight of children.
So what is the government's solution to helping the children of Canada and the world? It is to produce a document entitled, Children of Canada, Children of the World at a cost of $72,000 which contains nothing but statistics published elsewhere, yet more uninformative rhetoric about concern for children and a huge glossy photograph of the Prime Minister. This is only one of the costs of the summit and there will be many other costs.
Could this money have been spent better? Several organizations who are in a position to know certainly say so. For example, the World Health Organization estimated that four million children under the age of five will die this year as a result of gastro enteritis when a simple ten-cent package of sugar and salt would save them. Another 2.8 million children will die this year as a result of vaccine-preventable diseases. If the Canadian government really wanted to give a shot in the arm to the world's children, they could have spent $72,000 giving shots in the arm to 7,200 children and in the process saving their lives.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today under Standing Order 31 to point out that the Canadian government's actions have undermined their claims that they are negotiating at the GATT to strengthen Article XI to protect our dairy and poultry sectors.
In early July the Canadian government endorsed the GATT agriculture chairman deZeeuw's position paper and accepted it as the negotiating framework to reform world agriculture trade in spite of the fact that the paper failed even to mention Article XI.
When this government went to the Houston meeting of the G-7, they failed to include the strengthening of Article XI in the statement of their main objectives. This government helped draft and endorsed a resulting statement that failed to make any reference to strengthening of Article XI. At the end of August the Canadian government failed to table documents to further outline Canada's position. Only Japan and Switzerland tabled positions.
On October 1, the government has the opportunity to indicate through its actions that it is committed to maintaining and strengthening Article XI by not including our system of orderly marketing on that list of tariff equivalents that it will table at the GATT, clearly stating that they are not tariff equivalents. This will ensure that they are not on the sacrificial list to be tabled October 15.
It is time this government showed with its actions, not its hollow words, that it is committed to strengthening Article XI to allow our dairy and poultry sectors an equitable return for our Canadian farmers.

There is no correlation whatsoever to the situation that originated at Oka, not because of the Mohawk people whose peaceful traditions are well known to all Canadians, but because a small group of warriors have hijacked that situation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, however much affection and respect I may have for the authority of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, neither the Leader of the Opposition nor I need his permission to attend an important convention.
Yesterday's debate was highlighted by the significant and remarkable intervention of the member for Winnipeg South Centre. He spoke eloquently about the importance of the United Nations' summit this weekend and, unless I am mistaken, he did offer to co-operate fully with the government to support and promote approaches designed to help children in Canada and around the world. Having said clearly that I would indeed put to good use this outstanding gesture of leadership on the part of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I am amazed to see that the Leader of the Opposition should fail to draw inspiration from such leadership.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
We all know that the children of Canada are the jewels in our crown and our pride and joy. In the aboriginal community, they are our sacred trust and our future investment. Having said that, this summer, Liberal
members heard the testimony of members of the Oka defence fund who stated that restrictions on food impeded the free access of baby formula, resulting in children being fed sugar water.
Is it government policy to force unarmed children to go hungry? Is it government policy to make children pay the price for this minister's incompetence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, certainly this is not government policy. We certainly all respect the needs of children. I have written a number of times and spoken with the responsible ministers in the Government of Quebec to ensure that, at all times, food was allowed through the barricades when there were barricades up. I would say to the warriors that, if they were to allow the women and children to come out-who are completely free to come out-then all of their needs could be assured.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe a minister of the government who spouts the principle of democracy and does not allow people the right to choose what action they want to take.
If the minister does not agree with the statements just made, can he explain why the Canadian Human Rights Commission and the Human Rights Institute of Canada sent letters to the minister citing the need to prevent human rights abuses? Will the minister do the proper thing and resign?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member speaks of freedom of choice. The children and women- who in a way are providing a screen for the armed warriors-are free to leave and to seek the full benefits and comforts of Canadian citizenship.
I find it surprising that the hon. member would advocate having children sitting at the knee of armed warriors, learning how to clean a revolver.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It is not much wonder that Canadians have become cynical about the old style politics and have totally lost confidence in this government. Now, of course, we see the spectacle of the patronage Senate, with Liberals and Tories announcing
September 25, 1990

their intention to do what this government should have done a year ago, and that is kill the GST.
What does the Prime Minister intend to do now? Will the Prime Minister, instead of going on another binge of political and patronage appointments, kill the GST now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what it is about the NDP. It may be biological, but they are opposed to patronage appointments until one is offered.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!
Mr. Speaker, I was a bit taken aback by the Prime Minister's answer. I did not realize that he was being a stand-up comic and I was waiting for the answer.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. leader could put her question.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the Prime Minister that he once said "You had a choice". The choice is simple: continue handing out patronage appointments at an unprecedented rate, or drop this tax and present to the House a real tax reform which would put the interests of families and workers ahead of those of the rich and mighty.
Here is my question: will the Prime Minister take the right direction, drop this tax, and give Canadians a real tax reform?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a well-known fact that the idea of political appointments is repugnant to the New Democrats. Still, another principle is involved. Generations of New Democrats have adamantly insisted that the Senate has no moral authority whatsoever to kill a legislative measure from the House of Commons where members are duly elected by the people of Canada. Whether one accepts or not the outcome of the last elections, the fact remains that the Canadian voters had been made fully aware of the GST, the free trade agreement and the other political programs, and they chose this government and its programs, rightly or wrongly. Under our system, after
Oral Questions
it has been elected the Canadian government has the right to be heard and to implement its program once it has been accepted by the elected members. New Democrats may find political appointments repugnant, but we find repugnant any attempt at undermining the moral authority of the elected House.
Hear, hear.

My supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker.
The Prime Minister does not need to go to the boardroom for the country to get a vote on the GST. What he can do is either kill the tax himself or do the honourable thing, call an election, and let the people decide-
Hear, hear.
Call an election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just in case there is any doubt in my hon. friend's mind, I just want to reassure her that I did learn that a majority government term is five years, not three.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
That is too bad, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Today at the Canadian Bar Association meeting Roy McMurtry, the former High Commissioner to Great Britain, a very distinguished diplomat and jurist, said the following:
My deep concern is that Canada's role in the international community is being diminished by internal difficulties at Oka. We face a depressing spectacle. We are really on the verge of tarnishing our image in the world which will be very difficult to refurbish unless we get our act together.
Taking those important words of Roy McMurtry and supported by other members of the Canadian Bar Association, I want to ask the Prime Minister this. How can we go ahead on the world stage and argue for the

Oral Questions
protection of civil rights for other people when we are denying civil rights to our native people here in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 20 years ago next month the government of which my friend was a member invoked the War Measures Act and threw almost 600 citizens of the province of Quebec into jail without trial and that has been forgotten by my hon. friend and somehow-
Where did you stand on it?
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members will know that there is considerable contest in this Chamber for time in the Question Period. I would ask hon. members to keep that in mind. The right hon. Prime Minister will complete his answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
My hon. friend was a supporter of that government and information was supposed to be provided to the House of Commons with regard to that particular act. It never was and yet, somehow, the Government of Canada of the day and subsequent governments conducted themselves in such a way as to ensure that there was no dishonour brought to Canada's reputation internationally.
From time to time governments are confronted with difficult situations. This one here is a difficult situation. At Oka, following events that took place in May, for reasons that have a lot to do with the internal control of matters ranging from the illegal trafficking in arms, to cigarettes and to illegal gambling. There were two killings that took place on the Akwesasne reserve in the late spring. This was followed subsequently by the murder of a young member of the Surete du Quebec.
Murder?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: This is deeply regretted and deeply deplored by all-
Are you the judge?
Judge and jury.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Well, there was one of the members of the Surete du Quebec who was killed in the line of duty. The responsibility of the Government of Canada is to deal with this. We have sought to do so in a manner which ensures the ongoing respect for the rule of law, even if it means from time to time that we have got to get a black eye internationally in some fora. We will not accept that people will dominate this country at the point
of a gun because that is alien to everything that Canadians stand for.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take the supplementary to debate all the points but I would remind the Prime Minister that he has colleagues, including the gentleman sitting next to him, who also voted for that same act in 1970.
I want to ask this question: While it may be important to defend law and order, it is equally important to recognize fundamental human rights and fundamental civil liberties. Those are being denied to the people at the treatment centre on the reserve and this government has not moved to deal with the issues that are providing so much frustration and sense of grievance to native people.
Today, we are asking in Parliament: Why not set up a parliamentary inquiry or a royal commission? Why not show native people that we are prepared to deal with them fairly? Then you will get them to listen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend should not be exercised to that extent.
I have already indicated, as has the minister, our intention to join with him and other members of the House of all parties in devising and in setting out programs and policies that will bring a much greater degree of social justice and fairness to the native peoples across Canada.
With greater consultation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Indeed, with greater consultation.
My hon. friend is quite right: indeed, with a greater degree of consultation. I think that my hon. friend from Winnipeg would acknowledge the fact that before these matters can begin, it would be very important that those people who have hijacked an otherwise very peaceful group of native peoples near Montreal put down their guns and abide by Canadian law. Then we can get on with business.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Prime Minister refused to give us the names of Canadian native leaders with whom he has met to resolve the issue at Oka.
When are the Prime Minister and this government going to stop hiding behind a band of armed warriors just to ignore their responsibilities to all Canadian native
September 25, 1990

people? When is the Prime Minister going to sit down and start meeting with Canadian native leaders?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would offer the observation that the hon. member has it quite wrong.
It is the masked warriors who are hiding behind a barricade of razor wire from the justice system which all Canadians must abide by.
I will continue to meet aboriginal leaders, Grand Chief George Erasmus and the leaders of the various provincial first nations across Canada, as I have been doing for many months to help to address the important, social and economic needs of their people.

Well, Mr. Speaker, the minister has not been successful so far.
We want the Prime Minister involved. It should be the top person in government.

The Minister knows that the native children are faced with higher rates of poverty, illiteracy, malnutrition, disease and death than other Canadian children.
Considering such a deplorable situation, how can he justify to the Canadians and to the United Nations Summit on Children the fact that he has completely abolished the $60 million program for native children?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member could check the estimates. I can provide him with another copy of the vital information that I circulated to all members in June.
I will provide him with clear evidence of our increased commitment to the needs of aboriginal children. Certainly we recognize there are special social problems and higher than acceptable levels of difficulty in relation to child welfare, child sexual crimes and other matters. We are working on a new set of initiatives to address these in co-operation with the provinces.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House of Commons, the Prime Minister said:
The Government of Canada responded to a-request from the
Government of Quebec pursuant to the National Defence Act to
provide the Canadian army for peacekeeping purposes-
However, at a news conference on August 8 to announce the decision, the Prime Minister contradicted his friend, the Liberal premier of Quebec, and said that it would be inappropriate and misleading to describe the army's role at Oka as one of peacekeeping. Can the Prime Minister explain to the House on which occasion he was telling the truth?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rather than play on words, I think it is more important that the NDP recognize that the Canadian forces have been requisitioned under the National Defence Act in the aid to the civil power. It is a provision in the act that is available to every province in Canada when they need assistance because they cannot enforce civil law, have peace and security for their people, by either the municipal policing authorities, their provincial policing authorities or, in this case, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The Canadian forces were called in, have responded and, to the greatest extent possible, carried out their responsibilities with diligence, patience and understanding that I think even the hon. member would recognize.

Mr. Speaker, given that the army has been accused of provoking hostility, withholding food, denying human rights and trampling freedom of the press, why does the Prime Minister, with his Minister of Indian Affairs, continue to hide behind the army and why will he not take the responsibility now and commit himself to finding a political solution to this three-month-old conflict?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

June 28, a full two weeks before the tragedy occurred at Oka.

Over the course of the past week I have met with both of you, and your councils, to discuss the current situation in Oka and the long term needs of your respective communities.
With respect to the former, I understand that the Village of Oka's application for an injunction to remove the blockade of the Chemin du Mille is to be heard on Friday, June 29, 1990. Regardless of the outcome, I urge you both to meet, immediately following the court's decision, to discuss ways of diffusing the tensions that exist and restoring a climate of harmony until long term solutions can be found.
I am prepared to offer the services of Mr. Yves Desilets to assistyou in these discussions. I am confident-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. minister has read the appropriate parts.

Mr. Speaker, in a letter to John Ralston Saul, Chairman of the Pen Club International, a writers' association, the Defence Department stated, and I quote: "Material and films belonging to journalists can go through military barricades and we will allow journalists to receive food supplies." The Minister refuses to respect those commitments.
I ask the Minister of National Defence why he refuses to admit that these rights are absolutely fundamental in a democratic society?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has to understand that there are basic rights in a democratic society. The first right is that of respect of law. There are suspected law-breakers in the treatment centre at this time. The Canadian forces are acting as peacemakers and peace officers in this instance. With regard to food, I can tell the hon. member that we estimate there are some 53 people in the treatment centre. We are providing rations for 60 people. The other day we provided four eggs per person, some 240 eggs. They were so desperate for food that the warriors threw them at the army.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence

Mr. Speaker, first, I would like the minister to tell us what laws the journalists have broken.
Second, I would like the minister to tell us whether or not he believes that the public's right to know the real story at Oka, Kanesatake and the treatment centre is not a fundamental right.
Does the minister think that stopping access to films and tapes and the filing of stories is an absolute abridgement of fundamental rights in this democracy, that it is censorship?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should recognize that there are suspected law-breakers in the treatment centre.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If that is recognized by the hon. member then she, I believe, will concur with the actions that have been taken by the Canadian forces to limit inflow. There has been no limit to reporters wanting to leave. If reporters wish to leave, the door is open. If anyone wishes to leave, the door is open.
I ask the hon. member to understand that this is not a public event. These are actions that have taken place by people suspected of breaking the law. The Canadian forces are acting as peace officers under the jurisdiction of Canada. Perhaps the member will understand that these are not equals: one is enforcing law and the other is attempt to break law. We are making every effort possible to make sure there is a peaceful resolution.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Acadie-Bathurst on his confirmation as his party's financial critic.
May I remind him that in our most recent budget, we had indicated that the economy was under pressure following seven years of record growth and that it would require some slowdown in order better to adjust. Of course, we are now in this transition period and we certainly are quite concerned about the many bankruptcies, but the hon. member should recognize that there is a reduction in the number of businesses compared with an unprecedented high in Canada.
A look at some figures will show that nearly 150,000 new jobs per year have been created over the past ten years. Compared with 1982 when we had a Liberal government-admittedly a veiy difficult period-there are fewer bankruptcies today; there were then nearly 800,000 businesses, while there are now 1,600,000 businesses with the same number of bankruptcies. It is therefore a difficult and necessary situation which we monitor very closely in our efforts to avert inflation.

Mr. Speaker, my point in asking the Prime Minister the question is that the high interest rates we are suffering were not foreseen by the Minister of Finance. The deficit which the finance minister predicted is not at all in line with what it is going to be. Inflation is going to be fuelled by the GST. That is being confirmed by, for example, the IMF. These are all prime indicators that would require any thinking person to recognize that we must have a revised budget in this country that reflects economic reality.
I ask the Prime Minister: Is it not time to recognize the kind of damage his government is doing to the economy and to ask his finance minister to bring in a budget that reflects economic realities in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)

Canadian grain farmers are in a crisis position as far as cash flow is concerned. They have lots of grain but are unable to move it off the farm at any price. For a variety of reasons, among them the embargo against Iraq, prices have fallen and no grain is moving at all, which means the producers are virtually without any income.
Will the government now provide some immediate cash flow to grain farmers by providing them with an interest-free advance on this year's harvest?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member and other members of the House that I am very much aware of the serious cash flow situation in which the farmers find themselves.

Having said that, we all know that with the record crop, a serious slump in sales and the low prices that situation will deteriorate further still down the road.
We are looking at some options. As a matter of fact, the deputy ministers of agriculture are meeting in Toronto at this particular time. The crisis in cash flow is right now. When can the fanners expect some payment, either by payment for cash in the bin or deficiency payment for crops that will be sold to the Wheat Board later on? When can they expect some cash in hand?
I know the Saskatchewan election is on hold. Does that-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last week, the Minister of Finance practically admitted Canada was again on the brink of a recession. I have the following question for the Prime Minister. Since according to the Economic Council of Canada, the GST will aggravate the so-called slowdown or recession we are seeing now in Canada, is the Prime Minister prepared to join the members of the Senate of this country who want to kill the GST?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member forgot to mention, and her party certainly has not mentioned it either, that the GST has some very definite advantages-I am thinking of the role it will play in enhancing our exports-and will help inject into the
Canadian economy $9 billion worth of additional activities in the course of one year. That is something we should not forget.
Meanwhile, I may add that our policies are working if we consider that during the last few weeks and months there has been a gradual drop in interest rates. We find this very reassuring.

Mr. Speaker, maybe the minister has not heard the predictions of the Economic Council of Canada, but the Economic Council of Canada is predicting that there will be a 2 per cent inflationary result caused by the GST. speechtext:

A statement was made, and I quote it to my hon. friend: "It worries me that serious structural problems have been identified in the manufacturers' sales tax. To name just a few, in some cases its burden falls less heavily upon imported goods than on domestic goods. It falls unevenly upon competing goods which are marketed at different trade levels. It does not currently permit a meaningful appeal system. These problem areas in the law cannot be tolerated indefinitely-Before long,
I will have to assess the merits of all opinions and make a decision on the best course for the government to follow."
That was a statement by the Minister of Finance, Jean Chretien, on November 22, 1977.
Hear, hear.

September 25, 1990

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are back to the very important business of the day. Prior to the recess, we listened to the hon. Leader of the NDP make a very important intervention. I was very interested to hear what she had to say.
I know that the hon. member has a great concern for people of native extraction, Indians and Inuit, many of whom live in her riding, and I know she has a very deep and underlying concern about the condition of these people. She mentioned a lot in her talk about justice and fair play in Canada, and I heard that with a great deal of sympathy, as I am sure many other Canadians did as well.
The hon. member talked about how Canadians view themselves and this very special idea that we have about what we are like. We are tolerant, fine, fair-minded people who have a sense of social justice, who want to reach out to help their neighbours and each other. We certainly want to deal with the many injustices that we both feel Indian people have suffered over the centuries, certainly in the 120-odd years of Confederation.
The hon. member also pointed out that Canadians view themselves as a peace loving people. There was some dichotomy in what I heard because, if we are a peace loving society, how can we then assume that might is right and that he who carries a gun somehow has the moral authority to command special attention? Yet, the hon. member was espousing that very idea. If someone has a weapon combined with a just cause, that somehow gives him or her some special authority to get attention that we would normally not accord to anybody in our
September 25, 1990

society who took up arms against any other sector or segment of society.
Is the hon. member saying that when anybody wheels a gun, he or she deserves special consideration for his or her particular interest? Does this mean that anybody who feels he or she has a just cause can take up arms and then get some sort of special consideration? Should we sit down and negotiate the terms of the particular problem that that interest group might have at the point of a gun? If that is so, I find it difficult to put together in my mind with what the hon. member said about the just society, the way Canadians see themselves and how we deal with the perception, even internationally, that other people have of us.
It seems to me that there are many peace loving, law biding Mohawks and other Indians out there who do not condone the use of guns. In fact, Mohawk warriors are hiding behind the very legitimate concerns of the Indian people in the rest of Canada.
How does the hon. member condone the use of force and the use of guns? Does she believe that people who pick up arms should be given food because he or she points a gun in a certain direction? I wonder if the hon. member condones the use of guns.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, no, I have never condoned the use of guns. It is for that reason that I did not support the actions of the Surete du Quebec when it went in in a very violent way and, sadly, a young Canadian lost his life over this.
The hon. member across the way referred to these people, the aboriginal people. These people are Canadians and we cannot lose sight of this. Not only are they the people who the previous speaker refers to as "these people", but they are the first people of this country. There are many treaties that have not been honoured.
No, I do not condone the use of violence. I support Elijah Harper who has said that aboriginal people speak loudest when they speak with peace. No, I do not condone the actions of others who have also undertaken violent actions against aboriginal people, or indeed when
Government Orders
aboriginal people do the same thing. But we cannot avoid a discussion of the root causes of this issue simply by focusing on it and talking only about guns.
We are avoiding the issue of aboriginal rights and the acceptance of aboriginal rights in this country. By dealing only with the issue of guns and by pointing out that it is necessary to deal with the historical obligations of Canada and the historical and constitutional justice of aboriginal rights that are in our Constitution, and, indeed, rights to self-government that reports commissioned by the House have developed, we are simply avoiding the root issue.
No, I do not condone the use of violence. But I do not condone it by residents of Chateauguay, I do not condone it by the Mohawks, I do not condone it by the police, and I do not condone it by the army. The member across the way, of all people, should think that there is a different way to do things. Why do we always have to use the old way and, if I dare say, the macho way? Maybe it is time we started to sit down to negotiate and to deal with some of these issues properly.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question for the Leader of the New Democratic Party is one that concerns not only this issue, but a larger issue of which this is a microcosm, that is, the disrespect for the political process that we have seen this summer.
We have seen the abdication of political responsibility at both the federal and provincial level. As a leader of a major political party in Canada, how does she see this tragedy?

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands raises a very good point. It really is not the time to point blame at one group or another, but to look at what we are going to do collectively using good common sense in the House so that we are never faced with this kind of debate again. Is this not what we should be doing?

Government Orders
If the government had had respect for all of the members of the House, they would have recalled the House this summer to discuss the situation. This is an extraordinary situation. None of the aspects of the situation are happy, not for Quebecers, not for Canadians, and not for aboriginal people. It is not a situation we all wanted, but surely it was a time for the government to show leadership and to recall Parliament so that everyone in the House could offer their solutions for this crisis.
The kind of leadership needed in the country is leadership that listens to all the solutions. We cannot afford any more to only look at things from one perspective. If we have learned anything this summer, surely we must have learned that it is necessary to listen to all the voices in Canada. There are very legitimate concerns in Quebec after the failure of the Meech Lake Accord. There are very legitimate concerns of aboriginal people. There are very legitimate concerns of the people who, as we did in the debate yesterday, raised questions about our role in the Middle East.
Surely, it is the time to show some real statesperson-ship, to have people together to debate and discuss these issues. It takes everyone. Real leadership and government that cares about Canadians to ensure that that takes place.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the citizens of a region of my riding, particularly the residents of Oka-Kanesatake, Saint-Placide and Saint-Benoit, have lived through a summer of fear and terror. The nightmarish nights of women and children who were ordered out of their houses at gun point by masked Warriors on July 11, 1990 is an image which these peaceful people will never forget.
This is why I thank the House for this opportunity to express what I have been living through since 1984, and to shed some light on incidents of which members and Canadians alike have a right to be aware.
I was told during the 1984 election campaign that native people did not vote. At the time the chiefs asked me to leave Kanesatake. I was surprised because I
believed that native people were Canadians like all others and that they ought to exercise their right to vote.
After the elections I had many meetings with the residents of this Mohawk community who did not agree with the system under which the chiefs and the grand chief are elected by the clan mothers. Next came the compilation of duly signed petitions from 85 per cent of the people of Kanesatake urging the government to intervene.
In 1987 we asked for a referendum and the case was referred to the courts by then chief Alex Montour. The case is still pending and should be heard in the near future.
Right now, Madam Speaker, however well-intentioned, nobody-Conservative, Liberal, New Democrat, it does not matter-can negotiate with the Kanesatake Mohawk community. I would suggest there are too many chiefs and not enough Indians.
Six chiefs have held power since 1984. Only the highly-paid lawyers are interested in maintaining the existing system. The Mohawks must change this practice, for their future in Oka depends on it. Moderate Mohawks want to elect their leaders-I am talking on behalf of 85 per cent of the people of Kanesatake-for a term of at least three years and achieve the kind of political stability which, we are sure, will lead to economic stability. I agree with them and I am behind them all the way.
The government will have to deal with me if it seeks to negotiate the after-crisis and the land claim settlement within the current system and with chief George Martin who left his people in the dark when he fled from the reserve during the hostilities. He no longer speaks for the majority of his people. Perhaps I will antagonize some, but I certainly urge him to resign.
I urge the clan mothers not to insult their people by appointing another chief; the next chief has to be elected by the band majority, for only then will they have a strong voice which will make it possible for the government to settle the issue and bring the prosperity which the people of Kanesatake deserve and to which they are entitled.
I think that the unbelievable crisis we are experiencing could have been avoided. Tensions have gone up a few notches since the incident at the treatment centre where the Warriors are holed up. I hope the centre will not be ransacked as were the homes of white people, I hope
September 25, 1990

they have enough honour left to restore the building to its original condition so that native people who suffer from alcoholism may be treated. The centre had been the subject of controversy and we had to resort to various measures to make sure it would be built.
Then Jean-Roch Simon, a Kanesatake Indian who lives in the village and who has no use for municipal by-laws, decided he would build an eight-unit apartment building on his federal land. That is one of the problems at Oka. It is like a checkerboard, Madam Speaker, white land next to native land, and that makes for shaky relations between the two communities. And now we have all heard about the famous golf course. Does that case give a handful of armed warriors the right to hold a whole population hostage?
In passing, I might say that women and children who are victims of violence would be quite justified to ask the armed dissidents to protect them against their violent mates who seek them out in shelter homes. We are the laughing stock and this charade has lasted long enough! We must take drastic measures if that is the only way to force the fifteen-odd Warriors out of the centre so they will face Canadian courts.
Madam Speaker, after the Akwesasne incidents of last May I personally told the authorities and my caucus that the ongoing crisis out there was nothing compared to what was brewing in Oka. Arms have been piling up in Oka since last April. A couple of Warriors used their guns to intimidate ordinary citizens. There have been many blunders. I will mention first of all the hasty statements which Mr. Caccia made at the very beginning and which were challenged by the municipal authorities. I am not here to say whether the municipality was right or wrong concerning the golf course affair. Mayor Jean Ouellet did not nothing but carry out an injunction from the Superior Court ordering these Warriors not to block a public road.
At the time, Sam Elkas, the Quebec Minister of Public Safety, stated that he would not send the Surete du Quebec to act as cowboys in Oka. Well, on July 11, 1990,
Government Orders
he sent the members of his Surete to behave like Rambos, with the tragic consequences we all know.
Yves Desilets, a Federal negotiator, was sent to convince the Warriors to lay down their arms. The negotiation process he used at the time was wrong. I can really say objectively that this man was both arrogant and incompetent. I can understand that he may have been tired, but that is no reason for being incompetent, and he should have resigned at the very beginning and asked the Department to appoint somebody else to replace him. An investigation will show clearly the decisive influence he had, because the citizens from Oka got together as a group to defend their rights. It should be said also that the Kanesatake Mohawk people did not find in Mr. Desilets a worthwhile negotiator.
The whole staff of the Quebec Department of Indian Affairs should be fired and replace with new blood to manage the after crisis. Madam Speaker, how could we compensate our fellow citizens whose houses were broken in, wrecked and spattered with human feces and especially the older people who suffered enormously? Moreover, in their statements, the leaders of human right associations never mentioned the hard times the white people and the moderate Mohawks lived through behind the barricades. For the media, only the Warriors existed! I denounce misinformation. Has this been said? People should know that during the crisis, some reporters went swimming in the swimming pool of one of the evacuated citizens. That is unacceptable, Madam Speaker! The right of property was seriously infringed upon. How do you think the people in my region feel towards these Warriors? They call them savages! These people who ruined the reputation of the Mohawk nation should be damned! Canada and the rest of the world were in a state of shock when they heard that a man with a single semi-automatic rifle had terrorized and killed a group of young women at the Montreal Polytechnical School. In contrast, these Warriors with an enormous quantity of scary weapons were allowed to roam as they pleased. Yes, the Army did a magnificent job. They should have been sent for at the very beginning. Such an action would have spared millions of dollars which could have been spent improving the quality of life for the Mohawks in Kanesatake and the white people in the area.

Government Orders
Madam Speaker, I must admit I was filled with shame when the Ministers signed an agreement in the presence of an armed Warrior. I was also humiliated when some white people stoned Mohawks who were leaving the Kanhawake reserve and when Mohawks stoned soldiers who had been ordered not to reply in kind. I am proud of our soldier's sense of duty, self-control and proper behaviour. This crisis has at least made it possible for us to know the Canadian Army better.
Madam Speaker, the leader of the New Democratic Party mentioned a while ago a seven year old Mohawk boy who, following the crisis, was looking at a white reporter with hatred in his eyes. I can tell her that I saw the same hatred in the eyes of white boys looking at Mohawks. How unfair this is!
I have no objection to the setting-up of a Parliamentary Commission which the two Opposition Parties are seeking to look into the Oka and Kanetasake events to make sure that they will never happen again and that the guilty people will pay. I want to remind the House that a Royal Commission would help shed light on all the claims made by Indians in Canada to see whether or not they are realistic and reasonable.
Finally, I want to give the people in my riding the assurance that we will do everything that is necessary to restore a climate of trust in Oka-Kahnesatake. To do this, everyone will have to give a little. I want to say to those fifty or so people who do not want to go back to their homes that they will get all the attention and compassion they deserve. There will be a special project for the entire region which has already been proposed by the Regional Municipality of Deux Montagnes and I am sure it will be endorsed by the new leaders in Kahnesa-take.
People who will not be eligible for unemployment insurance this winter because they simply were unable to work will receive special attention from the government.
The Mohawks must redefine their relationship to the Warrior society. The Mohawks must choose their leaders and put an end to fruitless discussion. The white community must negotiate with them to decide on the territory they are to have, so that peace and harmony will return to this area. Stop the scare tactics and decide once and for all: a reserve or no reserve! The talks should be public. White people and Mohawks should discuss their
future together and do so in public. In Oka-Kahnesatake the situation is different because it is not a reserve and because these two communities have been living together, are living together now and will have to live together in the future.
We will have to investigate the role played by reporters. I feel that instead of informing the public, they often helped to increase tension. There should be an inquiry into the proliferation of arms in reserves, and we must find out why the Canadian Security Intelligence Service was unable to inform the authorities in time of these stores of weapons in Akwesasne, Kahnawake and Kah-nesatake. The Quebec and Canadian departments must find a way to either act as one or at least agree on policy in order to avoid duplication and confusion in native affairs in Quebec.
Although he signed the document in Oka it was probably a trap, Madam Speaker-in the presence of armed warriors, I would like to congratulate Minister Tom Siddon who in spite of everything, and as Minister of Indian Affairs during a very difficult and unusual period, stood firm before the native leaders when he denounced violence and the use of weapons.
Madam Speaker, there will have to be a lot of love and friendship on both sides if we are to restore the trust and respect the two communities have always enjoyed in Oka-Kahnesatake. We must make sure that Canada will never again have another crisis like the one experienced by the moderate Mohawks, and this is very important, Madam Speaker, because in Kahnesatake there is a serious leadership problem. For six years we have been unable to negotiate what they were entitled to, which was a more uniform territory. Every time we were close to an agreement, they changed chiefs. Of course, the Mohawks could say that we on this side changed ministers of Indian Affairs, and they would be right.
The fact remains that it is a very difficult situation, because the Mohawk community in Kahnesatake no longer recognizes its present leaders, and the community insists there should be a referendum on the electoral process. Only after a referendum is held and proper elections have taken place-this is not what I want but what they are asking- I say we must ensure this request gets the attention it deserves because we will never be able to negotiate any kind of agreement or settlement that will restore peace to Oka-Kahnesatake
September 25, 1990

unless Mohawks and White people can talk to each other and sign lasting agreements, Madam Speaker.
On the weekend, Chief Martin who was outside- these are moderate Mohawks who signed an agreement with the Quebec Provincial Police to have native people act as security officers. The next day, the agreement was defeated by other Indians by a vote of 45 to 42.
So you see, Madam Speaker, this is a very divided community, and so it is very difficult, almost impossible to conclude agreements. That is why I want to say to our various governments, to my own Prime Minister and the Minister of Indian Affairs and to the Premier of Quebec and Mr. Ciaccia, Minister of Native Affairs and to the Minister of Public Safety that as soon as there is a surrender in Oka, involving the Warriors, and as soon as peace is restored, a referendum must be held before we start negotiations that will ensure that, in the future, Mohawks and white people will continue to live together and that fairness and justice will prevail.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take the opportunity to thank all members for speaking to this very complicated and very sensitive issue.
I would like to ask the hon. member her view as to a body of opinion from Queen's University, a group of 20 scholars headed by Richard Spaulding and the Dean of Law, John Whyte, who indicate three points.
"(1) That there are legal arguments in favour of the Mohawk's assertion that their aboriginal and treaty rights entitle them to exclusive policing authority over Mohawk people.
The 1664 Treaty of Fort Albany under which the Mohawks first confirmed their relationship with the British Crown contains specific undertakings on this question.
(2) The actions of the federal and provincial governments and of the agents acting under their authority are unconstitutional if they interfere with aboriginal or treaty rights and cannot be justified on the basis of both
Government Orders
the purposes they serve and the methods they employ. (See the Crown v. Sparrow).
(3) Governments bear the burden of persuading the courts that actions which violate aboriginal or treaty rights are justified. Statements that the rule of law must be applied or that there is only one law for all "Canadians" will not suffice as legal justifications for actions which infringe on aboriginal or treaty rights".
These are comments that came from Queen's University. Since these people do not vote, how does the member feel about representing these people who believe they are sovereign and should be dealt with on a nation-to-nation basis?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member's question would be best answered by a royal commission of inquiry that would establish once and for all how Canada's native community should live with a new situation that has developed as a result of land claims. I think 20 academics- she mentioned 20 scholars from Queen's. Perhaps 20 scholars from the University of Montreal would have a different opinion. That is the problem, and I am convinced that these matters should be dealt with by a royal commission of inquiry, and I am sure that is what the hon. member wants as well.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was listening to the comments made by the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau who is also a Parliamentary Secretary, and I must say it is very disturbing for a member to hear an admission of defeat from a colleague who is sensitive to the needs of her riding.
During the past few weeks, I heard the hon. member being interviewed on the radio. In fact, she was trying to warn her government through the media, since the House was not sitting. Today, I find it very disturbing to hear a government member say the army should have been there from the very beginning, that she was ashamed of her ministers, that heads must roll and that people don't understand what happened, and especially when we realize that for quite some time the hon. member had been raising these concerns with her government. Today, the hon. member had to rise in the House and practically apologize for the fact that her government had ignored a situation she had most certainly brought to the attention of the Minister of Indian

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
Affairs and Northern Development-in an interview I heard her say she had been after the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, day after day to tell him that a crisis was brewing in this area. That is the very essence of Parliament. Today, we see a member who despite her convictions and arguments was unable to get the government to act, and who now has to admit defeat.
Madam Speaker, I think that today's debate has borne out the hon. member's concerns. I want to say to the hon. member that we heard her this summer, and that when she said it would take a lot of love and friendship, we knew she must have spent her entire vacation working on this problem. I want to say to the hon. member that if her government had shown the same sensitivity to these issues, there would have been no crisis.
While applauding the hon. member's efforts, I also want to tell this government it is a disgrace that the local member should have to come before the House today with this admission of defeat.
Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare: Madam Speaker, of course everybody in my riding, like all Canadians, felt it was disgraceful for ministers and a Quebec Superior Court judge to sign an agreement with a masked and armed person. I am only echoing what I have been hearing all summer. That image is imprinted in the minds of my constituents and in that of all Canadians, I am sure.
Madam Speaker, I say this, but I believe I also mentioned having been fully consulted by the Minister of Indian Affairs through the course of the summer. I was in constant contact with him through the phone. He never expected, as no one would have, the day would come when fifteen or so people would make a whole nation shake at gunpoint and could hold out against the Quebec Police Force and even the Canadian Army.
What I have said is that the time to act was in early April, when there were only two or three armed Warriors. Then was the time to prevent the situation from deteriorating and turn into a national or international
conflict, as it turned out, over a golf course. That is absolutely incredible!
However, I want to assure the member that the government has always considered Indians to be peace-loving people and still does. But the government never expected that there would be such people among the Indians, and among the Canadian population for that matter-We have seen Hell's Angels with guns too. Let's face it, the White people are not faultless!

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: But they were apprehended!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: That's right, they were apprehended. So, Madam Speaker, the minister never expected, and neither did the government, that the Warriors would pursue their action and that the native leaders would keep almost condoning there use of guns.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the government member.
I too am appalled at the use of arms to try to resolve situations, but what are native people to do when as young natives they are facing a 60 per cent to 70 per cent unemployment rate and they are not even acknowledged in the Constitution as being a founding people? It should come as no surprise that some native people have resorted to violence. The real surprise is that it has not happened sooner.
I would like to ask the member who represents this area what her thoughts were when the Prime Minister was selecting cabinet ministers. Four cabinet ministers have been replaced in the last six years in the Department of Indian Affairs which represents natives from all across Canada. To have a government majority of this size and to have to change ministers four times in five years shows the priorities of this government. Did the hon. member speak out against that and for a stronger selection of representation for the native people?
