speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
At the outset, may I say it must feel quite safe, in circumstances as complex

and unbelievable as the ones we have lived through, to be sitting on the opposition benches.
Madam Speaker, Mohawks and other aboriginal people in Canada most certainly have other means of pressuring the government than calling upon the Warriors society. There are other peaceful means which would be quite as effective.
In that regard, I must congratulate the hon. member, although I disapprove of his action in killing the Meech Lake Accord which would have finally allowed the premiers to hold a constitutional conference on aboriginal rights. I will never forgive him for killing the Meech Lake Accord, but on the other hand, he was the first to declare that the use of violence by aboriginal people was wrong and should be condemned.
There are all kinds of pressure tactics other than arms.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: The time allocated for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would just like to make a short comment. I believe I just heard the hon. member saying that she will never forgive-and I do not know who she meant-somebody for the failure of Meech Lake. Is it the aboriginal people?
However, I would now like to begin my speech. It is with great sadness and disappointment that I rise to speak on the motion of the government regarding the Oka crisis. How can the hon. minister move a motion commending the army when the standoff is still in progress, when Parliament does not yet have all the facts and when things still may happen? It is like jumping before looking.
I would also like to comment on some things that have been mentioned by hon. members across the way about how heavy the Mohawk artillery is. We have to make it quite clear that never have we said at any point that we condone violence. However, I would just like to point out that various members from the government side have referred to the arms, the arsenal, or the artillery in the Mohawk camp.
Government Orders
While this may be true, it does not excuse the fact that the army moved in with tanks, with machine guns, and with I do not know what else-with more arms-but it moved in with 3,000 to 4,000 army personnel against a group of something in the neighbourhood of 50 Mohawks, of which a number were warriors. I would say that is overkill. It is like sending the three frigates that we just sent over to the Persian Gulf against a canoe or a kayak.
It is important for everyone in this debate to rise above the actions of particular individuals and to focus on the broad issues which underlie this summer's tragedy. We risk missing the forest for the trees if we do not focus on principles.
Throughout this crisis Canadians have experienced a range of emotional highs and lows-shock, horror, disbelief, sympathy, compassion, anger, confusion, fear, sadness, frustration, helplessness, et cetera. I feel in particular for the children of this dispute, those who have been trapped in it from the beginning physically and emotionally, but also for all Canadian children who have seen or heard the events. What legacy is this crisis leaving them? What memories of fear, sorrow and horror have been inflicted upon them? What emotional scars will they carry with them for the rest of their lives? Surely it is obvious that once again history has repeated itself and the sins of the fathers are being visited upon the children. As the innocent world of these children has been shattered, so too has the Canadian innocence been lost. Canadians have witnessed ugly episodes of racism and hatred. We have seen a dark side of this country that we wish we had never seen and we will never be the same for it.
This is a complex situation. This is a unique situation. It cannot be seen in terms of black and white. There are many grey areas which I believe most Canadians sense intuitively. Certain means and methods may be condemned, but we cannot deny the justness of the cause.
That is why I have problems with this government's resolution. Canadians have experienced a summer of sorrow. Canadians have suffered throughout this ordeal. Canadians have been hurt. Canadians feel betrayed by their governments and they know they deserve better.
The government's motion, however, shows that it does not understand these emotions. The motion shows that the government does not understand the issues confronting it or the people it is dealing with. This government's approach is simplistic. It is one sided. It is

Government Orders
misleading. It is not conducive to a positive and just resolution of the issues involved.
We all want this crisis resolved peacefully and with good will. The Armed Forces at Kanesatake and Kahnawake should not be there. The families of these soldiers should not be in the positions they are in now of worrying about their husbands, fathers, sons, and brothers or sisters. The people in Kahnawake and Kanesatake and Oka should not be in the positions they are in now of worrying about their families. All Canadians should not be in the positions they have been put in of worrying about the safety of all involved and praying for no loss of life.
It has been said before, many times this summer, but it needs repeating: it should never have come to this. This crisis should not have occurred.
I want to express my deep regret and sorrow, as well as that of the rest of the members of the House of Commons, over the death of Corporal Lemay. All Canadians and all aboriginal people regret this unnecessary loss of life.
At times this crisis has seemed unreal: a nightmare. How many times did Canadians ask themselves: "Can this really be happening? Is this Canada? What has happened to us? What went wrong?"
These are questions we will be asking for a long time. The answers will not be easily arrived at. We will have to search within ourselves and not be afraid of what we may find in either our past or our present. This we must do if we want a future in which such a situation will never happen again.
Federal government ministers have made much in recent weeks of the necessity of having the rule of law apply and the government's resolution today says the laws of Canada must apply on all Canadian territory. While on the surface this is all very well and good, the government's definition and interpretation of the law is very selective.
Basic freedoms in this country-freedom of association, freedom of communication, freedom of movement, freedom of speech, and freedom of the press-are being violated in Kanesatake as we speak, but the government does nothing about these violations. It is, therefore, truly hypocritical for politicians to accuse
aboriginal people of being selective about which laws apply to them. These politicians are truly speaking with forked tongues.
In addition to permitting violations of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the government does not tell the Canadian people about the obligations it has toward aboriginal people which it is ignoring. It does not tell the Canadian people that it is in violation of its own laws all across the country when it comes to aboriginal people. The government's motion does not tell the Canadian people that Indian lands already have a unique status in this country.
Provincial laws do not apply on Indian lands and there are existing arrangements within this country where some federal laws do not apply to some Indian land. In addition, recent court decisions have thrown into question the application of certain other federal laws such as federal fish and game laws to Indian people.
The Constitution of Canada, the highest law of this land, recognizes and affirms aboriginal and treaty rights. This is not an empty affirmation. The past week the weight of the the highest court of this land, the Supreme Court of Canada, in a recent case known as the Sparrow case, confirmed that aboriginal and treaty rights have significant and contemporary meaning.
The court also issued a set of guidelines to the government on how it should conduct itself in its relations with aboriginal people. The court confirmed that the relationship of the federal government to aboriginal people is fiduciary-it is a trust relationship. The federal government has a constitutional obligation to protect aboriginal rights and interests, it said, and furthermore the government is obliged to justify any regulation, law or action which infringes upon and denies aboriginal rights.
The court said that the honour of the Crown is at stake in all of its dealings with aboriginal people. The special trust relationship and the responsibility of the government to aboriginal people must be the first consideration in assessing federal actions.
The Supreme Court has served notice to the federal government. The federal government is in breach of trust if it does not protect aboriginal rights from unjustified interference and infringement.
September 25, 1990

I suggest that the government has breached that trust and has failed the Supreme Court's test on numerous occasions since it took office. The tragedy of Oka is simply the most recent and glaring example of government failure.
Throughout this country, aboriginal rights have been, and continue to be, ignored and trampled upon. Justice has been delayed and denied, over and over again. Lands claimed by aboriginal people continue to be alienated by the government even while negotiations are proceeding. Exploration and development rights have been issued by the government to private companies on the traditional lands of aboriginal people with whom settlements have never been reached. Logging, mining, and other forms of resource development are allowed to continue on lands which still belong to aboriginal people.
Towns and cities have been built upon lands which have never been given up by aboriginal people. On the prairies many Indian bands are still owed lands that were promised to them a hundred years ago in treaties they signed. For over a hundred years these people have waited for what is rightfully theirs and they still do not have what was promised to them and are legally entitled to.
Across Canada aboriginal people continue to be harassed in the exercise of their aboriginal hunting, fishing, and trapping rights, despite court decisions in their favour, and the recognition of those rights in the Constitution of Canada.
When the 1987 constitutional conference on aboriginal rights failed, this federal government refused to re-establish aboriginal constitutional negotiations. In fact the Prime Minister shut down the 1987 conference several hours before it was scheduled to end. He threw up his hands and walked away from the table and then his government cut off constitutional funding to the aboriginal organizations.
As well it is this government that cut back post-secondary education funding for aboriginal students and denied native students the opportunity to pursue a higher education because the budget was capped.
It is this government which terminated funding to aboriginal communications societies and political organizations. It is this government which decided to increase
Government Orders
the freight rates on food items shipped to northern and remote communities and now northern people are paying almost $6 for one litre of milk.
All this happened under the Prime Minister who, in a public statement in April 1985, said that the special relationship between Canada and the aboriginal peoples should be strengthened. Aboriginal rights, especially the right of self-government, he said, should have constitutional protections.
The same Prime Minister went on to say that the current funding levels of programs designed to correct the serious inequities which exist for native people and native communities will be maintained. He added that policies regarding aboriginal people will be made after open, public consultation, especially at the grassroots level.
Is it any wonder that aboriginal people are frustrated and angry? Aboriginal people have seen their traditional lands and resources alienated; given away and sold without their consent and without, for the most part, any benefit to them. When there are some benefits, they are minimal and given grudgingly and only because the aboriginal people fought hard for them.
The land claims process in this country is not working well. The current comprehensive claims policy requires aboriginal people to extinguish their rights. The current policy does not allow for constitutional protection of self-government. How can the government justify requiring aboriginal people to extinguish their rights which, since 1982, have been recognized and affirmed in the Canadian Constitution?
The government has not taken any action to reconcile its policy with what the Constitution says. It is not prepared to recognize that self-government is an inherent right; that this right of aboriginal self-government does not come from this federal government or any other non-aboriginal government. It is inherent in aboriginal people and needs only to be acknowledged and recognized by the federal government.
These are issues which are causing much concern to aboriginal people. The government knows that if these issues are not resolved to the satisfaction of the aboriginal people, final settlements in the north may not be achieved.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
In addition to the limited number of claims the government is currently negotiating, there are hundreds of specific claims which remain unresolved and numerous comprehensive claims, most from British Columbia, which have never even made it to the negotiating table because the government refuses to deal with more than six claims at a time.
In many ways, I am bothered by the term "claims". I reject the implication or suggestion that aboriginal people are clamouring for something which the government may, in its generosity, give to us. We are not claiming anything from Canada. We are asserting what is rightfully ours; what belongs to us and what we are entitled to.
This government must understand that it is not doing us any favours when it enters into negotiations. It is we who are doing the government a favour by agreeing to sit down with them and determine how we will share with Canada, our land and our resources.
Most people in this country do not understand the land claims process. The government, in these negotiations, tries to keep the most it can. It gives up the least it has to. And it, for the most part, has held the big stick in these negotiations.
Many land claims negotiations have taken place under the threat of imminent resource development. Often settlements have been reached many years after developments have taken place and what the people have fought for has largely been turned over to someone else.
At times, the government has cut off negotiation funding or threatened to cut off funding when negotiations are not going its way. It has also threatened to stop negotiating altogether. In the negotiation of land claims, the aboriginal people have always been subjected to federal threats, intimidation and power plays.
Aboriginal people are saying "enough". We are standing on the power of our rights; rights which are affirmed in the Constitution of this country and which the Supreme Court has upheld. We have the power of the law on our side and the Government of Canada is subject to this law. Who determined that the Arctic was Canadian land? Were the Inuit ever asked? Where did the King of France get the right to give Mohawk land to Sulpician priests? These are the kinds of questions that Canadians must ask themselves. How would anyone feel, seeing the land you have lived and made your home on,
sold to others without your consent? How would you feel being squeezed onto smaller and smaller portions of land?
These kinds of expropriations without compensation have gone in this country since the arrival of the first Europeans. Last March, I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development a question in the House of Commons about the reports of the Canadian Human Rights Commission.
In 1988, the commission referred to the situation of the aboriginal people in this country as a national tragedy. In 1989, it said it had no reason to alter that judgment. I asked the minister at the time what immediate action the government was prepared to take to turn this tragedy around.
The minister gave the usual government response referring to how much money the government has spent, but at the same time agreeing with the human rights commissioner that the situation confronting the aboriginal people in this country needs to be vastly improved.
What has the government done to improve matters since I asked that question? Nothing, absolutely nothing. What the government has done is send in the army, between 3,000 and 4,000, to battle a group of 50 or less warriors.
From the beginning of the Oka crisis, the government tried to distance itself. It tried to absolve itself of any culpability and refused to accept any responsibility. An initial conflict over a golf course, a cemetery and sacred land escalated into a military confrontation the likes of which had never been seen in this country and which we hope will never be seen again.
The government's mismanagement of the Oka crisis has brought aboriginal people together in an unprecedented way.
In conclusion, we have all been shamed and diminished by the events in this summer of sorrow. But let us learn a lesson from this bitter experience. Force and violence solve nothing. They only breed more force and violence.
We need an independent commission of inquiry into the events at Oka, Kanesatake and Kahnawake estab-

lished immediately. Its structure and mandate should be determined in consultation with aboriginal people.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in his speech this morning made the most astonishing claim about the Canadian justice system. He said that our system of justice was the most fair and honourable system of justice known to mankind. I would like to ask the minister whether he asked Donald Marshall that question.
Has the minister not read the Marshall inquiry report which said that the legal system failed Donald Marshall at every turn? Does the minister not understand that the Canadian justice system of which he boasted this morning condemned a man to 11 years in prison for a crime he did not commit, because he was an Indian? If that is the rule of law the government wants aboriginal people to submit to, then we say: No thanks.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened to the hon. member from Nunatsiaq with a great deal of interest because we have many times stood in this House and had an opportunity to share some of our mutual concerns about native people across this vast land of ours.
I heard what he said about the Arctic and the land claims there. He asked the question: "Who gave permission for this land to be used?" But I wonder if he could tell us how he feels about the situation we are actually faced with today. In fact, in Canada we do have more than one peoples living in this land, and we do have treaties in many of the areas of the country.
I believe the member was talking about comprehensive claims rather than specific land claims having to do with certain treaties and certain parcels of land. How does he put that together in his own mind? How do we solve these issues that have to do with conflict of opinion over who owns what land when there are treaties involved and when there are people currently occupying these lands.
Perhaps the member could give us the benefit of his very valid advice on this matter.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
I am sorry I did not hear the entire question.
Government Orders
One point I would like to make which I mentioned earlier in this presentation, as I think the hon. member mentioned, is that there are no treaties in the eastern Arctic-absolutely none. No land has ever been given by the Inuit to any European or any other group of people other than the Inuit. As far as we are concerned, we live on that land, know the land, and own that land. If the government wants to negotiate with the people about who owns that land, then it should sit down on the basis that at this moment no other body owns that land, rather than saying: "We have one and a half million square miles of land and we would like to give you some."
All I am saying is that the attitude has been that somebody else owns the land and that we should claim back some of it.
In terms of treaty rights and treaties, we must remember that the Europeans came over, I think, starting in 1492.1 must also remind the hon. member that while she can record history in Canada by hundreds of years, we can record ours in thousands and tens of thousands of years.
When the Europeans came over they had in mind that this land was to be claimed for the Europeans. The people in North America, who had no concept of privately owning land and who shared the land at all times, were willing to share that land with the people who came over. There was a miscarriage of justice when the European people who were making those treaties were at an advantage. I have heard of treaties being signed with an x. Where is the justice if the treaties that were signed by people who did not understand what was in those treaties?
On the other hand, some of those treaties have not been honoured. I think the hon. member would be well advised to talk to the various aboriginal leaders and ask them what can we do to correct the situation? What can we do to correct the injustice that has been done to the aboriginal people?

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the member from Nunatsiaq. I think it does this place good to listen to somebody speak from a firsthand knowledge of the plight of native Canadians, the original Canadians, the first nations.

Government Orders
The member alluded in his comments to a statement made earlier today by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development concerning the justice system in the country.
I am from Nova Scotia and anybody who has lived in Nova Scotia or can read newspapers has read with great horror the findings of the Marshall commission of inquiry about the administration of justice in Nova Scotia. Madam Speaker, I do not know if you or other members of the House have read that document, but if they have not, they should. It is a stinging indictment of the justice system in Nova Scotia and a stinging indictment against systemic racism in the justice system right across the country.
I know that the issue of Oka is sometimes hard to separate when dealing with native issues, fundamental rights, weapons, the army, and all the other things, but there is one thing that is clear. It is clear that successive governments have asked the native community to live by our laws and told them that our way is a better way than their way. In doing that we have destroyed their language, we have assisted in destroying their culture, and we have almost destroyed the entire first nations of the country.
There is a double standard when we talk about justice and why the natives have to put down their arms because the law of the country must be supreme. The Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs is nodding. He knows that in Nova Scotia the Micmac community took the Government of Nova Scotia to court on the Treaty of 1752. The court affirmed the native rights when it went to the Supreme Court. Yet the Province of Nova Scotia, a province of the country and a sovereign government, has still denied the native community the rights the Supreme Court said they had subsequent to the Treaty of 1752. So, what we have is a double standard.
It is very, very easy to talk about upholding the law, but at the same time successive governments of Canada- Liberal and Conservative-and New Democratic governments in provincial jurisdictions have absolutely refused to honour the treaties they have with native peoples. The rights of everybody in this country-native and non-native-have been treated with a double standard.
I want to ask the member specifically about the UN Charter of the Rights of the Child. The Prime Minister is off this weekend to participate in the international conference and I hope he is listening. One of the articles deals with the right of children everywhere to be educated in their own language and their own culture. Yet, when the sub-committee travelled, it found that one of the number one concerns of the native community was that no resources were provided by the government to ensure the development of native curriculum and that languages of the native communities across the country were maintained.
I would like him to make a comment on that.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is very true that we are suffering from either a lack of funds or the way the funds are allocated within the education system in terms of our aboriginal languages curriculum.
Today in the Northwest Territories we have eight official languages, of which six are aboriginal languages. They also include French and English. I would hope that both the Government of Canada and the Government of the Northwest Territories would recognize the need to implement programs instituting or introducing aboriginal languages as a full part of that curriculum as we have down here with French and English. I must admit that in certain parts of the territory it has to be that way. In the eastern Arctic they should implement a full Inuktitut program. In some parts of the western Arctic they should implement some other languages.
I would hope that the Government of Canada and, through them, the Government of the Northwest Territories will recognize the need to put as much money as possible into language programs or reallocate the funds to them.
Very briefly, I would also hope that the Government of Canada would reconsider the post-secondary funding to the aboriginal people.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: The time allocated for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate. The Right Hon. Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since July, television has been bringing into Canadian homes alien images of barricades and masks and assault rifles. A dispute that began in Oka over land was hijacked by a group of heavily armed people, motivated by ideology and seeking to protect illegal commerce. Their tactics have been the tactics of terrorists. High-powered weapons, threats against the autho-

rities, trade in contraband goods, intimidation of law-abiding Mohawks, interruption of transportation, and destruction of property disqualified any claim the Warriors had to represent the grievances of law-abiding Indians.
What is taking place at Oka is not civil disobedience; it is violent activity that no community should be expected to tolerate. The ostensible reason for the conflict at Oka- and I do not in any way wish to downgrade major historic land claims by Native people, and I will get back to this later-was long ago removed when in July, the federal government acquired the disputed land, before the incidents took place, for the Mohawks of Kanesa-take. This step, incidentally, is in keeping with the goals of the framework agreement concluded a year ago this month between the Mohawks of Kanesatake, the town of Oka and the federal and provincial governments, an agreement that unfortunately was repudiated in March by a number of Mohawk leaders.

What has been at issue these past weeks is not the land, rather the warriors acting against all of the peaceful and noble traditions of Canada's Mohawks. The warriors, advised by foreign legal counsel, have been seeking recognition that their communities are independent and that the laws of Canada do not apply to their lands and to their activities which in the past have included smuggling and gambling on a very large scale. They have sought by various means to circumvent the Canadian justice system.
The warriors' demands are not simply ideas on which reasonable people can agree or simply agree to disagree. They strike at the very heart of what Canada is all about.
The warriors have been acting as if the concept of native self-government means national independence. I want to be very clear on this point. Native self-government is something that can bring great honour, great accomplishment, and great justice to native peoples and, indeed, it shall. But it does not and cannot ever mean sovereign independence within Canadian territory. Mohawk lands are part of Canadian territory and Canadian law must and does apply to us all. Everyone in Canada- members of this House, members of every house, war-
Govemment Orders
riors included-is subject to the Criminal Code of Canada. If exceptions to the Criminal Code were made on the basis of colour, race, or creed, where could the line be drawn in a country as diverse and as complex as Canada? What could be more repugnant in a democracy than a legal system based on birth rather than equality?
There are many non-violent avenues, political and judicial, open to people in the country to promote change. In fact, the traditions of Canada's native peoples have been peaceful and noble down through the decades, often under great assault and under great personal challenge. Any student of history, I am sure, would have wondered at the forbearance and the generosity of native peoples given some of the matters to which I will come very shortly. But the warriors opted for firearms and violence, concepts that are fundamentally alien to Canada and to the interests of all native peoples.
T\vo Mohawks were killed in a dispute over gambling at the Akwesasne reserve last Spring. Corporal Marcel Lemay of the Surete du Quebec was killed in the police assault on the barricades last July. These are the consequences when people decide that the law does not apply to them.
Conferring on the claims of the Warriors the legitimacy of the grievances of Canada's aboriginal peoples does the later's cause an enormous disservice. And glorifying violence and romanticising those who have recourse to it does democracy, itself, a terrible wrong. Masks and guns make compelling pictures and raise ratings and circulation. But they don't equate to noble purpose.
The armed forces have brought the barricades down and are gradually turning their responsibilities over to the Surete du Quebec. As this phase-out begins, I think all members would agree that perhaps the most edifying aspect of this whole tragic episode has been the professionalism of the Canadian Armed Forces.
The Canadian Forces, from General de Chastelain to Lieutenant-General Foster to Brigadier-General Roy are to be commended for the level of professionalism that has been evident throughout.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: It isn't over yet!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
No, it isn't over yet. The hon. member is right. However, they still deserve the respect and gratitude of Canadians for the truly outstanding way in which they carried out this difficult mission.
Lieutenant Colonel Robin Gagnon, Major Alain Tremblay, Private Patrick Cloutier-the young soldier who stood his ground coolly in a face to face challenge- and all the other personnel of 5 Brigade showed great courage and almost superhuman self-control in the face of extraordinary provocation.
There are no plans to attack the centre. No one is being interned there-least of all the innocent children who should be in school. They are welcome to leave at any time.

The armed people, behind the razor wire, can lay down their weapons and accept the offer of the Canadian forces to be placed in custody, and they should, they must. If they persist in staying there and they want to stay there themselves, let the children go. The children should be released; they should be in school.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Otherwise they can confine themselves to the detoxification centre indefinitely. Either way, the ultimate result is going to be the same. They will have to submit themselves, as all Canadians must, to the Canadian criminal justice system. Members of this House have an opportunity today to speak with one voice in calling upon the warriors to lay down their arms and submit themselves now to one of the finest justice systems in the world, the justice system of Canada.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Once the guns are down-

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Aboriginal exceptions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right. There are veiy tragic exceptions to this and I will be happy not only to-

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Aboriginal exceptions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Well, indeed, and I will be very happy to deal with it because the fact that we have an excellent
justice system which stands up admirably in comparison to any other in the world does not mean that there have not been serious errors and serious abuses. As long as those errors and injustices arise, and they have in recent times affected particularly native peoples, that is a special tragedy and that is one that all members of the House want to correct.
Once the guns are down, we will be in a position to hand over the disputed land to the people of Kanesa-take. There will also be freedom to explore new ways to resolve their historical land claims. In the meantime, there is much to do and many legitimate grievances to address there and elsewhere in Canada.
Over the past year, we have quietly discussed an agenda with native leaders to address issues of concern to all of Canada's native peoples. It is time to begin to put this agenda into operation. Canada's original peoples deserve a special place in this country as our first citizens based on the aboriginal and treaty rights recognized in the Constitution. Those realities have often been denied over decades and centuries in Canada and it is time that we began the process of making up this injustice.
Our agenda will be anchored in reality. It is no myth that native leaders have too often been treated insensitively, unfairly and often times illegally since the days that the first Europeans set foot on this continent. Canadian history records that Indian decency was too often met with cynicism and that Indian generosity was too often repaid with exploitation.
The cultures of Canada's native peoples have been poorly understood and little valued. Many people still remember Indian children being punished at school for speaking their own languages.
The first Canadians, our first Canadians, were denied freedom of speech in their own land.
Thanks to the Indian Act of 1876, people who had never known national boundaries found that they could not even leave reserves-pitiful, mediocre reserves- without a pass. In fact, only in 1960-to show the dimensions of both the tardiness and the enormity of the tragedy-were Canadian Indians fully enfranchised. And I may say, because I will be unveiling a statue of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson tomorrow, that this particular act was done while he was in the House and when the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker was the Prime
September 25, 1990

Minister of Canada, and it was roundly supported by all political parties.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
The ultimate irony is that the first Canadians were the last to get the vote, and it is a further reality that contemporary Canadians do not have to scour their history books for examples of the racism, paternalism and dependency that have been so destructive of native peoples' welfare and self-respect.
There is ample evidence that things remain seriously wrong to this very day, for example and most recently, the injustice done to Donald Marshall Jr., the Micmac Indian from Nova Scotia. I suppose that of all the tragedies of recent times that this one stands out for its poignancy. It is a tribute to Mr. Marshall and, indirectly I suppose, to all Canadians that even though it took that time, it was eventually corrected. My hope, as Prime Minister of Canada, is that that evil will never again be repeated against Indian people.
These failings sully our reputation and stain our history. If progress requires that we acknowledge historical realities, it also demands that we acknowledge contemporary realities as well. One of these realities is that Canada's aboriginal peoples benefit, as all Canadians benefit, from being part of a socially progressive and economically prosperous country.
Canada's native people enjoy the same rights as all Canadians under the Constitution even though you would sometimes have serious questions about understanding the application of those rights, and they are supposed to enjoy special rights available only to them, although those too are sometimes placed in jeopardy. In recent years Canada's aboriginal peoples have made progress. Consider the following excerpts from a statement by George Erasmus, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, in his annual report to his fellow chiefs meetings in Whitehorse this past May. I quote:
In the past twenty years, the landscape has changed a lot for us-
I can sum it up by saying that we have taken a good deal of control over our lives and affairs as First Nations persons.
Just look at where we were in 1970: all funding in 1970 was controlled by the federal government through the Department of Indian Affairs (DIAND); now, twenty years later, we're managing the bulk of our finances.
Government Orders
In Education, there's a tremendous number of schools now under
our control; twenty years ago, either Ottawa, the bureaucracy,
DIAND or the churches were in total charge.
In 1970, we didn't have as many as 1,000 post-secondary students;
today, there are nearly 17,000!
In fact, our figures show 18,500.
On-reserve housing continues to be a major concern but even here
there has also been improvement in the past couple of decades.
Chief Erasmus is right that despite the poverty that is too prevalent on too many reserves, progress is being made. More than 30 per cent of the current Indian housing stock has been built since 1984 and a further 35 per cent has been extensively renovated since then.
There has been progress in other spheres as well. For example, in 1960 the life expectancy of status Indians was 60; by this year it reached 70.
In 1960, the infant mortality rate was 82 per thousand live births; this year it has reached 13. These figures are either encouraging or depressing, depending on how one wants to look at them. But, I believe that if you place them in the context of what George Erasmus was saying, progress is often incremental, progress is often difficult to achieve. I agree with Chief Erasmus that when Canadians of good will combine and harness their activities with those of aboriginal peoples, solid and tangible progress can and has been made in Canada. I view the future for native peoples with optimism, provided we can maintain that degree of co-operation. I know that all members of all parties in this House of Commons are pledged to achieving precisely that.
It is also encouraging to note that while there were very few Indian-owned business on reserves in 1960, there are over 5,000 today.
Progress by Canada's native peoples in persuading the courts to endorse their aboriginal rights to the land has been substantial. In 1973, following the rejection by the natives people of the then government's white paper, the Supreme Court's Calder decision led to a re-evaluation of policy with respect to land claims. Substantial progress has been made since then in resolving comprehensive land claims.
I am referring to a series of agreements reached on claims with the Conseil Attikamek-Montagnais in June 1988, with the Nisga Tribal Council in July 1989, with the Council of Yukon Indians in March 1990, with the Dene-Metis in April 1990, although some Dene have

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
subsequently sought some changes, and with the Inuit of the Eastern Arctic in April 1990.
The Arctic claims, by way of illustration, just the Arctic claims, if ratified by all concerned, will put 575,000 square kilometres of land firmly and irrevocably under Indian and Inuit ownership and transfer more than $1.3 billion to them. Together, the land area passing into Indian and Inuit ownership is more than the combined area of the four Atlantic provinces and will make the northern natives the largest land-owners in North America. This I believe is not a miracle, but it is solid progress and it is an indication of what Canada can accomplish when all parties and all of us work together.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
So, progress is being made working within the law. On the constitutional agenda, progress on aboriginal issues, as on other issues, has proved more difficult. Neither proposals the federal government made on aboriginal self-government nor others made by provincial governments and aboriginal groups have been able to attract sufficient support to result in a constitutional amendment. And this summer, the planned series of First Ministers Conferences dedicated to matters of interest to aboriginal peoples died with the failure of the Meech Lake Accord. These setbacks aside, the Constitution, and the growing body of case law based on it, have strengthened the right of aboriginal Canadians.
Nevertheless, no one doubts that we still have a veiy long way to go.

I would like to outline very briefly, perhaps in a summary manner, the course of some of our government's plans to preserve the special place of our first citizens in this country based on their aboriginal and treaty rights recognized in the Constitution.
The agenda I believe we ought to be addressing will have four main pillars: land claims, the economic and social conditions on reserves, the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments, and concerns of
Canada's aboriginal peoples in contemporary Canadian life.
Consultation with aboriginal peoples respecting the fiduciary responsibilities of the Crown toward them will be built into the process from the very start, but we intend to go far beyond the status quo. On no issue is action more urgent than on land claims.
We intend to take three parallel initiatives. The first will be to accelerate the settlement of specific claims, that is those claims that result from past government non-performance or malfeasance with respect to existing treaties and to the Indian Act. We recognize that increased resources will be essential to make good on this undertaking, and they will be provided.
The second initiative that we propose to take is to ensure that the legal undertakings regarding land transfers to treaty Indians, given in some cases as much as a century ago, will finally be honoured. We have already reached agreement with the Government of Saskatchewan and with the Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations to begin negotiations. We are eager to initiate the same process in Alberta and Manitoba. I believe that once undertaken and once pursued with vigour by the federal government and encouraged by all parties in the federal Parliament, this will bring about major and historic beneficial results for Canada's aboriginal people.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Third, we will accelerate negotiations on modem treaties, the comprehensive claims which until now have had to be limited to six at any one time.
Comprehensive claims are negotiated where aboriginal title has never been legally ceded to the Crown, thus clouding land title for natives and non-natives alike.
Most of the outstanding claims, certainly thus far, are in British Columbia. In July Premier Vander Zalm reversed a decades-old British Columbia policy pursued by both NDP and Social Credit governments opposing provincial participation in such claims negotiations. That policy was wrong, and I want to salute Premier Vander Zalm for reversing a policy that should have been reversed a long time ago.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
To accelerate claims settlements the federal government will no longer limit itself to handling

September 25, 1990

six claims at any one time. We will consider other innovations such as regional or province-wide negotiations.
The second dimension of the government's agenda will be addressed to improving living conditions on Indian reserves. We are prepared to work jointly with Indian leadership and with provincial governments on a range of improvements in basic community programs and services such as water and sewage facilities so urgently required in so many areas across Canada.
We will expect those native communities with the resources to take on increasing responsibility for financing enhanced services and economic development.
Ensuring that all native Canadians have opportunities comparable to those of other Canadians to participate in the growth and prosperity of a country of this size is not an easy task.
I know there has been a contest in some quarters about the numbers, but it is a fact of life that federal and provincial governments already spend far more money on native programs than any other country in the world. The federal budget alone contains over $4 billion a year and still, in spite of these enormous expenditures, terrible problems persist.
The money has been spent. God knows we have the bureaucrats to prove it. Some of them are excellent and have done tremendous jobs, but the fact of the matter is that the problems are terrible. Unacceptable social problems persist from unemployment to problems with drugs, alcoholism, and abuse. All of these issues cannot be solved overnight.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: What about education?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
And education. I know that throwing money at it is not alone the solution, but certainly all Canadians recognize that we can do a lot better in Canada than we have done in the past.

Progress requires more than money. Progress will only be made if the degrading, antiquated and wasteful statutory relationship between Indian peoples and the government is changed.
Government Orders
The Indian Act is largely unchanged since the Victorian age. It fosters Indian dependency on the state, frustrates Indian self-sufficiency and undermines Indian self-respect. It deminishes Indians and non-Indians alike.
In the new year, building on work that is going on now with Indian leadership, we will bring in the first of many changes to the Indian Act. Consultation, and respect for the fiduciary responsibilities of the Crown toward aboriginal peoples, will be built into the process from the start.
But we intend to go far beyond the status quo. The objective will be the enlargment of aboriginal capacity for self-government, within the framework of the Canadian Constitution. While it is not perfect, the Constitution is sufficiently flexible to afford aboriginal people ample opportunity to develop their communities, en-hence their social and education systems and build their economies-in short, to live their lives according to their own cultures. For example, this government will find practical ways to ensure that aboriginal communities can exercise greater control over the administration of justice.
Self-government can mean a new relationship between aboriginal and non-aboriginal Canadians based on human dignity, trust and respect, all within Canada's Constitution and protected by Canada's laws.

Building such a relationship requires the understanding and the support of all Canadians. That is why later this autumn we intend as part of a broader initiative on Canadian unity to seek a thorough review of the fundamental place and the role of aboriginal peoples in contemporary Canada.
The agenda I have outlined is, I believe, very far-reaching. Its goal is to create a new relationship between aboriginal and non-aboriginal Canadians. There is no guarantee of success. There is ample precedent of failure over decades to indicate to all of us how difficult and how challenging it will be and, once we embark upon it, how important the responsibility that we all accept. It will take creativity and perseverance.
I believe that it will take the courage to see things as they are, the honesty to acknowledge them for what they have become, and the common resolve to correct them for future generations. Most of all, it will take sustained and firm leadership on the part both of governments and of aboriginal peoples, but with native and non-native

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
Canadians working together and with all members of the House of Commons co-operating on this vital dimension of our national life it can be done. I give Canadians the assurance of the Government of Canada that every effort will be deployed to ensure that it will be done.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Would it be possible to ask a few questions of the Prime Minister? He is the main spokesman for the government and the main guardian of aboriginal peoples. I hope I can demonstrate that it can be done in a very co-operative and non-confrontational manner, which I am sure he will not deny.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Prime Minister for taking the opportunity to address this veiy important question.
It has been a very difficult summer for all of us and things have become rather heated at times. I understand the onerous burden it is to deal with the specific problems facing the aboriginal people and the government at this point in time.
I appeal to the Prime Minister through a question. Why is it that through a series of moves over the last six months, Bill C-269, an act to establish an aboriginal language foundation, was denied? It would have helped to guarantee the linguistic and cultural rights, to some extent, of aboriginal peoples. I needed unanimous consent and the NDP agreed, but the government did not.
Why could we not have the suggestions of the Charest committee considered in our constitutional debate over the last six months? Why could we not get two sentences in the Constitution to recognize the specific wording the aboriginal people wanted to recognize them as a fundamental characteristic? Why is it that we have undergone
some severe cutbacks in native programming like native communications?
I say this to the Prime Minister because there is a real element of mistrust. I say to the Prime Minister in all sincerity that trust seems to be the problem here. The aboriginal community does not feel the element of trust is there. It does not feel that the efforts to negotiate a peaceful and honourable disengagement honestly, sincerely and genuinely have been exhausted, that all possibilities have been exhausted.
Can the Prime Minister assure the aboriginal people of Canada, including all Mohawks, that in fact what has happened is not an attempt to humiliate the aboriginal community because of Meech Lake and for other reasons?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Normally, I would not dignify that last part with a comment because I think my hon. friend knows full well that we undertook the Meech Lake Accord with a view to seeking a specific agenda. It failed, notwithstanding the very strong support it received from the Liberal Party in the House, the NDP and the Conservatives. At an appropriate time history alone will judge whether it was a beneficial attempt to bring about a degree of harmony and unity in Canada.
I would like to give the member an illustration of why I thought it was important. One of the duties that I inherited when I became Prime Minister was the responsibility of chairing meetings under the 1982 Constitutional Accord, seeking to bring about a constitutional amendment for aboriginal self-government. I believe I chaired two of those first ministers' meetings.
We came within a hair of securing an historic constitutional amendment that would have provided fundamental justice and a very beneficial change for the aboriginal communities across Canada. I do not know where it would have led but I had this strong view-and it was the view of the aboriginal leadership-that it had all of the earmarks of making a fundamental difference in the lives, eventually, of aboriginal peoples.
That constitutional amendment failed in 1985 and in 1986, because when it came time to go around the table to count heads, we were short one, and that was Quebec. Quebec was not participating at that time because in 1982 it felt that its own concerns, for reasons we will not go into here today, were not met. Therefore, to achieve
September 25, 1990

greater justice for aboriginal peoples it was necessary, in my view, to bring Quebec back, willingly, into the constitutional fold so that they could be there to vote in favour of aboriginal self justice.
Among my many regrets about Meech Lake-and as I say, we will let history look at it for all of us-is that I firmly believed the bringing back of Quebec to the constitutional table would bring about an affirmative position by the Government of Quebec and provide justice for the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
In response to the comment, I would like to tell my hon. friend that while no one gets everything he or she wants entirely, what I would want most of all in Canada, would be equality, fairness and justice for the native peoples of this country. Their denial and the denial of these fundamentals are something that one sees on a daily basis.
This is one of the problems that often occurs, for example, in an adversarial system in this House of Commons. Mention was made of the fact that there were cutbacks. That is true. What is not mentioned is that in the same time frame, there was an increase of $200 million to the aboriginal peoples of Canada in areas such as education and health and welfare. We decided in co-operation with others that it was better to take $20 million out of a given area and put $200 million into another.

subsubtopic: SITUATION AT OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: It was a mistake.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   COMPETITION ACT CONCENTRATION OF CORPORATE OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the House will be aware of the ruling in April of this year by the Quebec Superior Court that the Competition Act is unconstitutional. It seems to me that that was a clear signal to review the Competition Act and M-58 aims to do exactly that. M-58 proposes to look at the Competition Act, which has been in place since 1986, and with which we have had three year's experience. I think the time has come to look at our experience with the new Competition Act of 1986.
Much has happened in the last four years. We have had three record breaking years in terms of mergers and acquisitions with takeovers worth close to $30 billion in each year from 1987 to 1989.
This is a major restructuring of ownership in this country. It seems to me it is on a scale rarely seen in Canadian economic history. Many of us are very familiar with some of these major changes; Molson's acquisition of O'Keefe, PWA buying Wardair, the Amaco-Dome deal, Imperial Oil's takeover of Texaco Canada to name just a few.
M-58 aims to deal with one aspect of the Competition Act that is a source of concern. The fact is that mergers may be approved if "efficiency gains" can be seen as
emerging from a proposed merger. I believe that this criterion is too vague when assessing the major restructuring that we are now witnessing in the Canadian economy. It seems to me it gives too much discretionary power to the director of investigations and research at the competition bureau.
My motion's aim is to give greater guidance and direction to the director when assessing whether a proposed merger should or should not be approved. M-58 would ask the Competition Act to consider whether a proposed merger would lead to higher levels of corporate concentration and whether these higher levels would impact negatively on the Canadian economy.
Canada is one of the few countries where competition legislation does not take into consideration levels of market share in assessing mergers, for example, in comparable industrial economies in the industrialized world. German legislation limits markets shared to 40 per cent for a single firm for a particular industry. The limit is only 25 per cent if a conglomerate is involved.
Britain and the United States also have size criteria aimed at limiting corporate concentration. In any case, it is highly unlikely that these countries would allow a situation where two companies would control over 90 per cent of the beer market.
In Great Britain, for example, Elders who owned O'Keefe, were prevented three times from taking over another brewery because it would lessen competition. Our competition legislation makes no specific provision to ensure that a proposed merger will guarantee employment levels, or indeed, lead to increases in jobs. Surely, achieving higher levels of employment can be considered as "efficiency gains". It should be specified as such.
Another consideration is that of innovation. Our competition legislation should guarantee that innovative and dynamic firms are not stifled by larger firms more concerned about shutting out competition than with developing new products and new technologies. M-58 aims simply to make the Competition Act more specific in describing efficiency gains.
It seems to me quite a paradox that in a society where the corporate world stresses the marketplace and competition that we have even to consider legislation that forces them to compete.

The key principle of this Motion M-58 is that smarter, not bigger is better. It is an important principle if we are to develop a dynamic, competitive economy.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   COMPETITION ACT CONCENTRATION OF CORPORATE OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nickel Belt has asked the House to consider legislative amendment to the Competition Act to allow the Director of Investigations and Research to consider the extent to which concentration of corporate ownership is in the public interest when reviewing a proposed merger and whether the proposed transaction promises lower prices, innovation, employment, and other public benefits. However, the act already requires consideration of a number of these issues. Hence, there is no need for the House to consider further legislative reform.
Around the world, there has been an increased recognition of the desirability of market-driven approaches to foster economic growth and structural change. This is evidenced by the greater reliance on market mechanisms in a wide range of countries, both developed and developing. This trend reflects the numerous benefits of competitive markets.
From the perspective of consumers, including those who are less affluent, competition is a force that generates considerable savings and increased disposable income. It keeps industries sharp and efficient, characteristics which are of increasing importance in the more global trading environment.
Competition constrains the unilateral or collusive exercise of market power. It preserves a place for small businesses, providing opportunities for new enterprises and rewarding innovation. Moreover, freely competitive forces simultaneously preserve the democratic nature of Canada's political and social institutions. Thus, it is clear that competition is not promoted as an end in itself but, rather, as a means of enhancing society's welfare.
In Canada, the Competition Act is the principal piece of framework legislation which exists to protect and promote fair competition. The act is a general law of general application. To the extent the competition policy protects the forces of competition, it results in the movement of prices to levels which more accurately reflect demand and cost conditions, facilitating the flow of resources toward their most productive use. By promoting the efficient use of resources, competition
Private Members' Business
policy lessens the need for alternative, more interventionist forms of control such as regulations and public ownership.
In principle, it should only be necessary to ensure that market structure and conduct are such as to provide an acceptable degree of competition. The attainment of efficient industry performance can then be left to market forces without the need for detailed government intervention. To this end, Canadian competition legislation has consistently sought to prohibit certain practices in restraint of trade which serve to prevent the nation's scarce resources from being most effectively utilized.
The objectives of today's competition policy, as embodied in the purpose clause of the Competition Act, reflect these concerns and I quote:
The purpose of this Act is to maintain and encourage competition in Canada in order to promote the efficiency and adaptability of the Canadian economy, in order to expand opportunities for Canadian participation in world markets while at the same time recognizing the role of foreign competition in Canada, in order to ensure that small and medium-sized enterprises have an equitable opportunity to participate in the Canadian economy, and in order to provide consumers with competitive prices and product choices.
Merger review under the Competition Act is governed by this statement. Furthermore, the question of providing consumers with competitive prices and product choices is central to the notion of merger review. Mergers which are likely to substantially prevent or lessen competition in Canada, that is those which are likely to result in an increase in prices or decreased quality, et cetera, may be subject to an order of the tribunal except where there are offsetting efficiency gains. Clearly, consumers' interest in lower prices is protected by the existing legislation.
By forcing the movement of prices to levels which more accurately reflect demand and cost conditions, competition policy facilitates the flow of resources toward their most productive use. This in turn allows the Canadian economy to employ fully its labour force in those industries where we have a comparative advantage from a trading perspective and so the issue of employment is implicitly addressed.
The extent to which a proposed merger will affect research and development and innovative activity is specifically outlined by the act for consideration in merger review. Subsection 93(g) instructs the

September 25, 1990
Private Members' Business
competition tribunal and the director of investigation and research to consider the nature and extent of change and innovation in a relevant market when determining whether or not a proposed merger is likely to prevent or lessen competition substantially. The amendment which the hon. member seeks relating to innovation is a factor already explicitly contemplated by the existing legislation.
Finally, the act instructs consideration of "any other factor that is relevant to competition in a market that is or would be affected by the merger or proposed merger" when making the substantial prevention or lessening of competition assessment. I have complete confidence that the director of investigation and research is competently addressing the issues of lower prices, innovation and others when making merger assessments as the legislation instructs. Consequently, there is no need to legislatively amend the Competition Act as suggested by the hon. member.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   COMPETITION ACT CONCENTRATION OF CORPORATE OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague from Sudbury on bringing this matter to the attention of the House. It is certainly apropos, as will be seen in a few moments when I try to outline the effects of the Competition Act, how it affects Canadians and how it affects workers, contrary to what we have just heard from a member on the government side of the House.
I also want to compliment my colleague from Sudbury for being so perceptive in 1989 and bringing this matter to the House today. As I progress in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, you will see why it is apropos of the situation that we have before us.
We are talking today about the Competition Act. It is interesting because the Competition Act has to do with the economy of the country. Although we are all interested in other matters of great importance before the House, such as what is happening in Oka and the Middle East, we must always remember that there are other Canadians who are concerned about the economic conditions as they affect rural and small-town Canada: their livelihood, what is happening in the workplace, lay-offs and terminations. I am so pleased today to be able to speak on behalf of those people and how this Competition Act is affecting those people in rural and small-town Canada.
Perhaps I should talk about the failure of the Competition Act, the failure of its terms but perhaps more so the failure of the way the director of the Bureau of Competition Policy and the bureau itself to interpret properly the terms and the statutory obligations outlined within this act. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, as I carry on with this prime example of what this act is all about, that the interpretation of this act will be challenged in a tribunal other than this. It will certainly be up to the deputy directors who are entrusted with the administration of the act, the Bureau of Competition Policy itself, and even the Minister of Corporate and Consumer Affairs, who have to start applying this act, and the terms of this act, in the best interest of the Canadian citizen and the Canadian worker in the market-place.
The facts that I am going to relate are fairly simple and have to do with this act. There are two companies, two mega-giants in the food industry, Beatrice Foods and Palm Dairies. Beatrice Foods is a food producer across the country and Palm Dairies is a milk producer in western Canada.
Beatrice made an application to buy out Palm. It came to the Bureau of Competition Policy and it was approved. When Beatrice bought out Palm it was approved across all the centres in western Canada, including Thunder Bay. What happened in Thunder Bay? At that time there were only two milk producers in the city of Thunder Bay, Beatrice Foods and Palm Dairies. There are no other milk producers in the whole district.
Now that went to the Bureau of Competition Policy and the director of the bureau act to conduct an in-depth investigation into the affairs of how the elimination of competition in that market-place would affect the consumer. It was my understanding-and I am sure the understanding of all Canadians, particularly the people in Thunder Bay, the area I represent-that we would be protected by this act and the people who are charged with the responsibility of dealing with this act.
On August 28 there was no longer any competition in the milk industry in Thunder Bay. The director who was entrusted with completing an in-depth investigation into the affairs of the Beatrice-Palm sale issued a proclamation that after having reviewed the substance of this transaction he would not stop the sale of Palm Dairies to Beatrice Foods.

He stated in his reasons for making that decision that we were afforded the protection of the Competition Act. In that decision he stated that he would not stop the sale and that, even though there was a substantial lessening of competition, he would monitor the effects of the sale for the next three years to ensure that the consumer in the market-place was protected.
Now we all know that you cannot monitor situations on an ongoing basis in competitive industry. You either have competition or you do not have competition.
When the director chose to ignore that there would be a substantial lessening of competition in the most basic of industries, the milk industry-a basic food industry in the country-he chose to ignore the wishes of the people of that area and said that he would allow the sale of Palm Dairies to the Beatrice interests to go forward. There was no substantial lessening of competition. There was no threat of a lessening of competition.
In allowing that transaction to go through he completely eliminated any competition in that most basic of industries, the milk industry, thereby affecting almost every citizen in that community, especially young families.
He conducted what he said was an investigation as to how it would affect the market-place but in our conversations he said that we were conducting our own investigation.
Mr. Speaker, let me tell you just what we did so that the director could make an informed decision, we thought, with proper information.
When we found out that Beatrice and Palm were going to amalgamate, when Palm was going to be eliminated from the market-place, we went out into the marketplace to the independent grocery stores and independent merchants. People signed petitions and in a period of two days we got the signatures of over 2,000 people on a petition which stated that the people of Thunder Bay did not want Palm Dairies to be consolidated with Beatrice Foods because it would be a substantial lessening of competition. There are over 200 independent merchants in that particular area. We have over 200 petitions from those independent merchants exclusively which state
Private Members' Business
that they do not want the elimination of competition by Palm Dairies selling out to Beatrice Foods.
The Corporation of the City of Thunder Bay, the city council of Thunder Bay, realizing the import of this decision on the citizens of Thunder Bay, passed a resolution imploring the Board of Competition Policy not to proceed with allowing the sale of Palm Dairies to Beatrice Foods. That was followed by many of the other small communities: Nipigon, Red Rock, Hurkett, Do-rion, Murillo, and other small centres that said they would be affected, and implored the director of the bureau to stop the sale of Palm to Beatrice.
Given all of that information, they still made the decision to allow Palm to be sold to Beatrice in the community, which eliminated all competition. Just to bring it into focus, because I know my time is short, let me just read a press release on the results of that sale and let me put it down in perspective as to what this Competition Act truly means to the Canadian consumer when the terms of that act are not used in the best interest to protect the citizens of this country. This is dated today: "Beatrice Foods announced today that it plans to consolidate its Thunder Bay operations. This facility will undergo a major expansion of $1 million over the next 18 months to provide Thunder Bay with a modem processing plant."
Part of the consolidation plan-and their consolidation plan means closing the Palm Dairies plant, which is the newest and the most modem in the area and using the older one-is closing the Balmoral station, closing of the current Palm Dairies plant on Balmoral Street. With the move, approximately 20 people will be offered employment at the Beatrice plant and 35 people will be laid off effective tomorrow.
What this means, and this is an actual fact of what we are talking about here today, is that the Competition Act in this country is not being applied for the best use and the best interest of the average Canadian citizen. That is the result of what we are doing. We have got to stop it. We should not allow it.
