speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nickel Belt has suggested that the government should amend the Competition Act so that the Director of Investigations and Research shall consider, when reviewing a proposed merger, the extent to
September 25, 1990

Private Members' Business
which concentration of corporate ownership is in the public interest, avoids conflict of interest between merged financial and non-financial commercial operations and promises lower prices, innovation, employment and other public benefits.
Mr. Speaker, the concentration of corporate ownership is a complex phenomenon which cannot be attributed to a single factor. It is the result of various corporate decisions, dealing for instance with expansion projects aimed at greater efficiency and diversification.
The hon. member's suggestion seems to be based on the notion that concentration of corporate ownership is on the rise. As a matter of fact, since 1984, there has been a slight reduction in the number of concentrations generally and in the total assets, sales and benefits recorded by the top 25 companies in the economy. The level of global concentration among the top 1,000 corporations has remained the same since 1976. Therefore, I urge all hon. members to be careful when they interprete statistical data.
These matters are not so important as the impact of corporate concentration on the Canadian economy. It may have a positive impact such as the growth of Canadian corporations and the improvement of their position with respect to exports and world competition.
Just the same, Mr. Speaker, concentration of corporate ownership can give rise to a number of problems. The tools already exist to remedy them and we have shown that we are prepared to use them.
We showed we were ready to use them.
The government adopted a Competition Act whose deterrent effect on anti-competitive mergers have been proven. The Act enables the Director of Investigations and Research to prohibit mergers which prevent or substantially impede competition or will probably have that effect. Since the Act was passed in 1986, over 600 mergers and takeovers have been subjected to scrutiny. In more than 20 cases, changes were made or the case was simply dropped.
The federal government is presently reviewing the Canada Business Corporations Act to make sure that it protects efficiently the minority shareholders' rights in
the context of increasingly important and complex public offers.
Investment Canada reviews takeovers by foreign interests and approves only those that directly benefit Canadians.
There are also governmental programs to help workers who lose their job for some reason, such as retraining programs and mobility incentive programs.
Mr. Speaker, business concentration also causes concerns because of the concentration of wealth in Canada. I believe that the question is not so much to know who owns what, but to determine if the Canadian economy is growing and prospering. In fact, Mr. Speaker, our economy has grown by 16 percent since 1984. Between 1984 and 1987, the growth rate of the economy was higher in Canada than in any other OECD country.
Mr. Speaker, let us not be blind to the fact that concentration of corporate ownership also raises issues concerning the profitability and growth potential of smaller businesses in Canada's modem economy.
Canadian small business is indeed responsible for creating most new jobs and for an important part of the commercial growth, innovation and trade leadership. This sector has been very prosperous in the past five years, Mr. Speaker, and small businesses have held their own against larger companies over the last ten years.
Our government has launched a number of familiarization programs designed to promote the growth of small business. They include new tax incentives to encourage the management of retirement funds to invest in eligible small- and medium-sized businesses, not to mention other incentives like access to small business which makes it easier for them to land government contracts. Madam Speaker, these programs enable small businesses to take every advantage of opportunities flowing from freer trade and world-wide market expansion.
Madam Speaker, the increase in the number of takeovers and mergers in most countries-this is not restricted to Canada-points clearly to the need for a greater number of multinationals to be more competitive on world markets. This situation can easily prove to be a boon for small businesses that act as suppliers, which is a good thing, and in many cases the partners of the larger concerns they supply, for they gain better access to world

September 25, 1990

markets and new research and development opportunities.
Given the complexity of problems created by the concentration of businesses and its links with other fields of economic policy, the government has chosen a many-faceted approach instead of relying on only one legislative lever as advocated in the motion introduced by the member for Nickel Belt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   COMPETITION ACT CONCENTRATION OF CORPORATE OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you for the privilege of saying a few words on this private members' motion of the hon. member for Nickel Belt.
I congratulate him for throwing into the public mill a private members' motion that draws attention of members of the House, and more particularly Canadians, to problems as different people perceive them. We might have a little different perspective as to whether it is a serious problem at this moment, but nonetheless the extent to which governments permit the concentration of power in any one industry has always been a problem in every nation.
Of course, people are notorious for abusing their monopoly positions. It does not matter whether it is private business or people with too much power in public or private life. It tends to be abused, so the secret and magic of our society is to try to keep power dissipated so no one gets too much over anyone else.
For example, in the hon. member's home town of Nickel Belt, I suppose Inco is a very powerful player. I do not know even under the existing law whether Inco would have been permitted to become so big and powerful in Canada because, as he knows, for I guess 70 years the Competition Act was never changed. The merger test required the proof of criminal intent.
I think over the whole 70 years there was something like one conviction, many years ago. Successive governments had a chance to change that, including 1972 to 1974 when the NDP were really directing the Liberal Party and could have got it. None of us took time to do it when we had power, except 1984.
There are a host of other major problems that this country should have faced and solved 10, 15 or 20 years ago, whether it was the growth of government per se
Private Members' Business
becoming a monopoly, whether it was the lack of intellectual property protection, whether it was drugs or private breeders' rights or the Integrated Circuits Topography Act. There were all sorts of things that this country should have faced in the last 15 years but did not. The Prime Minister did take them on.
Free trade was done. The privatization of some Crown corporations was done, although there are still many Crown corporations. As a policy, the Conservative government agrees that there is a role for Crown corporations in this mixed economy of Canada. We have set some up. We will set more up.
One was the Competition Act. We came out with a whole new statute that took this criminal test on mergers, under which you could never get a conviction, and changed it to a civil test; the balance of probabilities. Under that, if my recollection is correct, there are at least four-I think there might even be up to six-mergers that have been absolutely prohibited. That is just one part of it, but it is significant in itself when there had not been any for 50 years.
The real point is that a host of proposed mergers were refused by the director, unless they made certain changes. For example, in western Canada, Safeway bought out a competitor and the director demanded that they sell certain stores in certain towns and cities. That has worked very well.
I think that is the type of power you need to have because each merger in each industry has to be assessed from a different perspective.
Every merger creates an opportunity. These firms have to compete not only in Canada, but on a global scale. I wonder if Inco would have amounted to the company it is and I wonder if Inco would be able to pay the tremendous salaries it pays now to my hon. friend and his constituents, because if it could not have operated around the world, it might have just gone right out of business.
What I am pointing out is that this thing is not just simple, but that does not take away from the spirit of the motion that my hon. friend from Nickel Belt has put in the House.
I can assure the member that this motion has been looked at very carefully by officials in the policy part of the department and in the directorate to see whether some ideas could be added to the statute. I want to tell

Private Members' Business
him not to write this off if it does not get through today. He might take it back and refine it a bit after talking with people and hearing members in the House give examples. He might well be able to come up with a motion for the next session that is much more appropriate and indeed will be accepted.
Another thing has happened, for those of us who have been around for a while. Private members' motions were never accepted in this House, but since we have become the government the Prime Minister and our government have accepted more private members' motions than ever before in the entire history of Parliament from 1867. There is a host of private members' bills. It has made life much more satisfying for us as individuals, because of course we come here thinking we have some ideas that are important for the private and public spheres.
I wanted to say in a more specific way what these merger tests involve. The issue of corporate concentration is best dealt with once one distinguishes three distinct areas of concern. There is concentration of markets, there is concentration of power, and there is concentration of ownership. We need to note that while any one of these three forms of concentration may coexist with another, the presence of one form does not necessarily imply the presence of another. Concentration of markets refers to the share of an industry's total output that is accounted for by a small number of firms. Typically this form of concentration is accentuated by horizontal mergers. Market concentration necessarily affects competition and thus possibly prices, but concentration of power and ownership in and of themselves do not do that.
This government has responded, as I have said, to concerns about the impact of market concentration on the Canadian economy by passing the Competition Act. Merger review in Canada has always considered the existing and prospective levels of market concentration when assessing the likelihood that a proposed merger will result in a substantial prevention or lessening of competition.
The legislation stipulates that this assessment is not make solely on the basis of market share or concentration figures. Other characteristics of market structure,
such as levels of foreign competition, product substitutability, barriers to entry, and whether effective and vigorous competition remains post-merger must also be addressed. The law also provides for consideration of efficiency gains or cost savings arising from the transaction. The Competition Act, by being designed to maintain and encourage competition while promoting efficiency and adaptability of the Canadian economy, has addressed market concentration concerns. There is no need for further legislative review.
That is the official position at the moment, but again I encourage my friend not to forget about his motion. If he feels that strongly about it, he should change some of the words and he will very likely have a successful motion when he brings it back the next time.
Concentration of power refers to the ability of a firm or a group of firms to influence regulators, legislators or other institutions. The government has taken action to ensure that large corporations do not have undue political influence. To ensure that the government's dealings with the private sector are open we passed the Lobbyist Registration Act, a statute that we should have had for years and years but just did not get done because of other priorities of other governments.
This legislation is intended to foster greater openness in the process of policy formation by allowing all Canadians to see who is lobbying and for what purpose. Canadians are then able to judge for themselves whether any particular group has undue influence.
The Competition Act also provides another example of open and arm's length dealings with business. The Director of Investigation and Research is statutorily independent of government policy makers and hence is free from government interference in matters subject to the Competition Act, including merger review. Moreover, the courts and competition tribunal, an independent, quasi-judicial body, perform all adjudicatory functions related to the legislation. In establishing the competition tribunal Parliament sought to combine the important element of judicial process with expertise in the fields of business and economics. I think it was a wise decision to go that way even though there have been some problems in the courts.

I appreciate that my time has expired. I know there are other members who wish to speak to this motion, so I will sit down now.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   COMPETITION ACT CONCENTRATION OF CORPORATE OWNERSHIP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak in support of my colleague's motion before this House, the member for Nickel Belt. The matter which he raises is an extremely important one and an extremely timely one.
As I know the House has already been informed, a company that now is the sole operator of a dairy concern in TTunder Bay and northwestern Ontario advised the media this morning that it was closing a plant it had just purchased, putting out of work 35 employees and affecting their families. This is all a direct result of the lack of a federal Competition Act which takes into consideration the needs of the smaller as well as the larger communities, the small as well as the large companies.
Let me elaborate, Madam Speaker. Earlier this year Palm Dairies, a company based in western Canada, owned by Peter Pocklington, decided that it wanted to find a buyer. What happened is very interesting because the initial purchaser-to-be was a western based co-op which the federal authorities deemed to be an inappropriate purchaser, because in their words the acquisition of Palm Dairies by this western based co-op would lessen competition so they ordered Palm Dairies to find someone else to purchase them.
They went to Beatrice Foods, a very large company which had already acquired one family owned and operated dairy in Thunder Bay a number of years ago. They agreed to purchase the assets of Palm Dairies in order to prevent a lessening of competition as decreed by the federal bureaucracy.
That was all well and good. I do not want to pass judgment on the impact on competition in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, but one thing that became eminently clear to us in Thunder Bay and in the Thunder Bay milk market was that the acquisition of Palm Dairies by Beatrice Foods would lessen competition in terms of fluid milk and, some of us believed, would eliminate competition in terms of fluid milk or what we call milk at the corner store.
We had already seen indications of that lessening of competition as store operators were advised that under
Private Members' Business
the new hierarchy the dairy would no longer come in and stock the shelves or rotate the stock. Over time it was suggested that the free freezers and the free refrigerators that were provided as part of a marketing plan by both Beatrice and Palm would no longer be provided. In fact the retailer would have to purchase those or find his or her own. Then we knew, based on what happened elsewhere in the country when an unregulated monopoly situation occurred, that prices would go up.
I take us back to Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario a number of years ago when it found itself in a monopoly situation for fluid milk. In a very short period of time that city by itself became the highest priced city in Ontario for the purchase of milk at the retail level. There was no competition. In the outlying communities such as Wawa and other areas around Sault Ste. Marie the price was even higher.
The only reason today that milk prices are lower in Sault Ste. Marie is the reality of American competition with a very high Canadian dollar that attracts Canadians across the border to pick up groceries like milk. That is the only reason that prices are depressed in Sault Ste. Marie. Because of this merger and because of the permission of the competition bureau, Thunder Bay and the area from White River to Upsala will now be in a virtual monopoly situation.
What did the competition bureau decide after literally hundreds of people from Thunder Bay, from Atikokan, and from along the north shore sent in comments and evidence indicating that they were concerned about the impact on them as retailers, as consumers, and as producers of milk? The bureau ruled that it could go ahead and they would monitor it over three years, as required under the Competition Act.
There is no longer going to be three years, because the moment that Beatrice closes Palm Dairies there is nothing to restart. The assets will be sold. The people will be moved out of town and will find other employment.
It just shows what kind of a farce is the existing act, the prime component in terms of which there is no appeal process. A bureaucrat in this national capital region makes an arbitrary decision based on confidential information provided to that person by the companies involved, and not to be released to any of us who have raised concerns about this matter. He and he alone has the decision-making authority. We cannot even appeal

Private Members' Business
to the minister because under the act he does not have the ability to overrule that decision.
This means that for the 35 employees who were told sometime today, I am told-or perhaps they are not even going to be told until tomorrow that they are out of a job-the company will try to find them employment elsewhere in their system, perhaps in Sault Ste. Marie or in western Canada. However, that is 35 less jobs in the community of Thunder Bay and on the routes that they service. It may in the long term lead to a reduction in the production of milk because, as we know, when the price of a commodity goes up the volume goes down, so there may be a direct impact on the milk producers in the Thunder Bay area.
We need motions like that of my colleague. We need a change in the act to change both the amendments made by the current Conservative government and the original bases for the act which are part of the appeal mechanism I was talking about that was put in by the former government, because it is unfair to see men and women put out of work just for the sake of corporate concentration.
We need a different way in this country. We need a better way. We need legislation, policies, and a government that cares about people first, not about the corporations.

Madam Speaker, I always enjoy listening to the hon. member for Nickel Belt who, eloquent and knowledgeable as he is, can get his parliamentary colleagues interested in various kinds of measures designed to make life easier for Canadians.
Unfortunately I believe that in fact the member for Nickel Belt is suggesting that the Competition Act, now enforced by the Bureau of Competition Policy, should be expanded into a domestic investment review legislation closely patterned-in spirit and scope-after the Foreign Investment Review Act of the previous administration in office before 1984.
The way I see it, widening the scope of the Competition Act to make it into a Domestic Investment Review Act would be a useless and unwise move.
Useless because the necessary mecanisms required to deal with the potential negative impact of a merger are already available to the Canadian government.
Some mergers may give rise to questions concerning the competition policy and have a negative impact on consumer prices and consumer options. The Competition Act which was amended by this government in 1986 has proved to be a very effective legislative tool to deal with all major mergers in all sectors of the economy.
Since the legislation was passed in 1986 more than 600 mergers and take-overs have been reviewed and in more than 20 cases they did not go through or they had to be changed because according to the Director of Investigation and Research they might have an impact on competition and consumption. If we compare the impact of this legislation with that of the former Combines Investigation Act, our conclusion must be that the latter failed to deliver a single conviction with respect to a merger. Other sections of the Competition Act, such as those dealing with abuse of dominant position and the refusal to sell, provide ways to deal with anti-competitive behaviour by larger corporations after a merger has taken place.
The merger provisions of the Competition Act apply both to foreign mergers involving Canadian assets and to purely Canadian mergers. Furthermore, Investment Canada is responsible for examining foreign investments to ensure that they contribute to economic growth and enhance employment opportunities in this country.
Some people are concerned that certain mergers may cause a loss of jobs. The enhanced competitive position of Canadian companies has increased employment opportunities. Since 1984, there has been a large number of mergers and takeovers in Canada. During this time, Canada has ranked first among OECD countries on number of jobs created. If they need assistance, workers who lose their jobs for whatever reason have access to a wide range of manpower adjustment programs that provide financial support while they look for another job, and also offer training and assistance in moving to another location.
As pointed out by the hon. member for Nickel Belt, mergers also raise concerns about conflict of interest, links between financial and non-financial corporations and corporate power. I repeat, the instruments we need to deal with these matters are already in place. The
September 25, 1990

Canada Business Corporations Act has been effective in providing shareholders with a mechanism to protect their right to fair treatment and adequate disclosure of financial information. Furthermore, the government recently passed the Lobbyists Registration Act to promote openness of relations between lobbyists and the public sector. The government's policy on business ownership is incorporated in new regulations for the financial sector in the form of legislation that will soon be tabled in Parliament.
Clearly the government already has a number of instruments to deal with any situation in which a given transaction raises or appears to raise concerns, and with any matter related to mergers in general. That is why I feel that the wide reaching legislation proposed by the hon. member for Nickel Belt to examine domestic investment is unnecessary.
If I may draw a parallel with the Foreign Investment Review Agency, abolished by the present government and replaced by Investment Canada, it is my firm belief that turning the director's office into a domestic investment review agency, to be established by amending the Competition Act in order to create business and employment opportunities for Canada, would in fact discourage Canadians from investing in their own country and thus lead to a substantial loss of investment.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today, we are confronted with a so-called Indian crisis, but strictly speaking, it is a crisis concerning relations between different groups of Canadians. The basis of that crisis can undoubtedly be traced back over 400 years of Canadian history. That crisis was aggravated by the government's inaction in the last six years, it has become an inextricable mess because in mid-july that government chose to let things degenerate.

Madam Speaker, Oka was no accident. This House needs no reminder of the tragedy that lies before us. Infant mortality rates simply stagger the mind. These people have a reduced life expectancy by 10 years of the average Canadian citizen. Those of you, and I, who have visited and spent much time on reserves, know that we are looking at a people uprooted, a people decimated. We are looking at each individual aspect of their lives. Whether it be housing or their traditional economic way
of life, we as a society have left a blight upon this nation's landscape. The government must now move to demonstrate that it understands the historical injustices that have been perpetrated on the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
This afternoon the Prime Minister indicated that finally he understands that a different approach is required. I would say that far more than that, the government must now be prepared to endorse fundamental and deep-rooted change. The government must stop the pablum. The government must now get specific. The time for pious wishes and promises without followup is over.
What must we do? Certainly, the first thing is we must recognize the absolute necessity of entrenching in the charter aboriginal self-government. Self-government is not something that you give to a people who have governed themselves for 15,000 years before the first white man or women arrived on these shores. Self-government is not something that needs detailed definition any more than freedom of association did. It is part of our system to establish concepts and let them evolve. Self-government is the culmination, the aspirations and the hope of a people who want to build and make for themselves a life comparable to those who live around them, and indeed in the terms of the exploitation and development of their own culture want to demonstrate that they can stand proud with anyone in the world.
Second, we must enhance the participation of aboriginal peoples in federal decision-making. Federal governments have consistently violated the fiduciary relationship which they have with the aboriginal peoples. You cannot consistently go to court with those with whom you have a trust relationship and expect that trust relationship to be valid any longer in law. As a result, I believe that the government should move immediately to establish a joint committee of ministers and aboriginal leaders to oversee the transition away from the Depart-

Government Orders
ment of Indian Affairs, to oversee the development and the ultimate implantation of aboriginal self-government.
Third, we have land claims. The government should appoint a minister whose sole responsibility is to deal with the task of concluding comprehensive land claims. This should be done in consultation with aboriginal leadership.
Fourth, the government should move to establish a specific claims tribunal. There are over 500 specific claims that remain unsolved, and the number is growing. Indeed, they are a profound source of friction and disaffection and that cancer must be removed.
Fifth, the government should rectify the injustice caused by constant broken treaty promises. It should establish a treaty commission whose sole purpose is to recognize explicitly that you do not solve the problems and the developing interpretation required of treaties by constantly going to court and engaging in litigation. It must be done by a body that understands the cultural background in which both treaties were signed historically and the modem needs of a modern nation.
Sixth, the government should take the lead in working with urban aboriginal Canadians. It must establish support of political, cultural, social and economic institutions so that those aboriginals living in large and small urban centres are not simply put on the dung heap of some suburb.
In the city of Winnipeg there are 600,000 aboriginal Canadians. We are talking about cities within cities, and as of yet this government has not even begun to recognize the nature of the problem.
I would join the Canadian Bar Association in the seventh and final recommendation. The government should accept its responsibility for Canada's Metis people. The Metis people of this country have been a ping pong ball between the federal and the provincial governments since Confederation. If you go into the urban cities that I have just described you see what the result is. It is politically immoral for the two levels of government who normally engage in fights over which has the jurisdiction to engage in fights over which should have the jurisdiction trying to put off their responsibility.
What I have recommended is not all that earth-shaking. What indeed is earth-shaking is that what I am recommending has never been done. We in the House sit
here and debate many issues. They are important issues. In not all of these issues, however, does the world simply stop and take note of our debates. In not all of these issues do we have it within our power to totally affect the world. But there are certain areas of human endeavour where we in the House can make a fundamental change in the way the world regards certain aspects of its policy. There are others where only those of us in the House can bring about fundamental change.
The problems of aboriginal Canadians is a Canadian problem. It is one that we must solve within this House. If there is any reason for any man or woman having gone into public life in this country, it is to make sure that in the course of the next decade we make sure that we leave a legacy so that never again must Canadians look upon armed standoffs on Canadian soil. Never again must we see Canadian soldiers putting barbed wire around other Canadians who are holding arms. Never again must we see the terrible sight of Canadians throwing stones at each other or bridges barricaded. We have our chance within this decade, within the hands of the men and women in this House. We have an opportunity to make an historical legacy not given to very many. We must not miss this chance.
There is one last point that I would like to raise within the context of this debate.

One month ago, the Quebec Government announced an indemnisation plan for the people of Oka and Chateauguay affected by that so-called Indian crisis. But really, we are talking about a matter that comes under federal jurisdiction. Yesterday, I asked the following question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, without getting an answer, I must say: Is the federal government ready to share the tax burden with the Quebec government? I asked at the same time: Is the federal Government ready to fully idemnify the residents of the South Shore, Lasalle, Emard, and the South West of Montreal who have received no compensation? I repeat because I think that it is capital, if we want to resolve the crisis currently affecting my province:

Reconciliation will not be attained if a group of people who should not have borne the brunt of this crisis feel that because of the historical injustices that have been meted out to the aboriginal Canadian that they are asked solely to bear the financial burden. I believe that it is the
September 25, 1990

responsibility of the federal government to share in the compensation for the southwest portion of Montreal, the south shore, and indeed for the inhabitants of Kanesa-take and Kahnawake. I believe that we have an opportunity now as Canadians to do something that very few have had before. But we will not grasp that nettle if the only thing that we do in the House is engage in empty rhetoric; if the only thing that we do in this House is make more vague promises; if the only thing we do in the House is talk, as opposed to laying down specific goals, objectives, and targets. If for the first time we say that the time for talk is over, the time for action is now. If we do that, then we will have justified our existence. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, I listened to my hon. friend with a great deal of interest because I thought I was hearing an echo. Many of the things that he has suggested this evening have already been suggested in the House just a very short while ago when the Prime Minister spoke.
If you will just bear with me for a moment, Madam Speaker, I will repeat some of the agenda that the Prime Minister very briefly shared with us this afternoon. He said, first, that consultation with aboriginal peoples and respect for the fiduciary responsibilities of the Crown toward them will be built into the process of negotiation from the start. The second initiative is that legal undertakings regarding land transfers to treaty Indians given as much as century ago will finally be honoured. Third, he said that we will accelerate negotiations on modern treaties-the comprehensive claims, in other words- which until now have been limited to six and, to accelerate claims settlements, the government will no longer limit itself to handling only six at a time. We will consider other innovations, such as regional or province-wide negotiations.
He said that the second dimension of the government's agenda would be addressed to improving living conditions on Indian reserves.
Government Orders
I will not get into all the specific details, but further he said that one of the very important objectives of the government would be the enlargement of aboriginal capacity for self-government within the framework of the Canadian Constitution.
I heard many of those things mentioned by my hon. friend opposite. Since as part of his government in power for so many years he had a wonderful opportunity to stop some of the inequities that he spoke about from ever happening in the first place, will he now be willing to stand when some of these these issues come before the House, to vote with the government as we pursue this very comprehensive and very positive agenda for the betterment of the Indian people in Canada?

I think that ought to be recognized.


I am not trying to be cute here, but I could listen to the kind of speech we just heard if it came from the hon. member from Western Arctic, who probably ten years ago was not a mover and shaker in the Liberal party, but I know that the hon. member who just spoke has been a mover and shaker in the Liberal party for long time before he reached the House. In that context, I remember the effort made by the NDP caucus in 1980 to have aboriginal rights included in the Constitution. We had to bargain very, very hard, threatening to withdraw our support for the constitutional initiative of former Prime Minister Trudeau, in order to even have that considered. Then, in the end, in the final document when it came out after the last First Ministers' Conference, many of us were tricked by the Liberal Government of the day when, instead of having aboriginal rights recognized, we had the word "existing" injected into the final document, at which time there was very little that anybody could do about it. We either had to vote for that or risk having the whole thing collapse.
I was involved in a housing project in Manitoba when there was a NDP government in power and I had a terrible time getting them to come to grips with it. I know the history of the CCF and the NDP governments in Saskatchewan. In terms of aboriginal matters, they were no more enlightened than any other government. I do not say this with any degree to attack and I certainly do not say it with pride. Every single government, federal, provincial, and, indeed, municipal, has very little to be proud of in this area. I do not think we should be pointing fingers. We should be doing something about the problem.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Quebec lived through difficult times this summer. And as this debate is going on in the House of Commons, it is worth mentionning that this crisis has not yet been settled and that the Canadian Army is still on Quebec soil.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
This Summer 1990 had begun with the failure of the Meech Lake Accord: the rejection by English Canada of an agreement considered by all in Quebec as a very strict minimum and by many as not enough. This failure was deeply hardly felt as a rejection of Quebec by English Canada.
It must be made clear that Elijah Harper blocked passage of the Meech Lake Accord because the national rights of aboriginal peoples were not recognized in it, whereas English Canada opposed Meech because they refused to recognize Quebec distinctiveness.
Following this rejection, this failure, thousands of Quebecers got together in the streets of Montreal last June 25 with a sense of pride and quiet confidence in their future. Quebecers never considered the problems in Oka as a revenge against the aboriginal peoples.
The aboriginal crisis broke out in a context where a majority of Quebecers were coming out in favour of Quebec sovereignty. And I want to say right away that we cannot but recognize, as the Quebec National Assembly did on March 20, 1985, the existence of aboriginal nations and that, yes, we have to speak in terms of self-government as Gil Remillard, the Minister of Justice for Quebec, said the Government of Quebec was ready to do without waiting for the federal.
According to some public opinion polls, there was in English Canada, unqualified support both for the Warriors and the aboriginal peoples themselves. This prompted a response from some chiefs asking that a distinction be made.
Moreover, these public opinion trends and others have been completely unfair toward Quebec and Quebecers on the subject of land claims. We must then set the record straight.
To begin with, I want to say that the inalienable rights of the native peoples do not justify the actions of the Warriors and that the unacceptable actions of the Warriors must not let us forget the historic and present rights of the native peoples.
We must also say that the govemement of Quebec has not waited for this crisis to occur in order to do
something. Indeed, the 20th of March 1985, the governe-ment of Quebec, then led by Rene Levesque, made the following statement recognizing ten native peoples on his territory, and took tangible measures designed to make real progress on the subject of the recognition of these peoples' rights. I will now read this resolution of the Quebec National Assembly:
That this Assembly recognizes the existence in Quebec of the following nations: Abenaki, Algonquin, Attikamek, Cree, Huron, Micmac, Mohawk, Montagnais, Naskapi, Inuit.
That it recognizes their existent ancestral rights and their rights which are written in the Conventions of James Bay, the North of Quebec and the North-East of Quebec.
That it considers that these Conventions, together with any other convention or future agreement of the same nature have the value of treaties.
That it subscribes to the negotiations entered into by the government with the native peoples in order to further recognize et clarify their rights, that process being based on historical legitimacy and on the importance for the society of Quebec to establish with natives peoples harmonious relations based on mutual trust and the respect of everyone's rights.
Urges the government to continue its negotiations with the native people on the basis, but not exclusively, of the 15 principles which were approved on February 9, 1983, in response to the proposals which it had received on November 30, 1982, and to make, with the nations which so wish or any of their communities agreements guaranteeing them:
a)	the right to self-government within Quebec;
b)	the right to their own culture, language and traditions;
c)	the right to own and control lands;
d)	the right to hunt, fish, trap, gather, and participate in the management of wildlife resources;
e)	the right to get involved in the economic development of Quebec and benefit from it, in order to develop as distinct nations having their own identity and exercising their own rights within Quebec;
Declares that native rights apply equally to men and women;
Affirms its determination to protect in its legislation the rights resulting from agreements with the native people of Quebec; and
Agrees that a permanent parliamentary forum should be set-up for native people to express their rights, aspirations and needs.
Moreover, since 1986, the year the policy statement of 1973 was amended, following therefore the adoption of this global land claim policy, the Federal government, according to an information bulletin published by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in August 1990, signed four territorial agreements with native groups, including three in Quebec and one with the Inuit in Northwest Canada.

*

September 25, 1990

Also, I wish to remind the House that the Quebec Government signed in 1975 the James Bay Agreement with the Crees and Inuit in Northern Quebec, as well as an agreement with the Naskapis Indians in Northern Quebec in 1978. In the same information bulletin, the Department indicated its satisfaction at the positive attitude and spirit of co-operation demonstrated by the Quebec Government in its negotiations within the framework of the amended legislation of 1986.
It would be interesting to hear the Minister inform the House of the level of co-operation demonstrated by the other provinces with respect to land claims, because we know that, except for the Yukon and Northwest Territories, the provinces must be involved in the negotiation of land claims if these negotiations are to result in negotiated settlements within a reasonable time frame, which is not the case now.
Besides, at the moment, five agreements are being discussed, and two of them will soon be reached. Moreover, according to the same department, nineteen other land claims are pending, most of which are in British Columbia.
Could the minister tell the House what means he plans to use to accelerate the settlement of those land claims in order to do justice to the legitimate claims of the native peoples and to avoid that situations similar to the case experienced at Oka, which was known for quite some time, deteriorate into crisis situations, as has been the case in Oka this summer?
Everyone recongnize that the limit of six land claims established by the government is absolutely unnacept-able, and that would result in the native peoples having to wait practically a hundred years before all of their land claims are settled.
Prime minister Mulroney announced he would improve this, but did not say how. If he means increasing the number of claims from six to seven, or reducing the deadline from 100 to 95 years, that does not solve anything.
In these circumstances, how can this government say that it has tried in every possible way and in good faith to avoid the Oka crisis which has still not been settled?
Government Orders
In this context, how can we not understand the legitimate frustrations of the native peoples which have grown over the years and which explain the explosion of violence that we all deplore, condemn, including the native chiefs themselves?
In this context where this government and his predecessors have so obviously dragged their feet without regard to the possible consequences of what is in fact a blockade of native claims, how, Madam Speaker, can this government put forward such a simplistic motion calling for the House to congratulate our soldiers, and merely reaffirm the primacy of law everywhere in Canada without uttering a single word on the core of the matter, the native issue?
I also noticed this morning that both opposition parties, the Liberals and the New Democrats, saw fit to join the government in congratulating the Armed Forces for their intervention.
Of course, in Oka, the military played its role and intervened at the request of the government. That is and was its role. Now, regarding the motion before this House, I think it would be better if the hon. members waited for the results of a public inquiry before handing out condemnations and congratulations. It seems to me that, at this time, such an approach is the most logical and respectful to the prerogatives of the public and members alike, based on complete information on the management and development of this crisis.
I would have liked to amend the government motion, but I am not allowed to. The amendment would have read as follows:
Replace the first paragraph and add the following after "That the
House-":
That the House recognize the basic rights of native peoples as the
Quebec legislative assembly did in a resolution dated March 20,
1985;
And that, in the opinion of the House, violence and arms will not
constitute acceptable means of solving this conflict.
However, the procedure does not allow me to make such an amendment. I maintain nonetheless that, under the circumstances that we know of, that is to say the present faceoff between armed Warriors and Canadian Armed Forces soldiers in Oka, near Montreal, the contribution of this House would have been much more credible in the eye of Quebecers and natives had the

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
House reaffirmed the following. First, the recognition of the national rights of native people in Canada.
Second, the commitment of the government to speeding up the settlement process concerning the native land claims through legal procedures and negociations to allow the peaceful resolution of this dispute. Third, the fact that provinces must take part in this negociation process in order to speed up the settlement of the claims. And fourth, to hold a public inquiry into the management and the causes of this crisis.
I think that, had it used such an approach, the government would have been more credible and would have contributed more to rebuilding the thrust and confidence needed to bring about the laying of arms without amnisty for the Warriors and to open negociations on the root of the problem.
The rights of some must not infringe upon that of others. While recognizing the validity of the native claims and condemning the armed violence of the Warriors as well as acts of agression against natives by protesters in the Chateauguay area, it must be realized that the citizens of Oka and Chateauguay had and still have to put up with major inconveniences because of a crisis in which they are merely helpless hostages. If expressions of intolerance such as the ones we have witnessed are to be avoided, and if we want and really have our heart set on rekindling the brotherly relations, neighbourly terms and mutual respect between the white communities, the Quebecers, and the native people, governments must assume their responsibities regarding the losses suffered by thousands of people. Otherwise, fine words and good intentions will again have resulted in nothing concrete. And results is what we need in the very short term if we are to restore good relationships between the native people and residents of Oka. I therefore ask the government to agree as soon as possible to Quebec's request to share in the financial compensation program and other measures taken by the government of Quebec.
The government must fulfill its responsibilities to all parties involved, natives as well as Quebekers.
Finally, I want to remind the House that, following the failure of the Meech Lake Accord, Quebecers have undertaken, under the authority of their National Assembly, and through a Committee on its Constitutional Future, a process supported by more than 60 percent of
Quebec citizens who long for Quebec's sovereignty, as shown by the polls.
The crisis in Oka demonstrates how important it is for Quebec to recover its full sovereignty so that it can, on its own territory, carry out the decisions taken in March 1985 by its own National Assembly and recognize the native people and their rights. I am sure Quebecers are prepared to give the natives the place they are entitled to on their territory and wish to see their nation establish good relationships with the native nation.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to take a few moments to put a question to our colleague on the other side of the House. I want to ask him if he might make what I would call a useful contribution. Given his long professional experience and his knowledge of the ins and outs of negotiations, I wonder whether he would make a useful contribution through a number of known regular channels instead of advocating in the House that some form of censure be applied and urging that positions be made clear. Perforce, he has been very theoretical because he admitted himself that if he had been able and if it had been possible-he does use the conditional tense-on one hand would it be useful to assist the whole House and all parties if we could take a better approach along the lines of his position and his input- On the other hand, Madam Speaker, how would he explain to me or to the House the fact that in his remarks he sought to depoliti-cize a situation, and yet almost in the same breath he ended up with a statement which to me, a French Canadian from Quebec, seems to be highly politicized? I would suggest that the ongoing situation at Oka-and this goes for Chateauguay as well but it is more obvious at Oka-must be depoliticized in this House. Having the opportunity to express his views, the hon. member should try to explain to us why he should want to politicize the whole thing by opening up a second front which has nothing to do with the issue under consideration.

Madam Speaker, I must say, first, that I was a bit suprised to be asked why we are bringing politics into those issues. I would have thought that the House was the right place to discuss politics and I am rather suprised by that question. That is a suprising question. And I say "poli-
September 25, 1990

tics" in the true sense of the word! I am not talking about petty politics.
Second, I did ask to meet the leaders of the native nations of Quebec and that meeting will take place in a few days. I hope to better identify the issues with them. Since you mentioned my past experience in the labour movement. I have also decided to meet with union representives who are actually preparing briefs on that question. Both native leaders and officials from Chateaugay and Oka have been invited to that meeting.
Contacts have already been made. I was explaining in my speech that I could not propose any amendment now since the Standing Orders do not allow me to do so, one amendment and one amendment to the amendment having already been tabled. But I say to the hon. member that that does not preclude anybody from proposing new ideas even if amendments are out of the question.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the member who just spoke.
How can he reconcile the statements made by his leader in the House who said it is evident that it is necessary to refuse sovereignty to the aboriginal people of Quebec and was speaking of the courage and the strength to say that it is not possible to have more than one sovereignty over one territory? I wonder how he reconciles that with what he said about the charter recently passed in the Quebec National Assembly. Is it possible for Quebec, as he perceives a sovereign Quebec, to allow sovereignty to native people within Quebec as those native people are requesting?
Furthermore, I would like to ask the member a question on the committee that was established to look into the constitutional future of Quebec by the Quebec National Assembly. Are there any aboriginal representatives on that committee in order to convey the aboriginal view?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
So, I start all over again. I suggest we should refer to the statement I made earlier taking all points into account. Mention is made of self-government and not sovereignty. It is there in so many letters. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Also, when I examine their claims, nowhere do I find that Native people refer to sovereignty, always self-government. It seems to me rather curious that some people should be more Indians than the Indians themselves. We must read their statements. They insist on self-government for reasons based on economic and political realities, while the Quebec nation has a sovereignty project which was developed on the basis of historic conditions of economic and political development. I suggest that within a sovereign Quebec, it will be possible to get along perfectly, and the evidence of that is that Quebec was the only province ever to sign agreements with them.
Under the NDP Government led by Premier Barrett who now sits in this House, no agreement was ever signed with the Natives although this is where the problem is the most crucial.
Let us remember the facts. On the commission established by the Quebec Government, we, of the Quebecois Bloc, insisted on the presence of Natives, among others. We insisted also on the presence of cultural and ethnic minorities, as well as women. Therefore, I fully agree that there should have been Natives sitting on that commission.

I am beeing asked hypothetical questions about the potential claims of the Crees in Northern Quebec while that is not what they are asking for at all.
