speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, regardless of what I feel about the motion on the Order Paper, I think it is worth while to have this debate to hear the range of views and understanding and information that members have on this important issue critical to Canada. It seems that some people have extremely different and diverse views as to what aboriginal people in this country are seeking and what has even been presented to this body or to politicians over the years. It is worth while to have this kind of debate in the House.
However, I want to say that I am completely opposed to the motion presented by the government at the opening of this session. The motion is an absolutely feeble excuse to explain the government's failure to deal with the issues at Oka and those issues which led to the
Government Orders
erection of the Mohawk barricades and ultimately led to the police attack on the barricades at Oka with the tragic loss of the life of Corporal Lemay and finally with the calling in of the army. It is a failure of the Conservative Party's leadership that has led to the situation we face today after 70 some days of a siege at Oka and Kahnawake.
Evident through the whole process was the failure of leadership on the part of this federal government. The failure of the Minister of Indian Affairs to become involved to the full extent of his jurisdiction, as the person who has under our Constitution jurisdiction over, as the Constitution says: "Indians and lands relating to Indians". The minister has through proclamations dating back to 1763 and through court decisions as recently as Sparrow, a trust responsibility to the native Indian people regardless of where they live in Canada. That trust responsibility was abandoned and that minister's jurisdiction over Indians and lands reserved for Indians, as spelled out in the Constitution, was abandoned. That is a shameful abandonment of leadership and jurisdiction and trust responsibility on the part of the federal government, including the Minister of Justice.
Where was the Minister of Justice when international human rights agencies as well as human rights agencies here in Canada indicated to the Canadian public that human rights violations were taking place? The Minister of Justice, who is responsible for reporting on issues of human rights to this House, was absolutely silent during the whole event. Not a single comment came from that Minister of Justice on the human rights abuses and what action she should take in order to correct those abuses.
Where was the Prime Minister of Canada, the man who came into this House claiming as his credentials and pointing to his resume as a man who was a skilled labour negotiator, a man capable of bringing people together and resolving problems between groups in conflict. During this whole situation, the people who have a leadership responsibility and a constitutional responsibility to deal with it were nowhere to be seen.
That is why we are dealing with a problem that is some 70 days old, that has become an embarrassment to Canadians, both in this country and overseas. It is why this Parliament is now dealing with this slippery resolution, to try to excuse the government from its responsibility to do what is constitutionally and morally required under its trust arrangements with the native people-

Government Orders
that is to face this issue and use eveiy effort it can to resolve it peacefully.
This is not the first time that violence has been resorted to in Canada. Rather than putting this in the very narrow perspective of what the parties are asking for at Oka, I think we should put this into a broader perspective and relate it to other conflicts that have taken place in this country dating as far back as 1837.
It is strange that when you look through the history books the same words are repeated over and over again, the same principles are repeated.
You will recall, Madam Speaker, the days of the-you will not recall because you were too young-Chateau clique and the Family Compact, and the rebellion of 1837. At that time people were interested in responsible government in Canada and in giving people the power of the purse and having elected parliaments-the kind of political freedoms we enjoy today. The Government of Canada of the day labelled those people as the Chateau clique and the Family Compact. They were labelled as dangerous terrorists, as criminals, as people who threatened and ignored the law of Canada that governs all of us and that before which we are all treated equally. Those people were labelled in very much the same way that the Mohawk people at Kanesatake and Kahnawake are labelled today. And this was back in 1837.
Madam Speaker, I think you will find that history has been much fairer to the people who took up arms against the Chateau clique and the Family Compact in favour of elected legislatures, of responsible government, and of turning over the power of the purse to the people-people like William Lyon Mackenzie who gave his name to one of our Prime Ministers in Canada and who later became a member of this body-than on those who stood in a chamber like this and insisted that people who took up arms against the country were terrorists and criminals and should face the full weight of Canadian justice. People have looked far more favourably on William Lyon Mackenzie than they have on the forgotten people who called them criminals and terrorists.
It is surprising how often Canada repeats the same mistakes over and over again. In what is called the North-West Rebellion of 1870, headed by one Louis Riel, and another rebellion in 1885 on the banks of the Saskatchewan River in the Northwest Territory at the
time, Riel and the Metis and a number of the aboriginal groups pulled together to attempt to have some government established in that territory that would recognize their rights and their role in the Northwest Territory or in the Manitoba territory of the day.
Again, it was a government of Canada headed by the same political party-John A. Macdonald was the Prime Minister then, and since he is departed from this room I can use his name rather than his riding. John A. Macdonald was the Prime Minister and I can recall him saying-I was too young myself at the time, Madam Speaker, but I can recall reading in Hansard about John A. Macdonald standing up in this House and calling Riel and his cohorts a band of criminals who defied the law of Canada and who were willing to take up arms against the legitimately constituted Government of Canada which, of course, treats all of its citizens equally.
Of course we all know the outcome of the North-West Rebellion and the Red River Rebellion of 1870. Louis Riel was hanged. But history has treated Louis Riel a little more favourably than some of the people who had him hanged.
Louis Riel is now considered a late Father of Confederation, one of the founders of the province of Manitoba and one of the leaders of the Metis and aboriginal people on the prairies who sought justice from the central government in Ottawa. I think that history has looked more favourably on Louis Riel and continues to do so than it does on those who said that nobody has the right to take up arms against this country and that blind obedience to bad law is the requirement of the day. I think history has looked favourably on those people.
None of us like to see Canadians being forced into the position of taking up arms against the government. None of us in this House would condone that kind of action on the part of any individual in this country. However, I think all of us understand that when a people is driven to the point of frustration, when they are constantly put down, when they are constantly treated like second class citizens, when they are constantly treated like colonial people, then the frustration builds, and builds, and builds to the point where those within the group who suggest a recourse to violence or to arms often obtain more credibility than those who wish to negotiate their griev-

September 25, 1990

ances and their concerns in good faith. I think that is what has happened at Oka and at Kahnawake.
I do not like the Mohawk Warrior Society and do not respect its objectives if they believe in using violence against the people of Canada. I do not like those objectives but I can understand them. If Canada drives those people to the point of frustration then the message that is carried by the Mohawk Warrior Society is going to gain a great deal of credibility among the Mohawk people because all other routes have failed. Recourse to the law of Canada has failed. Recourse to lobbying politicians has failed. Recourse to the media to demonstrate the conditions that they are suffering under and living under has failed. Recourse to local government to try to get them to stop, whether it is building a golf course on what is perceived to be Indian land or claimed to be Indian land, has failed. What are they expected to do? To simply submit. Madam Speaker, there are voices among the Mohawks which said that they were not prepared to submit and that they were prepared to take up arms against Canada and that is precisely what happened.
I do not think it is the fault of this government exclusively. It is the fault of people in this House of Commons, it is the fault of past governments, it is our fault because we as non-aboriginal people, have not recognized what aboriginal people are asking for and in fact, how moderate, how legitimate and how supportable are their demands. It is amazing that we have not listened to those people over the years.
We all come from various backgrounds where these kinds of demands were made in the countries from which we originated. One of the few things that I confess to is that I share in common with the Prime Minister of Canada that our ancestors came from the same country. That country is Ireland.
The conquest of Ireland by Britain began shortly after 1066. In fact, a small territory was set up in Ireland called the pale where the English were safe to live and beyond the pale-that is where the word comes from-was where all those savage, wild Irish like the Prime Minister's ancestors and my ancestors came from. It was not until the 14th, 15th and 16th centuries that England finally conquered Ireland and made it a part of England.
Government Orders
But when they did so, they could not understand why those Irish people did not consider themselves as British as every other Englishman; why they did not consider Ireland, to use the Prime Minister's own words, an integral part of the country over which another sovereignty could not survive.
Yet, in every single generation, from the time of conquest of Ireland, Irish people rose up in arms against the government, with their pipe poles and their declarations, demanded sovereignty over Ireland and, ultimately, in 1921 they gained it. Now, on what was considered an integral part of British soil, is a republic. As the old song went in Ireland, a nation once again and that was what the Irish people were seeking.
I do not think you could find a country that is more friendly with Great Britain than the Republic of Ireland, but all they wanted was the right to govern themselves within what they perceived to be their own territory and to co-operate with Britain as equals.
When native people in Canada talk about sovereignty, they are talking about nationhood. They are talking about being recognized as separate, legitimate nations. After all, they say, how could Britain and France come to North America and enter into treaties with those nations? One does not enter into treaties with dependants. One enters into treaties with nations who have the sovereign right as nations to enter into treaties with one and which are considered equal to one.
We are talking to people who have those kinds of treaties with Britain and with its successor, Canada. Those people consider themselves and have the legal documents to describe themselves as sovereign nations within Canada.
The world is changing dramatically and we cannot say any more that it is possible for a country to exist without recognizing the aspirations of the founding peoples within it. It is absolutely impossible.
When I look at what is happening in Europe or the Soviet Union today precisely the same thing is happening. The Soviet Union attempted to retain hundreds of nationalities, hundreds of separate countries within its own boundaries, and to control them from Moscow as if they were Russian people. Now the system has broken down and the nationality and the aspirations of those

Government Orders
people have come out again and they are demanding to be nations once again.
The people and the nations of the world looking at the process going on in the Soviet Union are excited about it. They are excited about the prospect of these, what were called nationalities in the Soviet Union, now seeking their freedom, now exercising their autonomy, and now becoming, as the Irish did in 1921, nations once again.
If we in Canada look at eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, see that these kinds of things are happening in those areas of the world and support it saying it is a good thing, then I am certain, in order to be consistent, we have to look at what the aspirations of the aboriginal people are in this country, because what they want to be are nations once again.
Going into this new world that is being described by what is happening in Europe in 1991, in eastern Europe, and in the Soviet Union, Canada has a tremendous opportunity, to go into this world of the future, recognizing the sovereign peoples within the country and developing a method of negotiating with those people and making settlements and treaties with those people. Rather than having what Lord Durham, in 1839, called "two nations warring in the bosom of a single state" or what could be today compounded with the aboriginal question, "many nations warring in the bosom of a single state", Canada has an opportunity to establish a model for the world as to how one state can recognize the sovereign aspirations of its individual members to become even more powerful and strong and even more of a teacher to the world than Canada is today. Unfortunately, what has happened at Oka has set us back as being a teacher to the world a decade or a century.
I was hoping that when we came into this Parliament for this fall session the Prime Minister in some way would have relented and in the resolution he presented to the House he would have recognized the faults in leadership that were made during the summer and the faults in interpreting the Mohawks demands, which the Prime Minister characterized as bizarre in the same way the British characterized the sovereign ambitions of his ancestors when they were revolting against the British crown.
I would have hoped that the Prime Minister of Canada in this fall session would have presented to us a mechanism which would have allowed for the honourable disengagement of the conflict at Oka so that there would be a basis for friendly, open, and productive negotiations between Canada and Quebec and the Mohawk people at Kanesatake and Kahnawake, and so that we could recognize some of their sovereign aspirations and work out ways of realizing some those aspirations while keeping this nation strong and united.
I remind the House that the country from which the Prime Minister's family originated is now one of the greatest supporters and allies of the country that it formerly opposed and rose up in arms against. There is a possibility of solution in this situation. Unfortunately, I cannot see any possibility in the current resolution, other than carrying on and making the dispute worse.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. I am especially concerned and interested in the government's resolution which is before the House because of the great concern that has existed in the many Indian reserves which are located in the Algoma constituency. I know that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who has just spoken represents bands in British Columbia. One of the special features about the whole situation which has existed this past summer is that right across the country, with bands from east to west, people are very concerned about what has happened.
The problems have arisen primarily because the government failed to act and resolve the issues with regard to land claims during the spring and summer months and the whole situation has deteriorated into one of the worst crises that I think we have seen. It has not only hurt us abroad, it has hurt relationships between with aboriginal peoples within our own country. I just hope that the efforts which are being made for negotiations will be enhanced and increased. I believe that there is concern and frustration building that will cause an incredible explosion among aboriginal peoples and Canadians generally if the matter is not resolved peacefully.
Our representative here in the House has called for a royal commission to look into the problems and difficulties that have arisen. A similar motion was passed by the Massey Town Council calling for a royal commission during this situation this past couple of months. To the credit of the bands in the Algoma district and Manitoulin district, there were a number of demonstrations along Highway 17, at Massey and at Garden River by the
September 25, 1990

Garden River Band, the Spanish River Band and the Wikwemikong Band, and they were all very peaceful. They were done on the basis of expressing the concern which aboriginal peoples felt with the situation as it has developed in Oka and in the way it was allowed to deteriorate.
We got a lot of wise advice from bands such as the Wikwemikong band where they were pleading that the Armed Forces not be used against First Nations. They were calling for negotiations to settle the underlying treaty and aboriginal claims problems, that the Surete du Quebec be kept at bay, and that the frustrations that were there be dealt with on a peaceful basis.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has outlined in his speech, I think this is a very serious matter that requires negotiation and a peaceful settlement so that we can get on with solving the underlying problems that have caused great anxiety and frustration among aboriginal peoples throughout the country-not just in Oka and Kanesatake and the bands in and around Montreal, but right across the country, including my own districts of Algoma and Manitoulin.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Is there a comment from the hon. member from Comox-Alberni?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure there is a question there, but certainly I have a response to the comment.
I think different aboriginal nations approach dealings with the government in different ways and there certainly are concerns among different nations as to what is happening in the Montreal area.
The Mohawks come from a very unique and different tradition. The incidents that have taken place very much reflect the tradition from which those people come and very much reflect the strong belief that they have based on treaties going back into the mists of time that recognized, on the part of the British crown, their sovereignty and ability to operate as a nation, to make war, and to conclude peace. One has to recognize that what is happening in Montreal is part of a unique Mohawk tradition.
Government Orders
There are other traditions across Canada and, in fact, many of the native nations in my province have preferred a route that does not involve the use of arms but the use of negotiation by sitting down and concluding treaties in that way.
However, I have to suggest that there is a frustration developing among the people in British Columbia that the longer the government delays, the more problems there will be for people to negotiate settlements at the negotiating table. More and more people will see the alternative taken by the Mohawk warriors as the way to go-
The Prime Minister's statement today-and I take him at his word-might lead to some breaking of the log-jam and hopefully some possibility, if the government lives up to its promises, of settling aboriginal claims against the Crown more quickly and more effectively.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the House reconvened we have spent some time discussing the situation at Oka, but what we have not done is taken affirmative action to find a peaceful solution to the problem.
Canada has been viewed traditionally as a leading force in promoting and defending human rights. We have earned a fine reputation at the international level, so we cannot continue to ignore our problems at home. We must address the plight of our native people, not just at Oka, but throughout Canada.
This issue has a far-reaching effect. Natives and non-native Canadians alike have voiced their concerns, and the eyes of the world are watching with interest to see how we resolve this crisis. At a time when many of the world's so-called closed countries are opening up, it is vital that we restore Canada's image as a diplomatic and caring nation. We must address the concerns of our native people and put fair and workable solutions ahead of taking arms in our hands.
We are traditionally a peaceful nation and must prove, not just to the world, but to ourselves that we can put aside our differences and negotiate.
Madam Speaker, the government must take positive steps to deal with native issues. We cannot afford to ignore justice, fairness and recognition of our native

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
rights. I call on the Prime Minister to get involved and find a peaceful solution and I call on the government to take affirmative action now and set up this royal commission which my colleague has been calling for.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I actually have a question for my colleague, the member for Comox-Albemi.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member will have a conversation with his colleague from Winnipeg-'Transcona. It does happen that someone from the same party does ask a question.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
You could not resist, Madam Speaker, could you. I will have a discussion with my colleague.
My question for my colleague from Comox-Alberni deals with the underlying issue of land claims. I heard the hon. member speak at a meeting on Manitoulin Island this spring of the northern council of the NDP. At that time he explained the economic impact on the region of a completed land claim.
I wonder if he might inform members of the House as well as those people watching of the positive aspects of why we as a society should finally deal with our aboriginal peoples and settle these outstanding land claims, some of which go back as long as this country has existed and even before.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
I was interested in a statement made earlier today by the member for Nunat-siaq, discussing what actually happens during a land claim. When the Prime Minister was making his speech, he indicated that land was being given to the Indians. In fact, when a land claim is settled Canada takes land from the Indians, gives them a bit of the remnant over which they have control and compensates them for the balance. So Canada is always the greatest beneficiary in a land claim settlement, or what the Prime Minister referred to as a modem treaty. Canada reaps the greatest benefit.
I would also like to point out that if you read the details of the framework agreement of the treaty for the Council of Yukon Indians, you will find that over the ten-year period that the Indians have agreed to take compensation, they have also agreed to phase out all of the exemptions from taxes that they enjoyed as a result of the previous arrangement they had with the federal government when the land claims were unsettled. That is an advantage to the Canadian people.
Another thing that happens and is clearly evident, for example in northern settlements, is that in the past forest and mining companies and oil companies have gone into the north, taken resources, taken profits and taken them to Montreal, New York or elsewhere in the world and discapitalized the area.
By settling land claims you are giving an opportunity for people who have lived in those areas from 8,000 to 13,000 years and are unlikely ever to move away, to spend that capital in the area in which they live so that it has the effect of recapitalizing areas that were previously discapitalized under the old system of Canadian economics.
We now see that native corporations own things like First Air and Air Quebec. They are forming their own transportation agencies, corporations, mining companies and trading agencies. Those things benefit all Canadians from the point of view of income, as well as from employment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: The period for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate. The hon. member for Chateauguay.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before I start, I would like to mention that I intend to take the full 20 minutes to which I am entitled, although this would hardly be enough if I were to talk about all the issues and all the pain and suffering the people of Chateauguay had to endure during the long so-called Amerindian conflict.
First of all, Madam Speaker, I would like to situate the riding of Chateauguay. It contains the largest and most heavily populated Mohawk Indian reserve in Canada. As you know, it is located southwest of the city of Montreal, just across the Mercier Bridge, where they set up one of the biggest barricades. The riding continues along the St. Lawrence in a westerly direction. This is a particularly beautiful and picturesque spot, a lovely contrast to the rest of the riding. I am not saying this because I happen to have the honour of representing Chateauguay but this riding is one of the most beautiful in Canada.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Now I would like to speak more directly to the subject at hand. So far, I was very surprised at the way my colleagues handled this topic. One after the other, they made some very eloquent and well-structured speeches, and I realize I have a lot to learn before I
September 25, 1990

reach that level. Of course most of these speeches were probably written by someone else, but in any case, they were very eloquent.
Everybody is talking about rights this evening, but not a word about duties. In our society, we have rights, and I think that is a very good thing, but we also have duties. And we tend to forget we cannot have one without the other. We are kidding ourselves if we claim we have certain rights and don't recognize the fact we have duties as well.
Speaking of rights, some Indians have been vigorously demanding the right to free movement-free movement of goods, persons, and so forth. Oddly enough, the same people who talk about free movement set up those blockades on bridges and highways. It seems to me they do not always practise what they preach. There is a very clear contradiction here.
If they want free movement, it seems to me that setting up barricades is not the way to go about it, and the people I have the honour to represent in Chateau-guay and the general area realize that. These people have not been able to move freely for over two months. There seems to be a double standard here.
Madam Speaker, I want to say that I have absolutely nothing against the Indians or the Mohawks who live in my riding. Far from it! I am proud to represent them and I am proud to be of service to them now and then. Even though this may sound contradictory, every week in my riding office I see more than fifty of them who ask for information and every kind of services. Rest assured that they are always and will always be welcome in my riding office.
But unfortunately another small group has infiltrated this group of Mohawks, most of them law-abiding citizens. I must say that perhaps-I am even sure of that-all these people are not even Indians residing in Canada. As you know the unfortunate reality is that we have to import a good many things, but we could probably have done without this kind of trouble.
I have another comment to make. The previous speaker dealt very briefly with the matter, namely the fact that our international reputation has been hard hit,
Government Orders
tarnished, and perhaps it is no longer as good as it once was. This would be very unfortunate if it were to be true.
I come from a country called Spain which is in Europe but which is now part of what is now known as the European Parliament. A few days ago in this European Parliament they voted on a resolution condemning Canada and singling us out for badly treating our minorities. Madam Speaker, unequivocally and unhesitantly I could tell you that Canada does not have to take a lesson from anybody whatsoever, not even Europeans.
I visited all the European countries, Madam Speaker, and lived in fifty-odd countries.
I should know. I can tell you that there is not a single country in the world that can compare with Canada, not one which has so much respect for its minorities and grant them so many privileges. It seems today that for people to belong to a minority is almost like having a certified cheque in their pockets, because everybody has rights. They only have to mention that they belong to a minority for the authorities to get on the defensive, for fear of being accused of racism, even when it is not the case.
During the so-called Native crisis in Chateauguay, I heard a number of reporters in the media accusing some Chateauguay citizens, if not all of them, of racism. But let us look at the facts. How could the Chateauguay people be accused of racism when they chose to elect as their representative a member of a minority. It is impossible! Nobody can be accused of racism in Chateauguay, in the whole area which I have the honour to represent or in its vicinity. Otherwise, I would not be here talking to you. I just cannot understand how some people could come to the conclusion that the peole in Chateauguay are racists.
In all this situation which was quite above me, something happened which I did not like at all. It was the day when some Ville LaSalle people, near Chateauguay, displayed quite an unfortunate behaviour. They were reported having thrown rocks at Natives leaving the reserve.
Madam Speaker, it is clear that violence must be condemned, no matter where it originates. I do not condone the actions of these people. But we should be realistic and understand the situation. Why did these people behave that way? It was somewhat in response to

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
another action. You know that it is very easy to condemn the majority by calling it all sorts of names. But in all logic and fairness, we must then also condemn the other side and ask for an investigation because Indians also threw stones, in fact not just stones, but projectiles.
They caused irreparable damage to property as well as to human beings. So, to be consistent I agree that there should be an investigation, of course, and that those responsible for such disgraceful behaviour should be tried and punihed. I fail to see how we could justify being so tough with a group of people whose actions were much less serious than those of others but who are singled out while everything else is forgotten.
I find it very hard, Madam Speaker, to accept that type of justice which really borders on injustice. Sad to say but what can we do. There is no escaping reality.
Anyone acting as did some of the Mohawks in Kahnawake who held a whole community hostage, who put up barricades on bridges and highways, should not realistically expect to be welcomed with open arms. That is unthinkable. There is no doubt that of all the people in the world, none are more calm, patient and tolerant than Quebecers. I should know. To put up with me sure takes a lot of patience! Yet, they elected me once in 1984, reelected me in 1988 and will elect me again in 1993 and so on, at least I hope so.
Our people have suffered enormously. I have urged our government to try and help them with some compensation for all or part of the losses they have suffered. Throughout this crisis, businesses and plants of all kinds had to close up. Let us mention only the case of a Chateauguay restaurant called Le restaurant rustique. It is well known across Canada and even the whole of North America, if I am not mistaken. The staff was reduced from 100 to 15. Imagine, 85 jobs were lost in a single restaurant. That means 85 families suffering the consequences of the crisis. There are farmers, carriers-
In the riding of Chateauguay, and more particularly in the city of Chateauguay, nearly half of the population goes to work in Montreal. These people commute via the Mercier bridge morning and night. To a large extent, they have been deprived of their work. Some have lost their job. So, I hope that my government will listen to the people of Chateauguay who are requesting financial
assistance for the area, by way of grants or whatever, because it is well know that many companies starting up request at the same time grants from the government. In this case, the government should say: "Your request will be considered, but you must settle in Chateauguay." The government usually tries to help when disaster strikes here or there. Well, I think that is our country I am talking about here. So we should be given the same consideration.
The truth is that, whatever our efforts to help people "recover" and to compensate for the losses they have suffered, it will never be enough. Their losses are too great and, in some instances, can not be quantified. For instances, there was a time when developers may have wanted to buy land here for industries. Well, they will prefer to look elsewhere. They probably went elsewhere. That lack of confidence can not be quantified, and there is no way of knowing how many jobs or millions of dollars were lost because of that. We know full well that we have lost a lot, and the hardship will persist for a long time in the population once the crisis is over.
I have a message for the Indian leaders. The chiefs have always advocated peaceful solutions, conciliation and good example. I would like to ask them this. If, in fact, you wish to remain credible, why not tell right now the Warriors behind the barricades to surrender immediately and to face the justice system. It seems to me that, by that action-despite the fact that some chiefs have already lost some credibility, but they may regain it at least partially-, they could put a stop to all that madness, I call it "madness of the century". There are also women and children behind the barricades, children who could go back to school and start leading a normal life again. And we too, as Canadian taxpayers, would stop paying for a totally irrational thing. Some estimate the total cost of the dammages in the billions of dollars. We cannot do that; we cannot afford it.
I appreciated what the prime minister said today, namely that they have to face justice. I agree with that. In our country, there should be only one justice. As long as it is enforced; otherwise, it is nothing but a sieve. I do not believe that our population deserves being harassed as injustly as this. Land claims I understand. But others claims are made as well. I have heard about requests for
September 25, 1990

a new reservation in Oka. I am very reluctant to agree with that.
To my mind, reservations are synonymous in many cases with ghettos. This is a solution which can create problems, as we have seen it. Creating a new reservation would amount to creating a new problem, and we already have enough problems. I quite agree that Indians should be treated fairly, the same as anybody else, but creating reservations around cities can only lead to problems for the future.
I hope the government will not fall into that trap which to me would be a serious mistake. I agree that Indians should be treated fairly. But to create problems in an attempt to solve other issues would be a mistake, Madam Speaker. No problem is solved by the creation of another. I thank you for your patient attention, Madam Speaker. I also hope also that my government will listen to me and take the matter under consideration, once the crisis is over. We cannot look back. However there is one thing the government could do now is to give some sort of compensation to the people who have been a victimized through no fault of theirs.

Madam Speaker, I would first of all like to salute the member. His speech tonight was obviously based on his first-hand experience this summer. I am sure it was very tough for him and his constituents.
I must tell the hon. member that there are many things he said this evening that I agreed with. No one in this country wanted to see a community go through frustration and inconvenience. Many people in my riding would phone every day and they could not understand what was going on. They could not figure out why there was so much tension.
It concerned me as well, Madam Speaker, and I must tell you that last week I went to Oka. I listened to some residents of Oka who were Mohawks. For someone living in Toronto the obvious question is: How did this all get started?
I was told by friendly Mohawks, not warriors with armed guns; I believe in the rule of law-about the background of the frustrations that were going on vis-a-vis the golf course, the 94 acres, and the municipal-
Government Orders
ity proceeding and totally ignoring some of the warnings that were given by members of this House.
Then I was told about how these barricades were set up near Oka and that on a particular day a group of mothers and children from the reservation were at a prayer ceremony and were confronted by the Surete du Quebec. How it happened or why it happened, obviously none of us in this Chamber want to judge right now, but shots were fired and to the great regret of everyone in this Chamber and in this nation a police officer lost his life. In the process of that experience everyone became frightened. The native community became frightened, the people of the area became frightened, and everyone got their backs up.
In no way, shape or form am I condoning ignoring the rule of law here, but I must tell you, Madam Speaker- and this is where I am heading with my question-that I went there last week to seek answers to questions to find out what was going on.
I was invited by two Mohawk residents of Oka to come into the community. As the cars approached the barricade by the Trappist Monastery, there were many people who got through the barricade. The press got through the barricade. I went there and I was stopped because I did not live in the community.
I was very polite to the police officer of the Surete du Quebec and I said with humility: "I am a parliamentarian. I have hundreds of constituents who are asking me: Are you asking questions? Are you getting answers? What is the point of view?'" I must say that I felt great tension and resentment from the people manning those barricades, not our Armed Forces. I found the Canadian Armed Forces to be very positive in their attitude and accommodating. That part of the Prime Minister's resolution I support, but there is some mystery here why the Prime Minister does not mention the other forces that are involved.
I personally encountered a very rough experience with the police force. We talk about decency and rule of law. What about the men who are holding those positions? The Prime Minister talked about masked men and guns today, but sometimes when we ask a person who is masked why he is masked, we find out that he is masked because he is afraid and he does not want to be intimidated or caught or whatever.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
Do you know, Madam Speaker, that I asked the officers of the Surete du Quebec if they would give me their numbers and they refused to do it? This is true. I am not trying to be difficult here. This is an absolute truth. Thank God I had cameras because I took their pictures. The law has to go both ways. These men refused. Their attitude promoted tension.
The hon. member mentioned development, tourism and other things that are important to the economic health of this country and that we must have galvanized communities. Does he not think that there is room for improvement in the attitude of the Surete du Quebec and those people who come into contact with them in relation to this crisis?

Mr. Speaker, there are several aspects to the question of my colleague and I will try to deal with them as best I can.
I deplore the fact that a parliamentarian cannot have access to what is going on on the other side of the barricades while a lot of other people do get through. In my opinion parliamentarians are just as good as any spiritual leader or any of the journalists. I am really sorry he could not go behind the barricades and see for himself what was going on so he could keep his constituents well informed.
It is quite deplorable. But you know, at times throughout this crisis the Quebec Provincial Police behaved impeccably, but they did act irresponsibly now and then. I am referring to the incident on the Saint-Louis-de-Gonzague bridge when a group of citizens blockaded the bridge and were rather savagely man handled by the police. Worse still, after the police ordered them off the site the people obeyed but the officers continued to hit them from behind and did some damage to their cars. I thought they acted like barbarians and savages.
But I can tell you that during the Indian crisis, as it is called, during these two months most of the time the QPP did an outstanding job. I want to thank them and pay tribute to them.
However you know that in the QPP as in any other police force there are good officers and others who are not so good. The experience you had was truly unfortunate and I deplore the situation as much as you do, but we should not blame every single QPP officer.
I want to say a few words about the other authority on the site, namely the Canadian Army. My hat is off to them! I knew that Canadian soldiers were highly competent, very human, well disciplined, but never to that extent. I think that just as I am doing all my fellow citizens and all Canadians will have to pay tribute to the Canadian Army.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to the motion of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In this motion the House is urged to
Government Orders
commend the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian Forces at Oka and Chateauguay.
The motion also mentions "That, in the opinion of this House, the laws of Canada must apply on all Canadian territory, including Kahnawake, and that all persons currently at the Kanesatake Treatment Centre should lay down their arms and submit to the processes of Canada's judicial system, thereby encouraging the creation of a constructive climate for discussions between governments and the Mohawk people on land claims and other issues;"
I am pleased to see the government has decided to have a debate on this important matter. However, I seriously question the government's refusal this summer to recall Parliament to discuss the conflict. It was high time the government woke up.
Mr. Speaker, what is particularly shocking about this whole affair is the government's inertia, its failure to act. It is clear the Conservatives have made a complete hash of the situation. They tried to ignore the conflict, hoping it would just go away. Unfortunately, problems that are ignored tend to get worse. In any case, the native blockade is a very complex matter and will take a lot of effort and imagination if it is to be resolved in the best interests of all parties.
Native people do not live in very fortunate circumstances. Just look at the statistics.

Mr. Speaker, I will just quote a few statistics. Reserve Indians have the lowest average personal income in Canada. Unemployment rates hover around 70 per cent and on some reserves the rate is as high as 90 per cent. Infant mortality rates for Indians are double the Canadian rates. Thirty-eight per cent of Indian homes on reserves have no central heating. The life expectancy of male and female Indians, aboriginals, is much lower than other Canadians. These statistics tell us a sad story. As the member for Western Arctic explained this morning in her eloquent speech, the native people of Canada do not need tear gas to make them cry.
The government has said that it wished to commend the exemplary work of the Canadian forces. That is fine, but how do we know that this is so because there is now a new blockade that has been set up that not many people have talked about today. That new blockade-just add an

Government Orders
"s" to the word "new" and you have a "news" blockade and that is where the problem is right now. I believe that this motion we are dealing with today does not deal with all of the issues and that one issue is very important.
What are the implications of a news blockade? Need I remind everyone present and those viewing that freedom of the press is one of the pillars upon which our society rests. This situation, this news blockade, undermines the public's right to know. How can we be expected to treat this situation rationally if we are denied the basic facts which are provided to us by the media? Censorship in any form is reprehensible. It undermines the foundation of democracy and, sad to say, paves the way to dictatorship. In fact, the media have a role to play and it should be unfettered.
What is truly amazing, Mr. Speaker, is that every time the Prime Minister is confronted by a crisis he tries to shift the blame. It is always someone else's fault. You will agree that this is a singular demonstration of lack of leadership. He has even had the gall to blame our party and even our leader. I want to make it clear that the Hon. Jean Chretien has done a great deal more about this situation than the Prime Minister will ever hope to do.
Let me outline just a few of those things. On July 20, Mr. Chretien went to Oka. He got in and he spoke to the Mohawks. Did the Prime Minister go? No. I do not know whether the Prime Minister has any intention of going.
On July 25, the Hon. Jean Chretien called together a special caucus committee to hear witnesses, to hear the concerns and try to find solutions that would come from consensus and understanding.
He also announced that the Senate committee on aboriginal peoples would meet and hear witnesses. Again, the Liberal Party was acting immediately. Mr. Chretien also called a national press conference on August 7. So that has all been done. He has been active on this issue.
The Liberal Party made numerous requests throughout the summer for the recall of Parliament. Many MPs have written to the Prime Minister asking for that recall.
I wrote a letter. I asked for a royal commission to be appointed and that a mediator be appointed. I said: "By failing to act on this matter the government has allowed the crisis to spread to other parts of the country and as a result fuelled an already volatile climate of intolerance". That was July 20.
I want to mention other actions taken by our members. On July 29, the Hon. Herb Gray and our critic for aboriginal affairs, the member from Western Arctic, also visited Oka to get a firsthand view. Did our Prime Minister go? No.
I believe that the Prime Minister has to start taking some responsibility. He tends to blame everyone else. The Prime Minister has to get out of his cocoon and stop playing hide and seek with these issues. I know his advisers have probably advised him that his poll ratings are so low he should keep a low profile, take a break for the summer. My gosh, he took them at their word. It is about time that the Prime Minister met his responsibilities.
I like to give a little bit of credit where it is due also. I was glad to see the Prime Minister enter the debate this afternoon. He made some comments in regard to what some of the actions will be on behalf of his government. I hope that he can come up with more specific solutions to the problems at Oka and Chateauguay.
I would also like to talk a little bit about my riding. Although the Oka crisis has monopolized a great deal of the media's attention, it is only the tip of the iceberg. In fact, there have been many demonstrations held by natives right across Canada over the last little while. Obviously they are a direct result of the federal government's failure to address the settlement of land claims and the demands of aboriginal organizations for selfgovernment.
In my riding of Restigouche-Chaleur, the Micmacs at the Eel River Bar Reserve blockaded Route 134 near the town of Dalhousie, New Brunswick in late July. They did this in order to manifest a solidarity and sympathy to the Mohawks. Although their original purpose was a show of
September 25, 1990

solidarity, Micmacs decided to exert a little more pressure for some of the outstanding claims and grievances that they had which were mostly with the provincial government. These grievances included the loss of fishing, water rights, as well as the employment question.
While speaking of the employment question, I would like to say that since unemployment is so pervasive among local natives, one of the things that they would like to see is more flexibility in the training programs, and in employment and immigration programs. I would like to see more flexibility with that and I would hope that the Minister of Employment and Immigration would note that.
There was a problem in my riding. They were trying to put pressure on the provincial government. What did the provincial government do? Unlike the federal government, the New Brunswick Government stepped in to help find a quick and peaceful solution to the blockade. They sent four ministers on site to meet with the Eel River Band Council and with those who were involved with the blockade-right on site. Four ministers went right in there and cleared it up. The aboriginal people were satisfied with the commitments they received from the New Brunswick government. Obviously the federal government should take some lessons on crisis management from the New Brunswick government.
I would like to congratulate the RCMP who handled the situation in my area in an excellent manner, the Micmacs of the Eel River Reserve, the band council, the chief, the local population for their patience and understanding, and certainly the provincial ministers who went in there to alleviate the situation as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the conflict in Oka and other demonstrations held by native people across Canada are a direct result of the federal government's failure to deal with land claims and requests for autonomous government by native organizations.
The Mohawks in Oka have tried, unsuccessfully, to obtain recognition of their claims. The government says the Mohawks do not have title since time immemorial to the lands around Oka and that the King of France
Government Orders
granted these lands to the Seminary of Saint-Sulpice, thus extinguishing the rights of the Mohawks.
The Mohawks and their legal advisors believe that recent judgments by the Supreme Court of Canada in the Sparrow and Sioui cases might provide new ways to support their land claims. According to these judgments, the courts are to apply a broad interpretation of subsection 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, and reject exception of so-called legal severance which has proved a stumbling block for many comprehensive claims.
The federal government has neglected to amend its land claims policy to reflect the recommendations of its own task force on comprehensive land claims, and it has refused to acknowledge the precedents created by recent court judgments on these matters, hence the conflict at Oka.
Already guilty by omission, the federal government, as a result of its complete failure to act, made matters in Oka and Chateauguay far worse.
Finally, when it was obliged to intervene, the federal government purchased the land in question from Oka and declared that it would resume negotiations with the Mohawks as soon as they took down the barricades and laid down their weapons. It also approved Quebec's request for bringing in the army, thus showing that it preferred to endanger lives instead of negotiating.
The actions of the federal government show that it is weak and that it will not resume negotiations unless threatened with a confrontation. It will not adjust its policies to reflect recent court decisions.

It is very important that the government realizes that it is a serious affair we are facing. It is important that it takes action. It is nice to put a nice motion on the floor here, but it is only a motion. We need action. I would only hope that the Prime Minister in his speech this afternoon was more than sincere and can convey a type of trust, not only the Mohawk people, but to all Canadians because Canadians are very concerned.
In conclusion, I would again call upon the government if at all possible to appoint a royal commission on aboriginal affairs to look at the whole question right

Government Orders
across Canada once and for all to see if we can come up with some solid solutions that would be acceptable to everyone.
I would also think that a public enquiry is a necessity. It is a necessity because there are so many unanswered questions. There are so many Canadians out there who are asking the questions: How did this happen? How did it happen in Canada?
As an immediate step in the right direction, I would hope that the Prime Minister would appoint a group of parliamentarians to go to the treatment centre to explain to some of the movement the government is planning, if it is planning any and to discuss with them their continuing concerns. An all-party group of parliamentarians must be sent to Oka to visit the treatment centre to help to resolve this conflict in a peaceful and acceptable fashion.

speechtext:
Having listened with considerable interest to the comments he has just made, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell my colleague the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur that I followed the events in Oka and Kahnawake all summer long because, like him, I have within my riding Native communities whose leaders and inhabitants were quite concerned about the goings on in Oka.
Having had the opportunity to talk several times with the elected leaders of the Montagnais communities within my riding, I can say that they found the situation very difficult because these hardworking and peaceloving people had managed over the past few years to implement a whole series of programs and set up various organizations which allowed them to assume their own shelter, educational and economic developments. If they were concerned about the action taken by a number of people within the Kanesatake and Kahnawake communities, it is because they feared they might lose the trust and credibility they enjoy within the other North Shore communities.
I am sure that, just like I did, he followed the development of this very difficult situation with considerable interest and that he was concerned about its possible consequences.
I have two questions for my colleague the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur. This afternoon, our colleague from Western Arctic referred to the Federal Government's fiduciary role with respect to the Native people of Canada. Although he certainly agrees, as I do, about the fact that the Federal Government plays a fiduciary role with respect to our First Nations and that it is responsible for ensuring their welfare, development and security, would he admit that this fiduciary role does not entail condoning actions such as those taken by the Warriors in Oka over the past summer? I fully agree that the federal Government is responsible for ensuring their security, welfare and development in every respect, as well as their full participation in Canadian life, of Canada, but I think it is going a little too far to suggest that the government of Canada condones such actions as those taken this year in Oka. So, I would like him to comment on that.
My second question to my colleague from Restigouche-Chaleur is this. He praised earlier the actions of his leader, the leader of the Liberal Party, during the summer. I would like to know if he agrees with the statement made by his leader to the effect that the Warriors should be free to leave, so they can be recaptured two days later.
Those were my two questions, Mr. Speaker.

thank you for that question, Mr. Speaker. Certainly, it is the responsibility of the federal government, as fiduciary, to protect the interests of the natives. I can tell you that I have disliked actions from both sides in Oka and Chateauguay in some instances, but I will not be the judge of that.
The other question deals with the policy concerning the 20 Warriors at the treatment center. There were 200 Warriors. So, where are the others? The Quebec government has let them run away. The federal government, your government, let them go. There are only 20 left. Where are all the others?
You have already implemented the same policy, a policy of carelessness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I acceded my spot to my hon. colleague from Broadview- Greenwood but I would like to take this opportunity to thank my colleague from Restigouche-Chaleur, first, for a very interesting speech and, second, for raising the issue of the news media black-out.
If anything could define a modern democratic society in today's world, it is, among other things, the freedom of association, the freedom of the press, and the kinds of institutions that allow full disclosure. I was very pleased to see him note that.
I was wondering how the hon. member reacted in Question Period today when the Minister of National Defence in a sense let us feel that the journalists who are on the scene essentially are part of the problem and not part of the people who could enable a better understanding and promote goodwill between people.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must thank my colleague for her question and her kind words. As I mentioned before, that new blockade that was set up, the news blockade, is certainly a problem. It has created a mistrust out there. It has created a situation in which some of the people behind the barricade are afraid in a sense that the information that is getting out from there might be a little different than what actually the facts are. There are a lot of things.
I happened to see a couple of news programs one day when some of the media were throwing their films to try get them out. There seemed to be a mad scuttle there to try to get them. In fact, in one case I saw the film taken away from someone who was trying to pick it up. It seemed to be someone in a uniform, so I wonder what we have to hide.
Some of the communication that is going on between the Armed Forces and the warriors in the treatment centre is by a sort of an educated mode, I guess. They use rocks. They tie their letter to a rock and throw it in. They throw it back and forth. It is not the way to act.
If we want a peaceful settlement, we must develop an air of confidence, of trust and I really think-

We should send a parliamentary committee in Oka to talk to the Mohawks, review their situation in Oka and see if they are ready to disengage under reasonable terms.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Restigouche-Chaleur.
He mentioned in his closing remarks how trust is really a key issue here.
I get many letters from my constituents. Today, I received one where the constituent talked about the fact that the native way of life was probably the original example of a sustainable society. Those of us who profess to be environmentalists are uttering words not worth a hill of beans if you do not immediately start to resolve native land claims issues. Probably many in this House do not realize but our member from Restigouche-Chaleur when he was working on Bill C-39, the forestry issue, forced the members of that committee to come up with the first definition of sustainable development that any act related to the environment in this Parliament of Canada has had, and I salute him for that.
My question is very specific. In keeping with his focused attention on sustainable development, does he not agree with those constituents who are saying that we in this chamber really cannot profess to be serious about the environment unless we begin looking after Canada's first environmentalists. I would like him to respond to that.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me a chance to reply to this question. I must thank my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood for the first question and his kind comments as well. I might hire him as a publicity agent to do some promotion.
I must say that it is true without going overboard with it. I think if we look at the state of our environment, not only here in Canada but around the world, we will find that it is a precarious state. I think if we turn back a leaf and look to our aboriginal people we will see how they managed the environment. They did not necessarily manage, but their attitude is so different. Attitude is one of the biggest environmental problems in the world, not only of a politician, but of normal everyday people who

Government Orders
are not willing to have their life styles change. They are not willing to make sacrifices. I think we can take many examples, not only from our own aboriginals here but from other peoples and other countries. I think it is very important that we use and take advantage of that situation while we can. As I mentioned, the environment is in a precarious position.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will start with one of my questions. I will give ask the hon. member the second question and I hope he will answer very briefly. I know when you are last to ask a question, there is not much time.
My colleague just said we should have a committee go to Oka to speak with the Mohawks. Well, I have been here all day and I have been listening to the speeches. Everyone spoke about the Indians and the Mohawks. I have the proper respect for that, but not one person spoke about the white people, those who lost their homes and belongings. I have been there. I had no problem going through the barricades. I have friends there.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: What's your point?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
My point is that when we talk and we tiy to solve a problem, we have two kinds of peoples to solve it. There is the respect we have when we speak. I saw Miss Gabriel speaking on TV. We have to respect our fundamental rights. Yes, but what about mine? What about my people who are there who lost everything? I do not think the committee should be there.

I would have another question, Mr. Speaker. Quebec had, and it still has, a great poet called Felix Leclerc, who said: "The surest way to kill someone is to pay him to do nothing". It is true that Canada is the fiduciary. We give money. That is very well, but there comes a time when you wonder if it would not be better to give responsibilities and dignity. So, if a committee is to go to Oka to solve the problem, I would want the basic rights of the people on both sides of the barricade to be respected. What good does talking do? People I know there told me they do not want to go back to their homes.
There is a problem: The most beautiful village in Quebec was destroyed. This is what the problem is: We can see only one side at a time. I therefore want my colleague to tell me if the government will continue providing money and nothing but money, not dignity for instance? Shall a word be put in for the other people whose houses were damaged? I would like to hear what my colleague has to say on that.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to answer the first question with regard to not only listening to the Mohawks, we must listen to all Canadians, I think that is important. I think that is being done in each riding on that issue and I would hope that this all-party committee would also listen to the concerns of the other side, if we can call it the other side.
The hon. member stated that no one has talked about that. I must point out that my hon. colleague and friend, the member for LaSalle-Emard, in Question Period asked about money to compensate the people who were put out because of the Chateauguay issue and Oka issue and residents on both sides of the river, all around the whole region, including natives and non-natives. He addressed that issue quite well and I must congratulate him on that.

I also want to tell you that I agree with you. We cannot keep on spending money without accounting for our actions but it is important that responsible programs be developed. Different programs are tested here and there. There are training programs. I have talked about those in my speech: We need training programs but training programs that are a little more flexible for aboriginal people. That would certainly be a start.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address this House on a motion respecting the situation in Oka and Chateauguay. This situation, with all its unpleasant and very serious threats to life, at times threats to innocent lives, happened for a reason.
If we put aside all the bad and negative feelings, what was the purpose and, indeed, what have we learned?

It is easy to point fingers and criticize. It is easy to look back and complain. What I think we ought to do though, is look ahead and ask ourselves, what is it that we must do now to heal the bad relations that have developed? What is it that we can do to seek positive solutions?
In retrospect, let us review the Kanesatake and Kahnawake situations. As one who has been involved directly with the advancement of native rights, seeking to do it positvely, I think I know and appreciate the frustration that my native leaders have felt. It is, nevertheless, unfortunate and sad that it has led to the taking up of arms.
The positive signal that this summer, difficult as it was, has sent to Indian country is that national unity and support behind a common cause is possible, just imagine what can be accomplished if the same energy can be expended toward positive goals.
An equally important result from this summer's incidents is that Indian issues are now on the national forefront. Before I propose some recommendations, as other members have done, may I remind the House of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and its second report. In that report, having heard witnesses, including National Indian Leadership, what the committee identified is an agenda for the 1990s. I quote from the report:
The committee invites all Canadians to become aware of the issues that face aboriginal Canadians, because these issues do not affect aboriginal Canadians alone. These issues affect all Canadians. They affect the future strength, prosperity, sense of fairness and tolerance that allows all Canadians to define themselves.
The committee also invites all Canadians to participate, each in their own way, to advance these issues. Awareness of aboriginal issues and challenges is a necessary first step.
I am very encouraged by the Prime Minister's statement a few minutes ago and I quote in part that: "It is time to put the Indian agenda into operation-one anchored in reality". One that will bring back the native dignity the Prime Minister referred to in his address and other colleagues who referred to it a few minutes ago as well.
Let me briefly look at what to me is a very serious negative message that has been sent to the aboriginal communities. The media coverage, although there have
Government Orders
been recent comments in its defence, could have in my opinion been better in some reporting because the message that was being encouraged to the native youth across Canada is that "if you have a problem, take up a gun. If you disagree", the youth is now encouraged "to take up a machine gun or mount an armoured tank". That is not the kind of Canada I want.
Another negative aspect is the disrespect of leadership. Leaders in any community deserve more than to get beaten up in their own homes. When a chief is beaten up in his own home, there is a loss for everyone because such action does not solve the problems. On the other hand, neither is it right that provocative actions by soldiers be taken against unarmed women and children, be they native or not, particularly in a traditional longhouse.
I have throughout this crisis maintained that violence is not the answer. I called on my own people, as I do now, to give tolerance and patience another chance. Continue the dialogue. I along with members from the Western Arctic and Nunatsiaq have perhaps one of the most unique opportunities in this House. As one of our most respected elders Chief Dan George wrote, and I remind the members: "I am a chief, but my power to make war is gone, and the only weapon left to me is speech. It is only with tongue and speech that I can fight my people's war".
But what about the future? I am being told by my own councils to get in there and do something about Oka. Mohawk spokespersons said: "No, you stay away from here". When I had the opportunity to work with an ad hoc committee of cabinet ministers for many hours, other constituents said: "You are spending too much time on Indian issues". Amid all of this I met with Indian leaders to ask them: "We have all had a very challenging summer, now what do we do to bring both sides back together". I indicated to them some of the not too pleasant comments and calls that my staff and I received in our offices. During my constituency tour last week, virtually everyone we spoke with wanted an immediate peaceful solution to the Oka situation.
Importantly, however, Mr. Speaker, we have to regain the positive work that was underway and is underway across Indian country. Mr. Speaker, allow me to give you and the House four suggested recommendations which I have received from my own Indian leadership.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
First, review immediately the land claims process with a view of considering an independent body or tribunal. The original problem, as I understand it, that sparked the Oka incident was the land claim. There have been many criticisms of the process, there have been many supportive blockades across Canada. We do not need any more evidence to encourage us to change. What is seen as a one-sided unfair process can be changed for improvement and I am pleased the Prime Minister addressed that this afternoon.
Second, consider immediately a new round of discussions or meetings similar to the First Ministers Conference. What is being suggested, however, is that the federal government meet with national aboriginal leadership bilaterally to discuss our future relations. I do not have to add the constitutional, legal and other obligations previous members of these Chambers have referred to in support of this proposition.
Third, I think for the first time the aboriginal leadership is calling on government to replace the Indian Act. Let us look at the alternatives for a new, positive relationship. We need to restore Indian dignity and pride. I encourage the Prime Minister's initiative for changes in the new year which he has just announced.
Fourth, as others have called for a royal commission, a public inquiry or whatever the name, what is needed urgently is a complete and comprehensive review of Indian affairs at all levels including the management by Indian leadership. I believe we will find the rightful place of aboriginals in Canada with this kind of effort.
In conclusion, I urge both sides in the Oka crisis, their leadership in particular, to begin new deliberations. They should put aside the hurt feelings, painful though that may be, and put down the weapons on both sides. This is a beautiful country and peaceful co-existence is possible in such a vast land. I believe we can continue to share. I believe we can continue to live together. Indeed we must.
To my colleagues, through you, Mr. Speaker, let me say that this is not an issue upon which we play political gamesmanship. This is not a matter on which we put blame. This is a time for us to work together. It is possible to come up with one mind, as the Prime Minister said, when Canadians of good will decide. It is possible to work side by side to continue to build a
stronger, more united Canada. As one native person in this Chamber, that is all I ask.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to commend my hon. colleague who has just given such an eloquent speech and to talk about the way we should be viewing the questions that have arisen in this House this evening.
My hon. colleague mentioned four things that he had in mind as being very positive initiatives. Some of those have been spoken to earlier today by the Prime Minister. He thought there was a very positive initiative to replace the Indian Act. I am wondering what sort of model he sees in terms of dealing with this issue.
The Indian Act has been around for a long time. There have been many attempts to try to change it, but it seems to me that it has always been changed in a top down way where somebody who is white and perhaps does not have very much knowledge of what life is like on a reserve makes decisions for people who have to live them out. I wonder if my hon. colleague would perhaps expand on this point just a little.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for her question.
It is a question that we have tried to deal with over the years to counter what has been the process in the past to which she referred, that top down change. We have some experience where a committee can be struck, one that represents the Indian leadership, one that represents justice, one that represents Indian affairs. We can work away at legislative amendment together and do it in a way where changes can be hammered out in a room that affect all sides and, indeed, have input from all sides. Although we have heated discussions in such a process, once that kind of procedure is established the legislative amendment that comes forward from that process has always been accepted by all sides because all sides have had input. I would encourage that kind of forum be undertaken for any proposed legislative amendment.
