subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too join with my colleagues on the other side to compliment the previous speaker, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. Many times in this House we are torn between loyalties and the greatest loyalty that we can have, of course, is to Canada. In so saying, I know that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin had quite a burden to carry this summer, along with many other people in the House.
My question to him is quite straightforward. Does the hon. member believe that if we had acted more quickly at the beginning of the crisis, if the federal government as well as the provincial government had moved to alleviate the crisis earlier, might not all of this have indeed been put behind us so that what he is talking about, a return to dignity, would not have been necessary and that the people there would have kept their dignity throughout this whole crisis?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hindsight being perfect, when I look back, I suppose one could say that, yes, it would have been better had we acted faster. At the same time, as my colleagues have said, nobody knew what was going to happen. I think that everyone in their own way suggested remedies to deal with the issue but no one knew, for example, that over the past many months, at least from what I understand, people had been preparing with arms for such an event and just waited for the timing to be right. When I look back, sure I could have said yes. We could have dealt with it earlier.
I think the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs even tried in its attempts to air out such issues during the past year. As I said, I find it very unfortunate and sad that we have had to get this far where both sides have taken up arms. I can only hope and pray that in the future we do not do this again.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too want to say that I found speech of the member for Wetaskiwin to be very sensitive and genuine. I know he has been in a tough spot. I totally agree with him, as I think do all members of this House, that violence is not the answer.
Government Orders
I gather that at first he did condemn the use of the army. Perhaps he could clarify that.
The first part of the government's resolution starts right away by commending the exemplary conduct of the army at Oka and Chateauguay. I gather from the content of his speech when he talked about some of the things that went on there that he feels like us, a little uncomfortable that the government proceeded right away on its motion with sort of the law and order approach rather than proceed with what he did in his speech, talking about where do we go from here and what are the positive measures like moving on land claims that we could do. I would like to ask him to clarify that.
The second matter I want to ask him about is if he is aware of the report on Indian self-government by the 1983 Penner committee wherein the committee recommended that the federal government establish a new relationship with the Indian first nations and that an essential element in this relationship be the recognition of Indian self-government. The committee also recommended that the right of Indian peoples to self-government should be explicitly stated and entrenched in the Canadian Constitution, that the surest way to achieve permanent fundamental change in the relationship between Indian people and the federal government was by means of a constitutional amendment, and that Indian first nation governments would form a distinct order of government in Canada with their jurisdiction defined.
Could the member say whether he agrees with the Indian self-government? I know he talked briefly about it. Does he see that to be in any way contradictory to what the Prime Minister has been talking about when he is saying that all the laws of Canada must apply equally?
I do not think the Prime Minister has reached the stage, quite frankly, where he has in his own mind to recognize we need a really new deal with the native people which may mean recognizing, as the Americans have, a form of distinct aboriginal government.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question and the opportunity to clarify what I said about the army's role. I did not condemn bringing in the army because as I understand it the initial request or the purpose for calling in of the army was to have it act as a

Government Orders
peacekeeper or a mediator between the animosities on both sides: the Quebec police and the Mohawks.
When a joint request came forward for the army to be present I agreed with it. I condemned specific actions that I disagreed with, actions taken against unarmed women and children in a spiritual place like the long-house. That is what I do not agree with. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that you or any member would appreciate such actions being taken by anyone in a spiritual place. I could not agree with that.
With respect to the report on self-government, if I may give a very personal opinion, it is necessary to recognize, perhaps in legislation, the existence of Indian government. I hear, of course, the proposition that there is only one law in Canada. In the Criminal Code there is one law, but the native people also have a criminal code and a criminal law, a code that is not written. Sadly it is one that is not recognized either. I do not think in my society, under our laws at home, that if a person commits a crime he can expect to get away with it. I do not think that is what is being requested.
Yes, we do have an Indian government, but we lack recognition. Perhaps a constitutional amendment recognizing that would be a simple step forward.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for his comments and I share with him the soul and the toughness of his position.
When the crisis broke I was overseas-and I have travelled extensively-and as soon as people talked to me they realized that I was from North America and asked me: "Are you from Canada or are you from the United States?" Every time I said that I was from Canada, there was a smile on people's faces. However, when I told them I was from Canada, I hesitated to continue by saying that I am a parliamentarian because I knew the next question to follow would be: "Why are you not in Canada? Why are you not dealing with the problem of your first citizens?"
The member for Chateauguay said that we have a duty and a right. Is it one of our duties as parliamentarians to have immediately recalled Parliament? Is one of our duties to our first citizens to look after them? Should we have recalled Parliament? Should the member's boss,
the Prime Minister, have acted immediately without any hesitation?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too was overseas throughout parts of the summer and throughout parts of the crisis. In fact I was at the United Nations in Geneva where some of the Mohawk leaders were and I had an opportunity to deal with them. This unfortunate incident did not only happen domestically. The story was carried elsewhere.
In retrospect, again I suppose it is easy to say that Parliament could have been recalled, but as was stated earlier in Question Period in response to similar questions, every request that came forward to reconvene was not accompanied by a purpose for reconvening.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to take the opportunity to thank my hon. colleague, the member for Wetaskiwin, for his speech. It is a very difficult position in party politics for aboriginal people in all jurisdictions. A very, very tough question that we have to deal with is this. Although we deal with a group of people who have taken up arms, there is the bigger question that the Mohawk Confederacy wants dealt with, that is the question of jurisdiction and sovereignty. I know his legal expertise and I respect his mind when it comes to these matters. I would like to ask him this. How does he feel we can grapple with this very difficult question which relates to law and order which the government is very concerned about and which Canadian citizens are very concerned about? How do we deal with the issue of sovereignty? As he advises his government, what would his advice be to the government on dealing with the issue of sovereignty and the Mohawk Confederacy?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Western Arctic says, it is a tough question. If I can relate back to my constituents, the second recommendation that they have presented was to consider immediately a new round of meetings similar to the first ministers' conferences. They did not set an agenda for those particular meetings but I am sure from previous and recent discussions one of those would definitely be to address areas of jurisdiction and sovereignty. I believe there are some areas where it is possible to delineate the responsibility and jurisdiction of one area, to delineate the jurisdiction and responsibility of another, just as we
September 25, 1990

do now with the federal and provincial governments under the British North America Act.
In those new discussions it might be just possible that discussions could lead to areas of shared jurisdiction. Maybe it is possible to recognize that there is in fact a third order of government. It is possible to use the word "sovereignty", although it is hated, in that kind of a context.
We have examples all over where it is possible for a smaller nation to be within a larger nation and yet not have to give up its jurisdiction. If we look south, for example, in the United States, some of the islands where they have their own governments have sovereignty yet use the United States currency, defence, and jurisdiction in a lot of other areas. In other words, they share areas of jurisdiction but yet they feel that they are sovereign. The Vatican, as I understand it, is sovereign in Italy but yet it has its own jurisdiction. Therefore, I think there are models elsewhere that we can use that would bring about this kind of possibility in a new round of meetings.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: The hon. member for Outremont, a very short question, please.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to put a question to my colleague and at the same time offer my sincere thanks for having the honour and the privilege of hearing what I just heard.
Since the start of this debate, positions have been taken and statements made which I would qualify as partisan. This afternoon, after the Prime Minister's speech, we heard a member on the other side of the House open her heart to the Prime Minister and talk about issues that came straight from the heart. I felt that was very moving. On the other hand, another member of this House who belongs to a non-party made a number of comments that I did not appreciate at all, and I am getting to my question, Mr. Speaker, but I thought it would be useful to make these introductory remarks.
Our colleague spoke from the heart, he talked about his people, not in an intellectual way but with great feeling and integrity. Could I ask the hon. member, who is part of this cultural reality-I imagine his answer will be affirmative, but I don't want to prejudge what he is going to say-whether if perhaps here in this House we
Government Orders
could raise the level of debate to that achieved earlier by our two colleagues, does he think that this House will be able to protect and enhance this cultural integrity Canada so desperately needs and which may provide the answer for other groups, including the one to which I belong?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. But, as his remarks are prefaced that it would be an affirmative one, yes, I see this House being able to protect all rights of Canadians.
I think sometimes of an analogy that could be used. It is not a melting pot but a salad, and within the contents of a salad the lettuce is able to stay as lettuce. If we can use that kind of analogy, I think as all Canadians, we can all be protected.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to enter the debate this evening. First of all, I would like to make a few points clear about the motion.
The motion, unfortunately, does not deal with the issue. The motion has been made very specific for reasons that are hard to understand when you first look at the situation we are dealing with.
For background information for those of the House who are here, the riding I represent has 46 aboriginal communities. This issue was debated very heavily over and over all summer. It was probably the worst summer I, as a politician, have ever had to face simply because I did not have an answer for the people I represented. The questions that were being asked over and over again were what does this all mean? When will this all end? And, just where do we go from here?
I would like to deal with where we have been and perhaps if time allows talk a little about where we should go. I would like to use an analogy that has probably been used often in the House in this issue. It relates to a lost generation of aboriginal people. That lost generation, for those of you who are not quite aware of the history of Indian Affairs, are the people who were put into residential schools in the 1940s and 1950s, and until the early 1960s when they were done away with. That is what the aboriginal people call the lost generation. That was a time when non-native governments tried to force their will on aboriginal people, and by doing that were

Government Orders
attempting to assimilate and do away with the race. As you know, that situation did not occur. It did not work.
I use that analogy in relation to Oka. The only thing that we achieved in Oka is we have attempted to break the spirit of one whole community. All the people who are alive today in that particular community will never forget this episode. We, as politicians might forget if we get carried away in discussing other issues of national importance, but the small village of Oka will remember this particular crisis and episode. That is really what this issue is about, the scars that are left after something that should never have reached a crisis situation becomes a crisis.
I use that analogy, Mr. Speaker, because that is about all we are going to get from the Oka affair when it is all said and done. We have affected and hurt a generation. We could never replace that hurt by handouts, money, or land. What is done is done.
I want to go back to what should have been and to what possibly members of this House should have paid close attention. Maybe I am naive but as a young politician who is very new in this place, I am very sensitive to what people tell me on the street. When I go up north I listen very intently to the 46 chiefs that I represent, their band councils, the elders and the people who are there.
When I was first elected in 1988 I went on a tour, as I am sure all members do in ridings as large as mine, to listen to the people. I came back to the House with this message and fortunately or possibly unfortunately, depending on how you look at it, the leader of our party gave me the responsibility of associate critic on aboriginal affairs. Therefore, I was on the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs.
One of the first things I suggested at committee was that a problem that I could easily see, that I was very sensitive to, was that was the leaders were telling me it was becoming more and more difficult to control their own people. The potential young radicals, a term I suppose is being used a lot in the media these days, are people who are no longer willing to wait 40 to 50 years for governments to act. The chiefs and councils and elders told me very bluntly that we have to start putting
those words that they hear from politicians at every election into action.
I came back to the House and I went to the standing committee to speak to my Conservative colleagues and my NDP colleagues. Of course, Ethel, being a member of that committee, knows very well what I am talking about. I said that we had better get moving very quickly because it is becoming very, very difficult out there for the leadership of the native community to control their own people.
Lo and behold, Mr. Speaker, nobody paid attention. What is so often sad in this House is that governments tend not to listen to opposition members. Why should they? They have a majority. What a waste of time. It is a lot of rhetoric, is it not? But there are some members who might have something to say, who have a little bit of sensitivity about this beautiful country of ours. So far I have not seen that sensitivity and that is why we are in this situation.
It would be nice to have had this debate a year ago to hear the types of very good suggestions that are being made today.
Some people have difficulty articulating the issue because they are not familiar with aboriginal people or their situation. Mr. Speaker, that is perfectly acceptable and understandable because aboriginal issues are not very high on the agenda of many politicians. There are those who, I am sad to say, have never been to a reserve and would not know one if they ran over it. They probably drive through one often because there are close to 600 reserves in this country.
The sad part of this whole debate is that we have come to the point of having to call the army into a situation that got out of control. Whether it is right or wrong, Mr. Speaker, we will not solve here tonight. As other colleagues have said we have to ask where we go from here.
First, that depends on whether members in this chamber really understand what we are talking about tonight.
I know we are not supposed to talk about what happens in caucus. I get a big kick out of this.
I listen to my colleague, the hon. member for Western Arctic, talk quite often about aboriginal affairs in caucus. We get these guys and gals and their heads are nodding up and down, indicating: "Yes, I understand what you are

September 25, 1990

talking about." But do they really know what this is all about? Do they know how complex specific land claims policy is and how complex the comprehensive land claims policy is and the political will it will take for us as parliamentarians to resolve that issue?
I suggest that more colleagues should stop nodding their heads when aboriginal people speak and start saying: "No, I do not understand." I suggest that they do not.
I represent a riding that has 14,000 aboriginal people and I say very frankly that a lot of my non-native constituents do not understand the issue. They think the specific land claims policy is a land-grab by aboriginal people wanting more.
Simply, it is trying to right a wrong that we as non-natives created a long time ago. Yes, we put in the Indian Act. Yes, we put in the Indian agents. Then we let the Indian agent have all sorts of powers. In those days the communications were not as good and the education level of our First Nations was not as exceptional as it is in some cases today. What happened was that pieces of their land were sold off. In some cases the land guaranteed to them in the treaties was never given. Do you know that there are 165 specific land claims in Ontario alone?
Today I listened very intently to what the Prime Minister said. I had waited a long time in the House for some indication of what my constituents in the aboriginal community call trust and honesty.
The aboriginal people are very difficult in the sense that they are not easily fooled. When you look them in the eye they will tell you right away, very quickly, in their own sophisticated method, whether you are full of it. I use that because it is probably the most parliamentary expression I can use referring to whether one was being just a simple politician or one truly means and understands what they are saying.
I have been through that process and this summer when I looked into those eyes up north it was very, very difficult. I said to myself: "Bob, you had better go back and tell your colleagues just how bad it really is for the 100th time. Just possibly they will listen this time or maybe they might understand."
As I have said in my press releases, letters I have sent to the minister, the request to the Speaker for emergency debate and the request to the House Leader to recall
Government Orders
Parliament, if we do not deal with this issue in a very comprehensive way, what we have seen over the summer is the tip of the iceberg. The young aboriginal leaders are not prepared to wait any longer.
The request of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin for people to be patient and continue with dialogue has come to an end. Aboriginal people have been dialoguing and speaking to non-natives for so long now that they just do not know what to say any more. They meet with the minister and members of Parliament and the heads keep nodding up and down: "Yes, yes, we understand what you are saying". The chiefs and the council go back to their community. A year goes by, two years go by, three years go by-nothing.
I want to bring into the debate a specific example. Here is one that belongs to my constituents. Here are six bands and I will name them for you: Kee-Way-Win, MacDowell Lake, New Slate Falls, Saugeen Nation and Wawakapewin. These six communities were given band status in 1985 by the present government. At that time, when they gave these six bands the hope of having their own community, it said: "Very soon we will give you reserve status." For those who do not know, reserve status means that they get a land base, something to work with, some hope of creating their own community and being independent to a certain extent. I know how much all people in Canada cherish their independence.
Well, it is five years later and this report here states: "Six Bands Five Years Later". That is the title. Lo and behold, there is no reserve status for these six communities. They live in total poverty.
One community lives exactly one mile away from a great big power line and it is not hooked up to the community. What do they do? Every winter they have little generators and little propane stoves and lights. It is an embarrassment to be a Canadian. But it is so far out of the way that these people here might never see that community in their whole lives. If they went there they would be ashamed. They would want to move away.
That is what we are talking about here, the understanding of the issue. People cannot continue-and I talk about parliamentarians and politicians-to talk and not act. That is why I am very sceptical about what the Prime Minister said today. In his discussion and in his speech there was absolutely no detail of where we are going and

Government Orders
no emphasis on timetable. Where will we be five years from now? Where will we be 10 years from now?
Give the aboriginal people a goal to set for themselves and something to work towards. Show them what we mean by improved infrastructure.
Of the 46 reserves I represent, a total of four have sewers and water. The Prime Minister said that we are going to start speeding up sewer and water situations and housing. This is a rough guess and a very conservative one, if you do not mind me saying, but there are at least 500 homes are needed in those 46 communities. There are two and three families living in a little home that we would probably call our garage. And we sit here and nod our heads. Oh, we understand, but do we really, really understand?
We presented a motion in standing committee that we do cross-country hearings. We also debated and discussed very heavily in the aboriginal standing committee about having-can you believe this, Mr. Speaker-cameras in our committee meetings. The ruling was, oh no, you cannot do that. We might say something that would embarrass the government. Good God, it is too late for that. We have embarrassed ourselves already. Look at what has happened.
What we want to do is we want to open the process up and, hopefully, through that we will educate non-natives who do not understand the issue. I do not say that to belittle anyone. If one does not live in that culture or in that world, one might not understand and that is perfectly acceptable. But if we do not turn the lights on, it will always be dark. As one leader said, I am getting tired of screaming in the forest. Do you know how many people hear you in the middle of northern Ontario, thousands of miles from anybody, when you scream in the bush? Absolutely no one. And that is exactly what is happening here.
I asked the members just for once-and I say that more specifically to the government who have a very important responsibility at this present time-to listen to members who might have something concrete to say. There have been many, many suggestions made in the House and those suggestions are for a land claims commission which would allow for a non-biased, nonpartisan approach, a resolution of these land claims issues which have to be sped up at a phenomenal rate with resources applied to it. Otherwise we will never, in my lifetime, go through them all.
Also, I think it is high time that we did look at a royal commission. At first, I disapproved of a royal commission and I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. There are so many reports like this one. There are hundreds of reports that are collecting dust on peoples' desks. Keith Penner's report in 1983 was very comprehensive and it cost the government millions of dollars to put it through. It would have showed us the way to change our approach to aboriginal affairs.
The reason I did not want to go along with this royal commission is simply this. It was another delay tactic, another way of stopping what should start immediately and that is to get into the very, very nuts and bolts of the issue. Now, I think maybe it would be good to air this whole issue nation wide. By doing that, maybe someone will learn something about aboriginal affairs.
I say this because I have learned a lot from my colleague who happens to be sitting behind me. Any member who really wants to learn something about aboriginal people, should come and talk to Ethel or to Jack. They will tell them what it is like. Or they should go and spend a few weekends of their precious time, as Dennis Mills did, up on a reserve in northern Quebec and they will find out what it is all about. Once we get to that point, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you we will, as parliamentarians, have done truly something exceptional. Until then, we will just stand up here and spin our wheels. Hopefully I will not have to do that.
Unfortunately, not being a pessimist but in this case having seen it before, we are in for a difficult time if these people here do not listen.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments and ask some questions to my colleague who has just spoken.
I can understand his deception to a certain extent. Mr. Speaker, it is often true that when we are confronted with problems in caucus or in meetings we have a
September 25, 1990

tendency to shake our heads and say: "Yes, yes, I understand."
I come from Beauhamois-Salaberry. For the benefit of those who do not know, Beauhamois-Salaberry is just after Chateauguay on the road which leads to the Akwesasne reserve. The Akwesasne reserve is in my riding and I might add a little detail which may seem meaningless. When I want to go on the Akwesasne reserve, and I go there regularly to visit the residents of the reserve, I have to go through the United States and Ontario and come back through the reserve. That is a small detail which goes to show to what extent they are sometimes badly treated.
But I want to say to my colleague who has just spoken that in the end the House of Commons may be a reflection of society. We really come to grips with problems when they are staring at us in the face. Three or four months ago when everything was going so bad on the Akwesasne reserve we did not have a great debate. We were saying: We will tiy to find a solution to the problem, we asked a few question and that was the end of it. But what was going on at Akwesasne? Akwesasne is where the traffic goes through. My colleague says he visits the reserves. Well, so do I, I visit the reserve located in my riding. I was in touch with reserve chief Mike Mitchell for whom I have the greatest of respect. He said to me: "Mr. Hudon, one of these days you will see things blowing up elsewhere because traffic interruptions here will have repercussions elsewhere". And we did have them this summer.
But we were all there, in the image of society. Nobody in Chateauguay or Beauhamois-and I said this to the people of Beauhamois and Melocheville during the meetings this summer-nobody among you has been unduly concerned about what was going on at Akwesasne. The situation was very serious. They had some problems in British Columbia, they had a very serious problem there as well.
But like we do they just stand there and wait. We say we will solve the problem whenever it comes up, in a more practical way, and then- But there is something I want to say. We have been here for two days. Yesterday we talked about Iraq. We had to put an end to the debate at 7 o'clock last night because there was no unanimous consent in the House. It is a good thing we did stop at 7
Government Orders
o'clock, for otherwise we might have found a solution to the conflict in the Gulf!
This is not the place where solutions are found. It is now 9.30 p.m.
We have been talking about the Oka stand-off for a number of hours and we could talk about it for many more. We are a reflection of what goes on in society. What the other guy just said is all wrong. The hon. member is perfectly right about that. People don't listen. They always say: he missed the point. That's not the right answer. The Prime Minister spoke and he didn't say the right thing. Well, I think tonight maybe we should start negotiating. I can hear people say: That doesn't make sense. It won't work here. I agree. The Prime Minister of Canada said that he was willing to accelerate the process. Unfortunately, today, the solution is not up to the House of Commons, although I am a firm believer in the parliamentary process and I think everybody should have his say. If we were really honest, maybe just a little more so than our society tends to be, and if we were also a little less hostile, we could all find a solution. However, we always disagree with what the other guy said.
I must say that I agree with the hon. member. Another member said we should have sent a group of parliamentarians. What is that supposed to do? How is sending in a group of parliamentarians supposed to settle the conflict? You didn't say that, it was one of your colleagues who spoke just before you rose, the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur.
Now let me see, this happened about two years ago on the Mercier Bridge. The bridge was blocked because the RCMP had seized cigarettes which it wanted to give to the Quebec Provincial Police. The politician arrived on the scene and just made matters worse. People were arrested with their cigarettes and the drugs they had at the time, but that was not the answer.
I think that if we were willing to sit down together without looking at the negative side of things, without necessarily-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for getting involved in the debate. I am not quite sure how to answer that question or to make a comment on his comments.
First of all, I would like to go back to what I talked about in the speech and that is that this issue is a lot larger than the reserve that he speaks of that is in his community. Yes, it is unfortunate that there are some situations there that have dictated the unfortunate scenes we have seen this summer, the one where we saw the young soldier, eye to eye with a Mohawk. But I would never stand in my place and say some of the things that this member has just said about people without a fair trial and having the judicial system rule on what in essence has gone on there. The reason I did not get into the debate about Oka the way possibly I would have if I were parked there on the doorstep is because I am not
from there. If I were to speak on what I saw on TV over the summer, I would have got a very slanted view.
I have been told by my French colleagues that the French media has reported much differently than the English media on what took place there. In order for us as parliamentarians to know exactly what did take place in this unfortunate incident, why don't we have a true inquiry so then we will know? I do not like to be dictated by the French or English media because I do not really know what their mandate is. Is it to sell newspapers? Is it to sell time on TV or is it to report to me the true facts and sensitivities of the Canadian people?

An excellent point.
Mr. Nault I suggest to you that because of that reason I stayed away from Oka. Maybe the member has some inside information that we as members do not have. I wished we would have pressed his Prime Minister to let us have this debate two months ago. I would have loved to come in the 1st of June or early July and talk about this before all-

speechtext: Well done.

speechtext:
Thank you. Just a brief comment and then a question. Mr. Speaker, I listened to the member's speech with interest. He raised the matter of a royal commission. At first he did not think much of a royal commission on native issues. Now he feels that perhaps it would be a good idea. I, too, think it would be a good idea.
I think it would be important for two reasons. One is to educate the public in these issues. That was done in a quick way with the Oka crisis this summer. Native issues have been on the back burner in spite of the horrible situation of native people in this country. It has always been on the back burner, even in this House of Commons.
The royal commission could do another thing. I believe it could define what we are looking for, the answer to a problem. The Mohawks talked about full sovereignty. The government cannot give that. The Prime Minister is talking about the status quo. He is not prepared to give anything on that. We have to get somewhere in between.
September 25, 1990

The royal commission, in my view, has to define self government. It is something less than full sovereignty but something more than the status quo. That is what I think the royal commission could do.
My question to the hon. member is this. I hesitate to be partisan here. Not ever being partisan, I always find Liberals sort of like jelly, trying to nail them to the wall. You know they sort of stand for this and then this and it is hard to pin them down.
Was the Liberal Party in favour of sending the army into Oka or not? Yes or no? It appeared from one member, the Whip I believe, that they wanted the army sent in. It appeared in Question Period today the Liberal Party was against the army being sent in. I ask the hon. member representing the Liberal Party, is it yes or no?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Let me answer the last question first. The answer is no. Anybody in their right mind who would suggest that allowing the army to go into any community to defend the interests of our society, be it judicial or not, because when you do that, it means that the ability to police yourself has completely fallen apart. I suggest to you, not being a lawyer and you being a lawyer, and you should know better, that under that scenario, not anyone in this House should have been in favour of the army going in. What I have said in the speech, and I thought I made myself very clear, is that the reason why I never talked about that situation was because you cannot right a wrong that has already been wronged. It has already been done. It has been dealt with. Let us look at where we go from there.
I want to talk a little bit about what I talked about before. This member should pay very close attention to this and not talk when I am speaking. I want to tell him a little bit about something he asked me which shows his lack of knowledge about aboriginal affairs.
He talked about the royal commission and the fact that it should define self-government. Any individual in this House who understands aboriginal affairs will tell you that you cannot define self-government. They are all different in every individual community in this country. That is why it has never been done before. Have you ever asked a chief or council to tell you what their concept of
Government Orders
self-government is? You get an interesting stare because it is very, very difficult. That is like defining distinct society. If you can define distinct society, I will define self-government. I tell you, it is impossible. That is why it is very, very important for this member to know that the reason we are having these debates is because you learn something. Tonight he learned something.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member, my friend from Kenora-Rainy River, has put some sense into the debate tonight and has taken most of the partisanship out of the debate.
This truly is an issue where every member from every side of the House has to feel something deep down in their guts. We are talking about an injustice that has been allowed to go on for much too long and has caused the situation to develop at Oka. Now the government would like very dearly not to talk about the problems that have caused the confrontation at Oka. They want to talk in a very sterile environment.
I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, if you look at the history of the civil rights movement in the United States, the blacks in the United States did not break laws in the United States through civil disobedience because they were law-breakers. They broke those laws to try to bring to the attention of the American people injustices that were perpetrated upon them, rights that they did not enjoy that the white population did enjoy. It was a final step to say to the larger society "For God's sake, wake up. I am human, too". That is exactly what has been happening in the native community in this country.

The Prime Minister said it earlier-
If I want to make a speech, I will. If you do not want to listen to it, that is fine. As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, great thinker she is.

Government Orders
The Prime Minister said it earlier, and I commend him for it. He said that the native people in this country are a gentle people. That is their history. They are not savages, contrary to what most of our schooling has taught in racist textbooks. They are not beasts, but enjoy a long and deep, rich cultural history.
What has driven a particular community out of that rich tradition to the problems that we see in Oka? It is a government and a society that does not want to deal with the fundamental problems in the native community.
I want to ask the member for Kenora-Rainy River this. Earlier the Prime Minister of Canada offered some possible solutions. I do not want to put the Prime Minister's intentions up to any scrutiny. I think he was honest this evening in wanting to do something. But, there is a problem here. The native community needs a sign of good faith by this government. It needs a sign of good faith. I am going to ask him, is this the type of thing that might lead to some movement, that might lead to restoring some of the trust that this government has destroyed with the native community if they went and did something simple, such as reinstate the funding that was cut through the Secretary of State for native newspapers in this country? Something simple like that.
In Nova Scotia, the Micmac community has lost its only form of communication among that minority community because the Secretary of State, through government cutbacks and government policies, has silenced the voice of the native community. Is this the type of thing I ask the member that the government could do to show their bona fides and to reinstate some good faith in the negotiations between the Government of Canada and our aboriginal peoples?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer that question simply by saying that this afternoon I listened very intently to what the Prime Minister had to say. The reason I did so was that I was looking for some sort of clue as to whether indeed the trust factor which has been eroded so severely over the years would possibly spark a bit of life back into the unfriendliness created over the past few years I have had the opportunity of being a member of Parliament.
To start off the debate properly and to turn the environment around somewhat on aboriginal issues, one of the nicest gestures that one could make is a small one
when one talks about $4 billion. The Prime Minister is very quick to tell us how much it costs. He is forever telling us how much it costs. I think it would be a very nice gesture if put back in place the funds cut from native communication societies in this country.
I was the recipient of one of those major cuts in Kenora-Rainy River at Wawate which my colleague and I visited. The damage it did to those people who use that radio station, the newspaper, and the bush radios which are there for the trappers was beyond description in this House, at least for me.
A little gesture like that would go a long way toward showing that we are on the right track. If the Prime Minister were serious about what he said this afternoon, he would start to implement this process or this new agenda very quickly. If he does not, it shows that he does not really have an agenda and that what he said today was a lot of rhetoric to get people off his back for a while.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comment will be very short.
Yesterday, on the opening day of the Parliament of Canada, most of the country had a pent-up expectation. Later on in the afternoon after Question Period, my office on the Hill received two irate phone calls from high school teachers who had organized their classes to watch Question Period. They called and echoed their disgust at what happened in this Chamber: the bantering back and forth and not listening to each other.
Today's debate in the House of Commons has been one of the most productive, positive, high-road debates that we have ever had. I would like to thank especially my colleague today from Kenora-Rainy River who pushed for a whole new level and tone toward working together and solving very serious issues. We should have a heck of a lot more of it in this House because I think it is basically what the people of Canada want.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence, Mr. Speaker, I wish to report to my colleagues and, through them, to all Canadians, on the way our military forces carried out the mandate they had received from the province of Quebec
September 25, 1990

following the breaking down of negotiations aimed at ending the Oka and Kahanawake crisis.
Everywhere in the world, Canada enjoys a tremendous reputation for respecting human rights and assuming peace keeping duties internationally. But now that I am personally involved with defence, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that the reputation we have abroad is somewhat different from that we enjoy within our borders. That is the reason many countries were watching us, wondering sometimes with scepticism how our Armed Forces were going to end a conflict which threatened to pitch brothers against brothers. As in many family quarrels, there comes a time when people loose sight of the real reasons behind the conflict.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to recall briefly the events which forced the Quebec Government to send for our Armed Forces. Over the past few years, through its Department of Indian Affairs, the Federal Government has worked diligently with the Mohawk tribe in Oka, in Kahnesatake, to formally establish a reserve. Considerable progress has been made. The government has bought lands from individuals to turn them over to native leaders. Early in May, the Municipal Council of Oka announced its intention to purchase the land next to their city's golf course in order to extend it. Following this announcement, the Mohawks set up barricades closing access to the contentious land. Because they had failed to obey to court injunctions, the Surete du Quebec received the order to dismantle the barricades. On July 11, this police force were confronted with heavily armed opponents, saw one of their men lose his life and incurred various material losses. To demonstrate their support for the Mohawks in Oka, the Mohawks in Kanesatake set up barricades to stop traffic on the Mercier bridge between the Southshore and the Montreal Island.
Following these tragic events, the province of Quebec, under Part XI of the National Defence Act, sent General John de Chastelain, Chief of the Defence Staff, a request to help the civilian power.
Armed assistance consists in providing Armed Forces personnel pursuant to a request received from civilian authorities requesting help to enforce Canadian laws.
Government Orders
Therefore, armed assistance necessarily implies a violent situation or threat of violence.
In our country, the concept of armed assistance is based on several principles that form integral part of our judicial system. The most basic of these principles is probably that any form of martial law is unacceptable; civil power remains the supreme authority and shall not be replaced. It ensues that troops can be called in to assist the civilian authorities. The Armed Forces are called in as a last resort, only when everything else failed to maintain or restore peace and order.
When armed assistance is requested, it is assumed that the civilian authorities at all levels have already done all they could to bring back to normal a situation that has deteriorated to the point of being very serious.
Provincial authorities can requisition-hear "demand" rather than "ask for"-troups from the Armed Forces in order to have them at their disposal when needed. Pursuant to the National Defence Act, the requests are made to the highest military authority, that is the Chief of Defence Staff, rather that to a minister of the federal government or to a political authority.
The following day, that is on July 12, after consulting the Quebec minister of Public Security, the Chief of the Defence staff asked the commanding officer of the Mobile Command to provide the Surete du Quebec with support equipment and personnel, such as armoured vehicles and their drivers, bulletproof vests, rifles, and also night-vision equipment. The troops were authorized to fire their weapons only in self-defence. The same day, July 12, 96 troops were dispatched from the Longue Pointe base, in eastern Montreal.
On August 6, negotiations between native people and representatives of the federal and provincial governments broke down. Therefore, under the provisions of the National Defence Act, the province of Quebec requested that Canadian Forces be called out in aid of the civil power to assist civilian authorities to restore law and order in Oka and Kahnawake.
When he involed the National Defence Act, the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Robert Bourassa, conferred upon the Canadian Forces the mandate to remove the barricades at Oka and Kahnawake, to ensure the free movement of vehicles on the roads and bridges, to take control of the fortified posts and to restore the normal

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
conditions essential to general welfare and public security-
When he instructed Lieutenant-General Foster to realize this mandate, General de Chastelain publicly committed himself to the peaceful dismantling of the barricades.
He said Canadian troops would not use force unless obliged to by the Warriors. Echoing the words of the Chief of the Defence Staff, the Mobile Command Commander also expressed his intention of proceeding without violence, but remaining ready to face any situation, confronted with Warriors equipped with military-type arms and entrenched behind fortifications that did not look the work of amateurs.
From the beginning of the crisis to its conclusion, which appears imminent, through the most recent tribulations of this conflict which are but too fresh to our memories to need to be recalled, our military maintained their quiet strength, inspired by their chief, a good balance of determination and calm. If a picture is worth a thousand words, the one of the terrible face to face of soldier Patrick Cloutier with a Warrior was shown everywhere around the world.
The step-by-step dismantling, without bloodshed, of the fortified road blocks, first in Kahnawake, then in Kanesatake, testifies to the impressive competence of the Canadian armed forces in peacekeeping operations. Our soldiers were able to combine some psychology, good sense and courage. They overcame with success several handicaps; those of having different ways of thinking, a different language and culture from those they were facing.
For many of our fellow citizens, the key role the army played in reducing tensions with aboriginal people, between aboriginal people and the people in the neighbourhood of the reserves, was a revelation. The media, particularly those of Quebec, generally conveyed with objectivity the positive contribution of the Canadian forces involved in the conflict I also experience as the member of a riding that includes the area of Chateau-guay.
A few days ago I heard a sociologist on the radio discussing the possible after effects of the conflict and whether there would be any harmful and lasting impact
on relations between the Mohawks and their neighbours. Mr. Speaker, I think we should make a very clear distinction between the legitimate aspirations of native people and the attitude of the Warriors, which is intolerable in a democracy. I am referring to these would-be soldiers, some of whom, in fact quite a number, were from outside Canada.
With the Canadian people, whose interests it reflects, the government has recognized the advantages of a quick and fair settlement of legitimate native land claims, but it had no intention of doing so at the point of a gun. Violence as a political tool or a pressure tactic was entirely unacceptable in a democratic system. Arbitrary actions can only generate fleeting successes and victories that are morally devastating. A democratic system like ours guarantees fair treatment for all citizens of Canada, as brothers who are equal before the law.
The Warriors' threats of violence will merely have postponed negotiations and as a result delayed solutions to problems such as settling the land claims of the Mohawks in Kanesatake and the transfer of 97 acres of land the federal government has purchased in the municipality of Oka.
The fact that dialogue is again possible today, Mr. Speaker, despite the pain and suffering on both sides of the barricades, the fact that there are no longer any barricades between men, women and children who share a common destiny which is to build this country, our country, is largely thanks to the fair, courageous and judicious action of the Canadian Forces. Justice, bravery and wisdom are, as we all know, platonic virtues, and I would like to take this opportunity to offer our congratulations and thanks on behalf of all Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Questions and comments. The hon. member for Saint-Boniface.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the hon. member's speech. Although I appreciated part of what he said, some of his comments I found rather alarming. If I understood correctly, he referred to a situation that had degenerated. He then tried to explain why.
It seems to me that there has been a quite extraordinary attempt to deny or to evade certain facts. What facts?

Is it not true that the Oka situation is in large part because of the failures of successive governments to respond sensitively and sensibly to the needs of our aboriginal peoples? Is it not true that this government's actions with regard to the capping of education funding, to the various budget cut-backs that we have discussed frequently in this House, to the unresolved land claims, to our collective inability to respond to their desire for self-government, to the lack of hope that our native brothers and sisters have in fact because of this series of broken promises, to this lots of talk and no action mentality and this series of broken promises, is it not all of this that is the real reason for what has happened in Oka?
I would ask whether or not my colleague would publicly in this House accept that this Oka situation at the very, very least is in large part a result of these failures.

Are you prepared to accept these facts? Are you prepared to condemn sending in the troops against our own brothers and sisters, against fellow Canadians?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Before the hon. member answers the question, I will recognize the hon. member for Victoria and then the hon. member for Nepean on a short question or comment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the hon. member's question because I believe he expects a reply. I think we must put the Oka situation into context. Oka is not and was not a reserve. So when the town of Oka decided to expand its golf course onto land that belonged to a resident of France, don't tell me this was not a legitimate request. A municipal council may, within certain limits, take certain initiatives. Two court injunctions authorized the town council to do so and to oblige people to take down the barricades. Previously, in the past year, the federal government had purchased several other properties to form a real reserve. Everything was fine. It is no more than natural for a municipality to want to add to property it already has, in a legitimate manner. People in other countries were
Government Orders
joking about the whole thing. I heard the news on French television and they said there was a major dispute in Canada between Indians and White people about a golf course. I think that is an exaggeration.
As for his comments on education funding, I think we shouldn't always think in terms of dollars and cents. I agree it is important. When we talk about cuts in education, as far as I know I don't have all my notes with me the cuts introduced last year do not mean, and I think Canadians should realize this and that you should realize it as well, do not deny native people access to university.
I am all for paying somebody's courses, their room and board and their books. More power to them. But, when they are enrolled in law school and the course takes four years, four years is all they are allowed. If the chancellor of the university says it takes an extra preparatory year, that will be paid for as well. That makes five years. After five years, no more. That is not what I call cutting off funding. It is just obliging people to observe a certain timeframe and do what you and I had to do when we were getting an education. These were constraints we had to live with.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the member's speech and on the situation in Oka and to use this opportunity to do so. What we have seen this summer is a terrible tragedy for Canada. I was listening this afternoon when the Prime Minister decided, in answering a question, to score a point on the basis of the violence that is being taught to young children behind the barricades in Oka, and the Conservative benches roared with laughter at the great score that he had made. This came across to me really as a form of racism, which underlies our whole reaction in Canada to what we have been seeing in Oka and to the real tragedy that has been happening there. Because the violence that we are seeing there behind the lines is really a product of the violence of our society and the terrible violence that we, in Canada, have wrought over hundreds of years on the aboriginal native populations in this country. The rape that happens to women, the sexual assault on children, the suicides of young Indians, the pain and agony that has come from the high populations in our jails, are all products of our violence against native people. And somehow this government keeps persisting in blaming the victims of the violence that has been wrought. It is time that this House

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
understood that we have to speak of reconciliation, of trying to come together to build a more just society.
Let me speak briefly about what this has done to the army. My new role in this House is as critic for our party on defence matters. I see what has happened to the army. The individual soldiers who are there have shown great personal courage but the government has put them and the army in a position in which its authority and its image in this country is slowly eroding. It puts them in a position where they are beginning to trample on the civil liberties of Canadians by denying communications and the right to communications to the press. The rights of journalists in Iraq are greater than the rights of journalists in the Oka area and behind the barricades.
The army is now imposing increased pressure on the people who are there. The image of the army is slowly eroding. The opportunity that it has to risk serious violence on the people there is a daily feature of the situation which this government's neglect has caused. I would ask the member if he would not concede that the time has come in this country for reconciliation and for resolving this matter, not with more violence but with peace and justice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Sure enough it is ingratiating. But there is a very simple way to initiate reconciliation. As long as armed people remain behind barricades and refuse to come out the process cannot begin.
That is not the way negotiations will get under way because if we begin to negotiate now I can tell you that the first item up for negotiation will not be the territorial claims, they will begin by negotiating safe-conducts for those peole.
They say that those people are traditionalists. I said a moment ago that I had visited the Akwesasne reserve in my riding, I got a book about the traditional values of the Mohawks as a present from chief Mike Mitchell because I had attended the opening of a housing project. I did not see any Mohawk warriors who had to be protected by women and children and move about with a rag over their face to avoid recognition! I did not see that.
A real Mohawk is someone who stood proud and was prepared to face the enemy. They are the ones we have always known and with whom we have always negotiated. They are not in Oka now. They are the ones who suffered in Chateauguay. A moment earlier you said something about suffering-we do not want to be racists and that is precisely what will prevent us from being so-when I consider what is going on in Chateauguay right now, with the solidarity committee which has been established in an effort to fight against such attitudes, because the effects of racism can be felt on both sides-
The real warriors are the people of Chateauguay and the native people who show respect for certain values and who, like you and I, have been taken hostage, just like the people of Melocheville or Beauhamois. Those are also Canadian values.
The negotiations were going well. No one likes the army. I said so in my speech. I had said that before in Haiti, when I was Chairman of the Parliamentary Commission on Haiti: In Canada, we feel towards military governments the way we feel towards hives. We do not like them. Nobody does. The purpose of my comment was to show that the army had behaved professionally. The first series of phone calls I got was for the army to come in and kill them all. That is not what we wanted them to do. De Chastelain, Foster, and Brigadier General Roy assumed their responsibilities and did so as gentlemen. They acted correctly, without violence. If there is still some violence today, let me tell you that we could put an end to it very easily. I could even call the Warriors tomorrow morning and tell them to lay down their arms and face their responsibilities.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: The hon. member for Nepean on a question or comment.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a comment first and then a question to the parliamentary secretary.
The recent clash and subsequent stand-off between the provincial police officers, the Canadian army and the Mohawk Indians is both tragic and unnecessary.
This government turned its back on an issue that is clearly theirs and one that it could have resolved in the first week of the crisis. This is a national tragedy and one that every member in this House should be thoroughly ashamed of. Canada's armed service men and women are being used as fall guys for a government that has been incapable of acting to end the tragic circumstances

Government Orders
in Kanesatake. None of us condone armed intervention. None of us condone violence. But I can partly understand it. When one consistently has one's back to the wall, when one's rights are consistently being trampled on, when one watches the federal government bend over backwards to accommodate a distinct society within that particular province, but does not include its native peoples in that accommodation, when one sees a federal government that does not appreciate or understand the national aspirations of its first citizens, then I understand their frustration.
A closer look at the crisis and its implications gives me cause to be concerned that the fundamental guarantee to basic human rights are not being met.
Amnesty International has the Oka situation under investigation at this very moment. They are in the process of collecting affidavits from those who have documented human rights abuses. Our international reputation as a strong human rights nation has been sullied by our government's failure to limit the many human rights abuses in this crisis. The United Nations has been asked to intervene and the UN Working Group on Indigenous Peoples has listed representations about the specific situation that we are debating today. Surely, if these international organizations are actively looking into the situation, there must be some legitimate concerns.
Does the parliamentary secretary believe that these concerns bear further examination? Does he think that they can only be given the attention they deserve through a full royal commission and judicial enquiry?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Human rights were trampled on. I should like to know by whom? By our Armed Forces? By the Canadian Government? I do not think so. Some rights were effectively trampled on. At some point during the negotiations, the Commission on International Rights was made up of 24 members. If these people keep quiet now, it is because they understand the situation better.
I must tell you, Madam Speaker, that if you try to make out of the problem in Oka and Chateauguay, a problem of a distinct society, you should pay a visit to my county where a bunch of people are doing exactly that. I received three kinds of phone calls as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence. The first series, until the army arrived came from people who wanted us to send in the army to kill them all! The second series was from the Pacifists. As soon as the army arrived, they were worried about our international reputation. I was afraid too. The third series was from people like you. You refuse the natives the right to a distinct society while you yourselves, as Quebec separatists, are demanding it for Quebecers. I can tell you there is a major difference between a distinct society and a distinct nation. As soon as Quebec has a referendum and a government bent on separation, then they will want a distinct society. I do not agree with that, Madam. But that is the difference between the two.
The legislation we amended in this House was different from the War Measures Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
