speechtext: Questions and comments are terminated. The next speech is for 10 minutes with five minutes for questions and comments. The hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that, indeed, is my constituency and I do plan to speak for 10 minutes, followed by the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam.
I am very pleased to be able finally to participate in this long overdue debate. The events that we have seen this summer of Canadians are ones which will be seared in our memories probably forever. They are shocking events: razor wire, dogs, search lights, women and

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
children being stoned in their cars, and food being withheld. Images that we, as Canadians, never thought we would see in this peaceful country of ours. A level of violence that ill-becomes us and is in no way part of our national identity, or so we thought.
Like the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, I, too, spent a good part of my summer touring Indian communities in my constituency. There are 13 and approximately 15,000 treaty Indian people in my constituency. My heart bled more than once at what I saw, especially among the young people, as they asked each other: "Are we prepared to die? Are we prepared to be like the people in Oka and Kanesatake? Are we prepared to die for our people if it should come to that?" And beyond that, the level of anger. In fact, that became perhaps even an attractive option, even to go so far as to think about taking life and becoming violent themselves.
I could understand the deep frustration of the Indian leadership in those communities and the sorrow of their elders as they saw the young people pick up that kind of thinking and those kinds of attitudes on the basis of what they saw over the summer.
We saw, too, the total abdication of leadership in the country and at the level that is probably unprecedented in our constitutional history when it comes to Indian people. Our Constitution is clear when it comes to the trust relationship which the federal government has towards the Indian people. We saw the Minister of Indian Affairs who hid. We saw a Prime Minister who hid.
At the same time, we were virtually in a situation of civil war between Indian people and our own military forces. We had a situation where Indian people were being denied food and medicine. Whole Indian communities were feeling themselves threatened and, in fact, Indian people across the country felt in the position where they needed to mobilize themselves to take action and we had a Minister of Indian Affairs who decided to hide behind the army and the police and a Prime Minister who decided to hide as well.
Therefore, I, like many other Canadians, was waiting very anxiously to see what the government's response would be when it got here to Parliament. What did we see? It was like a bad western movie. What we see here is talk about law and order. We see it repeated over and over again, a vilification of the warriors. Nobody condones the actions that some of the warriors have undertaken. Certainly nobody condones violence. But for the government to focus its attack exclusively on vilification of the warriors and justifying its actions on that very narrow basis, I think is an insult to thousands of Canadians. It is an insult to the thousands of Canadians who marched peaceably, to the thousands of Canadians who participated in peace camps, who attempted to get involved in the situation, who went to Oka, who went to Kanesatake to try to become personally involved in a constructive kind of way and were shunted away and driven away.
It is an insult to the Indian leadership who kept the situation very much under control throughout the country. It is an insult to those Canadians who made all kinds of efforts to become involved and to become informed, many of them for the first time, about the situation which in fact confronts Indian people in the country, the historical situation that we have allowed to evolve, and the situation of the lives of Indian men and women in Indian communities across the country. It is an insult to those Canadians who took this issue seriously for the government to turn around now and say that these are just lunatics that it had to look after. That is the sum total of the government's response.
I guess what sticks in my craw further to that is all this sanctimonious talk about the sacredness of the law and that the government's sole effort here, their sole motivation is to uphold that law. If it is so concerned about the sacredness of the law, why are groups like Amnesty International or the human rights commissions-100 of them from Quebec alone-investigating the situation there and coming up with condemnations one after the other of what they have seen happen? Why have we seen food used as a weapon? That is something we decry internationally when it happens, yet we have done it ourselves.
If the government is so concerned about the rule of the law, why do we see the muzzling of the press and the cutting off of communications? If it is so concerned about the rule of law, why did they use the National Defence Act which holds very little recourse by way of public accountability, as opposed to the Emergencies Act which would require Parliament to be called within seven days and require a public inquiry to be held when all the events had transpired so that there would be a full accountability to the Canadian public? If it was so
September 25, 1990

concerned about the rule of law, why did the government not use that mechanism?
Then we heard the Prime Minister this afternoon talk about how the warriors should give themselves up because they would only be giving themselves up to the finest legal system in the world, a legal system that they could have total confidence in because it is the same law for all. In fact, we have had a lot of talk about being the same law for all and there cannot be any exceptions and so on. Does the Prime Minister remember the Donald Marshall case? Does he remember the Manitoba justice inquiry? Does he realize that in my own province of Saskatchewan 80 per cent of the people incarcerated in that province are of native ancestry, although they make up only about 10 per cent of the population?
Does the Prime Minister not know that Indian people have a deep sense of laws being broken ever since 1763, the Royal Proclamation that said that they should not be disturbed at their hunting until treaties are concluded? We are still disturbing the Innu at their hunting without a treaty being concluded.
In my own constituency the Peter Ballantine Band has waited for 100 years now for 240,000 acres of land that are owing them. That is the law. The treaty is the law. They are to get that land. Yet, the Prime Minister says this legal system is something that is the finest in the world, that the same law applies to all and that the Indian people can have total confidence in the law.
Having said that, I would like to conclude by saying that I do agree that it is time for healing in the country. This has gone on for too long. We must reconcile the present situation immediately and the suggestion that a group of parliamentarians intervene immediately is a veiy good one. It would bring both public scrutiny and a sense of confidence that in fact the political process is working.
Second, I think we need to be honestly critical here. It is not acceptable for the Minister of Indian Affairs to stand up in the House and simply say that the government has nothing to apologize for. It has. Previous governments have things to apologize for and the Canadian people have things to apologize for. I think we need
Government Orders
to be honestly self-critical if there is to be understanding and reconciliation come out of all this.
We have to explore some useful ideas, and I give the Prime Minister credit for standing in the House this afternoon. I hope he was sincere. He floated some very useful ideas and I think it underlined again why we should have had this debate a long time ago. If the Prime Minister had come forward with some of the ideas he presented today six weeks ago, it could very likely be possible that a lot of events which have transpired since then would not, in fact, have occurred.
In that context, I also hope he takes very seriously our leader's suggestion for an aboriginal claims commission because I think that is an idea that is long overdue.
In closing, I would like to say that we need to go beyond what we can do as parliamentarians in the sense of law and the things we do as parliamentarians and develop a new sense of partnership between people, a sense of brotherhood and sisterhood to overcome the racism we see in our society, the distrust, and the sense that our children will grow up being each other's enemies. We need to bring peace, justice and love, not only in what we talk about and do, but in the way we conduct our lives so that, as our leader so eloquently put it today, we can turn a rebellion of despair into a revolution of hope.

speakeroldname: Miss Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend makes a very eloquent, albeit inflammatory and totally political speech full of all kinds of points that really do not get to the point at all.
The point we are dealing with here is one that is very serious, and most members in the House this evening have tried to stay away from political rhetoric. It has elevated the tone of this debate a great deal and it is a matter appreciated by many members of our listening audience across the country.
My question to the hon. member is very simple. How can the hon. member condone the taking of a life in the promotion of a cause, no matter how good that cause may seem to the people who are espousing that cause? Does the member believe that masked warriors dressed in full battle regalia, carrying weapons that one sees only

Government Orders
in movies about full-fledged war, promote the interests of the Indian people that he speaks so eloquently about?
The warriors are armed. We know that they were prepared to use those arms. I do not understand, and perhaps the member can tell me, how that kind of activity can do anything at all to promote the very just and legitimate cause of many of the Indian people who have very just and legitimate causes to be promoted across the country. How can he condone the use of armed force in the promotion of an idea?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have to start by saying that I think the hon. member misunderstood the point of my speech completely and that may well be my fault. I was trying to pack in a lot of ideas in a very short time.
In no way do I condone the taking of a life and what has happened here. I have been a life-long advocate of non-violent solutions to problems, including involvement in the civil rights movements in the United States and the anti-Vietnam movement where I personally have always advocated non-violence. I have done so as well in the Indian communities in which I move and take every step that I can to advocate peaceful, non-violent solutions to problems. In no way do I condone the fact that there has been an escalation of violence here.
The point that I am making, however, is that it is hypocritical-and I do not mean that in the partisan sense-to say that the violence is that of only a small group of people, the warrior society at Oka. I think the violence that has expressed itself has much wider origins than that and finds much wider expression than that. In fact, what is so tragic is that we did not respond to that situation at an early point in its evolution. What were we doing here? It struck me, are we so crazy that we are going to have a civil war in this country because somebody wants to build a golf course on a burial ground? The whole series of events that evolved have shown that certainly the Warriors Society has its way of doing things that I do not personally agree with but, as well, the government's response to that has been one, I think, of machismo as well in that you do not negotiate at the point of a gun and you keep ratcheting up the level of confrontation with lights and depriving a community of food until the whole country is anxious and up tight and in a tinder-box kind of situation. Therefore, I would say that I very much believe and hope that this can be resolved peacefully and, in fact, that this will be a lesson to all of us and one that will not be repeated.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. For the other half of that 20 minutes, the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I concur wholeheartedly with the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River, who has been a lifelong pacifist and has fought hard for the cause of pacificists and the cause of peace. I see the Minister of Justice in the House and I am hoping she will take some notes and reply to some of my comments.
I want to say right off the bat, let us make it quite clear, Canadians are against violence but they feel very strongly that this government has bungled this situation. That is what you get everywhere. As a matter of fact, I think the country would like to see the Tories and their politics out of Oman, out of Oka and out of office as soon as possible. I want to raise some legal questions tonight and, as I said, I would like the Minister of Justice to respond.
The first question is: who is in charge here, who is running the show? Is it the federal government, the provincial government, the army, who? Surely Canadians are entitled to know that. As part of that, how did this thing happen in Canada? How did we get to this horrible situation in Canada? I think you have to look at the political situation at the time this happened. You had a Prime Minister who was angry and wounded over Meech Lake and did not know what to do. He delegated the situation to a premier, Premier Bourassa, who was also angry and arrogant toward the native people and malevolent toward the native people, holding them up as the cause of the destruction of Meech Lake. I think that was the real politics and someone should say that and I have just said it. I think that is what happened. At the time, the Prime Minister delegated to Premier Bourassa, the Surete operation was bungled. If there ever was a police force in need of reform, it is the Surete du Quebec and it was bungled by the Quebec government which is the political master of the Surete and which is responsible.
Then the Prime Minister of Canada and this government used the Defence Act, not the Emergency Measures Act, the Defence Act. In my view that was unconstitutional and illegal. The Defence Act was not made for that purpose. The Defence Act, in my view, is made for a riot or a disturbance where the provincial premier could call in the army for a short period. Why else would it say in the act that the province is responsi-
September 25, 1990

ble but the federal government pays all the bills? Would Parliament leave that open ended? There is provision for a report to the Secretary of State, after seven days. Where is the report? I ask the Minister of Justice to show us that report here tonight.
Why did the government not use the Emergency Measures Act which is the reform of the War Measures Act, which is surely for an insurrection or something like this that happened in Oka? Why did the government not use that? Because they would have to recall Parliament and because there are certain civil liberties protections. I challenge the minister tonight to get up in this House and again justify the shameful conduct that is being applied as it relates to Canadian journalists. It is a clear violation of the Charter of Rights and it is a clear violation of freedom of the press in this country and an example of a bungling government and an example of the price that we are paying for this Oka situation. This is something that we have to look into when this motion goes to committee, the act that was used, the civil liberties violations and so on.
The resolution of the government is bad. The Prime Minister is hanging onto a law and order motion. Everybody, of course, is in favour of law and order but this crisis goes deeper. The Prime Minister is wrong in one aspect. He is in fact saying the law has to apply to all Canadians. There is a principle, of course, of equality under the law. But there are different laws for different Canadians. It is in our law and the Prime Minister fails to grasp this. For example, Quebec is treated differently. They have the Napoleonic code, civil law, a different language protection and different educational rights protection. Natives are distinct in many ways in our law; the fiduciary relationship with the federal government; hunting, fishing and so on and rights that have been recognized by the Supreme Court of Canada. The Prime Minister is wrong when he proceeds on this premise and the resolution is wrong when it proceeds on this premise.
The reason we need a royal commission, and it has to be an active royal commission and it has to go somewhere in defining between what the Mohawks have asked for, which is sovereignty, which no Canadian government can really recognize and, on the other hand, the status quo, which the Prime Minister wants to see.
Government Orders
We must find some way in the middle where there can be self government that can be defined. It is already in our law; it is already possible. The government is not grasping this and that is why this is a misleading resolution. The Prime Minister bungled the situation, retreated and handed it to the Premier of Quebec who bungled it malevolently, and then comes back in this House and wraps himself in the cloak of law and order. It is disgusting. As soon as the Canadian electorate can go to the polls, they are going to vote this government out of office.
I would like to end with a couple of other matters. It has been called the summer of discontent in Canada by my leader, and we all agree with that. When we saw the native and the old people being stoned at Chateauguay, it was a shame, it was the dark side of racism. But we should remember that that can happen anywhere in Canada. If the Lion's Gate Bridge in B.C. was blockaded, I am ashamed to say that you might see some similar conduct. Let us not just blame the people of Quebec because we all have that dark side to us in Canada. It is still a dark side and we should condemn it.
The second aspect of that is the Warriors. I am speaking for myself, Mr. Speaker, and I say this to many progressive people in Canada: do not be naive. We are against guns, we are against this kind of American conduct that the Warriors adopted. I see it as an almost fascistic takeover of a part of the Mohawk nation by a very, very ultra right-wing group that has been mixed up in some very questionable activities, and I think one has to say that. Having said that, where do we go from here? It is almost like, you know, it is the right cause. It is the cause and people understand the cause, but it is the wrong way to go about the cause. We have a choice in Canada; we can have more violence across Canada or we can tackle the legitimate claims of the native people.
You heard the member for Prince Albert say 80 per cent of the people in jail in Saskatchewan are native people. We must change that. We need to have a new relationship with native people in this country. I call upon the Minister of Justice tonight to begin by ending the Oka crisis. I heard them on television tonight. Call for an independent Crown attorney now. Is that really too great a thing to ask, and some protection from the army when they put down their weapons. I say put down

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
the weapons now. I say that the government agree to an independent Crown attorney and take charge. Don't just let Bourassa and the Quebec government deal with the whole thing. The Minister of Justice has a responsibility. You must give these people in there, whatever you think of them, a little bit of honour to get out of there because that honour will go on to the native people in this country who are looking for a little bit of honour.
Let me end on a positive note and I look forward to the Minister of Justice replying to my remarks. We all felt great, did we not, when the army and the natives got together and started pulling those barricades down on the bridge. We felt wonderful as Canadians, that was from the Canadian spirit, that was as a peaceful country. Let us get back to that. We are only going to get back to that by this Prime Minister cutting out the phoniness, facing the issue straight on and we, as a people, getting a new relationship with the native people and the federal government, through the Minister of Justice tonight taking over control of what is going on in Oka and negotiating at the last minute a settlement with honour.

Having said that, I want to refer to his comment that in the very outset that the government had bungled the situation. He used the word 'bungled'. In hindsight, as we heard from one of my colleagues this evening, I think that is a very serious mistake in terms because in fact the government has not bungled the situation.
How can the hon. member even suggest such a thing when the barricades have been removed? He alluded to this a moment ago and the good feeling that people had when the barricades were removed without incident and without any loss of life. How can he say that this government has bungled the situation when the volatility
of something that was very, very iffy, very touchy, was removed with cool-headed, capable, competent, calm action? How can he say that the situation has been bungled when in fact over 77 long days that were very trying and very emotional for all of us, not a single life was lost since the very beginning of the incident? How can the hon. member say that the government has bungled the situation? The government has shown the kind of leadership that was necessary to get through a difficult situation with honour, with integrity and without loss of life.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY

I think to get through the situation, in many respects it was the army and its their public conduct. There was some violence there. It was not exemplary, but the conduct got the government through and got us through. We are not through it yet. We are almost through it. The government should take some action tonight as I have suggested. It bungled it from the beginning. In my speech I suggested how in the beginning it bungled the matter. I suggest you ask any Canadian citizen out there. They will tell you they think the government has bungled the matter. The government is even worse, it is even more sleazy. It is now the Prime Minister who comes before the House and tries to wrap himself in this law and order stance. I am sure he has gone to Allan Gregg and looked at the polls. Well, Canadians like law and order. All right, we will go with law and order. You can see it. You can smell it from the man when he speaks. Where was he in the beginning of the crisis? Where was he hiding? Where was his minister? That is how the government bungled the situation because it was not there in the beginning. It could have made it a lot shorter.
With respect to the Emergency Act, I suggest the member read it. I ask the member to comment on my suggestion. Does she really believe that Parliament really intended to turn over a situation like this to a provincial premier and then let him run up the bills? We have to pay all the bills in this. I don't know if Canadians understand that. It is at the beck and call of a provincial premier. At some point he even said that he was not sure he was running. I call that bungling and I call that the wrong act. I think that the government has to respond to this when we get the committee.

Whip his writ. When he refers to the notion of the Prime Minister delegating this to the premier of Quebec, the hon. member knows the Constitution. He knows who has the constitutional responsibility for law enforcement. The Government of Canada worked very hard this summer to try and do what was ever within our constitutional power to contain the situation at Oka and to ensure that it was resolved in a way that did not result in loss of life. It was something that we agonized over. I would say to the hon. member that his comments about the warriors and what kind of people they are I find very welcome. They were pretty scarce in the early days, and I recall a time during this conflict, about the middle of July, when the Deputy Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development described the warriors in an unattractive way as criminals and thugs and was denounced roundly from one end of the country to the other.
Interestingly enough, about a week later in The Globe and Mail the story came out: "Mohawk chiefs decry paramilitary warriors, group called gang of criminals". Barbara Barnes, a spokesman for the chiefs' council did not mince words about the members of the Mohawk Warrior Society: "I agree with Harry Swayne 100 per cent, the warriors are a gang of criminals".
However, the fact of the matter is that this summer the government was doing a great deal, but it was doing it in the face of a very uninformed public opinion which in fact seemed to think that the warriors were heroes and
Government Orders
could not make the distinction between a group of armed warriors who had a particular interest that they wanted to defend and the legitimate aspirations of Indian people across this country.
I have talked to Indian people across this country who are themselves feeling disillusioned about the late arrival of people like Grand Chief Georges Erasmus on the scene to talk about what they really think of the warriors. Across this country there was a lot of confusion as to who these people were and an enormous amount of strained and tom loyalties among Indian peoples themselves as to how they should respond to the warriors.
I think it has been an enormously difficult situation because we had a group of very unpleasant people, many of whose chief victims have been members of their own community, who have been glamorized and idealized and set up as the champions of a cause in which they are not even faintly interested except in so far as it suits their own particular needs. I think to say that the government did not care, was not involved, bungled or delegated is completely wrong.
It would have been very nice if the Government of Canada had the constitutional jurisdiction to reinforce the law. It does not have it in Quebec. It does not have it in British Columbia. It does not have it in Ontario, which is why all of those situations which occurred this summer were dealt with by provincial authorities.
Once again, when we talk about the question of the honour to get out, the army made a very fair and straightforward offer to the warriors who are now in the treatment centre. I think this whole question of what is a fair and honourable denouement has a great deal to do with how one characterizes the warriors and who they are. I think a lot of people have lost sight of just who they are and what they represent.
I must say as Minister of Justice that I find it hard to answer the questions of people who say to me in my own riding and other parts of the country that if we appeared in masks carrying AK-47s, we would not be treated the way the warriors have been in Kanesatake. If a Chinese youth gang in Vancouver made a little trouble and appeared on the scene with masks and AK-47s, would they have been treated with that kind of patience? What about a group of young blacks in downtown Toronto or Haitians in Montreal?

Government Orders
It is a pretty tough question to answer, and frankly as Minister of Justice I am veiy troubled about that. I think the situation is not helped by people here fudging who and what the warriors are. I appreciate the hon. member's unambiguous statements that they should be the foundation of a reanalysis and a rethinking of the rest of things he said in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to rise today on the motion presented by my honorable colleague the minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
In that motion, the House is invited to commend the Canadian Armed Forces for their conduct.
I am sure that all the hon. members in this House will agree to say that our soldiers have demonstrated both courage and restraint in extremely difficult circumstances, as well as professionalism and discipline in emotionally packed moments and under very trying conditions.
Their exemplary conduct is worthy of the proudest Canadian traditions and of the Canadian Armed Forces.

The motion today goes on to call for the persons behind the barricades to lay down their arms and to submit to the processes of our nation's judicial system. This motion speaks to some of the most cherished of our democratic rights and freedoms.
My first career before I became a lawyer was as a political scientist specializing in the government and politics of the Soviet Union. My thesis adviser at the London School of Economics was a renowned scholar, Professor Leonard Shapiro, whose career was a mirror image of my own, since he went from the practice of law to academia, while I did the reverse. I believe that his distinguished career at the British bar provided the philosophical foundation for his later academic work. When he died in 1983 he was recognized as one of the great authorities on the Soviet Union.
One of the most important criteria by which he judged a society was whether or not it was governed by the rule of law. Sadly, during Professor Shapiro's lifetime that claim could not be made for the U.S.S.R., although recent changes have been dramatic.
My study of the Soviet Union in the pre-Glasnost era in my three months there in 1972 as well as travels elsewhere in the world have enabled me to gain some perspective on a concept which is taken for granted in Canada: the notion of the rule of law. It is the foundation stone of all our other values because it provides the rules of the game by which we reconcile the differences of interest, value, and opinion that are inevitable in human society. The challenge faced by democratic societies is to recognize that our values are often in conflict with each other.
When I taught political philosophy one of the most fascinating areas for my students was an examination of how different thinkers and different ideological schools of thought deal with the conflict between the values of equality and liberty. Societies cannot maximize either value without some cost to the other and an equilibrium struck in one era may not be acceptable to the priorities of another era.
How do we manage the conflicts in values and priorities in a manner which does not tear society apart? We do it through process which are enshrined in our law. Those processes and laws are themselves subject to change, but the confidence that the rules of the game will be observed is the foundation of our civility.
If one has never been in a country which is not a democracy, one perhaps cannot appreciate the significance of the orderly transition of governments based on electoral results. Notwithstanding the rhetoric that is frequently heard in this House, no one here is under any doubt as to the commitment of all members here to those fundamental rules, even if if occasionally we purport to think that the views of pollsters should substitute for a proper electoral mandate.
Even before but especially since the Charter of Rights and Freedoms became a part of our law, part of our rules of the game, courts have struck down the legislation of this House. However we may regard those decisions, it is unthinkable that we would not abide by their findings. Thus even those who made the rules are subject to constitutional limitations. These limitations and rules are not unchangeable. Sometimes we find them outdated or inappropriate and we seek to revise them, but by working with and through the law and democratic processes we make changes that are accepted as legiti-
September 25, 1990

mate, even by those who do not like them, because they been made according to the accepted rules.
The rule of law which binds governments as well as citizens is a call to an adherence to a reasoned and balanced process of law making in accordance with our Constitution. Fundamental to the principle and the process is the rejection of the arbitrary use of force, a rejection of violence.

We can review how the native leaders, governments and such and such locality responded to events in Oka and Chateauguay-Kahnawake.
We can discuss the wisdom of a specific line of conduct and the merits of the stand adopted by the Warriors. However, this debate must have for framework the fundamental principles of our society.
My colleague the minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development gave an excellent overview of the programs the government has implemented with the participation of the native leaders to protect the interests of the native peoples.

We know that we have a long way to go to ensure a rightful and fair place for aboriginal peoples in our country. We also know that a necessary precondition is the acceptance by all Canadians, without exception, of the rule of law. In the final analysis our primary concern must be to see that justice is served. The people of Canada, both native and non-native, demand it.
In current circumstances certain warriors have taken up arms and are resisting the enforcement of the law. Certain aboriginal leaders argue that peace officers should not search for illegal weapons on Indian lands because these lands are sovereign territory, not subject to the law of Canada.
The Government of Canada rejects the use of force by those with no authority under Canadian law. We reject any contention that the criminal law of Canada does not apply from coast to coast on public and private property, on Indian lands, or on land devoted for the use of some other group.
Government Orders
Justice must be applied to those who have consciously and wilfully resisted legitimate authority in the application of the law. We must not undermine the principle that everyone is subject to the law. We must not send a signal that laws can be ignored to suit individual circumstance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
The rule of law is the necessary precondition for a society in which our values can flourish. It enables us to weigh our actions, consider the consequences and know what to expect. We cannot pick and choose when we want to apply the law and we cannot pick and choose which laws we want to obey.
If one indulges in crime or civil disobedience, one does so with the assurance that actions have consequences. By the same principle, Canadians have the assurance that if legal consequences apply to them each Canadian enjoys the same guarantee of due process, the right to a fair trial, and the right to be heard.
Canadians have been shocked and deeply moved by the tragic events at Oka and Chateauguay-Kahnawake. Canadians have a deep sympathy for the grievances of native people, but one distinction must be kept crystal clear: we must not confuse the legitimate concerns of native people with the resistance to the rule of law by armed warriors at Oka.	.

I categorically refuse to equate the confrontation in Oka to pure and simple civil disobedience.
Weapons are not the tools of civil disobedience. Violence, effective or threatened, profits nobody. It makes innocent people suffer losses and gets in the way of rational discussions.
Violence cannot and will not be tolerated.
I also refuse to believe that the situation in Oka relates to land claims. That question was settled.
On the 27th of August, my colleague, the minister for Indian Affairs and Northen Development, announced

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
that his department had accepted to acquire 60 residential lots covering an area totalling 30 acres.
The lots in question at Oka will never be used for a golf course.
The government of Canada acquired them with the intention to negotiate their transfer to the relevant Mohawks authorities, as soon as all threats of violence will cease.
No, Mr. Speaker, the primacy of law is the question at stake.
The people concerned used very powerful arms to resist to the polices. A police officer was killed. Many innocent victims were threatened. Certain Mohawks were badly beaten.
Houses were broken into and vandalized.
That explains why, on August 27th, Premier Robert Bourassa, in accordance with the powers conferred on the provinces by the National Defence Act, asked the Armed Forces to remove the barricades, store the circulation on all streets and bridges, bring down all centres of resistance and store normal conditions of public order and security.

Under Canadian law, the Armed Forces are obliged to assist in the enforcement of the law when provincial law enforcement agencies are unable to prevent, suppress or control riots, insurrections or other disturbances of the peace. The Canadian forces have been called upon to do their duty and they will remain at Oka until such time as order is restored or the premier of Quebec requests their withdrawal.
I would like to remind hon. members that the Government of Canada has conscientiously avoided jeopardizing the efforts of the Government of Quebec to negotiate a solution to the situation at Oka. At the same time we have used our best efforts to assist in the negotiations.
Throughout the government has sought a peaceful resolution. We share the concern of many Canadians for the safety of the warriors now surrounded at Oka, but we would not agree with a decision to grant amnesty for their actions. No government can or should negotiate whether the law should be respected. No government can or should be expected to negotiate anything under the threat of weapons or violence. We do not accept that
the warriors are legitimate representatives of their people. The citizens of Kanesatake and Kahnawake do not accept them as such.
The Oka warriors will be given all the protection of the due process of law, for this too is fundamental to the rule of law. We will not invite a lasting disrespect for a system of justice that has served Canadians well, and we will not invite prospect of future violence against Canadians.

If the Warriors do accept the offer made by the Canadian Armed Forces to guarantee their safety, we will have to decide if criminal charges will be laid against them.
Individuals facing no charges will be released. Those who are will be entitled to a fair trial and the full protection of the Charter, the law and the courts.
In Canada, justice and fairness start with the rule of law. According to this principle, the government of Canada will continue to work with the native people to achieve their legitimate aspirations.

The government respects and honours all legitimate Indian leaders who come forward peacefully. The government welcomes the opportunity to sit down and discuss reforms to the justice system with these leaders but not with warriors with guns in their hands. We are prepared to move on many fronts. Last June, for example, I requested that the Law Reform Commission of Canada study the Criminal Code and related laws to ensure that any provision of the law that might impair the accessibility and fairness of the criminal law for aboriginal people be identified. I expect to receive their report in the summer of 1991.
The Government of Canada and the provincial governments are working toward reform of the justice system in native affairs. A recent meeting of federal, provincial and territorial Ministers of Justice agreed to hold a conference as proposed by my colleague, the Minister of Justice for the Yukon, on native justice issues in 1991 as an opportunity for governments and aboriginal leaders from all regions to discuss aboriginal aspirations for the justice system.
What have native communities asked for? Greater control of local police, new systems of dispute adjudica-
September 25, 1990

tion, tribal courts, community involvement in sentencing. Most of these demands are not unreasonable.
In looking at them the government is resolved to remain flexible and innovative. We are willing to consider alternatives to the present system, but these must respect the constitutional integrity of Canada and inviolability of the rule of law.

Mr. Speaker, all members of this House believe in a future where native people will feel confortable with the Canadian justice system.
I am convinced that by working together, we will make changes that will show our flexibility and our understanding and urge the native people to trust a justice system which really meet their legitimate aspirations.
We have a rather long way to go to deal with all the grievances that have been filed, but we have already made some headway.

We will continue to work with native people to accelerate programs for aboriginal self-government and resolution of land disputes. We will continue to examine alternatives to the justice system. We have learned the painful lessons taught by the Marshall inquiry in Nova Scotia, the testimony in the Manitoba inquiry and the Blood Indian policing inquiry in Alberta.
Even as we resolve to be flexible and innovative in the creation of our system of justice, we must renew our commitment to the basic human rights of all Canadians. Let us recognize once again that particular efforts may be required to ensure that universal standards are available to certain vulnerable individuals and groups.

Let's commit ourselves to implement a justice system that will take into acount our collective values, and suppress from our statutes all form of bias, and from the enforcement of the law, all form of discrimination.
Again, we have to try and establish a justice system that Canadians can continue to rely on.
Government Orders

Questions and comments. First I will recognize the hon. member for Winnipeg North, then the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Mount Royal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have several questions for the minister. Why did the government present this particular motion? Why is the conduct of the army on trial in Parliament and not the political marching order that was given by this government? I submit that what we should be debating is the political marching order given to the army and not the conduct of the army per se. I think this motion is misplaced and I would like the minister's comments on that.
The motion speaks about the applicability of Canadian laws on all Canadian lands and is asking the opinion of this House. This is most unusual. Is this an admission of failure on the part of this government? Is it an admission of the absence of federal leadership?
The motion also asks all of the people at the Kanesa-take Treatment Centre to lay down their arms. If this motion is passed and there are no peaceful negotiations in that area and the Indian people do not leave the centre, is the minister and this government then telling the Canadian people that it is creating another offence for the Indian people, that is contempt of Parliament? I think this is serious. This government is creating another potential offence for the aboriginal people of our country.
It is also repugnant to the principle of law. No ex post facto must be enacted. Here they are cornered by the army and now they are being forced to surrender and lose their dignity. If they do not do that, they can potentially be in contempt of Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, while the minister speaks of the rule of law that rejects violence, which I agree with, I would like the minister to also address the issue of where there is a conflict between the rule of law and the supremacy of justice. The minister knows that justice is the underpinning of any law. Even President Lincoln refused to

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
handle a client's case when he was being asked to collect from the very rich, which legally was right but unjust. Mr. Speaker, those are my questions to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief although there are quite a number of questions there.
First of all, the hon. member asks why this particular motion? This is the government's motion. If the hon. member wishes to bring forward a different motion to the House, he is free to do so. The motion is very broad and allows quite a considerable scope for debate. The point is, it does provide an opportunity for the members of this House to express themselves on an issue of veiy considerable public importance and I am sorry if the hon. member feels constrained by this motion and if he does feel constrained, then he can perhaps move his own. The wording of this motion is simply making a declaration on the part of Parliament.
The notion of contempt of Parliament if they do not surrender is totally misplaced. This House, on many occasions, calls on people to do things, calls on people to support something and the notion that somebody who refuses to yield to the call is in contempt of Parliament is totally ridiculous. I think it is perfectly appropriate for Parliament to make that call.
The member talks about the conflict between justice and the law. I would be the last person in the world to say that the law is always right. What I tried to point out in my speech was that there is a framework in which we try to change these things and I am not saying that it would never, ever be the case that dramatic events would not be required, perhaps to get attention. But we have in this country an enormous number of opportunities and processes through which people can attempt to change the law. That does not just mean the democratic process in Parliament, it means the ability to express one's self, to demonstrate, to vote, to mobilize, to organize, and to form associations. There is an enormous amount of leverage in the hands of people in order to influence the form that the law takes.
What I think was so important, and what I tried to draw attention to in my remarks in response to the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam is that part of the problem with this issue this summer has been the confusion as to how to characterize it. This is not, in my view, an issue where people are required to go to extraordinary lengths to get justice. The issue which stimulated the putting up of the barricades and the
taking up of arms, arms that are prohibited for Canadians, was an issue having to do with land and where the negotiations were ended by Chief George Martin in March of 1990. In August of 1989, the federal government met with the Kanesatake band council, the province of Quebec and the municipalities of Oka village and Oka parish to establish a committee to draft a framework agreement aimed at developing a unified land base for Kanesatake.
When I became Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development in January of 1989, one of the first issues I was briefed on was the land problem at Oka because the lands were dispersed and there was a need to develop an consolidated land base for more housing and community development. The efforts to try to purchase that land long predate this particular issue.
I think it is very important to understand that what was going on there was not a situation in which people were driven to extremes in order to achieve justice. From time to time, even some members of the Mohawk community have themselves been quite considerably intimidated, I think, by the presence of Mohawk warriors have spoken up. And what has distressed me is, who is listening to them? Who is listening to those who are saying, "We want them out of our community". Even Georges Erasmus is saying it now. Georges Erasmus was not to be heard in the early days of this particular confrontation but some people, with considerable courage, spoke up and said, "We want them out of our community". They went to my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs, and said, "Get these people out of our community". The chief and his son were beaten by warriors because they tried to stop them from vandalizing the house of the local veterinarian. The warriors will not be rebuilding the community relationship between the veterinarian and the other Indians. They will buzz off. They are not even from that community.
If you have been listening to what has been going on you hear the cries of the people who are in the community who are distressed that their community is being torn out by the roots, by warriors coming in with weapons and creating an atmosphere of violence and creating a division between the native and non-native community. They will not be around to heal. On the contrary, it will be left to others to heal. The actions they have committed have been in breach of the criminal law of Canada
September 25, 1990

and they should be held accountable before the criminal justice system.

speechtext: I have on my list the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam. I would hope that they would be more succinct. We have only four minutes left to divide.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will do my best to be succinct. The hon. member for Macleod wishes me luck.
I know that the minister's speech was a real mouthful. I want to congratulate her, though. I have not seen her since last June because Parliament has not been sitting all that time. I understand that her legal talents have now been recognized by her former mentor, the Premier of British Columbia, who has made her one of Her Majesty's counsel, learned in the law, and I wanted to pass on my compliments on this elevation for her. It is a distinction that I am sure is richly deserved as the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam will be able to attest, being a solicitor in her own province. I congratulate the minister on that.
With respect to her speech I had some difficulty because it certainly was full of a lot of-if I may put it politely-platitudes which sort of surprised me because when I heard the minister was going to intervene in this debate I was expecting some real pearls of wisdom.
One of the statements she made was: "We are prepared to move on many fronts". Well, today during the speech by my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Western Arctic, she referred to a proposal that had been sent by some professors at Queen's University. I do not know whether the minister had had the advantage of seeing the set of proposals that was addressed to her. I was sent a copy by the group of 22 professors who signed this particular document.
The paper suggested that one of the difficulties in the two Indian reserves where there are problems today was that the rule of law in Canada involved more than the Criminal Code, as the minister has been stressing throughout her speech. She seemed to suggest that there had been a breach of the criminal law and therefore the
Government Orders
law had to be applied with all its vigour and force, arrests made, charges laid, and so on.
The suggestion of these professors was that in fact Canadian constitutional law was involved. The law of aboriginal rights was involved. The law of the treaties that had been signed was involved. And international law was also involved.
I suggest to the minister that given the suggestion of these professors that perhaps it is not a simple, straightforward matter of criminal law. I invite her to look at the situation in that light.
Would she not agree with them that perhaps the reasonable solution and one of the movements she might make on one of the fronts that she might consider, is the appointment of the legal commission that they recommended, consisting of a group of distinguished jurists, aboriginal people, and others who could look at the situation and advise the minister with respect to how the matter could be handled, on the understanding that the natives who are behind the barricade, contained in the encampment at the moment, could be released and their fate determined based on the findings of the legal commission. It could decide how prosecutions, if any, were to be proceeded with. It could be determined whether or not they were subject to all the rigors of Canadian criminal law as the minister is suggesting.
It seems to be a way to avoid further bloodshed and to bring the matter to a peaceable conclusion. I think the suggestion was put forward by this distinguished group of men and women who are professors at the law school with the best of intentions and to assist the minister in the current difficulty. I wonder if she would comment on whether or not she is prepared to entertain that request and appoint a legal commission as suggested in the letter dated September 24.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal that the hon. member refers to is one that I have not seen so I cannot comment on the creation of a legal commission. But obviously as Minister of Justice I hope that it has probably been sent to me and actually has not come across my desk yet.

Government Orders
The hon. member makes reference to three particular areas of law that the learned scholars refer to: the law of aboriginal rights, treaty law, and international law. I know of no law under any of those rubrics that would in fact exempt the people who are now in the treatment centre at Kanesatake from the application of the criminal law of Canada.
I have done a fair amount of work on the question of aboriginal rights going back to my days as a policy adviser in the office of the Premier of British Columbia and I know of no interpretation or implication of any of the jurisprudence on aboriginal rights or aboriginal title that would serve to exempt Indian people from the application of the criminal law of Canada. I know of no treaty that would do so. It has been alleged that perhaps the Jay treaty provides that. I would respectfully suggest that is not the case in Canada, nor do I know of any provision of international law or any convention that we are signatory to that would be binding in Canada which would exempt them from the application of the criminal law.
The hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam will perhaps smile when I say it, but no matter which direction one goes-one can go up or down or side ways-wherever one goes, one comes face to face with the law. It does not fly.
All these things are very interesting, but once again it gets back to characterizing where one is there and who these people are. I do not see that any of these things would in fact exempt any of those people from the application of the criminal law.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister is referring to a case that I had with her father. He was a Crown attorney and I was defence counsel and I made a brilliant argument. He stood up and said: "No matter where my young friend goes, he goes up and down and around, and everywhere he runs into the law". He sat down and the judge convicted my client. So, that is where the phrase comes from.
By the way I would not cite my experience in Bill Bennett's government which did not recognize, as I recall, aboriginal rights. It is one of the reasons why we have so many problems with native questions in Canada. They were dragging their heels on that.
I do not want to ask the minister about her travelogue in the Soviet Union or her learned dissertation on the political science scene of the rule of law. She must be aware that the one of the officers of the Surete du Quebec filed an affidavit to get an injunction to interfere with the freedom of the press. One of the allegations in the affidavit was that the Lion's Gate Bridge which is in her riding in Vancouver, was blockaded. Absurd and yet they got the interim injunction and cut off press freedoms for a short period in Canada. How does she feel about that? Does she feel any responsibility for that area? How is she involved in this situation? Does she have any responsibility at all for the army down there or for the police?
My final question is this. What is the matter with trying to move in herself on the final negotiation and allowing these people to get out of there? Whatever we want to argue about the warriors, the fact is that other native people all across the country are looking and they feel humiliated. How about letting them out of there with a little honour and accepting some of the reasonable propositions, to wit, a trial under Canadian law, which I agree with, proper charges, proper defence counsel, a fair prosecutor, and some guarantee from the army that they will have some safety?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know the specific terms of whatever is on the table in front of the parties, but I remind the hon. member again that the prosecutions under the Criminal Code of Canada are not the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice.
If they were, I could barge in and do all sorts of things. They are not. They are the constitutional prerogative of the provincial governments. They are jealously guarded prerogatives, I am sure he is aware, given the fact of other federal statutes where the Government of Canada has wanted to prosecute the prosecutorial power has been seriously contested.
With respect to his comment about my providing advice in Bill Bennett's government, unfortunately when I was asked to get into the whole issue of aboriginal rights, titles and advice to the Premier, before I had a chance to give him my advice he decided to retire. So, I left his office with a head full of all sorts of no doubt
September 25, 1990

confused and erroneous ideas, but none of which I have been able to give the benefit of to the Premier.
With respect to the situation with the journalists, and I have read the reports about the affidavit, it is not for me to determine whether that allegation is fatal to the request for the injunction itself. That is for a court to determine and I do not think it is appropriate for me to comment on it. But the point is that there is recourse. That issue is before the courts now and the newspapers have challenged that decision. The only comment that I have made on this, which I made in the House and it appeared to create enormous discomfort among people, was I simply confirmed that the jurisprudence with respect to the right of freedom of the press as is in the Charter of Rights has indicated that the courts will, from time to time, recognize that it may be appropriate to limit the access of journalists to certain kinds of information.
But, once again, we have to think of what we are dealing with. We are dealing with a situation which is analogous to one where a group of people perform certain acts. They are in possession of prohibited weapons. They block public highways and destroy property. The police are attempting to arrest them. They take refuge in a building or a basement and they are armed. Therefore, the police are trying to determine how to arrest these people without loss of life for the suspects or for themselves. That is exactly the analogy of what we have in Kanesatake. I am not aware of any similar kind of circumstances where the press are allowed free access in and out and where this becomes a great public event.
The army is trying to conduct this law enforcement operation. It makes certain decisions, as does any kind of police department, about how it is going to do it and it is putting pressure on people there to surrender, exactly as one would if people were hold up in a basement somewhere or in a house or whatever trying to avoid arrest. I mean, one would not cater their meals and send out their laundry. We have to keep in mind what we are dealing with there and it is very difficult. None of us wants to see any injury and none of us wants to see loss of lives. No matter what offences may or may not have been committed, no one as yet has been convicted and we do not have capital punishment in Canada, so
Government Orders
shooting people is a bit extreme no matter what they have done and we do not want that to happen.
Those who are enforcing the law are trying to use as much patience as possible to get people to surrender. It is that context that you have to bear in mind. There is recourse in the law if the army has overstepped the Charter of Rights of members of the press and they will be held to account for it. When they go under under the civil power, they are each one of those members of the Armed Forces liable under the Criminal Code of Canada for what they do. It is a very accountable situation. That is all that would be appropriate to say. But people are seeking legal recourse.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating, as the Minister well knows, the role of the army and a whole series of issues that was placed on the Order Paper which I believe to be somewhat of a smoke-screen, notwithstanding her point of view which differs from mine.
One of the things which has been said in the House is the great deal of pride and sense of pride that one has had when we saw the picture of that young soldier standing there so well disciplined, face to face with this Mohawk. We sensed, in that one picture, the kind of role that the army was playing. There were errors and there were other things but, in a sense, good discipline.
We also were somewhat outraged by the picture of two ministers and a judge signing an accord with a Mohawk flag. There was no Quebec flag, no Canadian flag, but that picture will remain etched in the memories of a lot of us.
We also are well aware of what happened when the army rolled in. The photographers, the newspaper people, everyone has had a role to play in the media that has been very constructive. It has educated this society. There was that wonderful picture that was taken by Shaney Comolanen. She is still in that treatment centre. What was her crime and why was she deprived of both the entrance of food and equipment? Where was the Minister's role in speaking out with respect to the Charter and the abolition of human rights under that Charter? I believe the minister has something to tell this House with respect to her responsibilities for the media, for the telephones, for access to film material and the right to file their stories. Not to throw it out by-

speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard perhaps one of the most chilling speeches that have been given in the House of Commons in a long time. It is especially frightening coming from a minister who has taken an oath of office to protect justice in Canada. It is apparent that justice is not part of the vocabulary or lexicon of this minister.
The description, as she went through her long dissertation, of the rule of law being the foundation of society shows that she does not know her political science very well. There are others in the Chamber who have also had the occasion from time to time to teach political science and we know that a rule of law is not the basis of a civilized society, it is a question justice. It is a question of sharing power. It is a question of having a kind of society which recognizes individual rights and out of that one develops a rule of law around those basic concepts. Dictators and tyrants can use the rule of law as effectively as anybody in a democracy can. Oftentimes the rule of law is used by democracies to suppress the rights of minorities.
How would you think, Madam Minister, wherever you have gone, if you were part of a minority which for the
past three or four hundred years that has not been treated with any justice; who has signed treaties with all expectation of being treated honestly and fairly and had your land and hunting rights taken away? How would you like to be part of a minority where your leader in Manitoba was hung because of a question of law and order, even though he is defending the rights of the Metis people of Manitoba. We put Louis Riel on the gallows, saying that was a question of law and order.
At Duck Lake, we had the army once again go after the native people who had their lands and their rights taken away. Afterward, in the words of the then Conservative Prime Minister, John A. Macdonald: "We will then come down and settle your grievances once you have laid down your arms."
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, how do you talk about having a trust and confidence in a system of justice and this rule of law that the minister so patently described as the basis and foundation, when you have gone through the Donald Marshall case in recent history, or the Betty Osborne case in Manitoba, or the JJ. Harper case, where clearly law and order was not on your side? How do you develop a belief and a confidence?
Even in the Oka case, you find yourself being overtaken on a sacred burial ground by a group of municipal politicians who want to build a golf course. You protested that and the judge gives an injunction which allows the police to come in and take down your right to defend that sacred ground. Do you call that a system of law and order? A system of justice and fair treatment? Surely to goodness in this country of ours the concept of justice means that you recognize that there is an element of mercy, compassion, and distinction in that and that it is not some kind of rigid tool to be employed by the courts or the police or a blind Minister of Justice, to secure political ends. That is the real issue, because we are talking about a group of people who for hundreds of years have been powerless in this society to get the kind of laws that would treat them fairly. They have not had the political power. The laws have been made in this Parliament often without the consideration, consultation, or participation of native people. They have been dependent. They have been inJferior. They have been treated as second-class citizens. We have a Minister of Justice who says "All is perfect, forget it all. The rule of law is all that counts". What absolute nonsense. What a
September 25, 1990

disgrace to have a Minister of Justice who uses that kind of language in this kind of circumstance.
It is no wonder the Canadian people are crying in sorrow this summer about what is going on when we see the country turn in this direction. This is not the country that we have known. We have a Minister of Justice who shows no sign of compassion or understanding, or caring, or sensitivity to those basic minority rights, and then gets up in the House and defends this. What is going on in this country when we have a minister like that?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: It is pretty frightening, that's for sure.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
It is frightening and chilling, I say to you, Mr. Speaker. She talks about visiting Indians. I visited Indian country this summer, like many of my colleagues. I went in a canoe, travelled the old voyageur routes and visited 15 reserves. I spent time on the reserves and the Oka incident was happening at that time. I had to sit around the campfire with band council members who, when they looked upon what was happening, gave up and rushed off to Oka to find out what was going on. I can tell you what the reaction was in The Pas Indian Friendship Centre when the Prime Minister of Canada came on TV with his speech about this is by law and order. I will tell you the look of 30 or 40 native people in the friendship centre. They began to give up on this country. They realized that there was no one in Ottawa on the government side who cared about their interests. They were surrendering.
The real issue that is going on in this country today as we speak is a fight for the kind of moderation that has been shown by our Indian leadership, by the Phil Fontaines and the Georges Erasmuses of this world. How long can they hold to a moderate leadership when they do not have anyone responsive on the other side?
I visited those reserves. I will tell you there are hundreds of Okas waiting to happen in this country. I can talk about going to The Pas reserve and having the fishermen from that reserve talk about when the Saskatchewan government built a dam upriver on the South Saskatchewan and never paid them compensation. Their
Government Orders
livelihood disappeared and no one paid them a cent. It just disappeared.
I can tell you what happened at the Fairford reserve where 800 people are denied their right to vote because no one in this government has got around to passing an order-in-council to give them a new piece of land that was given in compensation for a new dam. So they have lived in a no-man's land for the last five or six years and treated as non-citizens.
I could tell you about a small fishing village up on Lake Winnipeg that had its hatchery closed down by the provincial government and therefore had the livelihood of 90 people knocked out in one fell swoop because some bureaucrat or Minister of Finance on Broadway Avenue in Winnipeg said that was a budget matter. So, you take away the livelihood. They have been writing letters to the Minister of Indian Affairs for the past two years saying help us, get the hatchery open. They have not been given a reply.
This is no different than the transgression of a burial ground at Oka. In its own way, it is a small incident that could explode in their face. And we have a Minister of Justice who said "We're really going to get them. We're going to make sure that all those bad guys are arrested". Well, I will raise a challenge to the government: Let's have an inquiry and find out what the real truth is. Let's find out who was responsible, who was inciting the problems, who was there with the weapons, who was using force. Let's get to the bottom of it. Let's not have this kind of manipulation that we see coming from across the floor, the attempt to do as they have done on the GST and on every other issue, to distort the truth and the facts, to try to manipulate public opinion, because that is what is going on.
Of course, there are people there with weapons. But, the government knew they had weapons two or three years ago. This is not news. They have been on the reserves, the RCMP were there, and they did nothing about it. If they were so concerned about that, where was the federal government and the Quebec government doing something about the law and order at that point in time? Well, it was too big a problem and they just let it slide by. It didn't touch it at all. We have in this country an incredible gap of trust. It is a growing chasm of confidence among the most oppressed minority of any civilized country. I say that with all the shame that every member of this House should share in saying that.

Government Orders
I posed the issue to the Prime Minister this afternoon in Question Period. How can we have the nerve to lecture to other countries about peaceful resolutions of conflict, about recognition of individual rights, about the whole belief in the idea of civil rights and civil liberties when we so blatantly disregard them in our own country when the occasion arises? The Prime Minister and others have said: Well, we had no choice, we were called in and we had to use the force.
Internal observers who were in attendance at the initial negotiation said they did not understand why the negotiations were broken off. Discussion was taking place, sides were being presented. The international observers had no axe to grind. They were not political parties. They were outside the country. People who had witnessed for many other kinds of situations the same kind of problems, said: Hey, it was beginning to happen. All of a sudden the federal government and the Quebec government pull out and say: No negotiations, sorry. They are not negotiating in good faith. Who do you believe? The negotiation was only allowed to get started for two or three days. My goodness, the Prime Minister used to sit across the table from labour leaders for months and prides himself on his skill and ability to work out a deal.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Supposed.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Why was the
skill all of a sudden absent? Where did it disappear? Where did it evaporate into air, this incredible skill to get a deal and to negotiate? The great believer, the gentleman who ran on the ticket of national reconciliation, all of a sudden finds that those talents that he had provided free of charge to the Canadian people for so long all of a sudden disappeared this summer. Where did they go?
We did not give negotiation a chance. I think we were stampeded by a certain public opinion that said use force, solve the problem. Goodness knows it was coming apart, but I have to say to you it was not just the fault of the natives that it was coming apart. I want you to take a good hard look at the responsibility of the provincial government of Quebec in this case because that kind of stoning that we saw which was a shame on this nation was not stopped by those who were standing around watching it happen.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: You are right on, Lloyd.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not hear any condemnation of law and order in this case. I am prepared to say it because I am embarrassed as a Canadian to have watched my country changing before my eyes and watching that kind of distortion take place. Mr. Speaker, I say to you and to members opposite, if you are going to base your case solely and exclusively on the fact that there was a group of armed warriors who took over the Indians nations, who took over the Mohawks and were the manipulators of them, then let us find out. What are you scared of? Let's have an inquiry, whether it is parliamentary or independent, but let's get to the facts of the case because until we get to the truth there will be no rebuilding our confidence or trust among the aboriginal people in this country. The truth is the mother of trust and as long as the truth is being distorted or hidden or being manipulated, there will not be any rebuilding. I do not care if the Prime Minister comes before this House and says that he is going to accelerate some land grants. You cannot buy off aboriginal people anymore. That is what happened this summer. The country can never be the same.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
