We did not
buy them off. In 1984 we brought in a bill to provide them with self-government and your government refused to pass it. You stood aside. There was a bill on the order paper in this Chamber offering self-government so that native people could find the self-sufficiency to handle their own affairs, and your government cancelled it out.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Bill C-52.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: That is what happened. Before you start talking, learn your history and learn your facts. Don't get confused simply by your opinions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: You don't even know where Oka is.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
I have been there, my friend, and I will tell you something. Every other Canadian knows where it is because it is at the very heart of what is sick and what is wrong with this government and with what is happening in this country and the way it is handled. My friend from Port Moody- Coquitlam said that it was bungling. It wasn't bungling, Mr. Speaker, it was worse than that. It was sheer,

unmitigated malevolence in this case. They were standing by and letting it happen. That great vacuum of leadership that everybody talks about, that perception is no accident because Canadians expected better from this Parliament and from any government. They expect people to approach the problems with some semblance of sensitivity and honesty and truthfulness, and they have received none of that up until now.
I can say that if you want to be challenged by members opposite, it is very easy to do. Open it up. Let us find out what really went on. Let us not try to hide it. Let us not try to box it in. Let us not try to turn on the old machine and get the public relations teams rolling. Let us get to the truth. Let us really find out. Do you have the guts to do that? I doubt it. You have not done it before but maybe you will have it in the future. This issue goes way beyond the life of one government or the life of one Parliament. It really goes down to some fundamental characteristics of what we are making this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: It started with your government.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear from my good friend from Winnipeg South, the neighbouring constituency. It started with the government, sure. We share responsibility in that. Every party does. I will not deny that. I think we were all sort of guilty. I do say that in 1984, as the member may know or should know, and if not go back into the records, there was a bill brought forward by the then Minister of Indian Affairs to provide for the beginning of self-government. Our government also began the constitutional recognition of aboriginal rights in the Constitution, none of which was honoured by the successive government to which that members belongs. Those are issues that I think are very, very crucial. I am not saying that we began, but what happened this summer perhaps may be an opportunity. Maybe that is the way we should really say to them that rather than coming down with the storm boots like we heard tonight from the Minister of Justice, maybe we should start using it as an opportunity to open a few doors. One would be to get to the truth, the other would be to take the Prime Minister not in his hazy promises but a timetable. If you want to use this Parliament for getting down to the serious business, fine. Members opposite, the member from Western Arctic has talked about it. My friend from Kenora-Rainy River
Government Orders
has talked about it. Let us begin to show that we mean business.
When we talk about an independent commission on land claims, we mean one that is accountable to Parliament that will not be subject to the whims and caprices of the justice lawyers and the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs. We have a Human Rights Commission that is accountable to this Parliament once a year and must report and is independent. We want an independent commission with a budget. That way we can begin dismantling and devolving the Department of Indian Affairs. How do you think any aboriginal person can deal with that department with any sense of responsibility when you have the deputy minister using the whips this summer. It is impossible to restore it. You are going to have to make major, fundamental, far reaching changes. We, members of Parliament, must take our accountability and our responsibility. The way we do it is to say we will set up, accountable to this Parliament, a commission and hold it accountable so that different bands can come forward with their land proposals and their self-government proposals and say: there it is, let us work it out. There will be a clearer timetable, you have five years to work these things out and here is your budget for it. If they do not do it, they are going to be in front of this Parliament every year being asked why.
That begins to make sense. If the government wants to show good faith, there is a way of showing good faith.
I think what we have to come to grips with is that this summer has brought about in this country for all of us, every single Canadian, a journey that we do not like. It has opened up inside us something that we did not like to see about ourselves as a people and as a nation. Now that we see it and now that it is exposed, let us do something about cleaning it up and changing it. Let us come grips finally. Let us turn this session of Parliament, beginning in the fall of 1990, into the Parliament of aboriginal rights. Let us go to work and get various bills done on the land claims issue, on the health issue. Let us not wait until the future. No mananas. Let us do it now. Let us at least say that we have learned those kinds of lessons.
We do not have much time. If we allow the prejudice and the handicaps of the past to hold us back, as well as that underlying sort of nastiness we saw exposed so badly this summer, all of us will be guilty, all members of

Government Orders
Parliament on all sides, of enormous failure of trust and confidence.
There is an opportunity. There is a small door open as long as we can retain the confidence of that Indian leadership which up to now has shown great restraint and moderation. If we do not act now and act with some courage and some imagination, that moderate leadership will be replaced and we will have hundreds of Okas across this country and this country will never be the same.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that my hon. colleague just gave quite a performance. I think it was one of his finest hours. I have often heard him speak with a great deal of eloquence and fire. He certainly had that this evening, and I guess he needed it because there was not a lot behind what he was saying.
It seems to me that my hon. friend speaks about injustices and natives as if they just started occurring yesterday. He admits that they did not, that they began quite a long time ago, and that they began to be built up over the years of Liberal government. I think those were the years when all these specific claims that we hear so much about were created out of betrayal, out of breach of trust, out of giving land to people and then taking it away, and out of making and breaking promises.
My hon. friend knows all about those things, but he expects us to believe that he can stand up here and say: "Oh, yes, I am sorry. Gee, we made a mistake. We were guilty, but we have changed our ways and from now on we are going to be the champion of native rights and we are going to be the ones with the pure white banner". I am afraid that I have a great deal of difficulty with that.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Mr. Clean.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Let me tell the member something. His current leader who brags about being the Minister of Indian Affairs for six years had a great opportunity to take control of some of these injustices that were built up by previous regimes and do something about them. What did he do?
My colleague says that they were about to pass a bill that would give us the beginning of self-government. My government has just quietly gone ahead and done it. We have started to create self-government throughout the
country. There are native bands all across this land that have benefited from the policies of this government since 1984. We did not make promises. We went out there and we did the things that the Liberals never even thought of doing until we came into government and started getting them actually into action.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that I am a very calm, cool, collected person. I really did not mean to get into the rhetoric, but my hon. friend across the way has a habit of getting my goat a bit and of getting me riled up once in a while. I will get to the question because I know you would like me to do that, Mr. Speaker.
What I would like to ask the hon. member is really very simple. It only requires a yes or no, if that is possible, just a simple yes or no. Does the hon. member support smuggling, violence, beatings? I want the hon. member to answer very clearly yes or no, just to answer the question with a yes or no. Does he support violence as a way to promote the better condition of the native people throughout this country? If he does not then he should say not. If he does then he should say he does and explain himself.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to disappoint the hon. member. I am not going to say yes or no. I am going to tell her a few things first and then I will give her the answer.
First, when I described the past I did not start with Liberal regimes. I started with Sir John A. Macdonald, the first Prime Minister of this country, who sent the troops in as well to justify the taking away of Indian land. His regime was responsible for hanging Louis Riel because of a belief in law and order in Canada. Since then we have learned, to our great sense of chagrin and embarrassment, just how wrong they all were.
I simply remind her of that because I would suggest that the speeches given by the justice minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, were about the same as the one we heard from the justice minister tonight. I am afraid that I do not want this country 120 years from now to be still trying to learn the lesson of just how wrong we were then.
I would also like to give her a small lesson in history, and that is that the Liberal government of which I was a part brought in a new Constitution in 1982 which gave aboriginals their first recognition in the Constitution. We
September 25, 1990

set forward a process that would give them further recognition until her government did not cany through.
We established the Penner commission which probably made the most far-sighted, insightful, useful recommendations dealing with the question of land claims and self-government. One of the direct results of that was a bill that was brought into this House in 1984 which set the framework of self-government, not small pieces of devolution, which again was not fulfilled.
I do not claim that is a perfect record, but I will tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker: a Liberal government would never have allowed an Oka to develop. We would never have allowed the kind of suppression of civil rights and civil liberties we have seen over the last 75 days. That is not the way we do things.
We would have had a justice minister who understood the real meaning of justice. We would have had an Indian affairs minister who cared enough about his portfolio enough to come back the first day from his summer vacation and do something about it. We would have had a Prime Minister who did not abdicate responsibility for two months. That would have made the big difference. We would have had Parliament back in session as a way of using this House to develop some understanding and consensus among members. That is the way we would have done it differently.
There are different ways of handling a crisis. There are different ways of coming to grips with issues.
The member once again throws out the question of smuggling of arms. Of course I do not support that, but I wonder where the federal government was all those previous months and years when it knew that was going on. Where was the Minister of Justice then when that was taking place? Did the member not believe in it then? Has she just discovered that that was taking place? Did it just occur to her this July that those things were taking place?
I have just finished reading a book by one of the experts that has a chapter on it. I would be glad to send it to the member. It was printed before Oka took place, and he describes it in his own book. The government itself had reports on it, but it did absolutely nothing
Government Orders
about it. It did not anticipate the crisis. It did not deal with it. It simply ignored it.
The deputy minister was anxious to run to the media for a backgrounder come mid-July about the problems in Oka. He knew all about it. Where was he?
That is why I say there is no trust or confidence in that deputy minister or that department any more. As the parliamentary secretary, perhaps the most important contribution she could make to this debate would be to go to her minister in cabinet and say: "Look it, we had better make a fundamental change. We had better do something that will turn some real power sharing over to the bands and their councils because that department no longer enjoys any trust or confidence with them".
Those are the kinds of changes that will have to take place immediately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to move away from the mutual confessions of my three colleagues from Winnipeg and move on to other issues.
I am delighted to seize the opportunity to speak tonight because I think today we are finally beginning on the road back from a disheartening summer of discontent, despair and disunity.
I suggest that we are on the road back to Canadian common sense, in part because of a series of commitments made earlier today by the Prime Minister in his remarks on this motion. I believe these commitments, and I say this recognizing the substantial efforts of the
past, particularly the recent past. I believe these commitments represent a change, a shift in perspective and commitment by the Government of Canada and the people of Canada.
I speak as a Canadian with a strong commitment to building understanding between native Canadians and non-native Canadians. That is one of the reasons when elected to serve in this House I asked to serve on the aboriginal affairs committee.
During the past year while I had the privilege and the challenge to chair that committee, I was proud of the efforts and accomplishments of all members of that committee from all sides of the House, from all three parties. We have toiled long and hard. I know it has not always been easy because the patience and the tolerance of all members have been tested. We have been tested because the more we learned and the more evidence we heard, the more we realized how much more work needed to be done. At times I felt-and I am sure the same is true for other members-that as we learned more, the greater became the weight of the task before us. The size of the task is overwhelming. I commend to all members and to Canadians in general the second report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs published this spring entitled: Unfinished Business, An Agenda for all Canadians in the 1990's.
We undertook this study. We consulted with native leadership from across Canada and we found that there was a multitude of issues that native leadership in this country felt that we, as a committee, should consider. Let me just run through some of them as an example of the depth and the breadth of the kinds of issues that we have had to deal with and the kinds of issues that I believe we have to deal with in this Parliament over the next decade. I will just go through some of the items in the Table of Contents.
Under the title "The Self-government Agenda", there is a list of issues including "Land Claims", "Other Land and Resource Issues", "Constitutional Issues", "Treaty Rights and Relations with Treaty Nations", "INAC's Self-Government Negotiations Policy", "Scope of Federal Activity Under s. 91(24) of the Constitution Act, 1867", "Indian Act Amendments and the Role and Mandate of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development", the DIAND's Lands, Revenues and Trusts Review", "Implementation and Impact of the 1985 Amendment to the Indian Act", Bill C-31, the question of "Traditional and Elective Systems of
September 25, 1990

Government", "The Trust Relationship", "Fiscal Arrangements", "Justice", "International Treaties Affecting Aboriginal Rights", the "Aboriginal Affairs Policy Development Process" and questions dealing with "Organizations Representing Aboriginal Peoples". That is just half of the list of the kinds of issues that we face. Some of the others include "Education", "Aboriginal Language Retention", "Childcare and Child Welfare", "Health", "Human Rights Issues", "Circumpolar Issues", "Northern Issues", "Housing", "Environmental Issues", "Off-Reserve Issues" "Aboriginal Women's Issues", "Economic Development Issues" and "Literacy". It is a very, very challenging area in which to work and I think it is also very rewarding for members of the committee who have worked on it and I look forward to continuing work in this area.
The committee, after completing this report in the spring also went on to do a study on literacy, the impact of possible changes in the field of aboriginal literacy and we held hearings across the country and it was very interesting. We expect to have a study to report to the House in the next few weeks. I think that that will be very instructive for the government as well. We look forward to making that report.
Last March, at the time that we decided to proceed with the literacy study, we also announced that we were going to be doing a study on land claims because we felt at that point that land claims was the most important issue, after literacy, that a committee of the House could deal with. That will be initiated as well this fall. It will consist of an examination of the process by which specific and comprehensive land claims are negotiated and settled and will be undertaken, obviously, without any intent to have any prejudice toward any existing claims negotiations. The analysis will include self-government issues, as they relate to comprehensive claims and public hearings on the subject of specific claims negotiations process will begin this fall.
I would like to highlight some of the points made by the Prime Minister earlier today because I think they are worthy of review. Judged in perspective, I believe this
Government Orders
path offers some leadership, offers a direction for all of us to work together as Canadians. The first point is that consultation has been going on over the past year and it is time now, after that consultation, to put this agenda into operation. Consultation was one of the issues that we heard a great deal about in our study on post-secondary education over a year ago. There was a great concern that there had not been enough consultation at that time.
The agenda that the government is going to institute will have four main pillars and I think they all hit at basic fundamental issues important to the aboriginal community in Canada. The first one is land claims; the second one is economic and social conditions on reserves; the third issue is the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments; and the fourth one concerns Canada's aboriginal peoples in respect of the fiduciary responsibilities of the Crown toward them. The Prime Minister noted today, as our committee had noted in the spring, that no issue is more important or requires urgent action more than land claims. The government intends to take three parallel initiatives. The first initiative is to accelerate the settlement of specific claims and I am sure the committee will have important observations on how that is to be done.
The second is to ensure that the legal undertakings regarding land transfers to treaty Indians will finally be honoured. The third one is to accelerate negotiations on the comprehensive claims, or the so-called modem treaties. Most of those are in British Columbia.
The government has made a significant commitment to expand its resources in this area and to expand the rate in which it deals with issues in this area.
A second dimension will be to look at ways to improve living conditions on Indian reserves, including such basic community programs and services as water and sewage facilities.
A third area of importance is taking some important looks, some important reviews of the Indian Act itself. The Prime Minister made a commitment to undertake that, in consultation that is currently ongoing with Indian

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
and native leadership, to bring in some changes in the new year to the Indian Act.
Consultation and respect for the fiduciary responsibilities of the federal government are essential elements of that process.
The government will also go far beyond the status quo to ensure that there are practical ways that aboriginal communities can exercise greater control over the administration of justice. I think this is an important element of self-government and I think that that is an important step forward.
We also have to look at the relationship between non-native and native Canadians, and that is an area in which I have found myself working hard, particularly over the summer, but also prior to that.
The Prime Minister indicated today that this fall the government intends to undertake a broader initiative on Canadian unity where the aboriginal peoples in contemporary Canada will have a full role. I think that is important. I do not think we can look at these issues in isolation and pretend that they are not connected. I think the agenda that was announced today by the Prime Minister is indeed far-reaching. I think it has gotten the ball rolling and I encourage all members in the House to get behind these initiatives to help ensure that they are not blocked by the lack of will in any sector of government. I encourage all members to take up the cause and to get involved in these issues.
It is obviously going to take creativity and it is going to take perseverance and it is going to take commitment, the kind of commitment that, I believe, was shown by members of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, but also the kind of commitment and perseverance shown by the moderate and modem native leadership who, over the summer, worked so hard to save the progress that they had achieved over recent decades. I speak here of the progress in terms of understandings held by all Canadians of aboriginal issues and aboriginal concerns. I think that is something that we all have to cherish.
I would also like to make an appeal to all Canadians both native and non-native. We faced a very difficult summer of discord and discontent and I think this, unfortunately, has stressed the bonds of relations between many groups of Canadians. So I appeal for moderation and common sense to prevail and I deplore
the intolerance which has flared up over the course of the summer at various times and any developments which have led to that kind of intolerance in the abuse of innocent individuals.
I call on all Canadians to reflect on what has happened this summer and what has led to heightened tensions across Canada between native Canadians and non-native Canadians. I think we have to reflect on that. Why has this come about? What is it that is behind these issues and what can we learn from this?
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre spoke of opportunity and I think we do have opportunities now, but to achieve the opportunity that is there, I think all parties have to work together.
I think we have to reflect on what we have learned about ourselves as Canadians over the summer. We have to be prepared to tone down our rhetoric and renew our commitment to reasonable common sense means of resolving differences. We have seen some progress, I think. In particular, I do commend the efforts of moderate native leadership in seeking a peaceful, reasoned resolution to these disputes.
I think we would all agree that Canada has a long way to go to balance social justice in this country. All Canadians need to work together in this regard.
Unfortunate incidents such as the stoning of a car cavalcade of innocent women, children and elders in Chateauguay are repugnant, unacceptable and are categorically rejected by all Canadians. There have been other repugnant developments in Canada over the summer. But we are all Canadians who have to live together and find ways to live together in peace. This is important, not only for those of us who live here in Canada today, it is also important for our children and our grandchildren and it is fundamental to establishing long-term solutions to long-term challenges. This is particularly important because of the tone it sets for the children and the grandchildren of all residents of Canada.
We need to set a new tone. Let us learn from this summer of discontent. Let us work together, native Canadians, non-native Canadians, parliamentarians and Canadians elsewhere, to start rebuilding a country that respects all individuals for whom they are and the potential they can offer to build a fair, secure and prosperous future for all Canadians.
September 25, 1990

One of the questions that I have had asked of me frequently over the summer is who will pay? Elow can Canada pay for the settlement of land claims and other outstanding issues? Well my friends, that is not the question we should ask. The question we should ask is: Who pays if we as a nation do not get our act together? The answer is shockingly apparent. Those who pay as a result of Canada not addressing these questions are those who are least able to pay; the children and the youth of aboriginal communities across this country, that 50 per cent of native population which is currently under the age of 23. It is hard to argue in this country that we cannot afford social justice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate this evening. I will tiy to be brief with my comments.
I understand the Prime Minister made a very forthcoming speech in the House earlier today that pledged the government to a serious effort finally to begin to address the fundamental concerns of the native people in Canada, the concerns which underlie the current crisis. Unfortunately I missed the speech but I look forward to reviewing it in Hansard. I sincerely hope that it signals a new attitude on the part of the government and that it will be followed up by concrete actions.
September 25, 1990

I am at a relatively early age in my education on the native experience in Canada and I watched for the most part the events of this summer from my constituency in Cape Breton Highlands-Canso where the weather was splendid, the parades were colourful, the square dances were lively, and the hospitality was second to none, as some members who came down had the privilege of experiencing.
What clouded this tapestry was the day-to-day barrage of news reports from Oka, Kahnawake, Kanesatake, and elsewhere in Canada that showed the deteriorating relationship between native people and other Canadians. They showed the escalating violence and the spirit of violence in the standoff between the Mohawk warriors, the government, the police in Quebec and later on the Canadian Army, and the general feeling which we saw in our part of the country that Ottawa was paralyzed, out of control and unable to deal with this situation. We saw with growing dismay the increasing expressions of racism and intolerance in various parts of Canada, and a sense that the whole country and the society was falling apart around this crisis.
There was a growing sense of frustration and despair among those people in Nova Scotia with whom I came in contact at what was happening to the relationship between aboriginal Canadians and other Canadians as we observed the events at Oka.
During the crisis I had an opportunity to spend an evening with someone who is a member of the traditional Mohawk leadership at Kahnawake who had come down to visit a friend on one of the reserves in my riding. The discussion was very illuminating with this very wise individual, whose name I will not mention.
He was a peaceful person and he did not condone the blockades and the violence of the warriors. Equally so, he condemned the response of both the Quebec and the federal governments, which was really to ignore the leadership and the concerns expressed by the traditional and moderate leadership of the native people and to focus their attention solely on the warriors and their weapons.
He, himself, was ignored, even though he had spoken out time and time again on native rights on his reserve and against the violence that was occurring. He de-
Government Orders
spaired of the message that was going out to native people across the country. The moderate, reasonable native people he knew who were being bypassed, who as a result of the government's handling of the crisis were receiving the message that the only way to get the government's ear, the only way to get their attention is put up blockades and to take up arms. It was a very disturbing message that was being sent out to the people across the country as the crisis evolved. There was a cry of despair from him at this message, what he was seeing and what it meant for the relationship and our ability in the country to come to a reasonable dialogue.
The Prime Minister was largely absent throughout the crisis. We never saw him, but he emerged to defend the efforts of his government on behalf of native peoples in Canada. I do not remember exactly how he phrased it, but essentially he claimed that each Indian in Canada receives something like $13,000 in government programs. Of course, that claim lead to a war of statistics and figures about whether, in fact, this was really finding its way to the native people or whether it was actually gobbled up by the bureaucracy that was delivering these programs. There were counter-claims that, in fact, only $2,000 eventually reached the destination and the rest of it was lost in bureaucratic overhead.
What was disturbing about this whole argument was the fact that the Prime Minister of Canada would attempt to justify his government's treatment of native people in terms of the dollars that were sent to them. Whatever the amount is, the whole argument missed a very fundamental point and betrayed something about the misunderstanding we have had in terms of our relationship with native people in the country. I think it is a tragic reflection of a kind of paternalism, a kind of paternalistic attitude that is at the root of our relationship with native people today. I think that it is this paternalism which is translating itself into a total loss of dignity and self-esteem and is translating itself into the dismal life which is so characteristic of our native communities and which manifests itself, as we all know, in the sub-standard housing, in social decay, in high suicide rates, rates that are multiples of what the rates are elsewhere in Canada, in family violence, in the whole litany of social conditions which characterize our native communities.

Government Orders
These conditions of life are present on the reserves in my riding, the reserves of Whycocomagh, Wagmatcook and Afton which too often are depressing and completely unacceptable by any contemporary standards, particularly in a country such as Canada, and where the official unemployment rate hovers between 75 per cent and 85 per cent and where many live in sub-standard housing with no plumbing and inadequate sewer and water and where alcohol and drug abuse is all too often rampant and where most of the natives spend their lives either on welfare or fighting through a maze of bureaucratic inertia in order to acquire the basic amenities of life, a job, housing, food, shelter or education. That is the situation in which all too often they find themselves. I believe that at the root of all of this is a kind of paternalistic attitude which characterizes our relationship with native people and which is symptomized by the statements of the Prime Minister this summer.
Nobody condones the taking up of arms or the use of violence to achieve political ends, be it by Mohawk warriors or by anybody else. I do not want to comment on whether or not the army should or should not have been sent into Oka or how best the standoff should be brought to a conclusion. That has been debated by others more qualified than I this evening. I want to make one point about that. It seems to me that there is a curious irony here and there is a curious irony in the government's insistence that Mohawks and other native people respect law and order, do not resort to blockades and do this as a precondition to being able to discuss what are fundamental questions about their basic human rights, questions which relate fundamentally to a litany of broken treaties, treaties which we have broken in our relationship with them and which have resulted, all too often, in their being pigeon-holed into reserves, having lost the basic elements of their livelihoods and having been forced into situations which are, by any standard, intolerable.
As I said before, I am at a relatively early stage in my education on the native experience in Canada, but I suspect that we can learn a great deal from them. We already have discovered through, I believe, the concern for the environment how the native relationship with the environment, the land and other creatures has in many
ways enriched our understanding of our environment, those of us who have grown up with the Judeo-Christian tradition or other traditions who have, in a sense, not understood that relationship which aboriginal peoples in Canada and elsewhere around the world have with the land and with other creatures who share the land with us. I think we have started to learn a little about the profound lesson that they have to teach us in that area.
Another area that I have personally begun to learn a little bit about is the law and the way in which we organize our society. I was reading about some of the ways in which the Micmacs have understood their treaties and their relationships with the British who came here two or three centuries before.
I would like to read a couple of brief quotes from a book called The Micmac Treaty Handbook. The Micmacs are the native people who live in Nova Scotia. I find it quite interesting to read what they have to say about treaties and the relationships that they have developed with Europeans.
The first two paragraphs read as follows: "Well before the arrival of Europeans, formal agreements equivalent to treaties were negotiated between sovereign nations of North America. The meaning and effect of these arrangements were not limited by a few words on paper as are present day business contracts. Rather, these treaties were living and evolving relationships among various indigenous nations. Like the members of a family, representatives of the nations that had entered into a treaty met from time to time to exchange gifts, to forgive one another and to renew their friendship. We, the Micmacs, related to Europeans the same way.
The 18th century agreements between the Micmac nation and Britain were and still are regarded by us as a form of brotherhood. When there was some injury or threat of conflict, we met to exchange reassurances and renew our engagements. That is why over several decades one finds half a dozen or more seemingly separate treaties between the Micmac and British Crown. The surviving documents are often incomplete summaries of meetings that typically required many days and were repeated every few years as necessary. By themselves the documents are fragments. Considered together, they constitute a great chain of agreement. In other words, the treaty documents that appear later in this book should be seen not as distinct treaties but as stages and
September 25, 1990

renewals of a larger agreement or pact that developed during the 1700s between the Micmacs and the British".
One of these treaties was a treaty of 1752, which essentially stated the relationships between the Micmacs and the British in Nova Scotia at that time. Successive governments have tried to wiggle their way out of this treaty and deny their importance and deny the validity of that particular treaty until the Supreme Court, in a decision in 1985, confirmed that particular treaty as a basis for the relationship between the Micmacs and Nova Scotians. In a meeting I had with the leadership of the reserves in my riding on Saturday, we discussed an agreement that they had just entered into with the Nova Scotia government on hunting rights. It is related to the quote I just read.
I found it quite interesting to see that this agreement, which essentially spelled out the number of moose that the Micmacs could hunt, where they could hunt, when they could hunt and a whole range of particulars related to hunting and fishing on and off the reserves in Cape Breton, spelled it all out in terms of saying what the Micmacs would agree to in terms of their obligations pertaining to those hunts. I found that particular agreement interesting because they showed it to me as an example of what was possible if the governments would be prepared to sit down and work out agreements with native people as equal partners, as people who were adults and capable of taking their own responsibilities and managing their own affairs, rather than treating them in some way as inferior citizens. I think that fundamentally, at least from what I have learned so far about this, that has to underlie whatever new relationship we engage in with native peoples in this country. What I have seen just from reading these two documents and that small experience is that really we have a lot less to be scared of in terms of entering into agreements with native people than perhaps we have had in the past.
Whatever relationship evolves out of this crisis, which I hope will be resolved very soon, I think it has to start with an acceptance by us non-natives in Canada that maybe over a long period of time we have been on the wrong track and maybe we have to accept a certain difference, a willingness to see things differently and to
Government Orders
look and see the reality of life, perhaps not from our own eyes, but maybe from the perspective that our native people have there to teach us. I think that has to be the basis of whatever new relationship, be it through the mechanism of a royal commission or whatever we enter into in this country. That is, in a sense, what I have learned from this and what I would like to contribute in this debate this evening.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso. I think it is much more sensible and practicable and much more knowledgeable, and I would not have been here this evening had I not heard the Minister speak earlier because this previous speaker, in contrast with the minister, made sense. The only reason I am down here is because the minister spoke. It showed a great deal of naivety. It was a treatise in law and order. It simplified a very complex issue. It is unbelievable that the minister of this government would speak in that way. I could not believe my ears.
I am not a lawyer and perhaps I am thankful for that. With the naivety that the minister expressed in her speech I could not believe my ears. I am glad it was a late hour because Canadians probably did not hear her either. John Wayne and GI Joe and the Prime Minister of this country, that kind of statement may be popular in the polls, but it is totally impractical, totally impractical. These are people who are grasping for any straw that might gain them some popularity with the Canadian public, but it will not wash. It cannot wash.
The reason that these people cannot speak with any sensitivity, I believe, is because they do not understand. They have not communicated with people on the other side of the issue. They say, "I have been to this reserve and I have been to that reserve", but I do not think they have communicated yet because their words belie their actions. There is no sensitivity in what they have said.
We may have Oka incident 1, 2,3, 4,5 and 25 unless we have some comprehensive ideas. This government saw the situation. It saw the problem before and let it fester and fester. In fact, it has festered for hundreds of years. But this particular situation had festered to a point where it broke out into what we saw this summer. After seven weeks, the Prime Minister comes to his senses and says, I am the white knight, here to-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Would the hon. member like to rebut?

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: I cannot rebut, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to thank the member for his compliment regarding my remarks. I may use it in my next householder.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
I stated that I did not believe that we could practise democracy in Canada at the point of a gun, and I still believe that. I also said that I believed that the native mandate which had been established so dramatically well by Elijah Harper was at risk of being diminished and damaged by the events of Oka and Kahnawake.
As many of my colleagues observed with considerable glee, the feather was removed from my hand by one of the elders and there was a sequel to that. About a week later I was invited to attend an Indian meeting around a camp fire in a large tepee in my riding in which a prayer vigil was held.
That feather was returned to me and I repeated the statements I had made in public. This time they were accepted with the dignity, the tolerance, and the patience that the process of the prayer vigil entails for Indian people.
In effect I took that as a statement of amends. In fact there was great glee that night in the tent when I decided in a lighter moment to comment that they had restored my dignity because-and this was said with great good will and was received with great humour-a bird without a feather was a very bald bird indeed.
I must say in that spirit that I have since met with the representatives of those reserves. In fact last week I met with the executive members of the Union of New Brunswick Indians. I said to them that I disagreed with their position in many areas of detail and that I could not support, even in principle, all of their demands. For example, I do not believe that we will ever be able to reconcile the idea of one country and one society of Canadians with separate societies of any kind, including native Indian societies as separate nations on an international sovereignty basis.
I said that notwithstanding those areas of disagreement I wanted to be their representative. I wanted to try to ensure that the process of communication, the process of dialogue, was always open. I must say that after a long, hard summer where the ripple effect of Oka and Kahnawake expressed itself in the Fredericton area, I feel encouraged that the lines of communication do remain open and that dialogue is taking place. I believe it is from that kind of base in every constituency in this country that we can move forward to the kind of higher ground that will bring resolution to many of the historic
Government Orders
injustices and grievances which legitimately have been expressed and which certainly must be resolved.
Another thing I did this summer in the course of these tensions was to try to understand a little more fully the background of the native Indian point of view. I engaged a distinguished teacher and gentlemen, a Malecite Indian who is a professor of Indian studies at St. Thomas University. After some hours with him I did have a new understanding of the aspirations of native Indians and of the complexities of the land claims issues, both the specific claims and the comprehensive claims. I had a better understanding of the deep spiritual roots which comprise the native way of life for many of their people; I would say the vast majority of their people. I was particularly impressed with their convictions about land, about the concept of mother earth and how it is really not there in their ownership but it is there in their trust.
I would urge all members of the House who have not had the opportunity to do so to examine those kinds of issues with native people. We are privileged in this House to have three, all in their own rights distinguished, who I am sure would be quite willing to enlighten those of us who are not conversant with the background of native Indian affairs. From that kind of dialogue, even on a quasi-partisan basis, I believe that much progress can be made.
I would like to say that I am willing and anxious. I would like my constituents on the reservations at home to know that I am committed to do everything I can to advance the legitimate native issues to which they aspire and which they hold but not under the practice or the threat of violence. Fortunately the native people of New Brunswick respect the rule of law. I am confident that we can and will work very well together.
Earlier this year I was privileged to serve on the special Meech Lake committee along with native members from Western Arctic and Nunatsiaq. We heard representations from all points in Canada about native concerns and native aspirations. This ended in the demonstration of democracy by Elijah Harper as he exercised his judgment, his courage, and his dignity in formally ending the Meech Lake process. While I disagreed and continue to disagree strongly with his judgment on that issue, I respect greatly his democratic and lawful demonstration of responsible representation. I believe that all natives and all Canadians could justly share the mantle of his performance, even those of us who found his decision very difficult to accept. Accept his decision we must, and

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
we will seek new horizons and we will find new horizons to unify and build this country.
However at Oka it was a different situation. Oka was a situation of violence. It was a tragedy. It was disgraceful. It was a situation that should never be tolerated again and should never be repeated again in this country.
I do not know how much time I have left, but I would like to move just very quickly to commend the government, as my hon. friend from Macleod has described to us, on the significant progress which is being made in terms of community dialogue in the direction of selfgovernment. I again commit to my constituents and to the government my best efforts to ensure that that process and that concept are advanced and engendered in every way that I can.
In closing, I guess I would merely like to echo the call of my colleague from Macleod to let us look to the future, all Canadians, with a commitment to work constructively and in good faith to create a society in which all may find their place in this country in dignity, in prosperity, and in peace.

speechtext: I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona and the hon. member for Chambly are going to split the next 20 minutes into 10 minutes each with 5 minutes each for questions and comments.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was just informed by the hon. member for Chambly that something may have happened at Oka, that events may have changed, and that there might have been either a settlement reached or something which has led to a change in the situation there but, until we find out more about it, I do not think it would make any sense to comment on it.
I wanted to try to place some of what has happened this summer in a certain historical perspective. I have listened to a lot of fine speeches this evening on both sides of the House, but I want to say that nevertheless the government motion itself contributes to and is part of the problem which led to the situation we find ourselves in. By this I mean that violence is often a response to the failure of the political process. By this I mean that violence is often a response to the failure of the political process. What we see in the government motion is an example of the failure of the political process. Instead of putting before the House a motion which might have brought people together and which might have enabled us to do something constructive,
instead the government did today, with respect to Oka what it did yesterday with respect to the Persian Gulf, and that is they put a motion in which they are trying to catch or trick the opposition and put it into a difficult position. It is this kind of political game playing that I think simply makes matters worse, instead of providing the opportunity for constructive debate.
I would like to go back to 1977, at a time when I was just coming out of seminary. It was the time of the final report of the Berger inquiry into the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. I think that was a culmination of a process that began in the early seventies. Out of that report came a new appreciation for the nature of the situation that native peoples found themselves in, the whole question of land claims. It was a time of great hope, not just for a moratorium on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline but also for a new era of recognition for native rights. Many of the current leadership of the native people in Canada came out of that experience and out of that time. At that time, without being too specific, a lot of them were in their twenties and a lot of them are pushing forty now, like myself.
They spent the mid to late seventies and all the eighties believing that the political process, duly invested in, would produce results. It did not produce results. What I think Canadians understand better than the government is that what you see in part and why there is so much solidarity with the action of the Mohawks at Oka, despite people's objection to the use of guns and arms is an expression of solidarity with this frustration that native people rightly feel about the failure of the political process over the last 15 years to respond to their needs. People feel that frustration for native people and it has enabled them and many Canadians-and I knocked on a lot of doors this summer because of the Manitoba election-not to completely put aside but to put in perspective their own objection to the taking up of arms, as has happened in this situation.
I think that many Canadians are able to hear in their own minds how hollow it must sound to the native mind to have people get up and talk about the rule of law when they know that the situation that so many native people find themselves in, is a situation that exists because there has been no respect for the rule of law, that is to say, the rule of the treaties that were entered into between native people and the British Crown or, for that matter, the Government of Canada over the years. How hollow it must sound to native people to hear
September 25, 1990

speeches by the Minister of Justice and others, as we have heard them tonight, talking about the rule of law when they know that the law has been broken, that agreements and treaties have been broken time and time again. It is in that perspective that we have to see what has happened at Oka and not be caught up just on the technicalities of the law although we need to obviously hold the law in great respect but we must hold it in respect in all of its dimensions and not just when it suits us.
The other thing I would like to say because I do have such limited time is that what we see here is the solidarity that I think a lot of Canadians feel with the Mohawks at Oka. It is no coincidence that this is over a golf course, or not over a golf course, but over trees. I think you will see that in the next decade, in the coming years, there will be more and more actions, perhaps not violent, perhaps not taking up of arms but civil disobedience in other forms of demonstration in which people are going to draw the line. They are going to say, no more. Unless they feel that the political process can save the environment, we are going to see these kinds of actions developing, not just with respect to aboriginal rights, but also with respect to the environment. Of course, the two are related because so many times it is aboriginal people who are called upon to defend the last vestiges of the natural environment, but it also will be non-natives. So there is solidarity between non-natives who are environmentalists and aboriginals who, by their very nature, are environmentalists. What we see here is a foreshadowing of the kind of events we may well see more of if the government does not get down to addressing some of the hard questions, not just with respect to aboriginal rights, but also with respect to the environment.
If people like David Suzuki are right-and he keeps saying these kinds of things-we have only got 10 years to save the planet. More and more people are going to say: "If we have only 10 or 15 or 20 years to save the planet, maybe it is about time I put myself on the line here". More and more people will do that, whether it is
Government Orders
stopping logging or whatever the case may be. That is the point I would like to make.
I would also like to say that there is another dimension to the solidarity that a lot of Canadians feel with aboriginal people. They realize that in many respects, not necessarily in Oka, but elsewhere, the reason that native Canadians have been denied their aboriginal rights and denied the kind of control they would like over their own resources and their own land is because that kind of control runs contrary to the corporate agenda in this country. Corporations do not want native people, or for that matter anyone else, to have control over oil, gas, minerals, land and water or whatever the case may be. They want to have unimpeded access to those resources so they can develop them for a profit, so that they can do their thing with planet earth.
In that sense there is a solidarity between the workers in my riding who are also victims of the corporate agenda and native people across the country who have been denied their rights by successive governments because those governments have been influenced by that same corporate agenda.
There were people in my riding who not only could not get to work easily like some of the people who had to go around the Mercier Bridge. There were people in my riding, not many but enough, who lost work altogether because of the cancellation of trains due to a blockade related to the Oka situation and who lost income. Some were not able to get to their cottages because they could only get to them by train.
I received very little complaint from these people, very little animosity. They called up to say that it was a problem, but at the same time I think they realized that the stake in how the government deals with native people is in some way related to their own future and how the government relates to them.
I call upon non-native people who are thinking about this to see the struggle of native people to control their own lives, the struggle of all of us to control our own lives in a context that is increasingly dominated by the corporate agenda, now a North American corporate agenda through the free trade agreement.
I recall the words of a chief in Manitoba who said before the standing committee on external affairs that was looking at the elements of the agreement in Winnipeg: "Free trade will make Indians of us all". Unless all Canadians can regain control of our own lives-not to be

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
too facetious about it, there may come a time when we will all be interested in reclaiming our country from the control of other powers and principalities, those people who have an interest in seeing that none of us, native or non-native control our own destinies.

speechtext: Questions or comments. Debate. The hon. member for Chambly. You are both taking up ten minutes.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As you said, I am the Member for Chambly, and I am probably one of the few people who are going to speak here this evening whose home is on the South Shore and who lived through those months, a very hurtful experience. And when I use the word "hurtful" I am speaking of the experience of the native people, of the people of Oka and of Chateauguay, and of the people of Quebec as a community, because in Quebec we have always treated native people with a certain respect. In 1985, as my colleague the Honourable Member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie remarked earlier, the Parti Quebecois recognized the autonomy, the existence of a distinct aboriginal society, if I can venture to use the expression now. Personally I am proud of that, but I am not proud of what happened this summer. I'm not proud at all. I'm not proud of the fact that our Premier, following the collapse of the Meech Lake Accord, held the native peoples of Canada collectively responsible.
I saw that, it was very clear, and I'm going to cite you the example of the federal government, which made a proposal just before the Meech Lake collapse, really a series of proposals, which I find progressive. They were good proposals. But once Meech Lake failed, the federal government said, "Tough, you were against Meech, so too bad, we're withdrawing our offer, and you can just wait, all you native people, and we'll get around to your grievances one of these days". I don't want to blame just the federal government for this. Even the provincial government, even Premier Bourassa, when he met with Mr. Sioui a few days after the Meech Lake failure, he said to him, "I hope the people of Quebec are going to understand you, Mr. Sioui". It was as if Mr. Sioui had been responsible for Elijah Harper, who was responsible for stopping the Meech Lake Accord.
As a journalist who knows what a powerful impact television images have, when it started appearing on television I felt how important it was, because I saw there a certain spirit.

I saw a certain spirit, a nasty spirit, a spirit which is un-Canadian, a spirit which is unnecessary, a spirit which is provocative. When you have this type of spirit from Quebec and you have the same meanness coming out of the federal government, I imagine if I were a native person, how would I react when I see the Surete du Quebec coming into where I call home, firing tear gas, heavily armed and trying to take away the peaceful barricades that we had up until that time? Quite frankly, I am ashamed that, in Quebec, 80 per cent of people who had been polled before this crisis had said that they were in favour of the land claims of the aboriginal people. Gosh, today that is almost as many people in Quebec who are against the GST but they were in favour of the land claims and I believe they still are. But what I find extremely hard to take is, when we are looking at the settlement of this controversy, we find a government wrapping itself in a cloak of law and order.
I am a former military man. I spent three years in the army. I believe in law and order, but I also believe in fairness. Here these concepts of fairness and equity are not present. There is provocation, meanness, and a minority of people turning towards the only defence they have, as warriors. I agree that the approach that the warriors took was wrong and I am going to emphasize that.
Armed struggle in a democracy, where one has the right to change the government through voting and through lawful dissidence, is wrong. I know of what I speak because, being an American by birth, I have worked with Martin Luther King. I never knew Martin Luther King to pick up an AK-47. I never knew Martin Luther King to have been masked. I understand how this could have occurred because of the feeling of weakness and of powerlessness of a minority. I do not think it is right to use these images to say that because of that we should permit ourselves to go in, shoot it out, take no prisoners, and get over with this entire situation. I do not think it is right.

I think what we need to do now-what the government has not done-is to come clean with the voters, with the people of Canada, and say that it was wrong and should have presented a series of propositions to our first peoples of Canada, whether Meech Lake passed or did not pass. It had no relevance to Meech at the time. It was used as a bargaining chip and we know that. But that is the way this government operates. Our Prime Minister, who likes to roll the dice, in this case decided to roll dice which were fixed. It wasn't fair. It wasn't honest. I think right now what is encumbent upon us after this controversy, after this conflict which has caused so many people to be inconvenienced, injured, and caused one death, that we learn from the tragedy-and I call that tragedy of Oka-that aboriginal people have got to be put on the front burner of our approach to this challenge of recognizing their basic rights.
If we talk about sovereignty for Quebec or sovereignty association, we have to also apply that to our nation's first people. If we missed this lesson, as we have missed so many lessons in the past as parliamentarians, then tonight at 1.20 in the morning we have missed this entire day and this entire Parliament in getting the message of what Oka has given us. That message is that it is time now, once and for all, to address the concerns of Canada's original peoples.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start off by congratulating my collegues on this side of the House, my colleagues from Chateauguay and Argenteuil, who have come through some difficult times this summer-I was in contact with them.
I listened to my colleague, the honourable member for Chambly, whose summer was probably just as busy. I don't know if people telephoned him to express their displeasure, but I am certain that if they did, they didn't all say the same things he has just said.
Mr. Speaker, this evening we have heard some emotional speeches. We have all lived through a long hot summer, that's for sure. I know Oka personally, because
Government Orders
I have many friends there; many of my constituents have summer homes there, and many pleasure boaters make a habit of using the marine there, which this year, unfortunately, couldn't operate. And I had to go there myself to see certain things with my own eyes so that I could contribute to the discussion.
This evening there have been people who told us how they visited reserves, they did this and that, but I think this evening we also ought to talk about the fact that cases like Oka, or Chateauguay, or Chambly, they don't happen every day. It was very hard for people.
Mr. Speaker, this year Laval is celebrating its 25th anniversary, 25 years of love and friendship. Oka is in the process of destroying itself, and the crisis has destroyed the prettiest village in Qubec, where I spent my summers when I was a student. They were wonderful summers. But this has been an Indian summer, and a bitter one.
The proverb has it, Mr. Speaker, that not all truths should be told. But one day the truth has to be faced. And the things I saw when I took my family on a few days of vacation, mainly in the United States, those things hurt me. When I saw cars, on television or in the daily paper of USA Today, a paper that sells 2.5 million copies every day, the first photo where there was a picture of a Surete du Quebec car with a Warrior and a sub-machine gun in his hands, people said, "Things are going badly in Quebec. The Warriors are holding a whole community hostage. A policeman has been wounded." That's what informed people were saying. There were other sources that were less informed: in Le Monde, from France, we read that it was an Indian who had been killed.
Mr. Jesse Jackson, who has forgotten the noble words of Martin Luther King-my colleague referred to him also, one would think he had read my notes-Martin Luther King never picked up a machine gun. He defended people's rights. Jesse Jackson arrives here, a fledgling journalist-recently recycled into American talk show journalism-and he says, "Two people have been killed here. Where are they?" Doesn't he even have a researcher, this guy? That's what has affected our morale, these international observers.

Government Orders
There was Archbishop Tbtu as well, who wanted to come and talk to the Prime Minister at a time when 450 people in his own country were busy killing one another, the Zulus. We saw some others like that, these international observers my colleague the Honourable Member for Winnipeg-North-Centre was mentioning earlier. He has left, which is too bad, as I would have liked to respond to him.
That's the truth. My pride as a Quebecer visiting the United States took quite a blow, I can tell you. I felt humiliated; the people of Quebec were being humiliated. To see the Surete du Quebec, a car overturned, Warriors with sub-machine guns, whether they call themselves Lasagna or Pizza or whatever- They made fun of us with masks, and people said, " You're maltreating the Amerindians." Well, isn't that dreadful!
I have a list of all the benefits we give them. There isn't a country in the world that treats its aboriginal people as well as Canada does-in any event I've never seen the figures that would prove it. And the village has been destroyed.
Earlier I spoke with the Mayor of Oka, who's a friend of mine. He's the one who managed to keep his cool and keep his townspeople within the law, too. No stones were thrown in Oka. Everyone came and went without making a fuss.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there are problems in Oka. There is good news this morning: everybody has come back to Oka; but there is bad news, too: there are people who don't have houses any more. There are people the law hasn't protected. Their houses have been destroyed, their goods stolen. Ask to see the houses that belonged to the Lemays, the Mongeons, the Imbeaus, the Legaults, the Dubes-what has become of their houses? Nothing remains but the four walls. Where is the law?
People thought the problem we were facing was the golf course. I hope we're not that naive! The problem is much more than that. The little bit of land wanted for the golf course (and it's a swamp, I know it very well), that wasn't the problem.
There has been a problem for the 14 months that they've been negotiating for the land. Before that they
negotiated for four years. Every time there was an agreement, they changed chiefs. There are serious problems. There's no more investment at Oka. There was a hotel that was supposed to be built there, a $9-million hotel, an open-air resort, because in that part of the country that's what there is: sports, the great outdoors, it's scenic, it attracts tourists. But that's all changed. There were houses that were sold-the buyers came wanting their deposits back. Nobody wants those houses any more, and why would they? I believe my colleague will have a chance to speak later. In the meantime, may I suggest that he do as I did, and listen? He might learn something.
The resort project: $8 million. The proposed marina at Pointe-aux-Anglais, is that going to go ahead? And there will be other surprises in the future, I'm sure. You know, Mr. Speaker, everyone has spoken, and rightly, about the native people, the Mohawks. Certainly the proposal before us must be discussed.
But I would just like to touch on the other side of the story, because I've spoken with the people on the spot. They are whites, non-Indians. You know, there was a poet in Quebec named Felix Leclerc, and he always said, "If you want to kill someone, pay him for doing nothing." So today, as in the past, it's a continuation of the past, the evil continues. We hand out money and more money and still more money, but money isn't always the answer. We are not giving these people the dignity they seek. We don't give them responsibilities, we give them money. Perhaps the Indians want some dignity. Perhaps they want to be self-sufficient. When someone earlier referred my colleague to the Vatican, I saw him smile, because the Vatican is independent, that's true. It would be quite something to see the Vatican, the same system they have for the independence of the Vatican, here.
You will tell me that the Canadian Constitution isn't perfect, and I agree. I may never be perfect. But all we are asking, all I want, all I would ask them if by chance someone is listening is: Lay down your arms. Nothing can be won with weapons. If there are people who think they're going to win with weapons, my regrets.
I listened to our Prime Minister this afternoon, I listened to his positive approach, and I retained something in particular from his speech:
September 25, 1990

Government Orders

Let the children go to school. That is where they belong now.

We see the Warriors, Lasagna and company, huddling close to children, families, women. That looks good, makes it easy to aim. And they call them "braves"! Personally, if I had something to settle, I wouldn't bring my children along, ever. I would confront the other person. They're putting children in danger. Why don't they put down their guns? Why don't our leaders-. Just now someone spoke of Mr. Sioui and of someone else. I'm not satisfied with the way the chiefs operate. I'm not satisfied when I see that people are being paid to do nothing behind all this. My colleague the Honourable Member for Chambly spoke of Mr. Sioui just now. I heard that too. Maybe I thought it was a threat too. I did think so. But if my honourable colleague is following the whole matter, he knows there is more to it. I could mention George Erasmus, who said,

We have never encouraged picking up the guns so that there would be bloodshed, but we have strongly defended our right to do everything possible peacefully to defend our rights.

I agree with him. George Erasmus, Grand Chief- [English]
Georges Erasmus, Grand Chief, said this on July 12 on Newsworld. Later, I saw him on TV say: "Indian people are not going to sit back and have their people butchered. What we are strategizing for is how to bring this country to its knees if it is not going to negotiate.

But in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, those are threats.
Yesterday I listened to George Erasmus, who has received $2 million in grants, who earns in the neighbourhood of $110,000 a year, and he came before Parliament to say, "It's not enough. You're going to have other Kahnawakes, you're going to have other Okas." Threats-And he doesn't pay income tax on his $110,000. He lives on a reserve. He says that the public, the MPs here, who earn $65,000 a year, are paid too much-and they pay income tax, too, which doesn't leave a lot.
So when someone bites the hand that feeds him, instead of finding a solution, because there must be a solution- Everybody talks about solutions. If one of them is a good one, let's run with that one! I'm not saying, "He's the one with the solution, or she is, or someone else is", but there must be a solution. But no, they criticize, they make threats. George Erasmus, Sioui. They don't want to respect the law, but they want the benefits of the law. And benefits the law certainly gives them.
It's true that the federal government has been under attack. It's easy for the opposition, it's easy to criticize those in power. It's easy to criticize the Prime Minister. He's to blame, he did it, they all dit it. It's governmentbashing time. It's like playing hockey, Mr. Speaker, and getting a 10-minute misconduct penalty when you weren't even on the ice. The Prime Minister has a 10-minute misconduct penalty, the Ministers of Justice and of Indian and Northern Affairs have also been given 10-minute penalties, and they weren't even on the ice, because the provincial government was there. But it's time they did get out on the ice. But there are laws, there are constitutions to respect. My colleague says No-he knows everything about Quebec. Probably he's never even been there. Bourassa, for him, doesn't count. For us, he's a Premier, elected as democratically as my colleague. Yes. But that probably doesn't matter to my colleague.
So, misconducts. And if you're in the opposition, it's so easy to criticize! And when they were in power? God save the country! You're so wonderful, but have you forgotten October of 1970, when you sent the army into Quebec? You're so wonderful, but you put Italians in prison, minorities, and why? They were interned because they were Italian. Minorities!

No respect for minorities and you tonight, like the member for Winnipeg South Centre, make a big speech with no content. He is an actor. I have content. I am going to give you proof of what you did, so do not give us any lessons. Go back in history, go back 20 or 30 years to what you did. You have no respect for minorities. We have.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I see people enlisted in this cause. One day they are egging the young people on, the next they're saying, "Hold it, hold it, no problem." One day they stir them up, the next day they calm them down. When is it going to stop? The people of Oka have returned home. They're eager for a peaceful solution. They're eager for everything to return to normal. They have lost a summer. They have lost their homes. They have lost personal property. And their eyes are smiling but not their mouths. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I say-

It is about time we got peace because these people did not ask for that problem. Non-Indian people there are suffering too. Nobody cares. We have everything on this side and we have nothing on the other side. I care for them. They are good people too.

speechtext: Is that a vote for me?

speechtext:
That is not a vote. They do not vote all for me, but I have got some friends that I respect very much. We were friends before politics and I hope we will stay friends. You see friends when you have problems. I went to visit and sympathize with them and tried to explain. Do you know what they asked me? They asked me, what would happen to me if I would go out with a machine gun? You would be arrested or shot, it is up to you. What would you like to do?
Even my kids said, "Dad, it is impossible that you guys cannot do anything about it". On TV I saw Lasagna playing the guitar with a big M-50 machine gun and then try to play with the arrow. Do you call that fun? Do you call that fun when kids are watching TV? Do you call that freedom of the press? Oh, the poor press, they suffer a lot. They show that almost live on TV. Playing the guitar with a machine gun in Canada when some poor taxpayers cannot even go through a red light without being put in jail.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: Freedom of the press.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue

speechtext: Yes, freedom of the press. One law with some exceptions. I do not know what the Liberals have to say. I would like to ask some questions of them but time does not permit, and I respect that. I would like to know if a lot of people here have the same solution as

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
let them go, catch them later. That is not what the people say in my area.
I met with all the people who have asked me to meet them on this issue. Why are we doing this? Why do I not have these benefits? Why do I have a special law? Why? What did we do wrong? We want to go to work. Ask the people at Chateauguay who have to go around. Nobody gave them anything free. Okay, now we will find some money, not too much, 10 cents a kilometre. When you drive a car it costs 36 cents a kilometre-41 now, my colleagues knows about it. It will be a present. My colleague from Chambly will understand that.
I did fight, too. I fought all my life for the consumer. We made a strike together. We had no guns and we won exactly what we wanted. I have a witness here. Thank God he is here to witness. We had no guns and we won. We won everything. Of course, there were some bad words going around. It is part of negotiations. We had something going on, but we did not have any machine-guns, thank God. We did not have any. What did we have? We had some friends who stuck together and we worked and tried to understand. When the minister called me and said we are ready to negotiate, I said, "Hey, boys, let's go back to work. These guys are serious". This was in the PQ time. He was there and saw what I did. We had 7,000 members on the road and everybody respected the law. If my people did not respect the law, we would not be here today.
I would like to finish with some-
