speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
These guys do not like the truth. These guys only like to criticize the government. But they have no solution. The only solution they have is to let them go. We will catch them later. Try to explain that to my people.
What I saw yesterday on TV was a real disgrace. Jesse Jackson came in and tried to play the new star on TV, just for the new talk shows in the United States. The researcher did not even tell him where Oka was. Somebody had to drive him there because he did not understand anything in this area. Thank God, he is not the President of the United States today because he would be playing golf the wrong way.
I was very surprised and shocked to see the international people who tried to give us lessons such as le journal le Monde en France. They do not understand this issue. They do not know what the hell is going on here. They do not know anything because on their first page


they wrote that an Indian was killed in Oka. It is not true. It was a Quebecer who was killed. He was a human being, too. Corporal Lemay was killed. Try to explain that to his wife, try to explain that to his kids. He did not even have the benefit of this person to rest in peace.

The respectful defenders of international human virtue did their usual turn, Mr. Speaker. The Right Honourable Joe Clark put it very well when he said that the observers tried to comment and find solutions when they had no idea what was happening. No idea! I was on the barricades one day, and the international observers came and they said, "How terrible", and then left. They didn't even go to the other side of the barricades. And at that point the army wasn't even there.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say to the people affected that I sympathize with them very much. I know their problems and I was there to help. I hope the two levels of government are going to do something to help them and also to restore some economic vitality to the town of Oka. I want to congratulate the Mayor of Oka, and extraordinary major who did extraordinary work, because he managed to keep the peace. And all his townspeople displayed extraordinary strength. They didn't criticize; they didn't act like the people of Chateauguay. Maybe they should have.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke to Mayor Ouellet earlier and told him that I would convey this message to the House. I congratulate him on his good work and I hope the government will do something to save this town, the prettiest village in Quebec.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess I am in a strange position having had my colleague, the hon. member for Laval-Est, put me in the same boat as he in the past. One thing that I have noticed with my colleague, the hon. member for Laval-Est, is that he has proven to me that anyone can become a member of Parliament regardless of creed, race or ability to understand a debate.
Government Orders
I think that what my colleague has said has been a mixture of insults to native people and an apology for the government. Unfortunately, I do not believe that he has really come clean in the sense of what he said publicly to the press. Before coming into the House today, he said publicly, and he had promised me that he would be saying that again today in the House, that he, as a member of Parliament, was very much upset by the way that his own government handled the native issue and that the members of his own party were not consulted and were left out and he felt very badly because of this situation. I see my colleague saying, yes, that is true and, at the same time I see other members of the caucus of the Conservative Party saying, no, that is not true. I think that is indicative of the fact that they were not able to get their act together before and they are not able to get their act together now.
To speak in terms of Mr. Erasmus, I do not agree with what Mr. Erasmus has said. I believe that he has been tendentious but I agree that the government has been equally tendentious, has been arrogant, has been wrong and has been provocative. To say that here is a man, a respected native leader and that we give him his food, to me, makes me feel dirty, it really does. It is not the appropriate kind of remark that we should make in Parliament about people who are Canada's original people.
I think that this entire debate has led itself to excesses on both sides and for one member of Parliament, my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Laval-Est to say that we have forgotten the other side, I do not think that is true. I have listened today. It is now almost two o'clock in the morning. I have listened because I figured I could make a better intervention if I heard what other people had to say, and I have heard, repeatedly, members from all the parties of this House saying that there has been a collective tragedy here on both sides. There have been people murdered-I am sorry, I must retract that-there has been one person killed, there have been people inconvenienced, there have been people injured, but I do not believe that we can put the blame on one side. I do believe that the government, as I said before must learn, and I wish that my colleague would learn, that this is a collective tragedy and that we should come out of this with the renewed desire to sincerely deal with native problems across the country.

Government Orders
One thing I would like to ask of my colleague and that is this: does he stand by the remarks he made outside of these halls, outside of Parliament, to the effect that the members of the Conservative Party-and I see him being coached right now by one of his colleagues and I understand he may need coaching but I would like the member for Laval-Est to answer on his own because he does that very well-did he not feel that the Conservative Party was running away from its elected members and it was really out of touch with native peoples?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I did tonight was try to explain that there are two sides to the story. The majority of our members tonight spoke about the Mohawk Indians. That was their right. I tried to touch on the other side a little, because these people need to be heard too. They are responsible people, good Canadians. They are taxpayers, and I have a lot of respect for them. I am a minority myself. I will not let anybody insult a minority in this House, even if my colleague tried a couple of times tonight.
The fact is that I was not informed. I said it and I will not hide it. There was a lack of information at the beginning. Of course nobody knew at the beginning where the story was going. I did inform my minister and we had some talks. I can tell the House that right after I was spoiled with information. There was a misunderstanding and some papers were sent to the wrong place. I accept that. I stand on what I said. On such an important issue people call their members of Parliament every day, people who were on both sides of the fence. At Oka and Chateauguay I have some people working there too who had lost their jobs. It is normal to be informed.
I did say that I was not well enough informed. I must say that after they did some research. Something happened and it was corrected, and after that I was spoiled with information. I must admit that I did not have very much time during the summer to read everything. I just wanted some important information about where we stood on the issue.
My hon. colleague from Chambly who asked me the question did not say a word in his speech about his constituents in Chambly. I met some people who were angry. I met some people who were not too happy about the crisis. They did not like the idea that they had to turn around and travel an extra 10 kilometres to 50 kilometres per day.
People called me from Ville La Salle. Maybe that is not exactly in the centre of Chambly, but I understand people called me because they knew me personally. Of course I am not their member of Parliament but I can still talk to these Canadians. They were unhappy. They did not like the idea, but that was the situation.
Of course they would like to have the situation changed after a phone call. I do not think anybody here has the right key for doing that. I hope that people understand that we try to do our best. We tried to work with everybody on both sides of the House and on both sides of the issue. I worked with the mayor, I worked with the people, and I think we did a hell of job.
I know my colleague from Argenteuil-Papineau spent many days there. I saw her on both sides, but most of the time she was on the other side of the barricade. I did not go on the other side very much. I was not allowed to go really. I stayed on this side of the barricade, and she was briefing me once a week.
The situation was not funny. We did not think for a minute that this thing would go on for 70 days or more, and the people sleeping in the homes at Oka tonight are not very secure. I understand that very well. If people here know Oka with the mountains, the golf courses and all the trees, they will know that they do not like that, but we assured them and the army assured them that there would be no problem. I am very happy that they went back to their homes tonight. I received that news at ten o'clock tonight.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on an issue of great importance and urgency to our country and indeed of great interest to the people of Haldimand-Norfolk.
This summer our country's own Armed Forces have been deployed against its own citizens. This summer shots were fired and a Canadian lost his life. Several hundred Canadians have experienced violations of their basic rights. We have seen footage and heard reports of police harassing Canadians and Canadians attacking police. Canadians have attacked one another with names and sticks and rocks. Our mood has become one of confusion, of anger, and of vengeance. Canadians know shame as a nation that they have never known before. The cause of this shame is our inability to deal peacefully and justly with the native people of Canada.
September 25, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I submit to you that a great deal of the shame must rest with with government and its inaction to deal with this situation.
In my time as a member of Parliament I have never seen such complete lack of confidence, such lack of understanding, and such lack of leadership as I have seen on this issue. In its souless, gutless manner we have seen throughout, the government is now trying to shift the blame away from its own inadequacies, away from its own lack of leadership, to a whole different issue.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development would rather talk about the conduct of our Armed Forces than to address the real issue, the real needs of our native Canadians. The Canadian Armed Forces are just that: they are Armed Forces. They were called into the communities at Kahnawake and Kanesatake and given a mandate in our society. They acted with discipline and efficiency, but the fact that the Armed Forces were called out at all was an admission of failure on the part of both this government and the provincial Government of Quebec, because arms are only taken up by people when they feel that all else has failed, when they feel that their governments have failed them.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development seeks to condemn the Indian people in their use of arms. These arms were taken up rightly or wrongly after decades of attempts to deal and negotiate a settlement with the Government of Canada. How long did the federal government wait to send in its Armed Forces? How hard did the minister and the Prime Minister try to negotiate before sending in the Armed Forces?
The minister could not negotiate because he was far too busy trying to dodge cameras and to figure out how he could twist the situation and how he could tell the people of Canada that it was not his responsibility, that it was not the responsibility of this government. I tell the minister that Canadians are not buying it.
From the early stages of this crisis the only information we got from the government, the only word that came from the government, was that it was a police matter and out of its jurisdiction. There has been no leadership
Government Orders
shown at all. It has completely abdicated the responsibility for first peoples.
That same point was made in a letter, of which I have a copy, to the Right Hon. Prime Minister from the Six Nations Council, from Chief Bill Montour. I want to quote a little from this letter because I think it is important:
The Six Nations of the Grand River are alarmed to be informed by Sue Nations negotiators in the Kanesatake territory that the federal government and the province of Quebec negotiators are unwilling to negotiate or entertain even serious discussions concerning the situation at Oka.
Later it says:
We feel your government has shown a total lack of responsibility and sound judgment, passing the situation off as a police action of the province of Quebec. Your inaction will only serve to regress the social relationship between this divergent cultural group and the aboriginal peoples in Canada to that of 100 years ago.
The Six Nations of the Grand River believe that it is your responsibility to take control of negotiations by defusing the trouble spots and negotiating a peaceful settlement with the Mohawks of the Kanesatake. Rather than allowing the bureaucracy to have total responsibility to uphold the honour of the Crown, we respectively demand that you recall Parliament to deal with the transgression by the province of Quebec.
May our creator guide your thoughts.
That was sent to the Prime Minister by Chief Bill Montour of the Six Nations, and with no response.
By abdicating its responsibility I believe this government has guaranteed, as my colleague from Rainy River said, that the threat of violence could continue. By abdicating its responsibility for aboriginal peoples and for the policies concerning land claims, this government has told Canadians that they are an instrument of choice when it comes to a crisis requiring leadership.
"Forget leadership, forget Parliament, forget serious negotiations, because I have always got the police. I have always got the army to bring in." That is the message from this government to Canadians. Then the government has the audacity to tell first peoples and to tell Canadians about this magical rule of law. This is the same government that stood by while food and medical attention were denied Canadians, the same government that is now trying to justify the violation of the freedom of the press, the same government that manipulates jurisdictions and legislation just to hide from this difficulty, the same government that on numerous occasions has

Government Orders
shown complete and utter contempt for this House. Now it wants to tell Canadians about the rule of law.
Let us talk about that point for a second. I am not a lawyer, but I did have the opportunity to contact the Library of Parliament to find out what exactly its definition of the rule of law is. They gave me a quote of the rule of law taken from the Oxford Companion which it reads:
The concept of the rule of law implies the subordination of all authorities, legislative, executive, judicial and other to certain principles-these principles such as the fundamental principles of justice, moral principles, fairness and due process. It implies respect for the supreme value and dignity of the individual. In any legal system, it implies limitations on legislative power, safeguards against the abuse of the executive power-
We all know-and even the government would admit it-that the treatment of aboriginal peoples throughout history on this continent has not been compatible with the fundamental principles of justice. The land dispute which gave rise to the blockades at Oka has its roots in the unjust allocation of land which arose when our society imposed concepts of land ownership and of land exploitation which were foreign and indeed caused conflict in this situation.
The rule of law implies supremacy of the moral principles and respect for the supreme value and dignity of the individual. Do we consider it morally right to deny food and medical attention to children? Do we abide by the violation of fundamental rights and freedoms?
All these things happened this summer and they are continuing to happen. Has this government done anything to solve these problems? Now government members opposite stand here before us and attempt to pass themselves off as defenders of this rule of law. What about the rule of law safeguarding abuse against executive power?
We on this side of the House demanded that the government recall Parliament so that representatives of Canadians from across this country could participate in a debate and that we could express to this government the anger and the outrage of many Canadians over this government's failure to act in this situation.
This government failed to commit the political will necessary to bring about a peaceful negotiated settlement to the situation and to preserve the dignity of all the individuals involved. This government refused to heed our call despite the fact that it had recalled Parliament to deal with events which while important were no more important than this situation. Members opposite like to talk about the rule of law and order, knowing that they are sacred cows which no one would dare contradict.
Let me express the perspective exposed by Ovide Mercredi, Manitoba Vice-Chief of the Assembly of First Nations. It is one I share with him. This government talks about law and order and what they do not seem to understand is that law and order is based on justice. Our population is law abiding because it believes in the justness of the law and the judicial system and where it does not agree with the law, it has confidence that the system will protect them and that it can be amended. We know that our judicial system, our police system and government have not treated aboriginals fairly or justly. How is it we expect unending patience, unending law and order from a group that we have endlessly abused and discriminated against? Does that mean that I think picking up a gun is a way to solve a problem? No, I do not.
What it means is that I believe it is abundantly clear that the current land claims system is a failure. It has little political legitimacy remaining and is in desperate need of reform. It is unacceptable that this government is trumpeting law and order and the rule of law as a new-found excuse to ignore and dismiss legitimate Indian demands. In fact, this government has violated the rule of law in almost every way imaginable in the last few months.
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to participate last Sunday in Simcoe at a rally by constituents of Haldi-mand-Norfolk. It was pouring rain and there were hundreds out there. They signed a petition which I have here and I want to read it because I think it is important. It says to the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premier

of the province of Quebec and all those who may be concerned:
"We citizens of the Haldimand-Norfolk area of Ontario gathered in Simcoe September 23, remind our federal and provincial governments of the meaningful aboriginal status of the native people of Canada, of the important contacts with land and community which has sustained them in such symbols as the Mohawk tree of peace, of the privation and suffering which Canadian and American policies continue to cause them, of the need in Canada today for generous and neighbourly treatment of all citizens including native people. We earnestly request our governments to address at once the many outstanding land claims of the native people of Canada, to recognize and respect all treaty rights of native people, to support the native people of this country in their search for a meaningful degree of self-government, to accept due responsibility for the deterioration of the quality of life in many reserves and to take appropriate steps to correct it. Finally, we request the federal government to establish an aboriginal rights commission to push these developments.
At this moment of confrontation at Kanesatake and Kahnawake in the province of Quebec, we think it essential that the federal government exercise its authority to cause a withdrawal from the scene of the Quebec police and after that of the Canadian military personnel who are at present on the scene and enter into meaningful discussion with the native councils of these communities with a goal of peace and the well-being of their people and in demonstration of our sincerity in these matters, we have gathered food and money to aid the people at Kanesatake and Kahnawake and signed our names to this petition."
This petition is clearly the feeling of a great number of Canadians. I know my time is up so in closing, let me return again, to the Oxford Companion's discussion of the rule of law. I believe that these words serve as a very useful commentary on the government's reaction to the Oka crisis and in particular to aboriginal issues in this country. It says, "The rule of law means more than that the government maintains and enforces law and order but that the government is, in itself, subject to the rule of law and cannot itself disregard the law or remake it to suit itself".

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you caught me unawares as I thought there might be some questions.
Government Orders
I take part in this debate this evening, or this morning, and I look at the resolution that we are debating, that this House commends the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian Forces at Oka and Chateauguay. We saw the TV coverage, particularly of the young soldiers who were pressed into something that I am sure that they did not enjoy, and the cool and patient way they approached a very tough issue facing Canada.
The second part of the motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the laws of Canada must apply on all Canadian territory, including Kahnawake, and that all persons currently at the Kanesatake Treatment Centre should lay down their arms and submit to the process of Canada's judicial system, thereby encouraging the creation of a constructive climate for discussions between governments and the Mohawk people on land claims and other issues.
I do not think there are many people in Canada who would not agree that the laws of Canada should be obeyed.
The last part of the motion reads:
That upon adoption of this motion, the said motion shall be deemed referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General.
If I may take a few moments, I would like to point out something that I think has been missing in the debate that I have heard here today. I think it has degenerated into a situation of blame back and forth which I do not think that really helps the House of Commons. It is very important that we in the House of Commons try to examine the issue and maybe even try and come up with some constructive ideas on the way to resolve a very difficult situation.
I think one of the things that has been overlooked repeatedly, not only in the debate here but in the news media in the past month or so, is the difference between the warriors, the Warriors Society and the Mohawk people. I would like to just briefly read an article which was printed July 4, 1990 by the Herald Journal of Syracuse, N.Y. after an interview. It is by M.C. Bums, who is a staff writer:
Louis Hall lives in an isolated trailer with battered typewriter he used to pound out his manifesto. Over the last 10 years, that document has inspired a divisive, militant resurgence in the Iroquois nation and fostered a rebirth of a warriors movement from Canada to Wisconsin.
When masked Mohawks with assault rifles blocked entrance to the St. Regis Reservation a year ago, Louis Hall was behind them -not physically, but his words put them there.
Those gunmen, members of the well-armed Warriors' Society at the reservation in New York and Canada, idolized Lewis Hall. Today, they are key players in the violence and the uneasy peace that exists in the place Mohawks call Akwesasne.

Government Orders
Halls writing, produced by slender figures rattling his Olympia, is outrageous, vehement and angry. "There will come a day", he wrote recently, "when the Indian will put the white man in a boat and send him back to Europe where he belongs and keep him there".
The manifesto reinterprets the Great Law Peace, the constitution of the Iroquois, and gives some Native Americans the rationale they need to carry weapons. In it, Hall asks, "What can the warriors societies do?
He answers: Dump bridges into rivers-which are now sewers-and into seaway, cancelling all traffic, knock out powerhouses, high-tension power lines, punch holes in the reactors of nuclear power houses.
He urges young Iroquois to reject the peace-oriented teachings of the traditional chiefs, including those who sit on the Grand Council of the Six Nations of Iroquois.
He believes that some traditional chiefs-including all of the ones who sit at the Onondaga Nation-have betrayed the Great Law, and for that they should be executed, Mafia-style, by Mafia hit men, if possible.
Hall is not kidding.
"They should be executing the traitors," he said in an interview. "But they would have to do it the way the Mafia do it -in secret and never see the victim again. No body. No case."
Some Warriors agree with him and do not question his teachings, even concerning executions.
"Yes, they should be executed," said Francis Boots, war chief of the Warriors Society of Akwesasne. "It's the law."
Boots usually has a copy of Hall's manifesto close by.
"But it is his actual presence that inspires us," Boots said. "He has the message, and he knows how to articulate it."
There is more that goes on and points out where the Warriors Society is coming from.
This is not supported by the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne. Let me show you a kit that I got from the Mohawk Council and I would like to point out just a few things. It is a chronology of violence and it basically states: "From Petty Offences to Multi-Million Dollar Crime". It is a brief history of events leading to the 1990 campaign of violence by the Mohawk Sovereignty Security Force (the Warriors) and the pro-gamblers.
In Akwesasne, May 1, 1990, ordinary people live in fear. Armed thugs rule the land. Gambling, narcotics, smuggling, beatings, and automatic weapons fire are everyday activities. Police protection exists only in some sectors and where it exists, it is overwhelmed by criminals. A ghetto in an American city? The Sicilian countryside? Life in Columbia? Not in this case.
The above description is of Akwesasne, a Mohawk Indian reservation with a population of about 9,500 located near Cornwall, Ontario, Canada and Massena, New York, in the U.S.A. It lies partially in Canada and partially in the U.S.A. How did a normally peaceful and law-abiding community become a war-zone reminiscent of Belfast or Beirut?
These are comments made by the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne. They wrote it. Jack Shields did not write it. This government did not write it. It is the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne who wrote this article.
From 1979 to 1980, the first step was smuggling cigarettes. They started out with petty crime. In 1981, a law enforcement vacuum-the bingo boom begins. A law enforcement vacuum was created on the American side of the reservation when the population disbanded the Tribal Police Force-that was on the American side-after charges of abuse and fraud. A high stakes bingo operator, partially funded by the smugglers and partially from outside sources, was allowed to set up under regulation of the Tribe. But he took advantage of the legal and enforcement vacuum to disregard the elected leadership and the deal that was signed with the Tribe.
In 1984, 1985, and 1986, speakeasies flourished; slot machines are added. As they accumulated wealth, the smugglers diversified into after-hours sales of alcohol and slot machines. Community objections increased after 19 people were killed in alcohol related car accidents as they left the speakeasies. Low skill jobs in the bingo halls and casinos attracted many young people away from continued studies. Community anger grew every day. Protests and attempts to have the illegal operations closed increased. The three Mohawk governments separately and then jointly attempted unsuccessfully to close them down. All of this supported by, not the Mohawks whom everyone talks about, but very clearly by this Warrior Society which was operating illegally among their own people, redefining what the Warrior Society was, following the teachings or the manifesto of Louis Hall.
In 1987, a chief of the longhouse, or the traditional government of the Mohawk people, is dehorned. He is

relieved of his authority and position for refusing to cease his involvement in the lucrative trade. He subsequently organized groups of young, unemployed men and boys to be runners or paid employees to help operate the business.
In 1987, the runners or foot soldiers of the smugglers received paramilitary training, bought sophisticated weapons and communications equipment, and emerged as the Warrior Society, later to become known as the Mohawk Sovereignty Security Force, MSSF or the warriors. They adapted and corrupted a tradition of the warriors which for centuries had meant societies which ensured protection of the nation, among other things. Traditionally, these societies were accountable to the traditional chiefs who call upon their services when needed.
In 1987, the MSSF claimed that their existence became necessary because the nation had been systematically attacked and rendered nearly powerless despite Mohawk protests. In reality, they emerged to protect the lucrative economic interests under the guise of Mohawk sovereignty because Canadian and U.S. officials and the good Mohawk people were becoming an impediment to business.
Again, I am saying, and I underline this, this is being written by the Mohawk council of Akwesasne. They are the ones who are saying this, not people in the House.
In 1988, 1989, and 1990, the warriors began to threaten and intimidate anyone who opposed the slots and bingos. Narcotics, especially cocaine and crack, became an increasing problem. Many people reported that warriors were dealing while others were often high while patrolling and handling their automatic weapons. Arrests were made of some warriors for attempting to take concealed weapons across the border. The State Police raided some casinos and confiscated slot machines but the operators replaced them and resumed full operations within twenty-four hours. Warriors began to run people off the road and ram vehicles. In Canada, you say?
In 1990, warrior violence increased. Beatings, threats, and shootings increased in frequency. Personal property such as homes and cars were damaged. Months of intensive efforts were made in vain to resolve the disputes through negotiation. The people, tired of federal and state inaction and wishing to stop their growth and eradicate the illegal activities, set up road blockades to stop the flow of clients to the casinos. That is the
Government Orders
Mohawk people doing this. Warriors' reaction was to shoot at Mohawk people with automatic weapons and to destroy the barricades.
Warrior spokespeople appeared on television claiming to protect the nation from outside forces and promising to do away with any opposition. The warriors developed a hit list of Akwesasne Mohawks who opposed them.
In April, 1990, warriors declared war on their own people. Hundreds of Mohawks fled the reservation to escape the "civil war" atmosphere. Why have we not heard about that in the debate tonight? Why has it only been an angry outburst of emotion saying that Canadians or the government is not interested in the plight of native people and land claims?
On May 1, 1990, two young Mohawk men were killed in gun battles. The non-Mohawk police finally moved in to back up the Mohawk police on the Canadian side. Mohawks on the American side saw law enforcement officials on the territory for the first time in a decade. In other words, the New York police were, for the first time in a decade, on the reserve.
In June and July of 1990, tensions persisted as the police forces from Canada, Ontario and Quebec and New York State came to Akwesasne to help Mohawk police maintain peace. Warrior spokesmen declare publicly their intention to take over control of all Indian reservations in northeastern North America through undermining means.
There is no doubt that in the past years since our forefathers came to this country native people were shunted off into reserves. There is no doubt in our minds that many of the land claims settlements have not been done. We have tried a number of things and other governments have tried a number of things. One of the things that I experienced was to throw money at the problem. We saw 10 or 15 years of throwing money at the problem and nothing happened. There is a clash in the way we look at it and it is a misunderstanding, many times, of what native people want and what Canadians see.
One of the things that I think is very important is that the young generation growing to be citizens of this country, native people, must recognize that there is not much future on a reserve. Our whole society in Canada is built on the idea that if you work hard, you accumulate

Government Orders
your worth or your wealth, you are able to own your home and you are able to pass on some of these things to your children. It is not so on a reserve. A reserve is communally owned. People living on the reserve do not own their own homes, it is a band house. We have passed the economic development to try to get the economy of the reserves moving to the band rather than to individuals. It has always been my contention that we should be looking more at individuals and saying to individuals on reserves: "Look, you, too, can prosper. You, too, can take part in this Canadian idea of getting into business, owning property, and profiting from your sweat, your work and the hard things that happen when you get into business or when you work."
The other thing that is a problem, and I have seen this time and time again, is when natives do become educated, become doctors, lawyers, and dentists and get into other professions or end up living not on the reserve but in a city, working at a steady job such as the oil sands, for example, in my area Syncrude and Suncor, the other natives on the reserve soon refer to them as Indian white men. The drag-down system starts because the whole philosophy on a reserve is that everyone should be equal. Everyone owns, in a communal way, everything on that reserve. It is run by a band chief and council.
I want to take one more minute, Mr. Speaker, if you will just give me another minute.
It must be totally devastating to a native man who is raising a family and does not have a job. He wants basically the same things that we do. He wants security for his family, he wants to see his family educated, and he wants them to be healthy and happy. That is not happening today. We, in this government, are committed to see that it does happen and that we become more involved through the consultative process to bring natives to the standard of living equal to anyone else in Canada.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I see that you are signalling me to stop.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: I regret that the hon. member's time has expired. On debate, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of sadness that I enter this important debate at this late hour.
I say with a great deal of sadness because, despite the many excellent and constructive proposals made by members of the House and by individuals and groups including aboriginal groups across the country, proposals to peacefully settle this long-standing dispute, members of the government continue to justify the insensitive and irresponsible actions that we saw throughout the summer. They continue to support this fraudulent, dishonest and demeaning motion which is before the House.
I am sad not only for what this motion says to the people at Kanesatake and Kahnawake, and not only for what it says to all aboriginal people in Canada, but also for what it says to Canadians and about Canadians.
During the last week of August and the first week of September, I was at an international conference in Geneva. Day after day in the news, in Switzerland and in Germany, Canada was portrayed as a banana republic denying basic rights to aboriginal people and using military might to force them into submission.
I refer to the resolution before the House as dishonest and fraudulent. Let me illustrate.
The resolution starts by commending the conduct of the Canadian Armed Forces. The issue that should be before the House is the conduct of the government. Why did the government not have the guts, the intestinal fortitude, to put a resolution to the House which would have addressed the real issue, which is the conduct of the Prime Minister and the Minister for Indian Affairs? That is what we should be debating. What a smoke-screen this resolution is. What a fraud this resolution is. It is an attempt to whitewash the irresponsible actions of the government.
The Canadian Armed Forces, of course, have long experience in peacekeeping. Nobody condemns them for what they do under direction of the government. They are a professional armed force. They follow the direction and the laws laid down by the government. The problem we are faced with is caused by the government and, if the government had any gumption, any guts, it would have put a resolution to the House dealing with its conduct,
September 25, 1990

and it did not do it. It is a shame for the House and for the country that it failed to do so.
Let us look at the second paragraph of this resolution.
That in the opinion of this House, the laws of Canada must apply on
all Canadian territory-
The implication of that particular paragraph is that all laws apply everywhere in Canada and that these Mohawks are wild, irresponsible people for suggesting otherwise. What is the government trying to say in that particular sentence? Does it not realize that the Indian Act, to start with, does not apply everywhere in Canada? The Indian Act itself applies to very particular people on very particular pieces of land, reservations and so on.
The government recognizing that Indian people were different in different parts of the country passed the Sechelt legislation a few years ago, whereby the Sechelt people in British Columbia were given a certain form of self-government and were exempted from the Indian Act.
If we look at the James Bay agreement, the James Bay legislation, there are provisions for those people living in northern Quebec which are quite different than the provisions under the Indian Act.
Many laws do not apply everywhere, and others that do should not in some cases, if we address them in a more critical fashion than we have in the past.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the whole resolution is a fraud. What does the government mean by that particular statement that the laws of Canada must apply in all Canadian territory. It certainly does not mean the Indian Act, or the Sechelt Act, or the James Bay and Northern Quebec Cree Act. Maybe they are referring to the Criminal Code. Maybe they are implying that the Mohawk people, the Indian people, feel they should not be covered by the Criminal Code.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, one might ask if the Criminal Code was applied equally to Donald Marshall, and one might examine the criminal justice system and how it applies to Indians and non-Indians in this country.
I listened to the hon. member for Athabasca reading a long list of accusations against the Warrior Society. No one is suggesting that if there are any crimes against
Government Orders
individuals or any crimes that are to be charged against individuals, they should not be charged with those crimes.
What I find is happening when I listen to the hon. member and others on the other side of the House is that they are trying to brand with a wide brush all aboriginal people and all Mohawks, including all those in the treatment centre, as being criminals and warriors, terrorists, and so on, following the lead of the Deputy Minister for Indian affairs who, in the month of August, more or less said that the people who were causing the trouble were criminals.
The fact of the matter is that there are many examples in this country of special laws for special peoples, depending on their circumstances. For many years in this country the aboriginal people have argued that many of the laws that apply to them were drafted and passed without their participation in a repressive, unjust, paternalistic and colonialistic fashion, and that their past, history, culture and backgrounds were never taken into consideration with the passage of those laws.
Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, this Parliament needs to recognize that. We recognize that to a certain extent in the James Bay settlement. We recognize that to a certain extent in the Sechelt Act. Some people will disagree with the Sechelt Act and say it is not really an act dealing with self-government, but despite that the Sechelt people were willing to accept it. So was the government and they made special provisions.
If we look at certain Indian nations in this country, they do have their own courts. They do have their own police officers. They do have their own probation and parole officers who understand their people and who apply their laws and customs in conjunction with the laws in Canada.
This conflict at Kanesatake and Kahnawake was a disaster from the beginning. It is a conflict that need not have happened. It should not have happened if the government had acted responsibly and correctly in the situation.
When I was Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs, if there was land under claim by an aboriginal group, we put a freeze on that land until the claim was totally settled. We would not allow oil and gas development. We

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
would not allow mining. We would not allow the construction of roads on that land while it was under claim.
Here we have the mayor of a small community deciding to expand a golf course and for that reason we have this dispute. If the minister and the government had been acting as they should have been, as trustees for the aboriginal people in this country, as they are supposed to do under the Indian Act and under our constitutional laws, and according to a recent decision of the Supreme Court, they would have immediately intervened and said it is irresponsible to move ahead with a golf course when this land is under claim. If they had done that, if the minister and the Prime Minister and the government had not been totally asleep with their heads in the sand, none of this would have happened.
However, here we are before this House debating a fraudulent, camouflage resolution about the conduct of the Armed Forces. Here we have this despicable conduct of the government, of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Indian Affairs and they have not even got the courage to put that to the House as they should have.
The conduct of this government in this matter from beginning to end was an abdication of responsibility. After the first incident of violence on July 11, we did not even hear from the minister or the Prime Minister for weeks on end. One wondered what had happened to the minister and to the Prime Minister. We heard from the Minister of Indian Affairs of Quebec, Mr. Ciaccia, we heard from Mr. Remillard, also with the Quebec government, we heard from Mr. Bourassa. There was a total abdication of federal jurisdiction over Indian affairs to the Quebec government. That was bad enough but once the Armed Forces were brought in, this same government abdicated responsibility and jurisdiction over important decision making to the army, and I will illustrate that in a few minutes.
Decisions that were political decisions and should have been made by the government through negotiation and through intervention were left to the Armed Forces, which are not equipped and should not be involved in political decision making or in key decisions which will affect the political results between two peoples, as we saw in Oka and in Kahnawake.
In the resolution they talk about the laying down of arms. They ask that the people in the treatment centre at Kanesatake lay down their arms and submit to the processes of Canada's judicial system. There have been several proposals agreed upon by the Mohawks and by the Iroquois Confederacy to do that, but it also involves some obligations on the other side. But these were not taken seriously by the Bourassa government nor by this government.
There was a very complete proposal to dispose of the arms under supervision and so on and if people were to be charged, let them be charged. Let us go through the process, even though the process has been very unfair to aboriginal people over the years. I have already referred to the Donald Marshall case and there are others as well.
I heard about the situation last week where John Ciaccia, the Minister for Indian Affairs in Quebec, was in Toronto and worked out an agreement with the Iroquois Confederacy to settle both the short term and the long term issues in dispute, a settlement that I understand dealt with the laying down of arms and dealt with the Warrior Society. The hon. member for Athabasca was pretending I suppose that we suggested that those who committed wrong or committed criminal offences should go free. Not at all. Nor did the proposed settlement of the Iroquois Confederacy and Mr. Ciaccia do that at all.
What happened with that agreement? Once concluded, one of the representatives of the confederacy was to discuss it with people in the treatment centre to see if it was acceptable to them. When he arrived in Oka to gain entry to the treatment centre, he was denied entrance by the Armed Forces. That was not a decision to be made by the Armed Forces. Here we have a potential solution to the standoff, to the problem which has existed for several months, and the man cannot even get inside to discuss it with the people involved.
The representative of the confederacy then went to Ottawa to speak to people in a higher position in the Armed Forces. At that time he was told that this is a political matter and he should discuss it with the political authorities, so he goes to the political authorities. What did they say? "This is a military matter, go back to the Armed Forces".
September 25, 1990

Talk about sticking your head in the sand and avoiding your responsibilities. That is what we should be debating today, the conduct of the government. It is not up to the Armed Forces to make key political decisions that would have led to a settlement in this particular case. The Armed Forces is a professional organization, as I said, and they follow the orders of the government, the direction of the government, and the law laid down by this Parliament. They are not meant to make key political decisions involved in the dispute.
That proposal, as I understand it, dealt with the short-term and long-term issues that are before us. The short-term, of course, deal with the standoff at the treatment centre and the long-term issues, the claim policy, the policy that the government has for settling claims and matters of self-government and sovereignty.
With respect to the longer term issues, they will have to be dealt with because if they are not dealt with, we will continue to have problems and trouble in this country. They have been looked at over and over again. I was a member of the special committee on Indian self-government called the Penner committee. We travelled throughout this country for nearly two years and made a report which made serious recommendations to deal with these issues.
We had the Coolican report which recommended changes to the claims policy, which recommended the end of the extinguishment policy and the end to the policy of superseding by law legitimate rights. That is the problem with our claims policy. Indians go before the courts. They go before commissions and bodies and say "Flere are our rights. We want them recognized". People in government keep saying "Well, those rights were extinguished by a law passed in 1905". They were extinguished by a law passed in 1917. They are superseded by law. But, many of those laws are unjust laws and that should not be an excuse.
At one time in our history we had laws on slavery. At one time in our history we did not allow women to vote. We got rid of those laws. It is time to get rid of a lot of other laws that affect our aboriginal people.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext: And laws on child labour, too.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Child labour, as my colleague mentions. There are all sorts of laws in our past history which were
Government Orders
unjust and unfair. Thank God we recognize that. But, we have not done it with respect to aboriginal people. We keep citing precedents of courts and saying that is what must govern. We keep citing precedents of laws that go back to a period when people did not have the same understanding they have today, or should have today.
Mr. Speaker, you are giving me the signal that my time is coming to an end.
In conclusion, I want to plead with the government to show a little humanity, a little compassion and a little understanding. They should try to put themselves in the shoes of the aboriginal people in Canada and try to understand how they feel in this particular situation.
I ask the government to forget this ridiculous resolution that is before us and get down to serious negotiation for a just, fair and peaceful settlement. For God's sake, Mr. Speaker, let's see some leadership.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just thought that perhaps it would be a good time to set the record straight about the story of the land at Oka because there seems to be some question in the minds of the members opposite about what the facts are.
I will go through it very briefly. It is a comment. It does not really require any response. This issue started, as some hon. members may know, back in 1717 when the seminary of St. Soltice acquired a tract of land from the King of France and set up a religious order there. They then brought some Indians with them from Montreal and included, not just Mohawks who are the ancestors of the present Indians, the group included Nipissing and Algonquins as well.
After a time, of course, the land was broken up. The religious order left and there was a dispute over whether or not the land that had been used by the Indians since 1717 was, in fact, theirs.
There have been numerous references to courts and to various methods of settling the dispute over the years, but I will just go quickly through some of the highlights. In 1851, in order to settle this dispute, a reserve was provided at Maniwaki and many of the Algonquins who were moving from Oka moved to this location, but many of the Mohawks stayed at Oka.

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
The dispute sort of continued. In 1881 there was another dispute and the Indians at Oka did not prevail. Finally in 1912 the judicial council of the Privy Council, at that time the highest court in Canada, ruled on this particular item and held at that time that the Indians at Oka had no title or right to control the administration of the land. At that time the highest court in Canada had decided that the interest in that land was not vested in the Indian people. It was vested in the other people who had been living there.
These claims continued. The hon. gentleman mentioned that if they were in power there would not be an opportunity to do anything on a piece of land that was under claim. Even though it had been finally settled by the the highest court in the land, the Mohawks submitted another claim, a specific claim, in June 1977 which was ultimately rejected in 1986. At that time the minister of the day, when he advised the Indians that their claim was rejected, told them however that he was willing to consider a proposal for an alternate means of redressing their grievance.
At that time they sat down and negotiated a framework agreement. We have heard much about it. It was initialled in September 1989. The rest is history. The leadership of the band changed and the land issue was once more in dispute.
It is important that hon. members recognize that this is a very unusual case. They should not ignore the facts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very much aware of that history. It only confirms the points I was trying to make.
The hon. member, for example, referred to court decisions which said that the claim was not justified because according to the laws of the land at the time another owner had the right to the land. In other words, laws superseded what were real rights, rights that had existed for a long time. Although it is true that band of people had moved from one place to another, promises had been made and for one reason or another the dispute carried on for years and years, sometimes with more visibility and more aggressiveness and at other times much more quietly.
If we examine what happened in a chronological way-and I have this record here before me-the negotiations this summer and spring were moving quite well, until once again there was a turndown of offer by the
band due to changes in the band administration and so on.
It was at that point that mistakes started being made. When the town of Oka decided to move ahead with the golf course, it was at that point, I submit, that the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs should have acted as a trustee for the Indian people and said: "Do not go ahead with that golf course, because this land is still under claim. There is no basis for proceeding with that golf course". It was that incident and the lack of action and involvement by the minister and by the government which led to all these problems.
The minister should have intervened at that point and said to the Quebec government and to the mayor of Oka: "Under no circumstances should you proceed with that golf course while this thing is still being negotiated". It is true that the negotiations had broken down, but with mediators and with conciliation they could have got going again, and they will go ahead again with good faith on both sides.
I blame the government for not taking action at that time, for withdrawing from the scene and for leaving it entirely to the Quebec government; then bringing in the army and leaving entirely to the army when the army should have been given more direction and when decisions that were made by the army should have been made by the government. I could list a whole raft of inactions which should have been discussed and blamed on the government.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in this debate. I cannot think of any other issue which has caused so much anguish among Canadians, so much lack of certainty about the purpose of their country, so much lack of generosity toward people who need some generosity and spirit from government, and some concern for their lifestyles and the peril they find themselves in.
I know that in Winnipeg North Centre, where close to 30,000 or 40,000 people of aboriginal descent live, this issue has been the one that caused the most anxiety this summer and the greatest number of phone calls, letters and demands for public action.
I ask myself why is it that in the organization of the business of the House of Commons such an important issue is being debated at 2.50 in the morning? I will tell the House why. It is because the government wishes to bury this issue. It wishes it to disappear. It wishes it to be

discussed in the darkness of night so that Canadians do not have to hear exactly what has been going on.
I can tell every member of the government sitting over there that we are not going to let this issue die, that we are going to keep fighting, that we are going to bring this to the public's attention, and that we are going to keep demanding a public inquiry because we have to get to the bottom of it and we have to stop treating aboriginal people as second-class citizens.
Mr. Speaker, tonight you have heard several times that the rule of law is the issue. The Prime Minister, in response to questions in Question Period, says that it is the rule of law, that we must have order. I used to be a political science professor before I took on this new task in life. I decided to go back to the textbooks and look up this concept of the rule of law. Apparently the Prime Minister did the same thing because in a speech given earlier tonight or late yesterday, depending on how one wants to count it, he too talked about the same writer, R. MacGregor Dawson, as he tried to justify why he is going to start appointing extra senators to beat back the Liberals in the Senate over the GST.
R. MacGregor Dawson wrote the book The Government of Canada, which is a basic text on understanding the Canadian government. I promise you, Mr. Speaker, that even though these quotations are long they are real eye-openers and you will enjoy listening to them.
Listen to what Mr. Dawson had to say, and I quote:
-Canadian inheritance which is closely identified with some of these fundamental rights of the citizen is the rule of supremacy of law, a long-established principle of the British constitution. The exact meaning and implications of this principle are not readily stated, but its essence is the restriction on arbitrary authority in government and the necessity for all acts of government to be authorized by "reasonably precise" laws as applied and interpreted by the courts.
When we talk about the rule of law here, we are not talking about the actions of the Mohawks. We are talking about the actions of the government.
When referring to this provision, for example, in the old American Constitution, he wrote:
Government Orders
-that "this shall be a government of laws and not of men" was clearly a vain hope, but it was an endeavour to state in one phrase substantially the same idea-the certainty of legal procedures, the absence of untrammelled official power, the protection of the citizen against unknown and unpredictable authority. The increasing complexity of modem government, the growing emphasis on the social rather than the individual good, and the resulting need for government intervention in almost all fields of human endeavour have inevitably resulted in far wider discretionary powers being given to executive and administrative officials, accompanied by a consequent narrowing of the rule of law. Thus the sweeping accountability of officials to the courts of law when the legality of their acts was in question has had its scope somewhat diminished by the grant of wider and more general legal powers, and this has tended to a limited degree to remove the acts of the officials from judicial scrutiny. Despite this modification, the rule of law remains a cardinal principle of the Canadian constitution and a sturdy bulwark against abuse of power.
The heart of the rule of law is not what the citizen is doing but is maintaining control over government. What have we seen in the last two months: that very concept, the essence of Canadian democracy, turned against Canadians and making them feel guilty about what they are doing.
