speechtext: Send it to the Minister of Justice.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Well, send it to the Minister of Justice. She does not read as carefully as the rest of us.
The second quotation is equally interesting. It is by Richard Van Loon and Michael Whittington. For the record, members might wish to know that these are people have been advisers to the government in Indian affairs and other matters related to that. They also talk about the rule of law. What is the rule of law according to these writers? It reads as follows:
The manifest function of any constitution is to define the relationship between the citizen and the state, and, to the extent that the relationship can be defined at all, every country can be said to have some form of constitution.
The principle of rule of law in the British and Canadian tradition asserts that any interference with the freedom of any individual must be performed only according to the legal process and carried out by legitimate authorities. No one is exempt from the law, neither citizens nor officials of the government, and no one can interfere with the rights of any individual, except through the legal process. Finally, the principle of the rule of law means, as well, equality before the law for all members of a political community. But if we grant that the Constitution of Canada is built on the principle of the rule of law, we must also ask why the rule of law is so important. The function of the rule of law is, briefly, to protect us, the citizens, from the arbitrary interference of government, or of government officials, in our

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
everyday lives. The relationship of the individual to the political system
becomes, to some extent, fixed and impartial.
By contrast, the rule of the most benevolent dictators-
And here I include the Prime Minister:
- could conceivably deteriorate to rule by whim and caprice, for even benevolent dictators once in a while get out of bed on the wrong side, and so forth. The law, on the other hand, is presumed to be impersonal, predictable and coldly rational rather than emotional or moody.
I understand that is a very dry way to get ourselves involved with such an emotional topic, but if we stop and think about how this issue has been portrayed to Canadians, that the actions on behalf of the people in these communities has been wrong by definition in the eyes of the government, hence the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Indian Affairs refused to negotiate. The heart of the matter is that they have deliberately, forcefully, and wilfully misinterpreted what is going on in order to satisfy their own political agenda.
The second point I would like to raise on this issue, which I think is important, is the great grief that it has brought to Canadians in the eyes of the world. One of the most memorable images that I have of democracy in the world was the site last June in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, China. There we had the sight of one man standing in front of a tank; the tank moves one way, he moves the same way, the tank moves the other way, he moves the other way, and there was a standoff.
I challenge the government to tell me what is the difference between that standoff and the standoff that we watched on Newsworld a few weeks ago between a Mohawk warrior and a Canadian army official? What is the difference? If you are sitting in China and it was the reverse than what it was last June, what would you think of the Canadian government? What would you think of that confrontation?
Or, I am drawn to remember in May when I visited Romania on behalf of the Speaker that outside of one of those major hotels, the Intercontinental in downtown Bucharest, there was a nightly demonstration of people talking about what it would be like to be in a democratic society. There was a second-floor balcony from which a student spoke and other members of the community. The crowd was of all ages and from all walks of life.
This summer I visited several times the peace village which aboriginal leaders in Manitoba erected on the legislative grounds to discuss the evolution of a democratic society in Canada, to discuss with political leaders such as members of Parliament and anybody else who would come forward to talk with them what it was that they were looking for. Everyone was peaceful. The leadership agreed to disband the camp during this week, the first week of Parliament, because they thought their point was made, and I agree with them.
Again, when the troops moved in in Bucharest we expressed shock and dismay that any government would turn on its people, but yet we do not even think about the peaceful demonstration taking place in Winnipeg. When I went there the leaders who are nationally known looked at me and said: "What do you think the Prime Minister is thinking? What do you think the government is trying to do to us? What do you think their ideas about us really are?" I stood there in silence because I could not explain to them what it was that the government was thinking. I could not explain to them why they were being treated that way.
However this has created a great unity among Canadians. Perhaps we are beginning to tie together different issues such as the environment and how we treat our land, because aboriginal people can tell us much about how not to spoil property, how to live for generation after generation. We should think of the changes to the lands of people who live in northern Quebec, and think of the way that people have changed their lives in northern Manitoba because of the northern flood agreement. We should think of all these changes and think of people who wandered through those areas and made their lives for generation after generation, and in two or three generations of Canadians we have managed to ruin that.
The peace movement which formerly looked outside of Canada for its issues now turns its attention to what is happening in our own country because we are on the battlefront. We can no longer take for granted the peace and security of our own citizens.
In Manitoba the peace community joined in at the Peace Village and this is why, in their own words: "We support the Mohawk nation and their struggle with the Federal government, Quebec government, Canadian
September 25, 1990

Army and Surete du Quebec, the Aboriginal people of Manitoba have established a Peace Village on the front lawn of the Manitoba Legislature" as a result of these events. In particular, we object to the Prime Minister who is responsible for this "by taking military action against the Mohawk nation. The Prime Minister has imposed a military solution where a political solution is required. This is a dangerous precedent, the security of all Canadians is at risk. The Mohawk people remain under siege with daily violations of their basic human rights."
Hopefully from news that we heard earlier this evening this is ending. "Children have been denied food and medicine, women have been assaulted and hospitalized, support and aid have been blocked by the army and the Surete du Quebec under the direct leadership of" the Quebec government. "The aboriginal people of Manitoba do not condone violence." They ask for our "continued support-to ensure that bloodshed is avoided and justice secured in this time of crisis." All Manitobans were welcomed to join in this Peace Village to show their solidarity. Many came bringing candles and tents and they joined in daily vigils and sunrise ceremonies.
I bring this to your attention and to the attention of the House to help us understand that although the House can fight over the specifics and disagree on the specifics, there is something at stake here which goes beyond the House. It is the transformation taking place in Canadian society. We can sit here and debate it all night, as we are doing today, because of the strong interest shown by this caucus in this issue or we can put our heads in the sand and pretend that if we ignore this or if the Oka crisis is settled this week that for somehow or another the whole issue will go away. In province after province, region after region, town after town and community after community this is going to be repeated until the basic injustices are settled.
It is up to us, members of all parties in this House, to work together with aboriginal leaders, with the support of the public who wish to no longer have to live through this nightmare, who wish to no longer hear about land claims not being settled, who wish no longer to hear about the poverty in urban Canada, who wish no longer
Government Orders
to hear about malnutrition on the reserves, who wish to hear some good news based on facts about improved conditions due to a commitment on the part of parliamentarians that they wish to see some recognition on the part of government that there is a commitment to improve conditions. Once that happens, then all parliamentarians can take pride in this institution. Until then there is a black spot on this institution, there is a black spot on this country and it remains for the government to take action and to get us going again.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, roughly 10 hours ago we heard a deathbed repentance on the part of the Prime Minister of Canada when he spoke in this Chamber. He delivered his commitment as to what he is prepared now to do. After having imposed financial cut-backs on native communications, after the post-secondary education fiasco last year, after having imposed cuts on friendship centres, after having imposed cuts to grants for native organizations, after withdrawing from past commitments, after having demonstrated to the country that not six months, not one year, not eighteen months but two years after the last election this government has not been able to introduce one piece of legislation that deals with the native and aboriginal people, after having failed to introduce measures in the light of what the nation learned about the Donald Marshall case on the application of justice when it comes to the aboriginal people.
In the environment we have seen month after month since the last election provocations and injustices and sheer follies. We have heard about the Cree Indians from James Bay who had to make their point by coming down by canoe, by demonstrating in front of the House of Commons, and then by way of the Richelieu River making their way down to New York in order to demonstrate their rejection of the James Bay II project to the United Nations.
We have heard for the past 20 months in Question Period the issue of the Oldman River dam and how the Peigan tribe is fighting against all odds in order to bring the white community to reason.

Government Orders
We have heard about the Algonquin of Barrier Lake and their frustration in getting the white society to accept some sensible principles of forest management.
We have heard about the Akwasasne reserve people who have to struggle with pollution in the St. Lawrence.
Many times we have heard colleagues in this House raising the issue of the Walpole Island native people and the water contamination that forces them to draw water from a distant region.
Everybody knows about the Wabagoon River and mercury pollution and what the native people have experienced over the last three decades.
We are now at the beginning of another saga in relation to the ALPAC development in northern Alberta where we are giving away the forests and the land on which the native people depend with potential serious contamination of waterways.
We all know and have heard about the Lubicon Indians and their struggle. It is very revealing to read what a writer in St. Bruno, Quebec, Marjorie Marc, writes about the Cree people in northern Quebec. I would like to quote a passage from her study where she says:

To deal with the problem of mercury contamination suffered by the First Nations, in particular the Cree of Northern Quebec, the Quebec government is encouraging them to change their eating habits. So far so good. But it happens that their eating habits are based on a way of life that goes back hundreds, perhaps thousands, of years, the fundamental pillars of which are hunting and fishing. In addition, native people's restricted incomes make it hard for them to obtain products from the South, which are more expensive for them than for us because of the great distances they have to be transported. Insisting that they eat tinned food means not only changing and limiting their way of life, but also putting their mental and physical health at risk. It is not by chance that Amerindians have a high alcoholism rate and the highest suicide rate in the world.

Mr. Speaker, it is not only with the environment that our native people have been increasingly fighting the establishment. When it comes to conflicts, a brief piece appeared in the Toronto Star of September 1 which encapsules the plight of the Innu of Labrador who are,
according to the writer from the Canadian Press historically, a peaceful, nomadic group which in recent years has repeatedly gathered at Canadian Forces Base Goose Bay to protest the low-level flying of NATO jets over their traditional hunting grounds.
You have the Micmac, traditional fishermen and hunters. During the 1950s their lives were disrupted by forest relocation. In the fall and winter of 1988 the Micmac in Nova Scotia protested provincial limits to moose hunting by hunting above the limits.
You know the saga in Temagami where after several years of protesting the extension of a nearby logging road this spring, the Indians won a say over the administration of part of the Temagami forest.
You have the Sarcee in your region, Mr. Speaker. In mid-August they marched on to the Canadian Forces Base in Calgary and claimed a large chunk of it saying the federal government stole it from them nearly 40 years ago.
You have the Peigan tribe, and I referred to them a moment ago when referring to the Oldman River dam. You have the Mohawks who are the subject and object of this particular debate today. It is worth while noting how, in the Toronto Star, Gerald Utting describes this history of Oka where reference is made to the fact that, and I quote:
The Mohawks say they have been provoked to taking action after years of keeping the peace despite continual (and undeniable) land grabbing by the white man. Mohawks lived at Oka before the British took Canada from the French in 1759.
These are historical facts that cannot be easily brushed aside. It is against this background of interference, conflicts and injustices that we read in the Order Paper, and we will debate today, the great vision of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. This vision is reflected by the motion that we are debating tonight in which he proposed that the House commend the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian Forces at Oka and Chateauguay, that in the opinion of this House, the laws of Canada must apply on all Canadian territory, including Kahnawake, and that all persons currently at the Kahnawake Treatment Centre should lay down their arms and submit to the process of Canada's judicial system thereby encouraging the creation, and so on and so forth.
September 25, 1990

What a vision on the part of a minister of the Crown whose task, whose assignment, whose mandate is that of speaking on behalf of the aboriginal people at the cabinet table, at the inner sanctum of power, federally speaking, and who takes this tack in this House, virtually abandoning the substance, the very essence of his political mandate as minister of the Crown in charge of aboriginal affairs.
For these reasons, and against the broader background that I have attempted to outline for you, Canadians have been asking questions all summer as to what is going on in this country. All of a sudden, why are we getting such bad press in virtually every country of the world. What is happening to our high reputation in international fora on human rights that we should all of a sudden, not only have a black eye but also be considered to be in a stage that we never thought we would be ascribed, namely, of neanderthalers?
We in the opposition have been restless all summer. We started urging the government to recall Parliament in July. There was a letter from the Leader of the Opposition on July 17 to the Prime Minister. We had a demonstration on the steps of Parliament to make the point with the help of the media to recall Parliament. Then, on August 22, the opposition House Leader, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier followed up that intervention with a letter of his own to the Prime Minister without avail, of course, as you know, Mr. Speaker.
Unfortunately, this debate has tended to polarize because except for some very rare exceptions this afternoon and this evening, the government back-benchers have been the champions of the law and order theme. It indicates no sensibility for the basic fundamental principles of justice, and have left the opposition to occupy the much broader territory, the much broader issue that endeavours to indicate that, because of historical facts and because of the fact that the law is meaningless and empty unless it is based on principles of justice, the approach of law and order in the context of what has happened this summer, and against the background of what has happened over centuries, does not make sense. But this is the kind of intellectual bankruptcy that we have to face more and more in this Parliament with this intellectually bankrupt government.
Government Orders
We actually do not have to go back very far to refresh our collective memories. We can go back just to 1983 and look at the Penner report on Indian self-government. I will just use a minute to go over the conclusions of that report because it is as valid today as it was then.
An all-party committee of the House in the Thirty-Second Parliament, three parliaments ago, said in the conclusion on page 148 of the Penner report:
As Indian First Nation governments exercise control over their own affairs, the committee strongly recommends that the programs of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development relating to Indian people be phased out. This process should be completed within five years. This recommendation does not affect the Department's mandate for northern development.
The committee believes that the best way to promote Indian rights is through Indian self-government and not by special representation for First Nations in Parliament. Nevertheless, the situation of Indian peoples will change with self-government, and special representation in Parliament might in future offer benefits that cannot now be anticipated.
Finally, this observation:
The committee has concluded that the implementation of this report in its entirety, legislatively and constitutionally, is the best means of satisfying international standards in relation to Indian First Nations.
I look forward to the Parliamentary Secretary getting up when I finish to indicate to me what has been implemented of this report of 1983, which is the most recent document produced parliamentarily in terms of a well thought out effort on the part of members of all three parties to launch a process. This was in October 1983.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to your attention the fact that in June 1984, Bill C-52 was introduced, an act relating to self-government for Indian nations. I would welcome an intervention by the Parliamentary Secretary to tell us what has happened since November 1984 in terms of introducing legislation in the House on self-government for Indian nations, apart from the legislation to which my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace referred to earlier. What has happened to the substantial body of legislative proposals that the Conservative Government found when it came to power in the fall of 1984?
I would also like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a paragraph which struck me as being indicative of the depths of thought and wisdom of the native people, produced on September 20,1990, five days ago, by the Six Nation Iroquois Confederacy. It is a fairly long document and I will read only one paragraph, because it is very relevant to the situation we are facing today. I quote:
Restricting negotiations at this delicate time to a military demand for an absolute surrender is, we feel, sadly short-sighted. We feel

September 25, 1990
Government Orders
our draft agreement with Mr. Ciaccia bears a real hope for a more lasting peace. Since Mr. Bourassa has announced his desire to negotiate with the Confederacy, and since Mr. Mulroney has stated his desire for a peaceful negotiated settlement, we hope they will agree to support this accord and join us in peacemaking, both for this immediate crisis and for the coming generations.
Time will tell whether this advice and this invitation will fall on receptive ears.
I must say that I felt deeply distressed by the wording of the motion proposed by the Minister of Indian Affairs. It strikes me as a motion that avoids the real issue before us. It almost brings back memories of Louis Riel, who also was described as being outside the law. It ignores the fundamental principles of justice and it reveals an attitude of a government that has to rely on the army because it has no other instrument at its disposal in dealing with a profoundly complex social issue that has been screaming for attention and screaming to heaven for so many decades and for so many centuries.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in debate at this early morning hour of 3.22 a.m. to add my voice to the consensus of my colleagues, the hundreds of constituents in my riding of Hamilton West and, I dare say, the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who agree that it has been a dark summer that has produced suppression, political interference, inaction and a failure of leadership and statesmanship on the part of our Prime Minister.
Even in the motion put forward by the Minister of Indian Affairs there is a degree of cynicism and political manipulation which I am sure all Canadians recognize and deplore. I draw the attention of the House to the first sentence in the government motion. It reads:
That this House commends the exemplary conduct of the men and women of the Canadian Armed Forces at Oka.
How can I support such a sentence in this motion when I do not have the full story? In fact, what I have are newspaper articles, reports from the scene, such as that given by The Globe and Mail reporter, Jeff York, who last Saturday walked out of the alcohol treatment centre where he and 11 other journalists have been cooped up by the military since one week ago Monday. York angrily disputed claims by the army that it has been acting in a disciplined and professional manner. York, in fact, says that the soldiers set off smoke-bombs, that they come behind the wire when they say they will not and they taunt the Mohawks by throwing rocks, trying to provoke violence.
In my experience prior to being elected in November 1988 of 16 years as a news journalist, I always followed that unspoken code of the news journalist. That code says that you must tell the truth, that that truth must be verifiable, that we must present a balanced story, both sides of the story, and, of course, that we do not say anything that is libellous. What we have seen is a gag on the media on this issue; in essence, a violation of the Charter of Rights. On my office wall here in Ottawa and in the constituency office, there hang framed parchments of the Charter of Rights. Under the heading of fundamental freedoms, number 2(b), is freedom of the press and other media of communication.
Tonight in my office I took a call from a constituent who passed along this comment. He said: "Stan, the Mulroney government has dealt more gingerly with Saddam Hussein than it has with Canada's native people. The media is permitted to report back from the deck of HMCS Protecteur in the Persian Gulf, but not from behind the razor wire at Oka."
Maybe what the Prime Minister fears most is the video image. It can be very strong, veiy powerful. There is the image, you can recall it, of women, children, and elderly people leaving Oka, and having stones thrown at them. There is the image of natives kicking and punching soldiers, and soldiers kicking and punching and using their gunbutts against the head of natives.
What this government is telling the Canadian people is that it does not trust news journalists because, in this
September 25, 1990

situation, it realizes it cannot manipulate the media. The government has branded the Mohawks as terrorists and will not allow them to negotiate before surrendering. In its opinion, the Mohawks are guilty. The journalists have attempted to give them a fair trial, but have been cut off from presenting their case by the Minister of Defence who is in essence managing the news by eliminating coverage of the events. As the Ottawa Sun reported just yesterday: "No court has declared them-the Mohawks-criminals. They want to negotiate with the province and the federal government but the army won't let them".
Here is the evidence. The letter is from the Six Nations Iroquois Confederacy and dated September 20, 1990. It states that "representatives of the Grand Council of the Iroquois Confederacy arrived at a draft agreement to end the crisis at Kanesatake and Kahnawake with Quebec's Minister of Native Affairs, John Ciaccia. Mr. Ciaccia was acting in his personal capacity and had no mandate from his government, but we, the Iroquois Confederacy felt that the proposed agreement represented a real opportunity for peace, not merely a temporary solution to the present situation".
It would have resolved the issues that must be dealt with immediately, but the Iroquois found out that there was virtually no co-operation from the federal, provincial, or military authorities. Both Canada and Quebec have said that the negotiating mandate has been given to the Armed Forces. Military authorities say that their mandate is limited to negotiating an absolute surrender.
Instant deadlock, Mr. Speaker. Even tonight the Iroquois Confederacy proposed that the laying down of arms could be carried out within hours if the government agreed and accepted its final offer which included a demand for an independent Crown Attorney. We have just heard from the Quebec government. It has rejected that proposal. All of it begs the question: Who is in charge? Is it the Quebec government? Is it the Canadian army? It should be neither. It should be this place. It should be the House of Commons. It should be the federal government.
What it all boils down to is two issues, land and the withdrawal of the Armed Forces. There are not many Canadians or I dare say many members of the House who understand fully the relationship that native people have with the land.
Government Orders
I have had the good fortune to attend many information sessions in my riding of Hamilton West and here in Ottawa and I have come to the conclusion that to the natives, the land is sacred. It provides and nourishes. One native person told me: "The land gives us life and it is to the land we shall return when we die." So it becomes increasingly clear when, in the case of Oka, the dispute originated over the expansion of a golf course, for pity sakes, the Mohawks finally decided to stand up for their rights, to speak in unison with indigenous peoples in Canada and around the world who have spoken out wherever oppression exists. Elsewhere in the world we applaud their efforts and in some cases, we even send aid. But here in Canada the Prime Minister calls the Mohawks terrorists and convicts and refuses to act unless they first submit.
Now, maybe as fond as he is of the American way, perhaps the Prime Minister would like to hear what the great statesman and a founding father of the United States, Thomas Jefferson, had to say on individual liberty: "The nation that tries to suppress liberty in the name of law and order inevitably loses both; liberty and law and order."
However the Conservative government, and in particular the Minister of Justice whom we heard from tonight, has hidden behind this notion of law and order and in the process has sent our peacekeeping army. The army we so proudly present as the bringer of harmony and peace in times of conflict, we have put up against a people begging and now demanding to be understood and treated with dignity. Instead, this government has dealt ruthlessly, arrogantly and with force, rather than leadership. Their philosophy is quite clear: that might is right.
Mr. Speaker, this is a power that cannot remain unchecked, for as John Stewart Mill noted in his book On Liberty: "The people may desire to oppress a part of their number and the precautions are as much needed against this as against any other abuse of power. In political speculations, the tyranny of the majority is now generally included among the evils against which society requires to be on its guard."
The real irony of this notion as applied to the situation we are faced with at Oka is that while the government is the tyranny with the majority, it is apparent to me that the majority of Canadians do not side with the govern-

Government Orders
ment and are in fact angry and frustrated with our "prime misleader".
The government claims that it has advanced the cause of native Canadians, but the record will show that we are talking about a government that has persistently delayed the aspirations of aboriginal Canadians. Only when Canadians are armed with the facts will they have a better understanding of the anger and frustrations of Canada's indigenous peoples.
I draw your attention to the "Budget in Grief". It was presented to the Assembly of First Nations on March 15, 1990. It tells us a few of these facts. The two-year federal reduction of $100 million is deceptively buried in the 1990-91 Main Estimates and the budget papers. Twenty-six million dollars was cut from approved levels for capital facilities and community services; $15 million from band management; $7 million from welfare services; $2 million from economic development for each of the two years.
With a crippled economic base and no tax base, just where do native people find the finances to offset lost federal revenue? First Nations have been trying to do so, but each year it drives them more into debt. To make up for the shortfall of federal budgets since 1985, over $333 million would have to be added to the 1990-91 Indian and Inuit Affairs program budget to compensate fully for inflation and extremely high population growth.
All this resulted in some appalling statistics. In 1989, 70 per cent of the reserve Indian population had become institutionally dependent on government social assistance, 164,000 reserve Indians lived on social assistance,
120,000	Indians living away from reserves received social assistance. It means that 61 per cent of them are on social assistance. That is greater than the combination of all four Atlantic provinces. There is only one business for every 30 Canadians but only one native business for every 100 native people. Life expectancy of male and female Indians will be over eight years lower than their non-aboriginal counterparts in 1991. Infant mortality rates are more than double the Canadian rate, 17.2 per cent compared to 7.9 per cent for 1,000 babies. It goes on, Mr. Speaker.
What native people have been telling me is that they are no longer interested in handouts, what they want is a helping hand. Canadians see the trail of broken promises, of suppressed culture, of deprived economies. And
while we must all take some responsibility for this tragic line of Canadian history, no government has ever been more blatant and more callous in its indifference, in its suppression of the needs of its indigenous peoples.
I want to conclude my remarks with a native myth, Mr. Speaker, the Indian myth about a tribe starving, unable to track the mighty buffalo herds. Two children brought the hunters' robes, made of coyote skins, begging that they wear them. Some of the hunters laughed, some were angry with the children's interference. But two elderly wise members of the tribe agreed to put on the coyote robes and, in doing so, found they had the vision of the coyote and were able to direct their people to the buffalo. Many stories of the great medicine wheel teach an important lesson that the government should learn and apply to the native crisis. To live in harmony and well-being we must see with the eyes of others, hear with the ears of others, speak with the tongue of others. I appeal to the government to put on the robes of the native people, to see and hear and thereby understand their hopes and their dreams.
Mr. Phillip Edmonston (Chambly) A comment, Mr. Speaker. I would just like to refer to my hon. colleague's remarkable and very well researched discourse on the present problem with the native peoples of Canada. I listened with great interest and I find that from his research he was able to give us a very good general sense of from where we have come and where we are right now with the native peoples, particularly in regard to Oka. I would like to make a comment and also follow it with a question.
I have learned tonight from a Canadian Press reporter, at this late hour, it is almost four o'clock in the morning, that there has been a declaration from the Mohawk warriors at Oka that they are prepared to surrender. They are prepared to unconditionally leave the detoxification centre as of Thursday or Friday next. If this declaration is followed by them, it would mean then that this entire controversy, which has taken up so much of our time and concentrated our efforts on looking for a way to resolve the issue, will have resulted in finally an end to a major conflict, I believe, between Canada's aboriginal peoples and the government, as well as the citizens. We have heard others say how much the citizens in the immediate area of both Oka and Chateauguay

were affected this summer. We have come to an end which is not a peaceful end. It has not been without a considerable amount of distress, inconvenience, even law breaking. We have to admit that. I am asking myself at the moment, are we going to be foolish enough, and I am speaking to my colleagues on the other side of this House, to feel that this is the end and that there is no more efforts that we must deploy in order to make sure that the conditions that bred this type of conflict no longer exist. Are we going to take this as the end of a conflict and that we do not have to turn attention to these problems? I certainly hope not.
If the Mohawks do surrender at Oka, and we have heard the government's promises, that it really wants to deal with the problems which are behind the grievances, initially of what the natives have brought to our attention so vividly through images, I trust and I hope the government will carry through with some of the comments and some of the promises it has made once again. However, understand we are in an area where the government has made many, many promises and that our native peoples have learned quite justifiably to be very suspicious.
What I would like to do in directing my question to my hon. colleague, and once again I would like to compliment him for a well researched job and very well presented, is ask him, in light of this new information, what concern he would have or whether he would share the same concerns that I have for the safety of the Mohawks in surrendering and the chances of having a fair trial. Finally, how does he see the next step for the government in light of perhaps-if what we hear right now at close to four o'clock in the morning is true-what he sees as the responsibility of us as parliamentarians. He has mentioned the ball is in our court and has to stay in our court. What is the responsibility of us as parliamentarians and on the government side? What is it in the very near future?

speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for his compliments and the question. The end, of course, might have been reached much earlier had the government acted responsibly in the beginning. The answer is probably simply this. The actions at Oka obviously loosened
Government Orders
the grip of the Prime Minister enough to force him to make the slew of promises that he made earlier tonight.
Yes, we heard the Prime Minister speak of the overhaul of native policies and changes to the Indian Act and speedier resolution of land claims, but you will have to excuse my scepticism if I say I have heard time and time again the right hon. member give us a record, be long on the promises but very short in the accomplishments.
Now I bring myself to putting aside the partisanship of the issue. We have made our point. We must act now together, as I explained earlier, to try to put ourselves in the position of our native peoples. We realize that may be an impossible goal but we must try to do that. Being able to see through their eyes and hear with their ears and speak with their tongues puts us in a better position to understand their problems, their uniqueness and their understanding and appreciation of the land. Therefore, we can work together, tiy to reach that goal and do what is right for our native peoples.

subsubtopic: THE SITUATION IN OKA AND CHATEAUGUAY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker for allowing me to speak and for your tremendous forbearance and an excellent job of chairing this House tonight.
To me this is a critical debate, not just in terms of what it means to Canada's native people, but what it means to all of us in Canada in terms of two very different systems of justice which are on trial before us. I am talking first of all about the type of judicial law-making system which is represented by this government's stand. Every one of the members from the Minister of Justice to the Prime Minister, to everyone who has spoken from that side, has spoken about law and order. Yes, this is one system of justice according to the principles of jurisprudence that is available in the western world and in all judicial systems throughout the world. The system of law and order in terms of jurisprudence is described generally as legal positivism or legal realism. It is represented by scholars such as Austin, Kelston and is maybe best expressed by the Swedish legal realist Lundsted, who said: "The assertion that law-makers and courts should be guided by ideals of justice, is completely useless".
In other words, the positives say if the law is properly passed, it must apply regardless. That is the government's position. That is their jurisprudential position. There is in jurisprudence one other position at least, and it is the one which is represented by persons such as Plato, Aristotle, Herbert Spencer, Lester Ward and W.R. Sorley. These are scholars who talked about the necessity for law, not just to be obeyed regardless, but

Government Orders
the necessity for the law to encompass equality andor freedom.
A more recent scholar in this area has been H.A.L. Hart. We go back to the Jeffersonian principles which he brought to the Declaration of Independence which again embodied the ideal that law is not right just because it is law. Law must satisfy the test of justice, and those tests for justice have often been the concepts, depending on the emphasis, of equality and or freedom.
I quote:
This latter school embraces the philosophy that no philosophical or sociological treatment of the law which refuses to face the question of the goodness of the law, in addition to that of its formal validity and technical organization can provide us with an adequate insight into legal reality.
For the Minister of Justice to have stood up tonight and done nothing to recognize that there are other schools of legal philosophy, other schools of jurisprudence other than legal positivism was, I do not believe, an attempt to mislead this House. I believe it was based on ignorance, an ignorance which has led to the type of crisis we are facing in Oka today and which, if blindly followed, is going to lead us to many more crises across this land.
If laws do not meet the test of justice, equality, and freedom, we have seen in the past how it is impossible for any elected or self-appointed government to deal with the civil disobedience that will inevitably arise. It was Ghandi who asked the people simply to make their own salt from the sea rather than capitulate to the monopolies of the capitalists, and he had a nation marching with him in peace.
We know that it is even a part of modern day law that if there is a patently unjust law on the books, it is a crime to follow it. That was the decision of the Nuremberg trials.
Even the United States Supreme Court has introduced these new principles, not illogical, legal positivisms, through Mr. Justice Holmes, in Brown v Louisiana when five blacks disobeyed a law which said they could not go to a public library and the court finally acquitted them. Even though they disobeyed that law the court said the law was not right.
We do have higher laws in this land than just the laws passed by Parliament. There are other laws. There is the Constitution with its Charter of Rights and Freedoms which provides an override for all the laws which may be passed.
We have other laws too: treaties, which are laws. We have the laws of reason, of justice, and of equality.
When we come to consider what has happened-and I hope the standoff at Oka is over-how are we going to assess the roles of all the people involved: legislators, native Canadians, police, army? How are we going to assess that unless we have a full inquiry into the facts that led to the resolution of what has been a blight on Canada's national reputation and has caused us great anguish in the international councils of the world?
I want this government to order an inquiry starting say last January and following right through. If it does not we are not going to be able to show people that justice was done or not done. It is not for us to prejudge it. We do not have all the facts. Facts coming out of that place are censured now. We cannot even get in to determine things.
Native Canadians cannot even get in to propose earlier resolutions to that conflict. We need an inquiry into all the facts called immediately.
When we are dealing in the future with this question of whether we are going to be legal positivists or whether we are going to have a broader social view of law, it is critical that we remind ourselves of the plight of Canada's native people.
In Canada we have 466,000 status Indians, 308,000 of whom live on reserves. Their income levels are atrocious: 61 per cent of all reserve and non-reserve Indians depend on social assistance. Their income is only 54 per cent of the national average. Their unemployment level is 70 per cent. Illiteracy among our native Canadians is 45 per cent versus 17 per cent among Canadians as a whole. Only 20 per cent of our Indian children have completed high school; it is 75 per cent throughout our population. Life expectancy is eight years less than for other Canadians. Infant mortality is two times as high. In their homes the overcrowding rate is 16 times as high as in all Canadian homes and 38 per cent of native homes have no central heating.
September 25, 1990

Native Canadians constitute 2 per cent of our population. However, they constitute 10 per cent of our federal penitentiary population. If that is not bad enough, look at native children. Four times as many native children are under child care agencies, and seven times as many native children commit suicide as other Canadians.
Today in this House of Commons the Minister of Indian Affairs talked about increases in spending on native programs. Since 1985, Canada's Indian and Inuit population has increased almost 34 per cent, the spending for them in real dollars over that period has declined by 11 per cent.
We know that money is not everything. Surely we have learned some lessons from Oka. We cannot tolerate this government hiding behind a few warriors in the treatment centre as an excuse for giving up on all of its responsibilities to Canada's native people.
What did this government do to resolve the issue more quickly? If it was a question of law and order, because some of these natives have guns, the government knew about it years ago. Did it step in then on the basis of law and order to deal with the issue? No, it was only when the barricades went up.
The barricades went up on March 11. According to the chronology in the minister's own communique on federal actions taken at Oka, the barricades went up on March 11-the first federal initiative is July 17. "Minister Tom Siddon issues statement explaining profile of federal government". That was six days after the Surete du Quebec went to the barricades, and the tragic death of one police officer. Where was the minister? Where was the federal government?
The Prime Minister admitted that he had not met with one native leader.
In the summer of 1985, 174 refugees were put ashore by boat in Canada. This House was called back because of that crisis and yet this government would not call back
Government Orders
this House to deal with the plight of our own native Canadians as epitomized by Oka.
We needed more negotiations and less force. Is it not ironic that at Oka we have deployed 3,300 armed forces? Heck, this government sent only 2,000 to the Middle East.
I hope we have learned from Oka. I hope we have learned that there is more than one concept of jurisprudence and that the modem concept, the concept that justice, meaning equality and freedom, must also be components of an orderly, legal system. I hope that we have learned that that was critical to all of our future deliberations in this House.
If one good thing has come out of Oka it has shown Canadian people the plight of many of our native Canadians. We must not let it die here. We must have a public inquiry as to the events leading up to Oka. We must have a royal commission to investigate the plight of natives in Canada. We must speed up land treaty negotiations. We must bring about conditions of economic and social justice for all of our native Canadians. Surely by now we realize that they have a claim on the conscience of all Canadians.
